Diagnosis
Treatment
rows: find the cause; pulse methylprednisolone ± cyclophosphamide/rituximab; plasma exchange for anti-GBM disease and selected vasculitis

ARDS-12.intro: COVID-19 tested the ideas of ARDS-09 and ARDS-10. In the early phase some patients were deeply hypoxaemic with fairly normal compliance, which pointed to a vascular problem rather than flooding alone.
why: **Often relatively preserved compliance despite severe hypoxaemia in the early phase.** Much of the hypoxaemia came from perfusion going to poorly ventilated lung rather than from loss of aerated volume. Gattinoni proposed two types: L (low elastance, so near-normal compliance; low lung weight; little to recruit) and H (high elastance, heavy lung, large shunt, recruitable). Larger cohorts (Grasselli, Lombardy; Ferrando, Spain; both 2020) then found compliance in ventilated COVID ARDS spread over the same wide range as classical ARDS, with no separate groups, and no trial has tested ventilation guided by L or H.

**Prominent endothelial injury and microthrombosis; hypoxaemia from loss of hypoxic vasoconstriction.** Normally, vessels to poorly ventilated alveoli constrict and send blood elsewhere; when that reflex is lost, blood keeps flowing through poorly ventilated lung.

**RECOVERY: dexamethasone 6 mg for 10 days lowered 28-day mortality in patients on oxygen or ventilation.** The dose was 6 mg once daily for up to 10 days (or until discharge). The largest benefit was in ventilated patients; there was no benefit in patients not on oxygen.
mimic: COVID vs classical ARDS
Mortality is similar; ventilation and stay are longer in COVID (ARDS-11c).
traps: “COVID ARDS needs a different ventilation strategy”
Ventilation is the same: low tidal volume and proning, as for any ARDS.
“Type L COVID ARDS should be ventilated with larger tidal volumes”
This was proposed from the L/H model, but compliance did not split into two groups in large cohorts and no trial supports it; standard lung-protective ventilation applies.
decode: [pattern] Steroid with mortality benefit in COVID-19 on oxygen or ventilation
Dexamethasone 6 mg for 10 days (RECOVERY).
[pattern] COVID pneumonia, severe hypoxaemia, near-normal compliance, little recruitability — which type?
Type L in Gattinoni’s model; type H is low compliance, heavy lung and recruitable. Large cohorts did not confirm two separate groups.
ARDS-12.punch: Early COVID ARDS may keep near-normal compliance because its hypoxaemia is partly vascular, but it is ventilated like any ARDS, and dexamethasone helps those on oxygen or ventilation.

ARDS-13.sub: Respiratory → ARDS → Revision: true or false
ARDS-13.intro: A sweep through the deck. Each statement turns on one detail from an earlier card.
why: **False — PAOP ≤18 was AECC.** Berlin removed the wedge pressure (ARDS-05).
**True — P/F 200 on PEEP 5 is moderate (101–200).** Each band includes its upper limit (ARDS-04).
**False — ALI was removed; it is now mild ARDS** (ARDS-05).
**False — moderate is the commonest grade in LUNG SAFE, 46.6%** (ARDS-02).
**True — hyaline membranes belong to the exudative stage, the hallmark of diffuse alveolar damage** (ARDS-08).
**False — type II pneumocytes proliferate in the proliferative stage** (ARDS-08).
**False — the ARDS lung is small, not stiff (baby lung)** (ARDS-10).
traps: “P/F 200 is mild”
Exactly 200 is moderate; exactly 300 is mild; exactly 100 is severe.
decode: [pattern] Statements about Berlin vs AECC
Wedge pressure and ALI belong to AECC only.
[pattern] Statements about pathology stages
Hyaline membranes early, type II hyperplasia next, collagen last.
ARDS-13.punch: Most errors on ARDS statements come from AECC leftovers (wedge, ALI), band edges (200 is moderate) and stage order (membranes, then type II cells, then fibrosis).

topups.topic: Goals in acute hypoxaemic respiratory failure
topups.q: Therapeutic goals in acute hypoxaemic respiratory failure?
a: - Least PEEP that gives SpO2 ≥90% on FiO2 <0.6.
- Least VT/plateau pressure compatible with pH >7.2 (accept hypercapnia).
- Least circulating volume/PAWP that keeps adequate O2 delivery and urine output.

x.sub: Respiratory → ARDS → Goals of support in hypoxaemic failure
x.intro: Step 3 explains why the hypoxaemia of ARDS comes from shunt and why the aerated lung is small. Support therefore has a cost at every point: more PEEP, more volume and more fluid each help one number and harm something else. The goals on this card (from Principles of Critical Care) are all written as the least that is enough.
why: **Least PEEP that gives SpO₂ ≥90% on FiO₂ <0.6.** SpO₂ 90% sits near PaO₂ 60 mmHg, the shoulder of the dissociation curve, so higher targets add little oxygen content. FiO₂ is kept below 0.6 to limit oxygen toxicity and absorption collapse, and PEEP is the tool that lets FiO₂ come down; beyond what is needed it overdistends the open lung and cuts venous return.

**Least VT/plateau pressure compatible with pH >7.2 (accept hypercapnia).** The baby lung (ARDS-10) is overstretched by normal tidal volumes, so CO₂ is allowed to rise; a pH above about 7.2 is well tolerated by most patients. This is the logic behind ARMA’s 6 mL/kg and plateau ≤30 (RESP01B).

**Least circulating volume/PAWP that keeps adequate O₂ delivery and urine output.** A leaky capillary floods with oedema in proportion to hydrostatic pressure, so the lowest filling that keeps cardiac output, oxygen delivery and kidneys perfused is the target; once shock has resolved, a conservative fluid strategy shortens ventilation (FACTT).
traps: “The goal is a normal PaCO₂ and pH”
Hypercapnia is accepted to protect the lung; the floor is pH about 7.2, not 7.35.
“Push PEEP until SpO₂ is 100%”
The aim is the least PEEP for SpO₂ about 90% on a non-toxic FiO₂; more risks overdistension and hypotension.
decode: Therapeutic goals in acute hypoxaemic respiratory failure — which is NOT one? [Marrow]
None: least PEEP, least VT and least volume are all goals.
Which target is acceptable in a ventilated ARDS patient: PaCO₂ 60 with pH 7.25? [pattern]
Yes — permissive hypercapnia within pH >7.2.
x.punch: Every lever in hypoxaemic failure is set to the least that works: enough PEEP for SpO₂ about 90% on FiO₂ under 0.6, enough volume for pH above 7.2, enough fluid for perfusion.

spine: Insults that injure the lung
ARDS follows a direct insult to the alveolar epithelium, such as pneumonia or aspiration, or an indirect one reaching the lung through the blood, such as sepsis or pancreatitis.
Diffuse alveolar damage in stages
The injured lung passes from exudative oedema with hyaline membranes, through type II cell proliferation, to fibrosis in some patients.
Leaky barrier, shunt, small lung
Protein-rich oedema floods alveoli that stay perfused, so hypoxaemia is from shunt and resists oxygen, and the lung left aerated is small rather than stiff.
Defining it: AECC to Berlin
Berlin defines ARDS by four criteria — onset within a week, bilateral opacities, oedema not fully cardiac, and P/F ≤300 on PEEP ≥5 — and dropped the wedge pressure and the term ALI.
Grading, global reach and burden

P/F grades it mild, moderate or severe; the 2023 definition stretches it to non-intubated patients and settings without blood gases; LUNG SAFE shows it is common, mostly moderate and under-recognised.
Mimics, prognosis and review
Several conditions meet Berlin criteria without being ARDS, and BAL, echo and CT separate them — which matters because some respond to steroids.
RESP01A.primer: The P/F ratio is arterial PO₂ in mmHg divided by FiO₂ as a fraction (PaO₂ 60 on FiO₂ 0.5 gives 120); the lower it is, the worse the oxygenation, and it is only comparable when PEEP is stated. PEEP is the pressure held in the airways at the end of expiration; it keeps collapsed alveoli open, so it changes the P/F ratio. Shunt means blood flowing past alveoli that receive no gas at all, whereas V/Q mismatch means alveoli that are ventilated, but too little for their blood flow — extra oxygen corrects the second, not the first. Compliance is the change in lung volume per unit of pressure; a low value means each breath needs more pressure.

ARDS-14.intro: The story starts before the tube. A patient with acute hypoxaemic failure, often early ARDS, can be given standard oxygen, high-flow nasal oxygen or NIV, and FLORALI is the trial that compared all three. The exam asks it two ways: what the trial showed, and what HFNC actually does to the patient’s breathing.
why: **HFNC vs standard oxygen (face mask) vs NIV, in acute hypoxaemic respiratory failure.** Frat and colleagues (NEJM 2015) randomised 310 non-hypercapnic patients with P/F ≤300, most with pneumonia; the NIV arm received HFNC between NIV sessions.

**Intubation at 28 days: no significant difference overall.** The rates were 38% with HFNC, 47% with standard oxygen and 50% with NIV — a trend, not a significant result, so ‘HFNC reduces intubation’ is not what the primary outcome showed.

**Lower 90-day mortality with HFNC; fewer intubations in the subgroup with P/F ≤200.** Neither is the primary outcome: 90-day mortality was a secondary outcome, and the P/F ≤200 intubation result came from a post hoc analysis, so both generate hypotheses rather than prove benefit. The hazard of death at 90 days was about twice as high with standard oxygen (HR 2.01) and two and a half times as high with NIV (HR 2.50), compared with HFNC. NIV did worst; its patients took large tidal volumes, which links this card to P-SILI (ARDS-17). Current ERS (2022) and ESICM (2023) guidance favour HFNC over conventional oxygen in acute hypoxaemic respiratory failure.

**FiO₂ 21–100%; washes out anatomical dead space; lowers work of breathing; gives a few cmH₂O of PEEP.** A flow of up to 60 L/min matches or exceeds the patient’s own peak inspiratory flow, so room air is not entrained and the set FiO₂ is the FiO₂ delivered — something no face mask achieves. The flow flushes CO₂ from the nasopharynx, so each breath carries less dead space; the respiratory rate and work of breathing fall, while tidal volume stays the same or rises. Heated, humidified gas is comfortable and keeps secretions moving. The PEEP is small — about 1 cmH₂O per 10 L/min with the mouth closed, less with it open — and it is neither set nor measured. Even so, among the common oxygen devices it is the only one that generates any end-expiratory pressure.
mimic: HFNC vs CPAP/NIV
CPAP and NIV set and hold a known pressure through a sealed mask; HFNC gives only a small, variable pressure through open prongs, but is far better tolerated.
‘High-frequency nasal insufflation’ vs HFNC
There is no distinct standard therapy by that name; the keyed answer simply describes HFNC — high flow, CO₂ washout, mild positive pressure.
traps: “HFNC reduces tidal volume”
It lowers the respiratory rate and work of breathing, but tidal volume is unchanged or larger; this is the false option in ‘all except’ questions.
“HFNC delivers higher pressures than CPAP” or “is CPAP”

Its PEEP is a few cmH₂O at most and falls with an open mouth. The DocT key ‘positive pressure to maintain airway patency’ (only 60% got it right) overstates this; it is still the best of its options, but the leading mechanisms are a reliable FiO₂ and dead-space washout.
“The elderly patient pulling off her mask needs a non-rebreather, mask CPAP or intubation” (only 43% got this right)

She is hypoxaemic but with a normal pH and PaCO₂, and she will not tolerate a mask: HFNC is tolerated through the nose and gives a reliable FiO₂. A non-rebreather is still a mask with an unreliable FiO₂; mask CPAP needs a cooperative patient.
“In FLORALI, HFNC lowered intubation”
Overall it did not (primary outcome negative); only the P/F ≤200 subgroup, in a post hoc analysis, showed fewer intubations.
decode: Which oxygen device can generate PEEP? [NEET 2025]
HFNO — not a non-rebreather, Venturi or Hudson mask.
Benefits of HFNC include all EXCEPT [DocT GT]
Reduce tidal volume.
Primary benefit of HFNO in ARDS [DocT QBank, three versions]

High flow with mild positive pressure, better oxygenation and less work of breathing — the option that does not claim CPAP-level pressure or a fixed tidal volume. Some stems put HFNO on an already ventilated patient; ignore that and answer the mechanism.
Elderly, confused, rib fractures, SpO₂ 89% on 8 L face mask, pulling it off — next step? [DocT GT]
Heated, humidified HFNC.
ARDS-14.punch: FLORALI’s primary outcome was negative, but HFNC was associated with lower 90-day mortality and fewer intubations when P/F was ≤200; it works mainly through a reliable FiO₂, dead-space washout and comfort, with only a little PEEP.

ARDS-15.intro: Once a patient is on HFNC, the danger is staying on it too long while failing. The ROX index puts oxygenation and breathing effort into one bedside number, so failure is seen in hours rather than at the point of collapse.
why: **(SpO₂ ÷ FiO₂) ÷ respiratory rate.** SpO₂ in %, FiO₂ as a fraction. Better oxygenation raises the top line, faster breathing lowers the whole, so the rate must be the divisor — SpO₂ 92% on FiO₂ 0.5 at 30/min gives 184 ÷ 30 = 6.1. It uses SpO₂, not PaO₂, because it is meant to need no blood gas.
**≥4.88 at 2, 6 or 12 h: low risk of intubation.** Roca and colleagues derived it in pneumonia patients on HFNC and validated it in 2019.

**Failure if below 2.85 at 2 h, 3.47 at 6 h, 3.85 at 12 h.** The failure cut-off rises with time, because a patient still struggling after 12 hours has less excuse. Values between the failure cut-off and 4.88 are indeterminate, so the score is repeated.
mimic: ROX vs HACOR
ROX is for HFNC and a lower value is worse; HACOR is for NIV and a higher value is worse (ARDS-16).
traps: “ROX = PaO₂/FiO₂ × RR” or “SpO₂ × RR / FiO₂” (69–83% got the formula right)
ROX uses SpO₂, not PaO₂, and the respiratory rate divides: a faster rate must lower the score.
“A higher ROX predicts failure”
A lower ROX is worse.
decode: Pneumonia on HFNC — correct formula for the ROX index? [DocT GT, three tests]
SpO₂/FiO₂ ÷ RR.
[pattern] ROX 3.2 at 6 h on HFNC — what next?
Below 3.47: high risk of failure, so prepare to intubate rather than wait.
ARDS-15.punch: ROX is SpO₂/FiO₂ divided by the respiratory rate; ≥4.88 predicts HFNC success, and values below 2.85, 3.47 and 3.85 at 2, 6 and 12 h predict failure.

ARDS-16.intro: HACOR does for NIV what ROX does for HFNC. NIV failure in hypoxaemic patients is common, and the harm lies in the delay, so the score is taken after the first hour.
why: **NIV failure in hypoxaemic respiratory failure.** Duan and colleagues (2017) built it from bedside variables to predict who will need intubation.

**Heart rate, acidosis (pH), consciousness (GCS), oxygenation (P/F), respiratory rate; consciousness carries the most points.** A falling GCS weighs most because a drowsy patient cannot protect his airway or cooperate with a mask: of a maximum 25 points, GCS ≤10 scores 10 on its own, more than the worst P/F (6), pH (4) or rate (4).

**>5 at 1 hour of NIV: failure rate above 80%; intubate early.** In the derivation study, among patients with a score above 5 at 1 h who failed NIV, those intubated within 12 hours had lower hospital mortality than those intubated later (66% vs 79%) — an association, but it is the reason the score is used.
mimic: HACOR vs ROX
HACOR: NIV, needs a blood gas, higher is worse. ROX: HFNC, no blood gas, lower is worse.
traps: “NIV suits moderate ARDS with distress, severe ARDS or shock”
NIV is reasonable only in mild ARDS without contraindications (ARDS-04c). The keyed option calls P/F 200 ‘mild’; by Berlin it is moderate — the option is still the best of the four.
decode: Most appropriate scenario for NIPPV in ARDS [DocT QBank]
Mild ARDS with no contraindications to NIPPV (83% got this right).
[pattern] HACOR 7 after 1 h of NIV — next step?
Intubate early: >5 at 1 h predicts failure.
ARDS-16.punch: HACOR (heart rate, acidosis, consciousness, oxygenation, rate) above 5 after 1 hour of NIV predicts failure in over 80%, so intubate early; for NIV a higher score is worse.

ARDS-17.sub: Respiratory → ARDS → Patient self-inflicted lung injury
ARDS-17.intro: Why does NIV do badly in hypoxaemic failure, and why does delay matter? Because the patient’s own breathing can injure the lung. A high respiratory drive generates large swings in pleural pressure, and the lung feels transpulmonary pressure, not the modest airway pressure on the screen.
why: **Lung injury caused by the patient’s own vigorous spontaneous effort, on NIV, HFNC or assisted modes.** Hypoxaemia, acidosis and inflammation drive breathing hard; in an injured, small lung, those big breaths over-stretch it in the same way that a large ventilator breath would (ARDS-18).

**Large negative pleural swings → high transpulmonary pressure and tidal volume; pendelluft (gas moving from non-dependent to dependent lung); raised transmural vascular pressure → oedema; patient–ventilator dyssynchrony.** On NIV, the ventilator’s pressure support and the patient’s muscle pressure add together, so large tidal volumes are easy to reach: in Carteaux’s cohort, patients who failed NIV averaged about 10.6 mL/kg PBW, against 8.5 in those who succeeded. In an injured lung, a forceful diaphragm contraction sucks gas from non-dependent into dependent alveoli before air enters from the mouth (pendelluft), stretching the dependent lung in a way the airway pressure does not show. Very negative pleural pressure also lowers the pressure around the capillaries, raising the transmural pressure across them and adding oedema. Dyssynchrony, such as double triggering, stacks breaths.

**Do not delay intubation in a patient with high drive; then sedation, higher PEEP, or neuromuscular blockade.** On NIV for hypoxaemic failure, an expired tidal volume persistently above about 9.5 mL/kg PBW (Carteaux 2016) predicts NIV failure, mainly when P/F is ≤200, even in a patient who looks comfortable — and NIV failure with late intubation carries a high mortality. After intubation, sedation lowers the drive, higher PEEP makes the injured lung behave more uniformly and reduces pendelluft, and paralysis abolishes the effort entirely in severe cases.
mimic: P-SILI vs VILI
Same physics, different source of pressure: the patient’s muscles in P-SILI, the ventilator in VILI.
traps: “She is comfortable, so tidal volumes of >9.5 mL/kg on NIV do not matter”
Read the volume, not the face: it marks high drive and P-SILI risk, and predicts NIV failure (81–94% got this right).
“High tidal volume on NPPV causes auto-PEEP or prevents recruitment”
The concern is P-SILI. The keyed wording ‘a marker of low lung compliance’ is loose: a large tidal volume marks high drive, which is dangerous because the lung receiving it is small.
“Airway pressure on NIV is low, so the lung is safe”
Transpulmonary pressure can be dangerously high while airway pressure looks safe.
decode: Hypoxaemic failure on NIV, comfortable, tidal volumes consistently >9.5 mL/kg — main concern? [DocT GT, two tests]
Patient self-inflicted lung injury.
NPPV in de novo hypoxaemic failure — concern about high tidal volumes? [DocT GT]
P-SILI.
Causes of NIV failure in ARDS [NEET 2024]
P-SILI, delayed intubation, mask intolerance, secretions, shock.
ARDS-17.punch: A patient with high drive can injure his own lung through large pleural swings and pendelluft, unseen on the airway pressure; a tidal volume above about 9.5 mL/kg on NIV is the warning, and early intubation is the remedy.

ARDS-18.intro: The ventilator can do to the lung what the patient’s effort does in P-SILI. Each type of VILI names a different way the breath harms the lung, and each is matched by a setting that prevents it — which is how the questions are framed.
why: **Volutrauma: over-distension from high tidal volume (high strain).** Animal work (Dreyfuss) showed that it is the volume, not the airway pressure itself, that injures: high pressure with the chest strapped, limiting volume, caused little oedema, whereas high volume at low pressure caused severe injury. Low tidal volume prevents it.

**Barotrauma: high transpulmonary pressure → air leak (pneumothorax, pneumomediastinum).** Over-stretched alveoli rupture, and air tracks along the bronchovascular sheaths into the mediastinum and under the skin, where on a chest X-ray it can outline the fibres of pectoralis major (the ‘ginkgo leaf’ sign).

**Atelectrauma: cyclic opening and closing of unstable units; shear (low PEEP).** Units that collapse at end-expiration and are forced open with each breath tear at the junction between open and closed lung. Enough PEEP keeps them open, which is why PEEP is started early, not just to raise the PaO₂.

**Biotrauma: mediator release from injured lung → distant organ failure.** Injurious ventilation releases cytokines into the blood; lower tidal volumes reduce them, which is one explanation of why ARMA lowered organ failure as well as mortality (ARDS-19).
**Ergotrauma: injury from total energy delivered (mechanical power) (standard teaching, not in your notes).** It brings rate and flow into the picture, not only volume and pressure (ARDS-27).

**Strain = tidal volume ÷ end-expiratory lung volume; stress = transpulmonary pressure.** Strain is how much the open lung is stretched relative to its resting size; stress is the pressure across it. They are linked by the specific elastance of the lung (stress = specific elastance × strain), so the same tidal volume is more harmful in a smaller baby lung.
mimic: Volutrauma vs barotrauma
Volutrauma is diffuse oedema from over-stretch; barotrauma is air outside the alveoli.
traps: “High PEEP is mainly to improve cardiac output or prevent hypercapnia”
PEEP raises intrathoracic pressure and can lower cardiac output; its purposes are recruitment, a larger end-expiratory lung volume (FRC) and prevention of atelectrauma (98% got this right).
“Barotrauma is caused by high airway pressure per se”
The injury follows high transpulmonary pressure and volume; airway pressure is only a proxy.
decode: FiO₂ 0.7, plateau 32 — strongest reason to start PEEP early? [DocT GT]
Prevent ventilator-induced lung injury (atelectrauma).
Primary rationale for high PEEP in ARDS [DocT QBank]
Recruits collapsed alveoli and increases FRC.
Post-ROSC, difficult bag-mask ventilation — expected chest X-ray finding? [Marrow]
Ginkgo leaf sign: subcutaneous emphysema outlining pectoralis major, from air leak.
ARDS-18.punch: Volume over-stretches, cyclic collapse shears, the injured lung releases mediators and the total energy adds up; low tidal volume and enough PEEP are the two settings that prevent most of it.

ARDS-19.intro: ARMA is the trial that turned the baby-lung idea (ARDS-10) into practice. It is the only ventilator setting in ARDS with a large mortality benefit in a randomised trial, so it is the answer to most ‘which strategy improves survival’ questions.
why: **Tidal volume 6 vs 12 mL/kg predicted body weight (861 patients).** The ARDS Network trial (NEJM 2000) compared a low tidal volume with what was then standard practice.
**Plateau ≤30 vs ≤50 cmH₂O.** The tidal volume in the low arm was reduced further, down to 4 mL/kg, if the plateau stayed above 30 (ARDS-22).
**31.0% vs 39.8% mortality (about 9% absolute reduction); stopped early for benefit.** About one death prevented for every 11 patients treated.

**More ventilator-free and organ-failure-free days.** Oxygenation was initially worse in the low-volume arm, yet survival was better: the benefit came from less lung injury, not from better gas exchange — so a better PaO₂ is not the goal of ventilation.
mimic: Therapies that improve oxygenation vs therapies that improve survival
Inhaled vasodilators and recruitment manoeuvres raise PaO₂ without proven survival benefit; low tidal volume (and proning in severe ARDS) improves survival.
traps: “Plateau pressure <35 cmH₂O” as the goal
The ARDSNet limit is ≤30.
“Intubated with P/F 86 on FiO₂ 1.0 — start VV-ECMO” (only 66% chose low tidal volume)
First ventilate protectively: 4–6 mL/kg with PEEP >5, then prone. ECMO comes after optimised ventilation fails (EOLIA criteria: P/F <50 for >3 h, <80 for >6 h, or pH <7.25 with PaCO₂ ≥60 for >6 h).
“Use actual body weight”
Predicted body weight, from height and sex (ARDS-21). Stems that say ‘ideal body weight’ mean the same thing.
decode: Primary goal of lung-protective ventilation in ARDS [DocT QBank]
Tidal volume 6–8 mL/kg predicted body weight (79% got this right).
Strategy most likely to reduce ventilator-associated lung injury [DocT QBank]
Low tidal volume (6 mL/kg ideal body weight) with appropriate PEEP.
Influenza, intubated, P/F 86 on FiO₂ 1.0 — next best step? [DocT GT]
Tidal volume 4–6 mL/kg with PEEP >5, not ECMO or CT.
ARDS-19.punch: ARMA: 6 mL/kg predicted body weight with plateau ≤30 cut mortality from 39.8% to 31.0% despite worse early oxygenation — protecting the lung, not the PaO₂, is what saves lives.

ARDS-20.sub: Respiratory → ARDS → Higher vs lower PEEP
ARDS-20.intro: After tidal volume, the next question was how much PEEP. Three trials compared higher and lower PEEP on top of low tidal volume, and the answer lies in who was studied.
why: **ALVEOLI, LOVS, ExPress.** ALVEOLI (ARDSNet, 2004) used a higher PEEP/FiO₂ table; LOVS (2008) added recruitment manoeuvres and pressure control; ExPress (2008) raised PEEP as far as a plateau of 28–30 cmH₂O allowed.

**No mortality difference; better oxygenation and less rescue therapy with higher PEEP.** Higher PEEP recruits lung and lowers FiO₂ needs, but in patients with little recruitable lung it only over-distends what is already open, so the net effect on survival was neutral.

**Moderate to severe ARDS (P/F ≤200) benefits from higher PEEP; mild ARDS may be harmed.** The individual-patient meta-analysis of the three trials (Briel, JAMA 2010) found lower mortality with higher PEEP when P/F was ≤200, and a non-significant trend to harm above 200. ATS guidance (2024 update) suggests higher PEEP, without prolonged recruitment manoeuvres, in moderate–severe ARDS; a later trial of recruitment plus PEEP titration (ART, 2017) increased mortality.
mimic: Higher PEEP vs recruitment manoeuvres
Higher PEEP is suggested in moderate–severe ARDS; prolonged high-pressure recruitment manoeuvres are not.
traps: “Higher PEEP reduced mortality in ALVEOLI”
No trial showed it alone; the benefit appears only in pooled data for P/F ≤200 (ARDS-29e).
decode: Septic shock, bilateral infiltrates, P/F 100 — ideal ventilator settings? [Marrow]
Low tidal volume with high PEEP.
[pattern] Which ARDS patients benefit from higher PEEP?
Moderate to severe (P/F ≤200).
ARDS-20.punch: ALVEOLI, LOVS and ExPress each found no mortality difference with higher PEEP, but pooled data favour it when P/F is ≤200.

ARDS-21.intro: Every tidal volume in the ARDSNet protocol is per kilogram of predicted body weight, so this calculation comes before the first setting.
why: **Men: 50 + 0.91 × (height in cm – 152.4).** A 170 cm man: 50 + 0.91 × 17.6 = 66 kg, so 6 mL/kg is about 400 mL.
**Women: 45.5 + 0.91 × (height in cm – 152.4).** At the same height a woman’s PBW is 4.5 kg less: a 160 cm woman is about 52 kg, so 6 mL/kg is about 315 mL.
**Lung size follows height and sex, not actual weight.** Fat does not add alveoli, so dosing by actual weight gives an obese patient a dangerously large breath.
mimic: Predicted vs ideal body weight
Questions use the terms interchangeably; both mean the height-and-sex formula.
traps: “Tidal volume by actual body weight”
Never: by predicted body weight (ARDS-29a).
decode: [pattern] 170 cm man weighing 110 kg — tidal volume at 6 mL/kg?
About 400 mL, from PBW 66 kg, not 660 mL.
ARDS-21.punch: Predicted body weight is 50 (men) or 45.5 (women) + 0.91 × (height in cm – 152.4), because lung size follows height and sex, not weight.

ARDS-22.intro: This is ARMA turned into steps at the bedside. The questions test three things: the tidal volume and plateau rules, what to do when the CO₂ rises, and when hypercapnia is itself dangerous.
why: **Start 8 mL/kg PBW; reduce by 1 mL/kg every ≤2 h to 6 mL/kg.** The mode is volume assist-control. Stepping down lets the CO₂ and pH adjust gradually instead of in one jump.
**Rate up to 35/min.** The initial rate is set to match the patient’s previous minute ventilation; raising the rate is the first lever for the CO₂ that rises when tidal volume falls.

**Plateau ≤30 cmH₂O; if higher, reduce tidal volume in 1 mL/kg steps to a minimum of 4 mL/kg.** Plateau is checked with a 0.5 s inspiratory pause. Six mL/kg is a starting point: if the plateau is still high, the baby lung is smaller than average and the breath must shrink further.

**pH 7.30–7.45. If pH falls, raise rate to 35; if pH <7.15 at rate 35, tidal volume may be raised and bicarbonate considered (permissive hypercapnia).** The CO₂ is allowed to rise because protecting the lung matters more than a normal PaCO₂, and it should rise gradually, so that cells buffer it and the pH falls less. Hypercapnia is not harmless: it raises intracranial pressure by dilating cerebral vessels, constricts pulmonary vessels (raising right-ventricular afterload), depresses myocardial contractility, stimulates a sympathetic surge and shifts the oxyhaemoglobin curve to the right. So it is avoided in raised ICP and used with care in right-ventricular failure.
mimic: Permissive hypercapnia vs chasing a normal PaCO₂
Raising tidal volume to normalise CO₂ undoes the lung protection; ARDSNet raises the rate first and the volume only below pH 7.15.
traps: “PaCO₂ 76 in the first hour — raise it faster, or accept SaO₂ 75%”
Let it rise gradually on the current settings; the oxygen target stays at SpO₂ 88–95% (ARDS-23) (100% got this right).
“Hypercapnia lowers ICP”
It raises ICP through cerebral vasodilation — the ‘NOT deleterious’ answer is decreased ICP.
“pH 7.27 on 6 mL/kg — continue current settings” (Marrow key)

Permissive hypercapnia is right in principle, and the tidal volume should not be raised. But by ARDSNet, pH 7.15–7.30 means raise the rate towards 35 if it is lower; choose ‘continue’ only if the options are between that and raising tidal volume. Conversely, Marrow keys ‘increase rate’ at pH 7.32 — the lever is right, but 7.32 is already within the goal.
“Your notes: pH goal above 7.2”
Many texts accept ≥7.20 in permissive hypercapnia; the ARDSNet protocol goal is 7.30–7.45.
decode: Pneumonia ARDS, P/F 120, AKI, MODS — ARDSNet strategy? [DocT QBank]
Low tidal volume (4–8 mL/kg PBW) with plateau <30 cmH₂O.
Influenza ARDS, normal echo, VT 500 — which therapy is best shown to improve survival? [DocT GT]

6 mL/kg ideal body weight — not diuresis, inhaled vasodilators or recruitment-guided PEEP titration (none has a proven survival benefit, and recruitment with PEEP titration increased mortality in ART).
Permissive hypercapnia, PaCO₂ 76 in the first hour — next step? [DocT GT]
Maintain settings and let it rise gradually.
On 6 mL/kg: pH 7.32/PaCO₂ 48, or pH 7.27/PaCO₂ 60 — next ventilator step? [Marrow]
The lever is the respiratory rate (to 35), not the tidal volume; Marrow keys ‘increase rate’ at 7.32 and ‘continue’ at 7.27.
ARDS-22.punch: Start at 8 mL/kg PBW, step to 6 (down to 4 if plateau >30), raise the rate to 35 for acidosis, and raise tidal volume only when pH is <7.15 at rate 35 — hypercapnia is tolerated, except where ICP is raised.

parts.q: Harmful effects of hypercapnia?
parts.a: **Raised ICP** (cerebral vasodilation), **pulmonary vasoconstriction** with right-ventricular strain, **reduced myocardial contractility**, sympathetic surge and arrhythmias, **right shift of the oxyhaemoglobin curve**. Decreased ICP is not one of them.

ARDS-23.intro: The last part of the protocol sets how much oxygen is enough, and how FiO₂ and PEEP climb together to reach it.
why: **PaO₂ 55–80 mmHg; SpO₂ 88–95%.** Above this range extra oxygen adds little to delivery, while the FiO₂ and PEEP needed to reach it add their own harm. Going lower is not free either: a trial of a more conservative target in ARDS (LOCO2, PaO₂ 55–70) was stopped early with a signal of harm: higher 90-day mortality and cases of mesenteric ischaemia in the conservative arm.

**Lower PEEP/FiO₂ table: 0.3/5, 0.4/5–8, 0.5/8–10, 0.6/10, 0.7/10–14, 0.8/14, 0.9/14–18, 1.0/18–24.** If the target is not met, move to the next pair; if it is exceeded, step back. PEEP of 10 belongs with FiO₂ of about 0.5–0.7. This is the table ARMA used; the higher table, from ALVEOLI, pairs each FiO₂ with more PEEP (ARDS-20).
traps: “Aim for SpO₂ 100% or PaO₂ >100”
The target is deliberately modest; hyperoxia is not the aim.
decode: Which settings are most consistent with lung-protective ventilation? [DocT QBank]
Tidal volume 6 mL/kg with PEEP 10 (86% got this right).
[pattern] ARDSNet SpO₂ target
ARDS-23.punch: ARDSNet aims for PaO₂ 55–80 and SpO₂ 88–95%, climbing the PEEP/FiO₂ table in pairs until the target is reached.

ARDS-24.intro: The plateau rule in ARDS-22 depends on reading the airway pressure curve. In volume control with constant flow, a pause at end-inspiration splits the peak into its two parts.
why: **Resistive pressure (airways, tube): flow × resistance.** When flow stops, this part disappears, so the pressure falls from peak to plateau.
**Driving pressure: the elastic load of the tidal volume.** It is the pressure needed to hold the breath in the lung against its elastic recoil (ARDS-26).

**End-inspiratory hold of 0.5–2 s (zero flow), in a passive patient.** With no flow, airway pressure equals alveolar pressure; an active patient’s effort distorts the reading. Total PEEP needs a separate end-expiratory hold, to include any auto-PEEP.
traps: “Peak pressure reflects lung stretch”
Peak includes the resistive pressure; plateau reflects the stretch.
decode: [pattern] Peak pressure rises from 30 to 45, plateau unchanged at 22 — cause?
A resistance problem: bronchospasm, secretions or a kinked tube.
ARDS-24.punch: Peak minus plateau is resistance, plateau minus PEEP is the elastic load; the plateau needs a no-flow hold in a passive patient.

ARDS-25.intro: Each named pressure on a ventilator is a difference between two points along the path from the ventilator to the pleura. Knowing which two points each spans answers both the calculation questions and the subtler question of when the airway pressure can be trusted.
why: **Pplat – PEEP = driving pressure, which reflects tidal volume ÷ compliance.** Use the total PEEP (set plus auto-PEEP).

**Ppeak – Pplat = resistive pressure, which reflects airway resistance.** This only works in volume control with constant flow; in pressure control the peak is the set pressure, and flow decays, so this gap does not measure resistance.
**Palv – Ppl = transpulmonary pressure: stress on the lung itself.** This is what over-stretches alveoli (ARDS-28).
**Palv – Patm = trans-respiratory pressure: lung plus chest wall.** In a passive patient at zero flow, this is the plateau; it treats the lung and chest wall as one.
**Ppl – Patm = chest-wall pressure: the chest wall alone.** A stiff chest wall (obesity, abdominal hypertension) takes a larger share of the plateau, so the plateau overstates lung stress.
mimic: Respiratory-system vs lung compliance
Volume ÷ (plateau – PEEP) gives respiratory-system compliance; lung compliance needs pleural (oesophageal) pressure.
traps: “Alveolar pressure during the hold is 32 (peak), 18 (plateau – PEEP) or 26” (62–81% chose 24)
At zero flow, airway pressure equals alveolar pressure: the plateau, 24. 18 is the driving pressure; 32 still includes the resistive part.
“Pressure control, paralysed asthmatic: compliance is reliable from Pinsp and volume, or resistance from peak – pause” (only 12% got this right)

Both statements hold only in other circumstances. In pressure control, peak is the set pressure, so peak – pause cannot give resistance; and with flow not reaching zero, or auto-PEEP in an asthmatic, Pinsp – PEEP is not the true elastic pressure. The keyed answer: once paralysis wears off, the patient’s own muscle pressure adds to the ventilator’s, so pleural (oesophageal) pressure is needed to calculate lung compliance.
decode: Volume control, end-inspiratory hold: peak 32, plateau 24, PEEP 6 — alveolar pressure? [DocT QBank, DocT GT, three tests]
24 cmH₂O (the plateau).
Asthmatic on pressure control, paralysed, VT 200 mL on Pinsp 25/PEEP 5 — most accurate statement? [DocT GT]
When paralysis wears off, pleural pressure is needed to calculate pulmonary compliance reliably.
ARDS-25.punch: Plateau is alveolar pressure; plateau minus PEEP is driving pressure, peak minus plateau is resistance (in volume control only), and only pleural pressure separates the lung from the chest wall.

ARDS-26.intro: Driving pressure brings the deck back to the baby lung. Six mL/kg PBW assumes an average lung; driving pressure measures the breath against the lung that is actually open.
why: **Pplat – PEEP = tidal volume ÷ respiratory-system compliance.** 400 mL into a compliance of 25 mL/cmH₂O needs 16 cmH₂O.

**Amato, 2015: of all ventilator variables it was the one most strongly linked to survival; changes in tidal volume or PEEP helped only if they lowered it.** A re-analysis of 3562 patients from nine trials: each rise of one standard deviation (about 7 cmH₂O) carried about 1.4 times the risk of death (relative risk 1.41). This is an association from secondary analysis, not a randomised test of a driving-pressure target.

**It scales tidal volume to the size of the baby lung (compliance) rather than to predicted body weight.** Two patients with the same height get the same 6 mL/kg, but in the one with less open lung that breath is a larger strain; driving pressure shows it. PEEP that recruits lung raises compliance and lowers driving pressure; PEEP that only over-distends raises it.
mimic: Driving pressure vs peak pressure
Driving pressure uses plateau, not peak, and total PEEP.
traps: “High PEEP or a high peak pressure predicts a better outcome”
Low driving pressure does.
decode: Predictor of a better outcome in ARDS [DocT GT PYQ; NEET 2024]
Low driving pressure (<14–15).
ARDS-26.punch: Driving pressure (plateau – PEEP = VT/compliance) sizes the breath to the open lung; below 15 is the target, and in Amato’s analysis it was the ventilator variable most strongly associated with survival.

ARDS-27.intro: Driving pressure looks at one breath. Mechanical power asks how much energy the lung receives every minute, which also counts how often the breath is given and how fast it is pushed in.
why: **Energy delivered to the respiratory system per minute (J/min).** Energy per breath (pressure × volume) multiplied by the respiratory rate.

**0.098 × RR × VT × (Ppeak – ½ driving pressure), VT in litres; bedside surrogate (4 × driving pressure) + RR.** The 0.098 converts L·cmH₂O to joules. RR 20, VT 0.4 L, peak 30, driving pressure 14: 0.098 × 20 × 0.4 × 23 ≈ 18 J/min.
**Tidal volume, driving pressure, flow, PEEP and respiratory rate.** Flow enters through the resistive part of the peak pressure, PEEP through the static part.

**Above about 17 J/min (12 J/min in ARDS in some studies) (standard teaching, not in your notes).** The 17 J/min figure is an association with mortality in large observational ICU data (Serpa Neto 2018); the 12 J/min figure comes mainly from experimental work. No randomised trial has tested a power target.
mimic: Mechanical power vs driving pressure
Driving pressure ignores rate; power counts it, so a very high rate used to compensate for a low tidal volume is not harmless.
traps: “Mechanical power is airway pressure × time, or pressure × compliance, or excludes PEEP” (only 34% got this right)
Energy is pressure × volume, not pressure × time; pressure × compliance gives a volume. Power is energy per breath × rate, and PEEP is one of its components.
decode: Best description of mechanical power [DocT GT]
The product of energy per breath and respiratory rate.
ARDS-27.punch: Mechanical power is energy per breath times rate (J/min), counting volume, pressure, flow, PEEP and rate; values above about 17 J/min are associated with higher mortality.

ARDS-28.intro: The plateau tells you the pressure across lung and chest wall together (ARDS-25). When the chest wall is stiff, part of that pressure never reaches the lung, and an oesophageal balloon is the way to separate the two.
why: **Alveolar pressure (airway pressure at zero flow) – pleural pressure; pleural pressure from an oesophageal balloon in the lower third of the oesophagus.** The oesophagus lies against the pleura, so its pressure approximates pleural pressure; position is checked by an occlusion test, in which airway and oesophageal pressure swings should match.

**Positive, about 0 to +3 cmH₂O (EPVent protocol used 0–10), so alveoli stay open; this is how PEEP is titrated.** A negative end-expiratory value means pleural pressure exceeds airway pressure, so dependent alveoli are squeezed shut; PEEP is raised until it is just positive.

**Stiff chest wall: obesity, raised intra-abdominal pressure, chest-wall oedema; plateau pressure overestimates lung stress here.** A morbidly obese patient may tolerate, and need, a PEEP and plateau that would be excessive in a thin one.
mimic: Oesophageal pressure vs alveolar pressure
Pes approximates pleural pressure, not alveolar, and it is affected by the weight of the chest wall and mediastinum.
traps: “PL = Paw + Pes” or “keep end-inspiratory PL above 35”
PL = Paw – Pes; end-inspiratory PL is kept below about 25.
“Oesophageal-guided PEEP is proven better”
EPVent-2 found it no better than an empirical high-PEEP table (standard teaching, not in your notes).
decode: Obese ARDS, end-expiratory Pes 20, PEEP 15 — interpretation? [DocT GT]
PL –5 cmH₂O: dependent alveoli likely collapsed; PEEP should be raised.
ARDS-28.punch: Transpulmonary pressure is airway minus oesophageal pressure; keep it just positive at end-expiration and below about 25 at end-inspiration — most useful when a stiff chest wall makes the plateau misleading.

ARDS-29.sub: Respiratory → ARDS → Revision: true or false
ARDS-29.intro: A sweep through the deck. Each statement turns on one detail from an earlier card.
why: **False — ARMA used predicted body weight** (ARDS-19, ARDS-21).
**False — a ROX of 5 at 12 h is ≥4.88, which predicts HFNC success** (ARDS-15).
**True — HACOR above 5 at 1 h predicts NIV failure in over 80%** (ARDS-16).
**False — driving pressure is plateau – PEEP, not peak – PEEP** (ARDS-26).
**False — ALVEOLI showed no mortality difference with higher PEEP** (ARDS-20).
**True — the ARDSNet SpO₂ target is 88–95%, with PaO₂ 55–80** (ARDS-23).
**True — PEEP prevents atelectrauma by stopping cyclic collapse** (ARDS-18).
traps: “A higher ROX is worse”
Lower ROX is worse; higher HACOR is worse.
decode: ROX formula on HFNC [DocT GT]
SpO₂/FiO₂ ÷ RR (83% got this right).
[pattern] Statements about scores and trials
ROX lower is worse, HACOR higher is worse; ARMA used PBW; no single PEEP trial cut mortality.
ARDS-29.punch: Most errors here come from direction (low ROX, high HACOR are bad), the plateau-not-peak rule and the negative PEEP trials.

topups.topic: NIV: CPAP vs BiPAP and contraindications
topups.q: NIV: CPAP vs BiPAP — what each pressure does, and who must not get NIV?
a: - CPAP = one continuous pressure: recruits alveoli, raises FRC and oxygenation (cardiogenic pulmonary oedema, OSA).
- BiPAP = IPAP + EPAP; pressure support (IPAP − EPAP) unloads breathing and clears CO2, EPAP recruits and oxygenates (and offsets auto-PEEP).
- Contraindications: GCS <8 or cannot protect the airway, apnoea/arrest, vomiting or upper GI bleed, shock, agitation/non-cooperation, facial trauma, undrained pneumothorax.
- Cardiogenic shock with confusion and hypoxaemic oedema → intubate, not NIV; overdose with GCS <8 and RR 6 → intubate.
topups.src: DocT ARDS Q04; DocT ARDS Q28; Marrow QB05-Q14; Marrow QB11-Q09; DocT GT CGT4 Q88; DocT GT CGT6 Q44

x.sub: Respiratory → Non-invasive support → CPAP, BiPAP and who must not get NIV
x.intro: Step 1 is support before the tube. Beside HFNC (ARDS-14), the two mask modes are CPAP and BiPAP, and they do different jobs: one pressure that holds the lung open, or two pressures that also help each breath in. The exam asks what each pressure does, then hands you a patient in whom any mask is the wrong answer.
why: **CPAP = one continuous pressure: recruits alveoli, raises FRC and oxygenation (cardiogenic pulmonary oedema, OSA).** The same pressure in inspiration and expiration splints collapsed alveoli open and raises FRC, so shunt falls; in cardiogenic oedema it also lowers LV afterload and preload. It gives no inspiratory help, so it does little for CO₂.

**BiPAP = IPAP + EPAP; pressure support (IPAP − EPAP) unloads breathing and clears CO₂, EPAP recruits and oxygenates (and offsets auto-PEEP).** The difference between the two levels is the inspiratory assist: it enlarges tidal volume and takes over muscle work, which is why it is the mode for hypercapnia. EPAP is simply CPAP at end-expiration; in COPD it also balances intrinsic PEEP so the patient triggers more easily (COPD-03).

**Contraindications: GCS <8 or cannot protect the airway, apnoea/arrest, vomiting or upper GI bleed, shock, agitation/non-cooperation, facial trauma, undrained pneumothorax.** A mask needs a patient who breathes, keeps the airway clear and tolerates it. Positive pressure into the stomach risks aspiration, raises intrathoracic pressure in a failing circulation, and enlarges an undrained pneumothorax.

**Cardiogenic shock with confusion and hypoxaemic oedema → intubate, not NIV; overdose with GCS <8 and RR 6 → intubate.** Cardiogenic oedema is the best indication for CPAP, but shock and confusion turn it into a contraindication. The overdose patient cannot protect the airway or generate breaths for a mask to support.
mimic: CPAP vs pressure support
CPAP raises FRC and oxygenation; pressure support helps inspiration and tidal volume. For low FRC in a spontaneously breathing patient, CPAP is the answer.
traps: “BiPAP works by decreasing lung compliance”
It recruits lung and improves compliance; the distractor reverses the physiology.
“BiPAP delivers a constant volume”
It is pressure-set; tidal volume varies with effort and mechanics.
“Hypoxaemic, low FRC, breathing spontaneously — pressure support”
CPAP raises FRC; pressure support only adds inspiratory help (DocT GT).
“Switch a ventilated severe ARDS patient to BiPAP”
The DocT stem is clinically odd: NIV is reserved for mild ARDS (ARDS-04, ARDS-14); answer the pressure question it asks.
decode: Characteristic feature of BiPAP [DocT; DocT GT]
Two levels: higher inspiratory, lower expiratory pressure (80%).
Primary advantage of BiPAP in this patient [DocT]
Spontaneous breathing with support in both phases (91%).
Spontaneously breathing, hypoxaemic from low FRC — best mode? [DocT GT]
CPAP.
Propafenone overdose, GCS <8, RR 6; cardiogenic shock, confused, hypoxaemic oedema [Marrow]
Intubate in both.
x.punch: CPAP holds the lung open, the gap between IPAP and EPAP breathes for the patient; and a patient who cannot protect the airway, breathe, cooperate or hold a blood pressure needs a tube, not a mask.

spine: Supporting the patient before intubation
High-flow nasal oxygen is the first-line non-invasive support in hypoxaemic failure, NIV is kept for mild cases, and ROX and HACOR tell you early when each is failing.
How breathing and ventilators injure

The lung is injured by the stretch it actually feels — from the patient’s own vigorous effort (P-SILI) or from the ventilator (volutrauma, atelectrauma, biotrauma) — so stress and strain, not airway pressure alone, are what matter.
Trials behind lung-protective ventilation
ARMA showed that 6 mL/kg predicted body weight saves lives; higher PEEP did not change mortality in three trials, but may help when P/F is ≤200.
Setting the ARDSNet ventilator

Calculate predicted body weight from height and sex, step tidal volume down to 6 mL/kg, keep plateau ≤30, accept hypercapnia within the pH rules, and pair FiO₂ with PEEP from the table to a modest oxygen target.
Reading the pressures on screen
A hold at end-inspiration separates peak (resistance plus elastance) from plateau (alveolar pressure), and an oesophageal balloon separates the lung from the chest wall.
Driving pressure, power and review
Driving pressure scales the breath to the open lung and is the variable most strongly associated with survival; mechanical power adds rate and flow to measure the total energy the lung receives.
RESP01B.primer: Respiratory-system compliance is tidal volume divided by the pressure needed to hold it (plateau minus PEEP); in ARDS it is low because the aerated ‘baby lung’ is small, not because that lung is stiff (ARDS-10). Plateau pressure is the airway pressure during a short pause at the end of inspiration with no flow, so it equals alveolar pressure; peak pressure also includes the pressure spent pushing flow through the tube and airways. What actually stretches the lung is transpulmonary pressure — alveolar minus pleural pressure — so a strongly breathing patient can over-stretch his lung even when the airway pressure looks low. HFNC delivers heated, humidified gas at up to 60 L/min through nasal prongs; NIV delivers set pressures (inspiratory support plus PEEP, or CPAP) through a sealed mask.

ARDS-30.intro: Once lung-protective ventilation is running and the P/F ratio is still below 150, the next step with a proven survival benefit is prone positioning. PROSEVA is the trial behind every number examiners ask: the P/F threshold, the hours per day and the size of the benefit.
why: **P/F <150 on FiO₂ ≥0.6, PEEP ≥5 and tidal volume about 6 mL/kg, confirmed after 12–24 h of stabilisation.** The stabilisation period matters: many patients improve once ventilation is optimised, so only those still below 150 after 12–24 h were enrolled — moderate-to-severe ARDS, not mild. That is why <150 is the keyed threshold, not <200 or <100.

**Within 36 h of intubation; sessions of at least 16 h a day (your notes: 12–18 h).** PROSEVA proned early and for long sessions (average about 17 h); patients stayed prone daily until oxygenation held in the supine position. Short sessions let the dorsal lung collapse again each time the patient is turned back.

**28-day mortality 16.0% vs 32.8%.** A halving of mortality, and the benefit persisted at 90 days. Current guidance recommends prolonged prone sessions — ESICM 2023 more than 16 h a day in moderate-to-severe ARDS, ATS more than 12 h a day in severe ARDS; it comes before ECMO, not after it (ARDS-35).
mimic: PROSEVA vs the earlier prone trials
Earlier trials proned later, for shorter sessions (some about 7 h a day) and included milder ARDS; they improved oxygenation but not survival. PROSEVA changed all three.
Prone vs ECMO for refractory hypoxaemia
Prone has a proven mortality benefit and is tried first; ECMO is for hypoxaemia that persists despite prone (ARDS-35).
traps: “Prone for at least 6 h a day is enough”
PROSEVA used ≥16 h; 6 h is a distractor. One DocT GT paper prints the keyed option as ‘≤16 hours/day’ — a misprint; pick the prone option whatever sign is printed.
“P/F 105 on FiO₂ 1.0, PEEP 8, paralysed — start ECMO, inhaled NO or oesophageal-pressure PEEP” (only 59% chose prone)

P/F 105 is below 150 and prone has not been tried, so prone is next. ECMO is not yet indicated (P/F not <80 and prone not tried), inhaled NO improves only oxygenation, and oesophageal-pressure-guided PEEP had no outcome benefit (EPVent-2).
“Avoid prone in severe ARDS”
The reverse: prone is recommended in moderate-to-severe ARDS, and severe ARDS is where it matters most. This was the NEET 2025 ‘should NOT be done’ answer.
“Proning improves oxygenation but does not affect mortality”
PROSEVA halved 28-day mortality.
“Methylprednisolone 2 mg/kg/day gives the most mortality benefit” (DocT GT distractor)

Prone ≥16 h has the largest and most consistent mortality benefit, so it is the answer. Early corticosteroids are now conditionally recommended (DEXA-ARDS; ATS 2024, SCCM 2024; ARDS-40), but that is weaker evidence than PROSEVA, and 2 mg/kg/day is not the regimen behind the current recommendation.
decode: At what P/F ratio is prone positioning recommended? [NEET 2024, DocT GT]
Moderate ARDS, P/F 140 on PEEP 10 — which intervention gives the most mortality benefit? [DocT GT]
Prone ≥16 h a day.
Intubated pneumonia, P/F 105 on FiO₂ 1.0, PEEP 8, paralysed — next step? [DocT GT]
Prone the patient.
Moderate–severe ARDS: which should NOT be done about prone ventilation? [NEET 2025]
Avoiding prone in severe ARDS.
ARDS-30.punch: PROSEVA: P/F <150 on FiO₂ ≥0.6 after 12–24 h, proned within 36 h for ≥16 h a day, cut 28-day mortality from 32.8% to 16.0% — so prone comes before ECMO, nitric oxide or HFOV.

ARDS-31.intro: Why should turning a patient over halve mortality? In the supine ARDS lung, the weight of the oedematous lung, the heart and the abdomen squeeze the dorsal regions shut, so a small ventral lung takes every breath. Turning the patient prone changes where that weight falls.
why: **The pleural-pressure gradient becomes more uniform and the dorsal lung is recruited (more lung mass lies dorsally).** Supine, pleural pressure is much less negative over the dependent dorsal lung, so it collapses. Prone, the dorsal lung becomes non-dependent and re-opens, and because more of the lung’s tissue lies dorsally, more lung is gained there than is lost ventrally. The shape of the lung also fits the chest wall better prone, so ventilation spreads more evenly.

**Perfusion stays mainly dorsal, so V/Q matching improves and shunt falls.** Pulmonary blood flow goes mostly to the dorsal lung whichever way the patient lies. Supine, that well-perfused lung was the collapsed part — shunt; prone, it is re-aerated, so ventilation and perfusion now meet in the same regions.

**The heart and abdomen no longer compress the lung; the right ventricle is unloaded; secretions drain.** Prone, the heart rests on the sternum rather than on the lower lobes. Recruitment and a lower PaCO₂ reduce pulmonary vascular resistance, which offloads a strained right ventricle (acute cor pulmonale, ARDS-43). Gravity drains secretions from the dorsal airways.

**More homogeneous strain → less VILI.** When ventilation is spread over more open lung, each alveolus is stretched less, and fewer units open and close with every breath. This, not the higher PaO₂, is thought to be why survival improves.
mimic: Oxygenation response vs survival benefit
In PROSEVA, the gain in PaO₂ after proning did not predict who survived; patients whose PaO₂ does not rise still benefit, so a non-responder is not a reason to stop.
Prone vs raising mean airway pressure
Inverse-ratio ventilation, HFOV and recruitment manoeuvres open lung with pressure; prone opens it by redistributing weight, without raising pressure.
traps: “Proning works by raising mean airway pressure”, “by reducing dead space through airway patency” or “by improving chest-wall compliance”

Its main effect is redistribution of ventilation to the dorsal lung, where perfusion already is. The keyed options say ‘V/Q matching by redistributing ventilation to dorsal regions’ or ‘to more compliant regions’.
“The main goal of proning is to prevent pressure sores or remove lung fluid”
Pressure sores are a complication of proning (ARDS-32); the goal is recruitment and oxygenation.
“Severe ARDS, FiO₂ 0.8, Pplat 30, pH 7.22 — increase VT, reduce PEEP or target PaCO₂ <40” (DocT keys inverse-ratio ventilation)

With prone not offered, IRV is the least harmful option because it raises mean airway pressure without raising tidal volume or plateau pressure. It has no outcome evidence and is in no ARDS guideline; pH 7.22 is acceptable permissive hypercapnia, so do not chase PaCO₂ <40. If prone is offered, choose prone.
decode: Primary mechanism by which proning improves oxygenation? [DocT]
Better V/Q matching by redistributing ventilation to the dorsal lung.
Image of a prone patient — primary goal of this position? [DocT]
Alveolar recruitment and oxygenation.
Which statement about proning is true? (≥6 h, ‘no mortality effect’ as distractors) [DocT]
It improves oxygenation by redistributing ventilation and perfusion.
Severe ARDS, Pplat 30, pH 7.22, no prone option — best strategy to improve oxygenation without VILI? [DocT, DocT GT]
Inverse-ratio ventilation (best of the options; prone if offered).
ARDS-31.punch: Prone re-opens the heavy dorsal lung where the blood already flows, so V/Q improves; its survival benefit comes from spreading strain evenly and reducing VILI, not from the rise in PaO₂.

ARDS-32.sub: Respiratory → ARDS → Prone positioning: contraindications and complications
ARDS-32.intro: Prone is the step that saves lives, so the questions test when you cannot do it — and then what comes instead — and what goes wrong when you do.
why: **Contraindications: unstable spine (absolute); raised intracranial pressure; open chest or abdomen; recent sternotomy or tracheal surgery; facial or pelvic fractures; massive haemoptysis; severe haemodynamic instability; life-threatening arrhythmia; late pregnancy (relative).** Each is either something turning could injure (an unstable spine, fresh wounds, fractures that bear weight face-down), something prone worsens (prone with the head turned can raise ICP and impede venous drainage), or a patient who cannot be resuscitated face-down. When prone is contraindicated and the patient meets EOLIA criteria, VV-ECMO is the next step (ARDS-35).

**Complications: tube obstruction or displacement; loss of lines and drains; pressure sores (face, chest, knees); facial and eye oedema; brachial plexus injury; feed intolerance and vomiting; transient desaturation.** The dangerous ones happen during the turn — the tube and lines. Pressure sores are the commonest, on the face, chest and knees, which bear the weight. Facial and eye oedema, and eye injury from pressure, are why the face is padded and moved regularly.
mimic: Raised ICP as contraindication vs complication
Raised ICP is a reason not to prone; facial and ocular injury is the keyed ‘major complication’ of proning itself.
traps: “Increased intracranial pressure is the major complication of proning” (only 67% chose facial and ocular injury)
Raised ICP belongs to the contraindications. The keyed complication is facial and ocular injury, which follows from lying face-down for 16 h.
“Polytrauma with uncleared C-spine and chest lacerations, P/F <150 — prone the patient” (only 52% chose ECMO)

Prone is contraindicated (unstable spine, open chest-wall wounds). With PaO₂ 67 on FiO₂ 1.0 — P/F 67 — for 6 h despite optimal ventilation and paralysis, he meets the EOLIA oxygenation criterion (<80 for >6 h), so VV-ECMO is next.
Two correct options in one DocT GT question

‘Proning improves oxygenation by redistributing ventilation and perfusion’ is keyed, but ‘proning is contraindicated in spinal fractures’ is also true (unstable spine is absolute). Pick the keyed mechanism statement.
decode: Major complication of prone positioning? [DocT]
Facial and ocular injuries.
Uncleared C-spine, ventral chest lacerations, P/F 67 for 6 h, paralysed — next step? [DocT GT]
VV-ECMO (prone contraindicated).
Proned, ventilated TBI patient desaturates acutely — what to assess first? [Marrow]
Tube dislodgement or obstruction.
ARDS-32.punch: Do not prone an unstable spine, raised ICP, an open chest or abdomen or a peri-arrest patient; when you do prone, watch the tube and lines at every turn and the face and eyes for pressure injury.

parts.q: A proned, ventilated patient suddenly desaturates: first step?
parts.a: **Check the tube first: displacement or obstruction** (Marrow), before blaming the lung — the turn is when tubes move.

ARDS-33.intro: If collapsed lung can be re-opened with pressure, why not do it deliberately? A recruitment manoeuvre is a brief, high pressure to open collapsed alveoli, followed by enough PEEP to keep them open. The idea is sound physiology; the ART trial is why it is no longer routine.
why: **Sustained inflation: CPAP 40 cmH₂O for 30–40 s.** The pressure must exceed the opening pressure of collapsed units. The other method is stepwise (staircase) recruitment: PEEP is raised in steps, then lowered in a decremental trial while static compliance is tracked — the step at which compliance suddenly falls is the derecruitment point, and PEEP is set about 2 cmH₂O above it after re-recruiting. Whatever the method, the gain is lost unless PEEP holds the lung open afterwards.

**Hypotension (fall in venous return), barotrauma, desaturation.** High intrathoracic pressure squeezes the great veins and loads the right ventricle, so cardiac output falls during the manoeuvre. Over-stretching already-open alveoli can rupture them (pneumothorax). Oxygenation can fall transiently as blood is pushed towards unrecruited lung and output drops.

**Stepwise recruitment plus PEEP titrated to best compliance vs low PEEP: higher mortality and more barotrauma with recruitment.** ART (Cavalcanti, JAMA 2017; about 1000 patients with moderate-to-severe ARDS) found 28-day mortality 55.3% vs 49.3%, with more pneumothorax needing drainage. ESICM 2023 and the 2024 ATS update both make a strong recommendation against prolonged high-pressure recruitment manoeuvres, and ESICM also suggests (weakly) against brief high-pressure manoeuvres.
mimic: Derecruitment vs pneumothorax as a cause of sudden desaturation

After open suctioning or a disconnection, the lung derecruits and compliance falls; a pneumothorax adds unilateral absent breath sounds and haemodynamic collapse — exclude it before any recruitment manoeuvre.
traps: “Recruitment manoeuvres every 4 h maintain alveolar stability”
Routine, repeated manoeuvres are not recommended; ART showed harm.
“PEEP after a recruitment manoeuvre is to prevent over-distension or improve cardiac output”
It is there to keep open what the manoeuvre opened (DocT GT, 100% right).
“Recruitment manoeuvres are a grade B recommendation”
In the Harrison table Marrow uses, recruitment manoeuvres are grade C; low tidal volume is A, and conservative fluids, higher PEEP, prone and ECMO are B.
decode: Recommended sustained-inflation technique? [DocT GT]
CPAP 30–40 cmH₂O.
Purpose of PEEP after a recruitment manoeuvre? [DocT GT]
To maintain the recruitment achieved.
Decremental PEEP trial: static compliance suddenly falls before oxygenation worsens — what happened? [DocT GT]
Alveolar derecruitment.
Desaturation after open suctioning in ventilated pneumonia — next step? [Marrow]
Recruitment manoeuvre (after excluding pneumothorax).
ARDS-33.punch: A recruitment manoeuvre (CPAP 40 for 30–40 s) opens lung only if PEEP then holds it open, costs blood pressure and risks barotrauma — and in ART, recruitment with compliance-titrated PEEP increased mortality.

parts.q: Desaturation after open suctioning in ARDS: why, and what then?
parts.a: **Disconnection loses PEEP and the lung derecruits.** Exclude pneumothorax, then recruit; pre-oxygenate with FiO₂ 1.0 and use a closed in-line system when PEEP or FiO₂ is high (Marrow).

ARDS-34.intro: HFOV takes the open-lung idea to its limit: hold the lung open with a constant high mean airway pressure and move gas with tiny oscillations, so there is no cyclic stretch at all. In theory it is the ideal lung-protective mode; two large trials in 2013 showed it is not.
why: **OSCAR: no difference in mortality. OSCILLATE: higher mortality (stopped early).** OSCAR (UK, about 800 patients) found 30-day mortality almost identical in the two arms. OSCILLATE (Canada and elsewhere, about 550 patients) was stopped early because in-hospital mortality was higher with HFOV (about 47% vs 35%).

**High mean airway pressure → haemodynamic compromise, more vasopressors, sedation and paralysis.** HFOV holds a constant high mean airway pressure for oxygenation, which reduces venous return and raises right-ventricular afterload. In OSCILLATE, the HFOV arm needed more vasoactive drugs, midazolam and neuromuscular blockade.

**Not recommended for routine use in adult ARDS.** The ATS/ESICM/SCCM 2017 guideline makes a strong recommendation against routine HFOV in moderate-to-severe ARDS; the 2023 ESICM guideline did not revisit it.
mimic: HFOV vs high-frequency jet ventilation
HFJV pulses small jets at about 100–200/min with passive expiration; its niche is airway surgery and a large bronchopleural fistula, not ARDS. Neither improves adult ARDS survival.
OSCAR vs OSCILLATE
OSCAR: no difference. OSCILLATE: harm. NEET 2024 asked OSCAR: ‘HFO in adult ARDS — no benefit’.
traps: “HFOV provides low inspiratory pressures”
It runs a high mean airway pressure; its theoretical advantage is tiny tidal volumes at high rates, not low pressure.
“In HFOV expiration is passive” or “raising the frequency clears more CO₂”
Expiration is active; lowering the frequency lengthens each cycle, enlarges the tidal volume and clears more CO₂.
“HFOV is the preferred rescue over prone positioning”
Prone has the survival benefit; HFOV harmed or did nothing.
“The keyed ‘advantage’ means HFOV is recommended”
DocT keys the theoretical mechanism (small volumes, high rates, less VILI); the trials failed, so it is not recommended routinely.
decode: Primary advantage of HFOV in ARDS? [DocT, DocT GT]
Very small tidal volumes at very high rates, minimising VILI (in theory).
How is gas transported during HFOV? [DocT GT]
Taylor dispersion and pendelluft, with tidal volumes smaller than dead space.
Primary advantage of HFJV in ARDS? [DocT, DocT GT]
Very small tidal volumes at high rates (theory only; no outcome benefit).
OSCAR trial was about? [NEET 2024]
HFOV in adult ARDS: no benefit.
ARDS-34.punch: HFOV oxygenates with a high mean airway pressure and moves gas below the dead space, but OSCAR showed no benefit and OSCILLATE showed harm, so it is not used routinely in adult ARDS.

HFOV
