COPD-29.sub: Respiratory → COPD → Revision: true or false
COPD-29.intro: A sweep through the deck. Each statement turns on one detail from an earlier card.
why: **False — auto-PEEP is measured with an end-expiratory hold** (COPD-18).
**False — dynamic auto-PEEP is lower, reflecting the fastest units only** (COPD-19).
**True — external PEEP at 80% of intrinsic PEEP relieves trigger load safely** (COPD-21).
**False — a high flow (80–100 L/min) lengthens expiration and reduces trapping** (COPD-15).

**False — the target is pH (his normal pH), not a normal PaCO₂** (COPD-16). His normal pH is the one he lives at, reached by returning to his own baseline PaCO₂; in the acute phase a pH above about 7.2 is accepted, and a textbook pH of 7.35–7.45 is not forced by over-ventilation.
**True — terbutaline 0.25 mg SC is preferred in pregnancy** (COPD-22).
**False — clinical judgment has a sensitivity of 35% and a specificity of 79%** (COPD-27).
traps: “A low inspiratory flow is gentler on the lung and reduces trapping”
It lengthens inspiration and shortens expiration; trapping worsens.
decode: [pattern] True/false on auto-PEEP and ventilation in obstruction
End-expiratory hold, dynamic lower than static, PEEPe 80% of PEEPi, high flow, target pH, low density.
COPD-29.punch: Most errors here come from direction: hold at end-expiration, dynamic is lower, flow goes up not down, and the target is pH, not a normal PaCO₂.

topups.q: MDI on a ventilated patient — how do you maximise delivery?
a: - Spacer in the inspiratory limb ~15 cm from the Y-piece; actuate at the START of inspiration.
- Low inspiratory flow, VT >500 mL, longer Ti with a pause; remove the HME (or place the device between HME and patient).
- Wider ETT helps; deposition falls with high flow, small tubes and humidified gas; typical dose 4–8 puffs.

- Nebuliser with the HME left in place: the filter traps the aerosol and almost no drug arrives — remove the HME during nebulisation; volume control with a square, low inspiratory flow carries aerosol more consistently than pressure control.
- Vibrating-mesh nebuliser is electrically powered: no added driving gas, so VT, trigger and FiO2 are undisturbed and it refills without breaking the circuit; a jet nebuliser adds 6–8 L/min of gas.
topups.src: DocT GT GT3 Q88; DocT GT CGT5 Q8; DocT GT CGT6 Q8; DocT GT CGT6 Q9; DocT GT GT4 Q116

x.sub: Respiratory → Drugs → Inhaled bronchodilators on the ventilator
x.intro: Step 4 gives the drugs for the attack; on the ventilator the question becomes how much of an inhaled dose actually reaches the lung. Aerosol must travel through tubing and an endotracheal tube, and most of it can stick to the circuit on the way. Every rule on this card either gives the aerosol a slower, larger, longer breath to ride or removes something that traps it.
why: **Spacer in the inspiratory limb ~15 cm from the Y-piece; actuate at the START of inspiration.** The spacer lets the fast MDI plume slow down and evaporate into fine particles before the tube. Firing at the start of inspiration means the breath carries the aerosol in; fired during expiration it is lost down the expiratory limb. The exact distance matters less than the position: the 2023 international aerosol consensus (Ann Intensive Care 2023) asks for the pMDI with a spacer larger than 150 mL in the inspiratory limb before the Y-piece and gives no fixed distance.

**Low inspiratory flow, VT >500 mL, longer Ti with a pause; remove the HME (or place the device between HME and patient).** Slow flow means less turbulence and less impaction in the circuit and tube; a large tidal volume and an end-inspiratory pause carry particles deep and let them settle. A heat–moisture exchanger is a filter and traps aerosol. These settings come from bench and small clinical studies; the 2023 consensus advises against changing tidal volume, flow pattern or mode solely for aerosol delivery, so in a lung-protective ARDS patient the low tidal volume is kept and the dose is titrated to response instead.

**Wider ETT helps; deposition falls with high flow, small tubes and humidified gas; typical dose 4–8 puffs.** Narrow tubes and fast flow make particles impact on the tube wall; humidity makes them grow and rain out in the circuit. Because so much is lost, the usual dose is higher than in a spontaneously breathing patient.

**Nebuliser with the HME left in place: the filter traps the aerosol and almost no drug arrives — remove the HME during nebulisation; volume control with a square, low inspiratory flow carries aerosol more consistently than pressure control.** A poor response with the HME still in the circuit is a delivery failure, not resistant bronchospasm. Volume control guarantees the breath size, whereas pressure control’s tidal volume falls exactly when the airways are tightest. This is the exam answer; in practice the mode is not changed just to give a nebuliser.

**Vibrating-mesh nebuliser is electrically powered: no added driving gas, so VT, trigger and FiO₂ are undisturbed and it refills without breaking the circuit; a jet nebuliser adds 6–8 L/min of gas.** Extra gas from a jet nebuliser enlarges delivered volume, dilutes FiO₂ and can make triggering harder; the mesh device avoids all three and leaves less drug unused.
traps: “Increase inspiratory flow to push the drug in”
Higher flow increases impaction and reduces delivery; flow is lowered.
“Reduce tidal volume below 400 mL”
Larger tidal volumes (>500 mL) improve delivery.
“Pressure control or a square waveform?”
DocT keys volume control; a square low flow is the waveform volume control usually delivers, so read the options carefully when both appear.
“Minimal response to nebulised salbutamol — refractory asthma”
Check the HME first; left in the circuit it traps the aerosol.
decode: MDI with spacer near the Y-piece — which other adjustment improves delivery? [DocT GT ×2]
Deliver during the inspiratory phase (75–80%).
Nebulised salbutamol, minimal response, HME left in the circuit [DocT GT]
Markedly reduced drug deposition.
Ventilator setting giving the greatest aerosol delivery [DocT GT]
Volume-controlled ventilation.
Main advantage of a vibrating-mesh nebuliser over a jet nebuliser [DocT GT]
Electrically powered — no added gas.
x.punch: Aerosol on a ventilator is lost to fast flow, small tubes, humidity and filters, so fire it at the start of a slow, large inspiration with the HME out of the path.

spine: Ventilating the obstructed lung
Once intubated, the obstructed lung is ventilated for expiratory time — small breaths, a slow rate, fast inspiration — accepting a high PaCO₂ while the pH stays above about 7.2.
Seeing and measuring trapped air
Expiratory flow that does not reach zero shows that air is trapped; an end-expiratory hold measures intrinsic PEEP, and the trapped volume (Vei) is the validated marker of danger.
Undoing auto-PEEP
Lowering minute ventilation is what empties the lung; external PEEP below intrinsic PEEP does not empty it but makes triggering easier for a patient who breathes for himself.
Drugs for the attack

Inhaled salbutamol with ipratropium and a systemic steroid treat both diseases; IV magnesium is the add-on for severe asthma that has not responded, and antibiotics belong to COPD with purulent sputum.
Supporting the ventilated patient
Hypercapnic acidosis dilates cerebral vessels and constricts pulmonary ones, and over-correcting it, overfeeding or overloading with fluid makes weaning harder.
Weaning, extubation and outcome
A COPD patient who passes a spontaneous breathing trial is extubated to NIV; prognosis after ventilation for COPD is poor, worse than for asthma.
RESP02B.primer: On a volume-controlled breath the peak airway pressure is the pressure needed to push flow through the airways plus the pressure needed to stretch the lung, while the plateau pressure, read during a short end-inspiratory hold when flow is zero, reflects the stretch alone; so a peak that rises with an unchanged plateau means more resistance, and both rising means a stiffer or fuller chest. An end-expiratory hold closes the valves at the end of expiration so that the pressure in the alveoli shows on the airway gauge; any pressure above the set PEEP is intrinsic PEEP (COPD-03). Minute ventilation is tidal volume times rate, and in an obstructed lung it decides how much air is trapped (COPD-02). Permissive hypercapnia means deliberately accepting a high PaCO₂ to avoid the trapping and barotrauma that normal ventilation would cause.

RSC-01.sub: Respiratory → Sepsis → Oxygen and non-invasive support
RSC-01.intro: The deck opens with the septic patient whose lungs fail before any tube goes in. The guidance answers two practical questions — how much oxygen to aim for, and how to give it without intubating.
why: **2021: insufficient evidence to recommend conservative over usual targets. 2026: titrate to a conservative or a liberal target by patient; SpO₂ 90–96% is taught (SEP-50).** Trials of conservative oxygen in the ICU have not shown a clear benefit overall, so the 2026 guideline makes only a conditional, low-certainty suggestion to titrate to either target by patient factors; most trials compared a lower target of about 90–93% with a higher one of 96% or more, and the panel reported aiming for 90–96%. The band avoids both hypoxaemia and sustained hyperoxia.

**High-flow nasal oxygen over NIV (weak recommendation).** In hypoxaemic (non-hypercapnic) failure NIV by face mask is poorly tolerated and can let the patient take large, injurious breaths. High flow delivers a reliable FiO₂ (21–100%) at up to 60 L/min, washes out dead space and gives a little PEEP, and in FLORALI (which excluded patients with PaCO₂ >45 mmHg) it lowered 90-day mortality (12% vs 23% standard oxygen vs 28% NIV) without a significant difference in the intubation rate overall (38% vs 47% vs 50%). The 2026 update keeps a conditional suggestion for high flow as the initial therapy over NIV.

**Post hoc: point estimates suggested possible harm with conservative oxygen in sepsis; liberal oxygen may be preferred.** In the 251 patients with sepsis in ICU-ROX, 90-day mortality was 36.2% with conservative oxygen vs 29.2% with usual oxygen, a difference that was not statistically significant (P = 0.24) in a post hoc, underpowered analysis. It is a signal to avoid driving septic patients to low saturations, not proof of harm.
mimic: Hypoxaemic vs hypercapnic failure
Hypoxaemic, non-hypercapnic failure (sepsis, pneumonia): high flow first. Hypercapnic failure (COPD, obesity hypoventilation): NIV first (RSC-13).
traps: “Surviving Sepsis suggests NIV over high flow in septic hypoxaemia” (RSC-16a)
It is the other way round: high flow over NIV.
“FLORALI showed fewer intubations with high flow”
The overall intubation rate did not differ significantly (P = 0.18); fewer intubations were seen only in the subgroup with P/F ≤200, and 90-day mortality was lower.
decode: [pattern] Septic patient, SpO₂ 86% on face mask, not hypercapnic — preferred support?
High-flow nasal oxygen over NIV.
RSC-01.punch: In sepsis-induced hypoxaemia give high-flow nasal oxygen rather than NIV, and do not chase a low saturation: the ICU-ROX sepsis signal leaned against conservative oxygen.

RSC-02.sub: Respiratory → Sepsis → PReVENT: low tidal volume without ARDS
RSC-02.intro: Many septic patients are ventilated without having ARDS. PReVENT asked whether the ARDS tidal volume should be used in them too.
why: **Ventilated ICU patients without ARDS.** Patients expected not to be extubated within 24 hours, with ARDS (Berlin) an exclusion (Simonis, JAMA 2018; 961 patients).

**Low tidal volume (4–6 mL/kg PBW) vs intermediate (8–10 mL/kg).** The low arm started at 6 and came down by 1 mL/kg each hour towards 4 mL/kg; the intermediate arm started at 10. PaCO₂ on day 1 was higher in the low arm, but the use and duration of sedatives and neuromuscular blockers did not differ.

**No difference in ventilator-free days.** Ventilator-free days at day 28 were the same in both arms (median 21), as were mortality, ICU and hospital stay, and complications such as ARDS, pneumonia, severe atelectasis and pneumothorax. Surviving Sepsis 2026 accordingly suggests 6–8 mL/kg rather than 4 to <6 mL/kg in sepsis-associated hypoxaemic failure without ARDS.
mimic: PReVENT vs ARMA
ARMA (ARDS): 6 vs 12 mL/kg, mortality fell from about 40% to 31%. PReVENT (no ARDS): 4–6 vs 8–10 mL/kg, no difference. The proof of low tidal volume is in ARDS.
traps: “PReVENT showed benefit of low tidal volume without ARDS” (RSC-16b)
It showed no difference; an intermediate 8–10 mL/kg PBW was as good.
decode: [pattern] Ventilated patient without ARDS — does a tidal volume of 4–6 rather than 8–10 mL/kg improve outcome?
No: PReVENT found no difference in ventilator-free days.
RSC-02.punch: Without ARDS, going down to 4–6 mL/kg PBW gained nothing over 8–10 mL/kg in PReVENT; the 6 mL/kg rule belongs to ARDS.

RSC-03.intro: When sepsis does cause ARDS, the ventilator becomes part of the treatment and can itself injure the lung. The one real question checks the core of lung protection, and it is the same set of rules as any ARDS.
why: **Tidal volume 6 mL/kg PBW** (strong recommendation). A smaller breath limits the stretch of the small aerated part of the ARDS lung; the ARDSNet protocol targets 6 mL/kg within a range of 4–8. The resulting rise in PaCO₂ is accepted.
**Plateau pressure <30 cmH₂O.** Plateau pressure is the end-inspiratory alveolar pressure; above 30 the risk of over-distension and barotrauma rises, so the tidal volume is lowered further if needed.

**Avoid incremental-PEEP recruitment manoeuvres (barotrauma).** In the ART trial a staircase of rising PEEP (25, 35, 45 cmH₂O) followed by decremental titration increased 28-day mortality (55.3% vs 49.3%) and barotrauma (5.6% vs 1.6%), so it is recommended against (strong). Surviving Sepsis 2021 still suggested traditional, sustained-inflation recruitment in moderate–severe ARDS.

**Prone ventilation as needed.** Prone for more than 12 hours a day is advised in moderate–severe ARDS; PROSEVA enrolled P/F <150 on FiO₂ ≥0.6 and PEEP ≥5 after a stabilisation period and roughly halved 28-day mortality (16% vs 33%), because turning makes ventilation and lung stress more even.

**Intermittent neuromuscular blocker boluses rather than infusion.** After ROSE found no benefit from routine early infusion, the guideline suggests boluses, keeping an infusion for persistent dyssynchrony or the need for deep sedation.
**VV-ECMO in refractory cases.** For severe ARDS when conventional ventilation fails, in a centre that can provide it.
mimic: Traditional recruitment vs incremental-PEEP strategy
Sustained inflation was suggested (weak) in 2021; the incremental PEEP staircase of ART is recommended against (strong).
traps: “Permissive hypercapnia with tidal volumes targeting a normal PaCO₂”
These contradict each other: permissive hypercapnia means accepting a high PaCO₂ so that the tidal volume can stay low.
“High tidal volume with high PEEP protects the other organs”
Large breaths cause ventilator-induced lung injury, whose mediators spread to other organs; low tidal volume protects them too.
decode: CAP, ARDS with P/F 120 and AKI (MODS) — lung-protective strategy by the ARDSNet protocol? [DocT QBank, 97% right]
Low tidal volume (4–8 mL/kg PBW) with plateau pressure <30 cmH₂O.
RSC-03.punch: Septic ARDS is ventilated as any ARDS: 6 mL/kg PBW, plateau <30, prone when severe, NMB boluses not infusions, no incremental-PEEP staircase, and ECMO when all else fails.

RSC-04.intro: The second part of the deck moves to the lung after surgery. Anaesthesia and an abdominal or thoracic wound reduce FRC, weaken coughing and stiffen breathing for days, so the complications on this card follow.
why: **Atelectasis.** General anaesthesia causes collapse of dependent lung within minutes of induction, from high FiO₂ (absorption), loss of muscle tone and the diaphragm pushed up by the abdomen; after surgery, pain and opioids limit deep breaths, so it persists.

**Bronchospasm, pneumonia, exacerbation of chronic lung disease, upper airway obstruction, sleep-apnoea complications, pleural effusion, tracheal injury, abdominal compartment syndrome.** Most follow from collapse, retained secretions or residual drugs; the last links to RSC-10.

**Older age, emergency surgery, hypoalbuminaemia, heart failure, COPD or smoking, lower respiratory tract infection.** Patient factors add to the procedure’s own risk, which is highest for thoracic, upper abdominal, aortic and neurosurgical operations and long or emergency surgery. A serum albumin below 35 g/L is the most useful laboratory marker of risk (ACP 2006), reflecting frailty, poor nutrition and weak respiratory muscles.
mimic: Atelectasis vs pneumonia after surgery
Atelectasis appears early (first days), with volume loss on the X-ray; pneumonia brings purulent sputum, a rising white count and consolidation (RSC-05).
traps: “Pneumonia is the commonest post-operative pulmonary complication”
Atelectasis is (RSC-16g); it is also the soil in which pneumonia grows.
decode: [pattern] Commonest post-operative pulmonary complication?
Atelectasis.
[pattern] Which pre-operative laboratory value predicts pulmonary complications?
A low serum albumin.
RSC-04.punch: Atelectasis is the commonest post-operative pulmonary complication; age, emergency surgery, low albumin, heart failure, COPD or smoking and recent chest infection raise the risk.

RSC-05.sub: Respiratory → Post-operative lung → Melbourne Group Score
RSC-05.intro: Trials of lung protection need an agreed way to say that a complication has happened. The Melbourne Group Score turns a bedside judgment into a count of eight items.
why: **A post-operative pulmonary complication: 4 or more of 8 items in the same 24-hour period.** No single item is specific; requiring four together in one day makes the diagnosis reliable enough to compare groups.

**New abnormal breath sounds; yellow or green sputum; temperature >38°C and SpO₂ <90% on room air, each on more than one consecutive day.** The sputum must differ from the patient’s usual sputum before surgery.

**Chest X-ray collapse or consolidation; unexplained white cell count >11 × 10⁹/L; positive sputum culture; physician’s diagnosis of chest infection or antibiotic prescribed for it.** Published versions give the white count as >11.2 × 10⁹/L, and the later version (MGS-2) replaces breath sounds with readmission to, or a prolonged stay in, ICU or HDU for a respiratory problem.
traps: “Any one item, such as fever with a raised white count, makes a pulmonary complication”
Four of the eight are needed, within one 24-hour period (RSC-16c).
decode: [pattern] Melbourne Group Score — how many items define a post-operative pulmonary complication?
4 or more of 8, in the same 24 hours.
RSC-05.punch: The Melbourne Group Score diagnoses a post-operative pulmonary complication when 4 or more of its 8 clinical, radiological and laboratory items occur within one 24-hour period.

RSC-06.sub: Respiratory → Post-operative lung → Prevention, ICOUGH and ERAS
RSC-06.intro: Since atelectasis is the root of most complications (RSC-04), prevention is mostly about keeping FRC up and secretions moving. The one real question asks for the least invasive way to raise FRC in an obese patient after surgery.
why: **Lung-protective ventilation, good analgesia, restrictive fluids, low-dose relaxant with full reversal, early mobilisation, physiotherapy, upright position, CPAP/NIV.** Pain-free deep breathing and coughing reopen collapsed lung; residual neuromuscular block weakens the upper airway and cough; sitting up lets the abdomen fall away from the diaphragm. Going from supine to upright raises FRC substantially, which is why position comes before pressure.

**Incentive spirometry (10 times an hour), Coughing and deep breathing, Oral care (twice daily), Understanding (education), Getting out of bed (3 times a day), Head of bed up 30–45°.** A nursing bundle from Boston University Medical Center; in its before-and-after evaluation pneumonia fell from 2.6% to 1.6% and unplanned intubation from 2.0% to 1.2%, by keeping the lungs expanded and secretions cleared.

**Enhanced Recovery After Surgery: pre-, intra- and post-operative bundle (carbohydrate loading, no prolonged fasting, opioid-sparing and regional analgesia, early feeding and mobilisation).** Each element shortens the time the patient spends weak, sedated and in bed.
mimic: Raising FRC by posture vs by PEEP
Sitting up is the first, non-invasive step; PEEP or CPAP raises FRC further but is the escalation and can lower venous return.
traps: “Obese patient supine with falling SpO₂ after surgery: first apply PEEP 10”
PEEP would raise FRC, but the question asks for the least invasive step: sitting him up 45° comes first. Only 73% chose it on DocT GT.
“ERAS is Early Rehabilitation After Surgery”
The standard expansion is Enhanced Recovery After Surgery.
decode: Obese post-operative patient, supine, hypoxaemic — least invasive way to improve FRC? [DocT GT, 73% right]
Elevate the head of the bed to a 45° semi-recumbent position.
RSC-06.punch: Prevention keeps FRC up and secretions moving: sit the patient up first, then add pressure if needed, with good analgesia, full reversal, the ICOUGH bundle and ERAS.

RSC-07.sub: Respiratory → Post-operative lung → IMPROVE vs PROVHILO
RSC-07.intro: Two trials split lung protection in theatre into its parts. IMPROVE tested the whole package against old-style large breaths; PROVHILO kept the tidal volume low in both arms and tested PEEP alone.
why: **IMPROVE (Futier): VT 6–8 + PEEP 6–8 + recruitment vs VT 10–12, no PEEP, no recruitment (400 patients). PROVHILO: PEEP 12 + recruitment vs PEEP ≤2 without recruitment, same low VT.** IMPROVE studied major abdominal surgery in patients at intermediate to high risk; PROVHILO studied 900 at-risk patients having open abdominal surgery, with 8 mL/kg in both arms.

**IMPROVE: complications 10.5% vs 27.5%; less atelectasis and pneumonia; hospital stay 2 days shorter. PROVHILO: no difference in pulmonary complications; more hypotension and vasoactive drugs with high PEEP.** IMPROVE’s 10.5% vs 27.5% is a composite of major pulmonary and extrapulmonary complications within 7 days; fewer patients needed NIV or intubation (5% vs 17%). PROVHILO’s complication rates were 40% vs 39%. Since only PEEP differed in PROVHILO, the benefit in IMPROVE probably came mostly from leaving large tidal volumes behind.
mimic: PROVHILO vs PROBESE
Both found no benefit from high PEEP with recruitment and more hypotension; PROBESE did it in obese patients (RSC-14).
traps: “PROVHILO showed fewer complications with high PEEP” (RSC-16d)
No difference; more hypotension.
decode: [pattern] Open abdominal surgery, low VT in both arms, PEEP 12 + recruitment vs PEEP ≤2 — result?
No fewer pulmonary complications, more hypotension (PROVHILO).
RSC-07.punch: Low tidal volume protects the lung in theatre (IMPROVE); routinely high PEEP adds hypotension without fewer complications (PROVHILO).

RSC-08.sub: Respiratory → Post-operative lung → Driving pressure and FiO₂
RSC-08.intro: If PEEP alone does not help (RSC-07), which number does? Pooling the surgical trials pointed to driving pressure; the card ends with the other setting that touches atelectasis, FiO₂.
why: **17 trials, 2250 patients: driving pressure was the variable linked to post-operative pulmonary complications (odds ratio 1.16 per cmH₂O).** Driving pressure is tidal volume divided by compliance, so it scales the breath to the lung actually open; tidal volume was not associated (OR 1.05), and PEEP alone had too small an effect to enter the model (Neto, Lancet Respir Med 2016).

**More complications. PEEP helps only if it lowers driving pressure.** If PEEP recruits, compliance rises and driving pressure falls; if it only over-distends, driving pressure rises and so do complications (odds ratio about 3 when a PEEP increase raised driving pressure).
**No effect on short-term mortality; high FiO₂ may increase atelectasis.** Pure oxygen in poorly ventilated alveoli is absorbed and not replaced by nitrogen, so the alveoli collapse.
traps: “More PEEP is always more protective”
Only when it lowers driving pressure; PEEP that raises it is linked to more complications.
decode: [pattern] Which intra-operative ventilator variable is associated with post-operative pulmonary complications?
Driving pressure.
RSC-08.punch: In theatre driving pressure, not tidal volume or PEEP alone, tracks pulmonary complications; PEEP helps only if it lowers it, and high FiO₂ adds atelectasis.

RSC-09.sub: Respiratory → Post-operative lung → NIV for post-operative failure
RSC-09.intro: When prevention fails and the patient becomes hypoxaemic after surgery, the cause is usually atelectasis, which positive pressure reverses. That is why NIV works here better than in most hypoxaemic failure.
why: **Suggested (conditional recommendation, moderate certainty).** The ERS/ATS NIV guideline (2017) suggests NIV for acute respiratory failure after surgery; by contrast it makes no recommendation for de novo hypoxaemic failure.

**Mortality relative risk 0.28; intubation relative risk 0.27. It improves aeration and oxygenation and reduces atelectasis.** These are the guideline’s pooled estimates (mortality moderate certainty, intubation low certainty, wide confidence intervals). Positive pressure reopens the collapsed bases and lowers the work of breathing.

**Gastric insufflation, regurgitation, anastomotic leak.** Mask pressure can push air into the stomach; after upper gastrointestinal surgery that distends a fresh anastomosis, so the pressures are kept modest and a gastric tube is considered.
mimic: Post-operative failure vs de novo hypoxaemic failure
After surgery (atelectasis) NIV is suggested; in de novo hypoxaemic failure (sepsis, pneumonia) high flow is preferred (RSC-01b).
traps: “NIV is contraindicated after abdominal surgery”
It is suggested; the anastomosis is a reason for care with pressures, not a ban.
decode: [pattern] Hypoxaemia on day 1 after abdominal surgery — role of NIV?
Suggested: it reduces intubation and mortality.
RSC-09.punch: NIV is suggested for respiratory failure after surgery, cutting intubation and mortality by reopening atelectasis; watch for gastric distension and the anastomosis.

RSC-10.intro: The abdomen is part of the chest wall, so a tense abdomen pushes the diaphragm up and stiffens the whole respiratory system. The key point for the next card is which compliance falls.
why: **Sustained IAP ≥12 mmHg; compartment syndrome is >20 mmHg with new organ failure.** These are the WSACS 2013 definitions, with IAP measured through the bladder, supine, at end-expiration and zeroed at the mid-axillary line. Normal IAP in the critically ill is about 5–7 mmHg; IAH is graded I 12–15, II 16–20, III 21–25 and IV >25 mmHg.

**20–80% (about half).** Reviews put the average near 50%, but the fraction varies with the patient and the chest wall, so pleural pressure cannot be calculated from IAP; it is measured with an oesophageal balloon when it matters (RSC-11d).

**Chest-wall (and so respiratory-system) compliance falls; lung compliance is unchanged.** With healthy lungs the lung tissue itself is not stiffer; the container around it is (if the lung is already injured, its compliance may fall as well). Plateau pressure rises because part of it is spent pushing the diaphragm and abdomen out.

**FRC and lung volumes fall, compression atelectasis; pleural, peak, mean and plateau pressures rise; PVR rises; shunt, dead space and PaCO₂ rise; difficult weaning.** Collapsed bases cause shunt, and raised intrathoracic pressure lowers venous return and raises pulmonary vascular resistance.
mimic: Stiff chest wall vs stiff lung
Stiff chest wall (IAH, obesity): high plateau with high pleural pressure, transpulmonary pressure may be normal. Stiff lung (ARDS, fibrosis): high plateau with high transpulmonary pressure.
traps: “Lung compliance falls in intra-abdominal hypertension” (RSC-16e)
Chest-wall compliance falls; the lung is unchanged.
“IAH starts at 12 cmH₂O”
The consensus unit is mmHg: IAP ≥12 mmHg.
decode: [pattern] Intra-abdominal hypertension raises plateau pressure — which compliance has fallen?
Chest-wall (and respiratory-system); lung compliance is unchanged.
RSC-10.punch: Intra-abdominal hypertension (≥12 mmHg; compartment syndrome >20 mmHg with new organ failure) stiffens the chest wall, not the lung, so plateau pressure rises while lung stress may not.

RSC-11.sub: Respiratory → Abdominal hypertension → Ventilating abdominal compartment syndrome
RSC-11.intro: Because the high plateau in RSC-10 comes partly from the chest wall, the usual targets would force needlessly small breaths. This card adjusts them, and the one real question tests the reason: lung injury follows transpulmonary pressure, not airway pressure.
why: **6–8 mL/kg; driving pressure <15.** Lung protection still starts with a small breath on predicted body weight.

**Usual plateau target + (IAP – 13) ÷ 2, IAP in cmH₂O.** Roughly half the abdominal pressure reaches the thorax (RSC-10b), so the plateau limit is raised by that share. Example: IAP 25 mmHg is 34 cmH₂O, so the limit becomes 30 + (34 – 13) ÷ 2, about 40 cmH₂O. In mmHg the same formula reads target – 7 + 0.7 × IAP. It is a physiological correction proposed in reviews, not a target tested in trials.

**PEEP by best respiratory-system compliance; higher pressures are needed for recruitment.** The stiff chest wall absorbs part of each pressure, so more is needed to reach the alveoli; PEEP is titrated to the compliance it produces, not to a fixed number.

**Oesophageal balloon: end-inspiratory <25 (over-distension); end-expiratory kept positive (your notes: 3; EPVent 0–10) to prevent collapse. Transpulmonary = alveolar – pleural (oesophageal) pressure.** EPVent set PEEP to keep end-expiratory transpulmonary pressure at 0–10 and limited end-inspiratory to below 25 cmH₂O. This measures what the lung actually feels: with a plateau of 38 and a pleural pressure of 20, the lung is stretched by only 18.
mimic: Airway (plateau) pressure vs transpulmonary pressure
Plateau is lung plus chest wall; transpulmonary pressure is the lung alone. When the chest wall is stiff, plateau overestimates lung stress.
traps: “Plateau 38 cmH₂O with markedly raised pleural pressure means alveolar rupture, volutrauma or high transpulmonary pressure”
With a high pleural pressure the transpulmonary pressure may be well below 20–25, so it can be a safe distending pressure. ‘Safe’ is an inference; an oesophageal balloon confirms it.
decode: Morbidly obese, plateau 38 cmH₂O, pleural pressure markedly raised by abdominal and chest-wall compression — interpretation? [DocT GT]
Safe distending pressure: injury follows transpulmonary pressure.
RSC-11.punch: With a stiff abdomen, plateau overstates lung stress: raise the plateau limit by (IAP – 13) ÷ 2 in cmH₂O, or measure transpulmonary pressure and keep it below 25 at end-inspiration and positive at end-expiration.

RSC-12.sub: Respiratory → Obesity → Respiratory changes and obesity hypoventilation
RSC-12.intro: Obesity is the everyday version of the stiff chest wall in RSC-10: the weight of the chest and abdomen lowers FRC, and some patients also stop driving their breathing enough. Five real questions test this card, mostly on obesity hypoventilation, which the card mentions in a single line.
why: **FRC and ERV fall; airway closure, atelectasis, intrinsic PEEP, V/Q mismatch.** Abdominal contents push the diaphragm up, so FRC falls, mostly by losing expiratory reserve volume; TLC and residual volume change little. When FRC falls below closing capacity, small dependent airways close during quiet breathing: the alveoli behind them are perfused but not ventilated (V/Q mismatch, hypoxaemia), gas is trapped behind closed airways (intrinsic PEEP), and they collapse (atelectasis). All of this worsens supine and under anaesthesia, which is why sitting him up raises FRC (RSC-06).

**Chest-wall and total compliance fall; abdominal pressure rises.** The patient breathes on a stiffer system at a lower volume, so the work of breathing and oxygen consumption rise, and plateau pressures read higher on the ventilator without the lung itself being stretched more (RSC-11).

**Difficult airway, obstructive sleep apnoea; low drive in obesity hypoventilation syndrome.** Obesity hypoventilation is defined as BMI ≥30 with awake daytime hypercapnia (PaCO₂ ≥45 mmHg) after other causes of hypoventilation are excluded; hypoxaemia is not part of the definition. Its cause is not the load alone: a blunted central response to CO₂ (with leptin resistance) is central, sleep-disordered breathing adds nocturnal CO₂ loading, and the kidneys retain bicarbonate, which further blunts the drive. About 90% have OSA, but the OSA can be mild — so a BMI of 40 with a PaCO₂ of 50 and only mild OSA is explained by diminished drive.

**Poor chest X-ray and ultrasound windows; difficult transport for CT. Always rule out pulmonary embolism.** Obesity is a major thrombotic risk and a hypoxaemic obese patient may be untestable by the usual routes, so embolism must be actively sought rather than assumed absent.
mimic: OSA vs obesity hypoventilation
OSA is obstruction during sleep with a normal daytime PaCO₂; obesity hypoventilation adds daytime hypercapnia from low drive.
Raised HCO₃⁻ in obesity: metabolic alkalosis vs compensation
In an obese patient a raised bicarbonate is usually renal compensation for chronic hypercapnia — the ABG shows it.
traps: “Hypoxaemia on room air is required for obesity hypoventilation”
The definition is BMI ≥30 plus awake PaCO₂ ≥45 mmHg with other causes excluded; hypoxaemia is common but not required.
“Obese patient with HCO₃⁻ 35 and a chest infection: start antibiotics or a sleep study first”
The raised bicarbonate signals chronic hypercapnia: an arterial blood gas comes first.
“Obesity hypoventilation is just severe sleep apnoea”
Hypercapnia with only mild OSA points to diminished ventilatory drive.
“Supine obese patient desaturating: start PEEP first” (73% right)
Sit him up first; it is the least invasive way to raise FRC.
decode: Obese post-operative patient, supine, hypoxaemic — least invasive way to improve FRC? [DocT GT, 73% right]
Head of bed up to 45°.
Obesity hypoventilation syndrome — most accurate statement? [Marrow]
Awake daytime PaCO₂ >45 mmHg.
Obese patient, HCO₃⁻ 35, respiratory infection — next step? [Marrow]
Arterial blood gas.
BMI 40, awake PaCO₂ 50, mild OSA — best explanation? [Marrow]
Diminished ventilatory drive from obesity.
RSC-12.punch: Obesity lowers FRC below closing capacity, causing airway closure, atelectasis and V/Q mismatch; obesity hypoventilation is BMI ≥30 with awake PaCO₂ ≥45 mmHg from low drive, flagged by a raised bicarbonate and confirmed by ABG.

table.title: Obstructive sleep apnoea vs obesity hypoventilation
head: OSA alone
Obesity hypoventilation
rows: CPAP if severe OSA; **NIV (bilevel)** if OSA mild or absent

parts.q: Obese OSA patient, hypercapnic after surgery on morphine — CPAP improves which volume? [Marrow]
parts.a: Functional residual capacity: CPAP lifts FRC above closing capacity; residual volume and TLC are unchanged. If tidal volume needs support, use bilevel NIV.

parts.q: When is a bicarbonate used to screen for obesity hypoventilation?
parts.a: ATS 2019: in an obese patient with sleep-disordered breathing and low suspicion, a serum HCO₃⁻ <27 mmol/L makes it unlikely; a raised value or high suspicion needs an ABG.

RSC-13.sub: Respiratory → Obesity → Non-invasive support and the airway
RSC-13.intro: The low FRC and low drive of RSC-12 decide how the obese patient is supported before and around intubation. The two real questions test which non-invasive mode fits obesity hypoventilation and what prevents a disaster at intubation.
why: **Hypercapnic failure, sleep apnoea or obesity hypoventilation. Settings: avoid high tidal volumes, adequate PEEP, high back-up rate. Start CPAP 2 weeks before elective surgery.** UK perioperative guidance (CPOC) aims for 4–6 weeks of CPAP before planned surgery, so 2 weeks is a minimum rather than the ideal. NIV (bilevel) adds inspiratory support, which a low-drive, hypercapnic patient needs; high flow and CPAP do not support the tidal volume. PEEP holds the airways open above closing capacity, and a high back-up rate covers the hypoventilating patient who stops breathing in sleep. So BMI 50 with mild OSA (AHI 7), nocturnal desaturation and a raised bicarbonate points to NIV: the problem is hypoventilation, not obstruction.

**Respiratory complications relative risk 0.33; unplanned ICU admission 0.43. First-line for post-operative failure in obesity.** These come from a 2016 meta-analysis (11 studies, 768 patients with BMI ≥35, NIV around induction and after surgery): the fall in respiratory complications was significant (95% CI 0.16–0.66), but the 0.43 for unplanned ICU admission was not (95% CI 0.16–1.15), nor was the fall in re-intubation. After surgery the obese patient’s FRC falls further; positive pressure reverses the atelectasis (RSC-09).

**Semi-sitting; pre-oxygenate with CPAP/NIV plus apnoeic oxygenation; rapid sequence induction; videolaryngoscope recommended.** A small FRC is a small oxygen store, and oxygen consumption is high, so the obese patient desaturates within a minute or two of apnoea. Head-up positioning and positive pressure enlarge the store, and apnoeic oxygenation extends the safe time. Mask ventilation and laryngoscopy are harder, so the airway is assessed in advance (neck circumference, Mallampati, mouth opening, the 3-3-2 rule) and senior help is present before induction.
mimic: NIV vs CPAP in obesity hypoventilation
CPAP holds the airway open (severe OSA); bilevel NIV also supports ventilation, needed when OSA is mild and drive is low.
traps: “The obese asthmatic’s arrest after failed RSI was due to the induction drug or the tube size”
It was preventable by assessing the high-risk airway beforehand and planning (videolaryngoscope, senior help, pre-oxygenation).
“Mild OSA (AHI 7) means no positive pressure is needed”
Nocturnal desaturation with a raised bicarbonate is hypoventilation; NIV is the next step.
decode: Obese asthmatic arrests after failed RSI — what would have prevented it? [Marrow]
Assessing the high-risk airway beforehand.
BMI 50, AHI 7, nocturnal desaturation, HCO₃⁻ 30 — next step? [Marrow]
Non-invasive positive airway pressure (NIV).
RSC-13.punch: In obesity choose NIV for hypercapnia and hypoventilation, use it after surgery, and intubate semi-sitting after CPAP/NIV pre-oxygenation with apnoeic oxygen, a videolaryngoscope and a planned difficult airway.

RSC-14.intro: Once the obese patient is intubated, the settings follow from two facts already met: lung size follows height, and the chest wall is stiff (RSC-12). The one real question is the same transpulmonary pressure point as RSC-11.
why: **Tidal volume 6–8 mL/kg predicted body weight.** A patient 160 cm tall has the lungs of a 160 cm person whatever he weighs; 8 mL/kg of an actual 140 kg would be about 1100 mL, against about 450 mL on his predicted weight (about 57 kg for a man).
**PEEP 5–10 cmH₂O (keep alveolar pressure above closing pressure).** The weight of the chest and abdomen raises pleural pressure, so without PEEP dependent airways close at the end of every breath.

**Recruitment may need CPAP up to 50; risk of hypotension, barotrauma.** The stiff chest wall takes part of the pressure, so higher pressures are needed to reach the alveoli. In PROBESE (2013 patients with BMI ≥35, 7 mL/kg PBW), PEEP 12 with recruitment vs PEEP 4 did not reduce pulmonary complications (21.3% vs 23.6%) and caused more hypotension (31.6% vs 17.2%) and bradycardia, although less intra-operative hypoxaemia.

**Plateau target + (IAP – 13) ÷ 2 (IAP in cmH₂O); driving pressure <15–17 cmH₂O.** As in RSC-11, part of the plateau is spent on the chest wall, so the plateau limit is adjusted and driving pressure, or transpulmonary pressure, judges lung stress.
mimic: Predicted vs actual body weight
Predicted (from height and sex) sets the tidal volume; actual weight is used for many drug doses but never for the breath.
traps: “Tidal volume in obesity is set on actual body weight” (RSC-16f)
Predicted body weight; actual weight over-distends.
“A plateau of 38 in a morbidly obese patient means volutrauma”
With a high pleural pressure the transpulmonary pressure may be safe (RSC-11).
decode: Morbidly obese, plateau 38 cmH₂O, markedly raised pleural pressure — interpretation? [DocT GT]
Safe distending pressure.
RSC-14.punch: Ventilate the obese on predicted body weight (6–8 mL/kg), PEEP 5–10 to stay above closing pressure, and judge stress by driving or transpulmonary pressure, not the raw plateau.

RSC-15.sub: Respiratory → Obesity → Prone positioning and extubation
RSC-15.intro: The last clinical card follows the obese patient to the two hardest moments: turning prone and coming off the ventilator. Both are shaped by the abdomen and the low FRC.
why: **Yes: feasible and safe with a trained team; improves P/F; may reduce mortality.** Obese patients have more dorsal collapse, so turning them reopens a large area; a French case–control study (De Jong 2013) found oxygenation improved at least as much as in non-obese patients without more complications, though mortality benefit is not proven in this group.

**Careful abdominal positioning; reverse Trendelenburg.** The abdomen must hang free or be supported so that it does not push on the diaphragm and raise IAP; tilting head-up lets the abdomen fall away and reduces facial and airway oedema.

**T-piece, or pressure support 0 with PEEP 0.** With pressure support and PEEP the ventilator does work that the patient will have to do after the tube comes out; a trial without them shows the real post-extubation work of breathing in the obese.

**Stop sedation; extubate to NIV/CPAP (prevents atelectasis and re-intubation); pre-operative settings may be used.** As FRC falls again after extubation, positive pressure holds it up; a patient on home CPAP or NIV goes straight back on it.
mimic: Weaning trial in obese vs non-obese
In the obese, support during the trial hides the load; a T-piece or zero support and zero PEEP is closest to life after extubation.
traps: “Obesity is a contraindication to proning”
It is feasible and safe with a trained team and careful abdominal positioning.
decode: [pattern] Which weaning trial best predicts post-extubation work of breathing in the obese?
T-piece, or pressure support 0 with PEEP 0.
RSC-15.punch: Prone the obese when needed with the abdomen free and the bed tilted head-up; wean with a T-piece or zero support and extubate to NIV or CPAP.

RSC-16.sub: Respiratory → Special situations → Revision: true or false
RSC-16.intro: A sweep through the deck. Each statement turns on one detail from an earlier card.
why: **False — high flow over NIV** in septic hypoxaemia (RSC-01b).
**False — no difference** in ventilator-free days with 4–6 vs 8–10 mL/kg PBW (RSC-02).
**True — 4 or more of 8 items, in one 24-hour period** (RSC-05).
**False — no difference in complications; more hypotension** with high PEEP (RSC-07).
**False — chest-wall compliance falls**; lung compliance is unchanged (RSC-10c).
**False — predicted body weight**; actual weight over-distends (RSC-14a).
**True — atelectasis is the commonest post-operative pulmonary complication** (RSC-04).
traps: “Low tidal volume and high PEEP are proven for every ventilated lung”
Low tidal volume is proven in ARDS; PReVENT (no ARDS) and PROVHILO and PROBESE (high PEEP in theatre) found no benefit.
decode: [pattern] True/false on special-situation ventilation
High flow in sepsis, PReVENT no difference, four MGS items, PROVHILO no difference, chest wall not lung, predicted weight, atelectasis.
RSC-16.punch: Most errors here come from overextending ARDS rules: low tidal volume is proven in ARDS, high PEEP is not proven in theatre, and in IAH and obesity the chest wall, not the lung, is stiff.

topups.q: Respiratory failure types I–IV — mechanism and typical setting?
a: - Type I (hypoxaemic): V/Q mismatch/shunt; PaO2 <60 with normal or low PaCO2 (pneumonia, ARDS, oedema).
- Type II (hypercapnic): alveolar hypoventilation; PaCO2 >45–50 with acidosis (COPD, opioids, neuromuscular).
- Type III (perioperative): atelectasis from low FRC, pain and splinting after upper abdominal surgery; mainly hypoxaemia, CO2 may rise.

- Type IV (shock): normal lungs and pump, but respiratory-muscle hypoperfusion and high ventilatory demand (sepsis, cardiogenic shock) → fatigue; ventilate to unload the muscles until shock is reversed.

x.sub: Respiratory → Respiratory failure → Types I–IV
x.intro: Step 2 asks what goes wrong with the lung after surgery, and the four-type classification (Principles of Critical Care) gives post-operative failure its own place. The types are sorted by mechanism, not by the blood gas alone, and the exam tests exactly that: a stem whose gas fits one type but whose setting fits another.
why: **Type I (hypoxaemic): V/Q mismatch/shunt; PaO₂ <60 with normal or low PaCO₂ (pneumonia, ARDS, oedema).** Alveoli that are perfused but flooded or collapsed cannot oxygenate the blood through them; the patient breathes harder, so CO₂ is normal or low.

**Type II (hypercapnic): alveolar hypoventilation; PaCO₂ >45–50 with acidosis (COPD, opioids, neuromuscular).** The pump — drive, nerves, muscles or the load on them — cannot move enough air, so CO₂ rises and pH falls; PaO₂ falls with it.

**Type III (perioperative): atelectasis from low FRC, pain and splinting after upper abdominal surgery; mainly hypoxaemia, CO₂ may rise.** Anaesthesia, a painful wound and opioids shrink FRC below closing capacity, so dependent lung collapses (RSC-04). It is a type I lesion with a type II component, given its own label because the setting and the treatment — re-expansion — are specific.

**Type IV (shock): normal lungs and pump, but respiratory-muscle hypoperfusion and high ventilatory demand (sepsis, cardiogenic shock) → fatigue; ventilate to unload the muscles until shock is reversed.** In shock the respiratory muscles take a large share of a cardiac output that is already too small, while acidosis and sepsis drive ventilation up; they fatigue and CO₂ rises. Ventilating them frees that blood flow for other organs.
mimic: Type III vs type II after surgery
Both can show a high CO₂; type III is atelectasis in the post-operative setting, type II is a primary failure of the pump.
Type IV vs type I in sepsis
Type IV has clear lungs and fatigue; type I has infiltrates (pneumonia, ARDS).
traps: “Day 1 after upper abdominal surgery on opioids, pH 7.30, PaCO₂ 58 — type II”
DocT keys type III from the setting (56% and 72% chose it); the gas is hypercapnic, so type II is defensible — in the exam, a post-operative stem goes to type III.
“Sepsis, clear lungs, rising CO₂ from fatigue — type II”
The pump is normal; the failure is demand outstripping supply, which is type IV.
decode: Post-op day 1, upper abdominal surgery, opioids, drowsy, PaCO₂ 58 [DocT GT ×2]
Type III — perioperative.
Sepsis with normal lungs and a normal respiratory pump [DocT GT]
Type IV (88%).
Post-op sepsis, clear lung fields, progressive hypercapnia, intubated for fatigue [DocT GT]
Type IV — increased ventilatory demand.
Smoker, PaO₂ 55, PaCO₂ 70, hyperinflation [DocT GT]
Type II from COPD (94%).
x.punch: Type I is a lung that cannot oxygenate, type II a pump that cannot ventilate, type III the collapsed post-operative lung and type IV normal lungs failing because shock starves the muscles.

topups.q: Lymphoma with a large anterior mediastinal mass needs intubation — best predictor of collapse at induction, and the plan?
a: - Symptoms when supine (orthopnoea, cough, stridor) predict compression; normal PFTs or auscultation do not reassure.
- Induction, paralysis and positive pressure remove the muscle tone and negative intrathoracic pressure that hold the airway open, so the mass compresses trachea, bronchi or pulmonary artery.
- Plan: CT first, keep spontaneous breathing (awake fibreoptic intubation, sitting up), rigid bronchoscope ready, ECMO standby if high risk; steroids or radiotherapy can shrink the mass first.

x.sub: Respiratory → Airway → Anterior mediastinal mass at induction
x.intro: Step 5 turns to the airway that is harder to secure. A large anterior mediastinal mass is the extreme case: an airway that stays open while the patient breathes and may close the moment anaesthesia is induced. The exam asks which bedside finding predicts that collapse.
why: **Symptoms when supine (orthopnoea, cough, stridor) predict compression; normal PFTs or auscultation do not reassure.** If lying flat already narrows the airway, the patient is relying on posture and muscle tone to keep it open. Normal tests done upright and awake say nothing about the anaesthetised, supine state; an echo looks for cardiac or vascular compression, not the airway.

**Induction, paralysis and positive pressure remove the muscle tone and negative intrathoracic pressure that hold the airway open, so the mass compresses trachea, bronchi or pulmonary artery.** Awake, the negative pleural pressure of inspiration pulls the airways open and smooth-muscle tone stiffens them. Anaesthesia lowers lung volume, abolishes that tone and replaces negative with positive pressure, so the mass meets less resistance; a tube may pass the narrowing yet the bronchi beyond it can still collapse.

**Plan: CT first, keep spontaneous breathing (awake fibreoptic intubation, sitting up), rigid bronchoscope ready, ECMO standby if high risk; steroids or radiotherapy can shrink the mass first.** CT shows where and how badly the airway is narrowed. Keeping the patient breathing preserves the forces that hold the airway open; a rigid bronchoscope can be passed beyond a compression, and ECMO (or bypass) supports a patient whose airway cannot be rescued. Treating lymphoma first can shrink the mass but may compromise the histology, so where possible tissue is taken first, often from a peripheral node or under local anaesthesia; when the airway cannot wait, a short steroid course is given after discussion with the oncologists, who also watch for tumour lysis.
traps: “Normal recent pulmonary function tests make induction safe”
They are done awake and upright; supine symptoms are the predictor (65% chose correctly).
“An echocardiogram best predicts airway collapse”
Echo shows cardiac and vessel compression or effusion, not the airway.
“Standard rapid sequence induction with paralysis”
Paralysis removes the tone that keeps the airway open; keep spontaneous breathing.
decode: New lymphoma, widened superior mediastinum, needs intubation — best test of airway-collapse risk? [DocT GT]
Ability to lie supine without orthopnoea or cough.
x.punch: An anterior mediastinal mass is held off the airway by the patient’s own breathing, so the best predictor is whether lying flat already causes symptoms, and the plan is to keep the patient breathing.

topups.q: Ventilated patient, sudden hypoxaemia not fixed by FiO2/PEEP/tube check; CXR: retrocardiac triangle with loss of the left hemidiaphragm — diagnosis and next step?
a: - Left lower lobe collapse ('sail sign'), usually from a mucus plug.
- Next: therapeutic bronchoscopy to clear the plug (plus suction, humidification, physiotherapy).
- Not needle decompression (tension pneumothorax is hyperlucent with shift away); not advancing the tube (right mainstem intubation collapses the whole left lung).

x.sub: Respiratory → Post-operative lung → Lobar collapse on the ventilator
x.intro: Step 2 makes atelectasis the commonest pulmonary complication; lobar collapse is its sudden form. A ventilated patient with secretions desaturates, and the usual fixes — more oxygen, more PEEP, checking the tube — do nothing, because no gas reaches a lobe sealed off by a plug.
why: **Left lower lobe collapse (‘sail sign’), usually from a mucus plug.** The collapsed lobe lies behind the heart as a triangular opacity; it removes the outline of the medial left hemidiaphragm and the descending aorta, and gives a double cardiac contour. It is easily missed because the heart hides it.

**Next: therapeutic bronchoscopy to clear the plug (plus suction, humidification, physiotherapy).** Removing the plug reopens the lobe, so the shunt closes. Physiotherapy and suction often work as well: in Marini’s 1979 randomised trial of acute lobar atelectasis (31 patients), bronchoscopy added nothing to vigorous respiratory therapy, and an air bronchogram (patent proximal airways) predicted slow resolution with either. So in a stable patient chest physiotherapy comes first; bronchoscopy is chosen, as here, when hypoxaemia is severe and has not responded, when physiotherapy cannot be done or has failed, or when the absence of air bronchograms suggests a central plug.

**Not needle decompression (tension pneumothorax is hyperlucent with shift away); not advancing the tube (right mainstem intubation collapses the whole left lung).** Collapse is white with volume loss, and the mediastinum moves toward it; tension pneumothorax is black and pushes everything away. A tube already checked is in place; pushing it 3 cm further enters the right main bronchus. Prone positioning is for ARDS, not a plugged lobe.
mimic: Lobar collapse vs tension pneumothorax
Collapse: white, volume loss, shift toward it. Tension: black, no lung markings, shift away, hypotension.
Lobar collapse vs ARDS
Collapse is one lobe with volume loss; ARDS is bilateral opacities without volume loss.
traps: “Advance the tube by 3 cm”
The tube was already repositioned; advancing it causes right mainstem intubation.
“Needle decompression”
Nothing on the film is hyperlucent; this is collapse, not tension.
“Prone him”
Proning treats diffuse ARDS; a plugged lobe needs the plug removed (only 28% chose bronchoscopy).
“Bronchoscopy is always better than physiotherapy for lobar collapse”
Marini 1979 found no difference overall; bronchoscopy is for severe or refractory hypoxaemia, as in this stem.
decode: Ventilated, productive cough, hypoxaemia not fixed by FiO₂, PEEP or tube repositioning; CXR retrocardiac triangle [DocT GT]
Bronchoscopy.
x.punch: Hypoxaemia that ignores oxygen, PEEP and the tube, with a triangle behind the heart, is a plugged left lower lobe, and the treatment is to remove the plug.

spine: Sepsis: oxygen and ARDS ventilation

In sepsis-induced hypoxaemia high-flow nasal oxygen is preferred over NIV, and once ARDS develops the ARDS rules apply — 6 mL/kg PBW and plateau <30 — while lungs without ARDS gain nothing from going lower than 8–10 mL/kg (PReVENT).
What goes wrong after surgery
Atelectasis is the commonest post-operative pulmonary complication, and the Melbourne Group Score calls a complication when 4 or more of 8 items occur in the same 24 hours.
Protecting the lung in theatre
Low tidal volume protects the lung during surgery, routinely high PEEP does not, and the pressure that tracks complications is driving pressure; NIV is suggested when failure follows surgery.
The stiff chest wall
Raised abdominal pressure stiffens the chest wall, not the lung, so plateau pressure overstates lung stress and the targets are adjusted for abdominal pressure or read as transpulmonary pressure.
Obesity: lungs, drive and airway

Obesity lowers FRC towards closing capacity, so dependent airways close and the lung collapses; some patients also lose ventilatory drive (obesity hypoventilation), and the airway is harder to secure.
Ventilating and weaning the obese
Set tidal volume on predicted, not actual, weight, use enough PEEP to keep FRC above closing pressure, prone if needed with care for the abdomen, and extubate to NIV or CPAP.
RESP03.primer: Predicted body weight comes from height and sex, not from what the patient weighs, because lung size follows height; tidal volumes are set in mL/kg of it. The respiratory system is the lung and the chest wall (rib cage, diaphragm and abdomen) in series, so its compliance falls if either one stiffens, and the plateau pressure (end-inspiratory pressure at zero flow) reflects both. Driving pressure is plateau minus PEEP, the pressure that stretches each breath; transpulmonary pressure is alveolar minus pleural pressure (estimated from an oesophageal balloon), the pressure that stretches the lung itself. Functional residual capacity (FRC) is the volume left at the end of a quiet breath; when it falls below closing capacity, small dependent airways shut during normal breathing and the alveoli behind them collapse.

RSC-17.sub: Respiratory → Immunocompromised → Causes of acute respiratory failure
RSC-17.intro: The deck opens with the question every immunocompromised patient with new hypoxaemia poses: what is it? Most causes are infections and treatable, so the cause, not the oxygen device, decides the outcome.
why: **Infectious about 60%; non-infectious about 25%.** The non-infectious share is drug toxicity, the disease itself infiltrating the lung, haemorrhage and heart failure; the rest stay unexplained.

**Bacterial infection 33%; then viral 13%, Pneumocystis 8%, invasive aspergillosis 7%, disease-related infiltrates 7%, cardiogenic 3%.** Ordinary bacteria still come first even in deep immunosuppression, so empirical antibacterial cover is never omitted. In EFRAIM (1,611 patients, 2017) the order was the same: bacterial 29.5%, viral 15.4%, fungal 14.7%.

**15% undetermined, and an undetermined cause carries a worse outcome.** If the cause is not found, it is not treated. In EFRAIM an undetermined cause (13.2%) was linked to both intubation and hospital death, which is why the diagnostic work-up (RSC-20d) is part of the treatment.

**The type and mechanism of immunosuppression, and the nature, phase and duration of treatment.** The defect predicts the organism (RSC-18), and the phase matters: a neutropenic patient in the first weeks of chemotherapy is at risk of different organisms from one on long-term steroids or months after a transplant (RSC-19).
mimic: Infection vs the disease or drug itself
Infiltrates may be leukaemic or lymphomatous infiltration, drug pneumonitis or haemorrhage; these are found only by looking for them once infection has been sought.
traps: “In the immunocompromised, opportunistic organisms are the commonest cause”
Ordinary bacterial infection is the single commonest cause; Pneumocystis and aspergillosis follow well behind.
decode: [pattern] Commonest identified cause of acute respiratory failure in immunocompromised patients?
Bacterial infection.
[pattern] Which factor in the work-up is linked to higher mortality?
Failure to identify the cause.
RSC-17.punch: Bacteria are the commonest cause, the immune defect predicts the rest, and an undetermined cause carries a worse outcome, so finding it matters more than the oxygen device.

RSC-18.sub: Respiratory → Immunocompromised → Immune defect and typical infections
RSC-18.intro: Step 1 continues: the kind of immune defect narrows the list of organisms before any test returns. Each defect removes one line of defence, and the organisms that line normally handles take over.
why: **Neutrophil defect (acute leukaemia, chemotherapy): Gram-negative and Gram-positive bacteria, Candida, Aspergillus.** Neutrophils kill extracellular bacteria and the hyphae of moulds. Without them, gut and skin bacteria invade within days, and Aspergillus becomes the threat after about 10 days of profound neutropenia. Long-term steroids add to this risk, because they impair neutrophil and macrophage killing too.

**T-cell defect (steroids, calcineurin inhibitors, lymphoma, transplant): Pneumocystis, CMV and herpes viruses, mycobacteria, Nocardia, Listeria, Legionella, Cryptococcus.** T cells control organisms that live inside cells or that need cell-mediated immunity, so the infections are slower, opportunistic and often reactivations. A patient on long-term prednisone with a lung nodule and a brain lesion has Nocardia (RSC-20).

**B-cell or antibody defect (myeloma, CLL, rituximab, asplenia): encapsulated bacteria — pneumococcus, H. influenzae.** A capsule resists phagocytosis unless antibody and complement coat it, and the spleen removes coated bacteria from the blood. Without antibody or spleen, pneumococcal pneumonia and sepsis can be fulminant.
mimic: Neutropenia vs T-cell defect
Neutropenia: acute, bacterial and mould infection within weeks of chemotherapy. T-cell defect: subacute Pneumocystis, viral, mycobacterial and Nocardia infection on steroids or after transplant.
traps: “Aspergillus is a T-cell infection”
Invasive aspergillosis follows neutropenia (and steroids); neutrophils kill hyphae (RSC-29b).
“Pneumocystis follows neutropenia”
Pneumocystis follows loss of T-cell immunity: steroids, transplant, lymphoma, HIV.
decode: [pattern] Prolonged neutropenia after induction chemotherapy, new nodules — likely organism?
Aspergillus.
[pattern] On rituximab or after splenectomy, fulminant pneumonia — likely organism?
Pneumococcus (encapsulated bacteria).
RSC-18.punch: Neutropenia lets in bacteria, Candida and Aspergillus; a T-cell defect lets in Pneumocystis, viruses, mycobacteria and Nocardia; an antibody or spleen defect lets in encapsulated bacteria.

RSC-19.sub: Respiratory → Immunocompromised → Lung complications after stem-cell transplant
RSC-19.intro: Step 2 narrows to the patient after a haematopoietic stem-cell transplant (HSCT), the card asked most often in this deck. Immunity returns in a predictable order — neutrophils at engraftment, T cells over months, antibodies last — so the number of days since transplant tells you which infections and which non-infectious syndromes to expect. The questions test the non-infectious syndromes, each defined by its timing and by what the lavage does or does not show.
why: **About two-thirds of patients.** Most reviews give 30–60%, depending on the transplant and the era, so two-thirds is at the high end; lung complications account for about half of transplant-related deaths.

**Pre-engraftment (first month): bacterial, fungal and viral infection; drug toxicity, engraftment syndrome, diffuse alveolar haemorrhage.** The patient is neutropenic, so bacteria and moulds dominate (RSC-18). Engraftment syndrome comes within 96 hours of neutrophil engraftment: by Spitzer's criteria, three major features (fever without infection, an erythematous rash, non-cardiogenic pulmonary oedema with hypoxaemia) or two major plus one minor (weight gain, liver or renal dysfunction, transient encephalopathy). The returning neutrophils release cytokines and make capillaries leak; it responds to steroids. Diffuse alveolar haemorrhage (DAH) is diagnosed at bronchoscopy, when successive lavage aliquots return progressively bloodier; haemoptysis is uncommon despite the name. It affects about 5–12% of recipients, with a median onset that varies by series from about day 11 to day 30, and it carries a high mortality and is treated with high-dose methylprednisolone and correction of platelets and clotting.

**Early post-engraftment (to day 100): CMV, fungal and Pneumocystis infection; acute GVHD, idiopathic pneumonia syndrome, radiation pneumonitis.** Neutrophils are back but T cells are not, so the T-cell organisms take over. Idiopathic pneumonia syndrome (IPS) is widespread alveolar injury — multilobar infiltrates, symptoms and signs of pneumonia, a raised A–a gradient or new oxygen need — with no active lower respiratory infection and no cardiac failure, acute renal failure or iatrogenic fluid overload to explain it (ATS 2011). It usually appears within the first 120 days, with a median onset of about day 21–65 in different series; donor T cells and TNF-α drive it as well as conditioning toxicity, and mortality is 60–80%, above 95% once ventilated. Treatment is high-dose steroids with antimicrobials continued; etanercept was added on the basis of the TNF-α link, but the adult phase III trial (BMT CTN 0403, 34 patients) closed early for slow accrual and showed no difference in response at day 28 (62.5% with etanercept vs 66.7% with placebo).

**Late (after day 100): encapsulated bacteria, fungal and viral infection; bronchiolitis obliterans (chronic GVHD), post-transplant lymphoproliferative disorder.** Antibody and splenic function are the last to recover, so pneumococcus returns. Bronchiolitis obliterans syndrome is the lung form of chronic GVHD: an obstructive defect (FEV₁/FVC <0.7 and FEV₁ <75% predicted) with air trapping on expiratory CT, appearing a median of about a year after transplant.
mimic: Engraftment syndrome vs acute GVHD

Both cause fever and rash and both respond to steroids. Engraftment syndrome comes with neutrophil recovery and brings capillary-leak lung; acute GVHD targets skin, gut and liver, and whether it injures the lung directly is not accepted.
DAH vs IPS
Both are diffuse, non-infectious and early. DAH is defined by blood in the lavage; IPS is the diagnosis left when lavage shows neither blood nor organisms.
traps: “Rash, fever and lung infiltrates at 4 weeks: acute GVHD of the lung and skin”

This picture at neutrophil recovery is engraftment syndrome; acute GVHD targets skin, gut and liver, and acute lung GVHD is not an accepted entity. DocT keys GVHD because engraftment syndrome is not offered — the least wrong option, chosen by 59%.
“DAH is diagnosed by more than 20% haemosiderin-laden macrophages in a lavage taken in the first 24 hours”
Haemosiderin-laden macrophages take 48–72 hours to appear; the early, defining finding is aliquots that become progressively bloodier.
“IPS is purely conditioning toxicity, or needs documented lung GVHD”
Donor T cells and TNF-α contribute, and GVHD is not required; IPS is a diagnosis of exclusion.
“Stop the antibiotics once the lavage is negative”
Antimicrobials are continued while steroids start, because a negative lavage does not exclude every infection.
“Iatrogenic fluid overload is an IPS criterion”
It is an exclusion: fluid overload, cardiac failure and renal failure must be absent (93% got this right).
“DAH is a late complication” (RSC-29c)
It belongs to the first month.
decode: ALL, 4 weeks post-HSCT, fever, maculopapular rash, respiratory distress, lavage negative, perivascular lymphocytes on skin biopsy [DocT, 59% right]
GVHD of skin and lung as keyed; engraftment syndrome is the better answer whenever it is offered.
Post-HSCT, sudden dyspnoea and haemoptysis — which lavage finding is most diagnostic of DAH? [DocT GT]
Successive aliquots that become progressively more blood-stained.
Day 20, bilateral infiltrates, no cardiac failure, lavage negative for all organisms — true statement about IPS? [DocT GT]
High-dose steroids with possible etanercept, because TNF-α drives IPS.
Which is NOT a criterion for IPS? [DocT GT, 93% right]
Iatrogenic fluid overload (it is an exclusion).
RSC-19.punch: After stem-cell transplant the day decides the cause: engraftment syndrome and alveolar haemorrhage in the first month, idiopathic pneumonia syndrome before day 100 once infection, heart, kidney and fluid are excluded, and bronchiolitis obliterans after.

RSC-20.sub: Respiratory → Immunocompromised → CT pattern and diagnostic work-up
RSC-20.intro: Step 3 turns the clinical picture into a diagnosis. CT narrows the organism by pattern, and the questions pair a pattern with the immune defect and ask for the organism or the test that confirms it.
why: **Ground-glass opacities: Pneumocystis, viral (CMV), atypical bacteria.** These organisms fill alveoli with fluid and protein and thicken the interstitium without solid consolidation. Ground glass with interlobular septal thickening (crazy paving) in a patient on steroids, cyclophosphamide or after transplant is Pneumocystis until proven otherwise; it is confirmed by immunofluorescence or PCR on lavage or induced sputum, and a raised serum beta-D-glucan supports it.

**Nodules with or without cavitation: Aspergillus, mucormycosis, Nocardia, mycobacteria, S. aureus.** Angioinvasive moulds infarct lung around a nodule: a halo of ground glass (haemorrhage) appears early in neutropenia and an air crescent later, as neutrophils return; mucormycosis may show a reversed halo. Nocardia gives nodules or cavities and spreads to the brain, so a lung nodule with a brain lesion in a patient on long-term steroids is Nocardia; the brain is imaged in every case and treatment is high-dose co-trimoxazole (with imipenem or amikacin for brain or severe disease) for 6–12 months, and at least 12 months when the patient is immunosuppressed or the brain is involved.
**Consolidation: bacterial pneumonia, aspergillosis.** Lobar or segmental consolidation is usually bacterial, the commonest cause overall (RSC-17).

**Non-invasive tests first (induced sputum, nasopharyngeal viral PCR, urinary Legionella antigen, serum galactomannan and beta-D-glucan, echo, BNP); bronchoscopy only for diagnostic uncertainty, because it is risky on high oxygen.** Lavage in a hypoxaemic patient can precipitate intubation. Each test answers a specific question: galactomannan for Aspergillus, beta-D-glucan for Pneumocystis and other fungi, echo and BNP for a cardiac cause.
mimic: Pneumocystis vs CMV pneumonitis
Both cause ground glass after transplant; crazy paving with a high beta-D-glucan favours Pneumocystis, and CMV is shown by PCR or antigen in blood and lavage.
Nocardia vs tuberculosis
Both cavitate; a lung lesion with a brain lesion in a steroid-treated patient points to Nocardia.
traps: “Sarcoidosis on prednisone, seizure, lung nodule and brain lesion — tuberculosis or sarcoid”
The lung-and-brain combination on long-term steroids is Nocardia. Only 19% chose it on DocT GT.
“Ground glass in the immunocompromised: send a serum galactomannan”
Galactomannan detects Aspergillus, which gives nodules; ground glass and crazy paving call for lavage for Pneumocystis.
“Crazy paving 4 months after lung transplant is CMV”
CMV also gives ground glass, but crazy paving is keyed as Pneumocystis (68% right).
“Bronchoscopy first in every immunocompromised patient with infiltrates”
Non-invasive tests come first; lavage on high oxygen can tip the patient into intubation.
decode: Systemic sclerosis on cyclophosphamide, insidious dyspnoea, ground glass with septal thickening (crazy paving), antibiotics failed — confirmatory test? [DocT, 71% right]
Lavage for Pneumocystis immunofluorescence.
4 months after lung transplant, fever, dry cough, crazy paving on HRCT — organism? [DocT, 68% right]
Pneumocystis.
Sarcoidosis on prednisone 10–60 mg for a year, seizure, 2.5 cm lung nodule and 3 cm brain lesion [DocT GT, 19% right]
Nocardiosis.
RSC-20.punch: Ground glass means Pneumocystis or a virus, nodules mean moulds or Nocardia, and a lung lesion with a brain lesion on steroids means Nocardia; non-invasive tests come before bronchoscopy.
