RSC-21.sub: Respiratory → Immunocompromised → NIV and high-flow oxygen: the evidence
RSC-21.intro: Step 4 asks how to support the failing lung. Intubation used to carry a very high mortality in these patients, so avoiding it with a mask was attractive; the small early trials supported that, and the larger modern trials did not.
why: **Early trials: NIV better than oxygen, but small and with a high control mortality.** Antonelli (2000, 40 solid-organ transplant recipients): intubation 20% vs 70%, ICU mortality 20% vs 50%. Hilbert (2001, 52 patients with infiltrates, fever and hypoxaemia): intubation 46% vs 77%, ICU mortality 38% vs 69%, hospital mortality 50% vs 81%. Control mortality that high reflects an era when intubating these patients was often fatal.

**Lemiale 2015 (374 patients): NIV vs oxygen, no difference in mortality.** Day-28 mortality was 24.1% with NIV vs 27.3% with oxygen alone; intubation (38.2% vs 44.8%), ICU-acquired infection and length of stay did not differ either. With modern care control mortality had fallen to about a quarter, leaving far less room for NIV to help.

**HIGH trial 2018 (776 patients): high-flow vs standard oxygen, no difference in mortality.** Day-28 mortality was 35.6% vs 36.1% and intubation 38.7% vs 43.8% (not significant); only oxygenation was better with high flow. Among the 82 immunocompromised patients in FLORALI, a post hoc analysis found intubation in 65% with NIV (alternating with high flow) vs 31% with high flow alone and 43% with standard oxygen; but FLORALI-IM (2022, 299 patients) then found NIV alternating with high flow no better or worse than high flow alone (day-28 mortality 35% vs 36%).

**LUNG SAFE: NIV used more often first-line in the immunocompromised (20.9% vs 15.9%), and failed more often.** About half of those given NIV were intubated, and in LUNG SAFE their mortality matched that of patients intubated at once; other cohorts (Azoulay 2014, ARDS in malignancy) found NIV failure linked to higher mortality.

**A time-limited trial of NIV or high flow in early or mild disease; invasive ventilation with shock, renal failure or high work of breathing.** The risk is a late intubation after hours of large, injurious breaths. ERS/ATS 2017 still says “we suggest early NIV for immunocompromised patients with ARF” (conditional, moderate certainty, weighted by the early trials); ERS 2022 conditionally prefers high flow over NIV in hypoxaemic failure generally.
mimic: Where NIV works vs where it fails

It works where positive pressure reverses the problem: COPD hypercapnia (COPD-10), cardiogenic pulmonary oedema, high-risk extubation. It fails in severe hypoxaemia and in an exacerbation of ILD, where stiff lungs do not recruit.
traps: “NIV helps an exacerbation of interstitial lung disease”
Stiff, non-recruitable lungs make NIV fail in most patients, and it delays intubation; ILD is the condition where NIV is NOT useful [NEET 2025].
“Hilbert proved that NIV saves immunocompromised patients”
Its control mortality of 69–81% belongs to another era; Lemiale (2015) found no difference.
“The HIGH trial showed lower mortality with high flow” (RSC-29d)
No difference: 35.6% vs 36.1%.
“NIV failure was linked to higher mortality in LUNG SAFE”
In LUNG SAFE mortality after NIV failure matched that of primary intubation; the excess appears in other cohorts.
decode: NIV is NOT useful in which: ILD exacerbation, cardiogenic pulmonary oedema, COPD exacerbation, high-risk post-extubation? [NEET 2025]
ILD exacerbation.
[pattern] Immunocompromised, hypoxaemic, no shock — what did Lemiale 2015 or HIGH 2018 show?
No difference in mortality with NIV or high flow.
RSC-21.punch: Early small trials favoured NIV, but Lemiale, HIGH and FLORALI-IM found no mortality benefit from NIV or high flow, so either is a time-limited trial and shock, renal failure or tiring mean intubation.

RSC-22.sub: Respiratory → Immunocompromised → ARDS: ventilation and outcome
RSC-22.intro: Step 4 continues once the patient has ARDS. About one in five patients with ARDS in LUNG SAFE was immunocompromised, and their hospital mortality was higher (52.4% vs 36.2%) despite similar severity; the card asks what predicts it.
why: **No: the same ARDSNet strategy, and plateau, driving pressure and compliance predict mortality as usual.** In the EFRAIM ARDS analysis (789 patients, hospital mortality 56.3%) higher driving pressure and plateau pressure and lower compliance were each linked to death, and tidal volume was not; the rules of ARDS-19 and ARDS-26 apply unchanged.

**Vasopressors, renal replacement therapy, ARDS of undetermined cause.** Each raised the odds of death (adjusted odds ratios about 1.9, 2.0 and 1.7 in EFRAIM); organ failure beyond the lung and an untreated cause (RSC-17c) are what kill.

**Not linked: neutropenia and the type of underlying disease.** Neither neutropenia on admission nor the kind of malignancy or immunosuppression predicted death once organ failures were counted, so neither is a reason to withhold ICU care.

**ECMO: 6-month survival 30%; worst with haematological malignancy; better with a recently diagnosed immunodeficiency.** In 203 immunocompromised patients given ECMO (Schmidt), cannulation within 30 days of the diagnosis was linked to lower mortality, so ECMO is kept for patients with a realistic prognosis (ARDS-35).
traps: “Neutropenia predicts mortality in immunocompromised ARDS” (RSC-29a)
It was not linked once vasopressors, renal replacement and an undetermined cause were counted.
decode: [pattern] Immunocompromised ARDS — which factor is NOT associated with mortality?
Neutropenia (or the type of underlying disease).
RSC-22.punch: Immunocompromised ARDS is ventilated as any ARDS, and death follows vasopressors, renal replacement and an undetermined cause, not neutropenia or the type of disease.

RSC-23.intro: Step 5 moves from infection to a mechanical problem: a hole between the airway and the pleura. On a ventilator, gas goes out through the hole rather than into the lung, and the questions test when a leak means an airway injury and when air outside the lung can be watched.
why: **A communication between a bronchus and the pleural cavity with a persistent air leak (beyond 24 hours).** In ventilated patients a leak lasting more than 24 hours is the usual threshold; after lung surgery, a prolonged air leak is usually defined as one lasting beyond 5–7 days.

**Lung resection, trauma, mechanical ventilation, ARDS, spontaneous pneumothorax, radiation or radiofrequency ablation, infection.** Resection leaves a bronchial stump that can break down; necrotising infection and ARDS weaken the lung, and positive pressure forces gas through any weak point.

**Loss of PEEP and of tidal volume (expired below inspired), hypoxaemia, persistent surgical emphysema or pneumomediastinum, bubbling in the water seal.** The difference between inspired and expired tidal volume measures the leak per breath. After chest trauma a persistent large leak, or a pneumothorax that recurs despite a working drain, means a tracheobronchial injury until bronchoscopy proves otherwise.

**Mortality 27–50% (other reviews 18–67%).** The 67% comes from an older series in which 39 of 1,700 ventilated patients had a leak beyond 24 hours, ventilated with tidal volumes far larger than today's (about 14 mL/kg); with lung-protective ventilation the figures are lower.
mimic: Air leak through the lung vs air outside it

A fistula leaks into the pleura and bubbles in the drain. Pneumomediastinum and pneumopericardium in ARDS are air tracking along the bronchovascular sheaths (barotrauma, ARDS-18); if the patient is stable they are watched, not drained.
traps: “An occult pneumothorax needs a drain, especially on positive-pressure ventilation”
A stable occult (CT-only) pneumothorax can be observed even on positive pressure (OPTICC).
“Every traumatic haemothorax needs a drain and VATS”
Only a retained collection (more than about 300 mL) after tube drainage needs VATS.
“Pneumopericardium in ARDS needs pericardiocentesis”
Without haemodynamic compromise it is observed with serial chest X-rays; drainage is for tamponade.
decode: Trauma, right haemopneumothorax with rib fractures, chest drain inserted — true statement? [DocT GT, 65% right]
A persistent air leak or recurrent pneumothorax should prompt evaluation for tracheobronchial injury.
ARDS with pneumomediastinum and pneumopericardium, haemodynamically stable — intervention? [Marrow]
Observe with serial chest X-rays.
RSC-23.punch: A leak lasting beyond 24 hours on the ventilator is a bronchopleural fistula, shown by expired volume below inspired; after trauma it means an airway injury until bronchoscopy says otherwise, while stable air in the mediastinum is watched.

RSC-24.sub: Respiratory → Air leak → Ventilator and drain strategy
RSC-24.intro: Step 5 continues with how to ventilate around the hole. Every setting is judged by one question: does it raise or lower the pressure pushing gas through the fistula, and for how long?
why: **The transpulmonary pressure gradient (airway minus pleural pressure) and the duration of inspiration.** Flow through the fistula follows the pressure across it and the time that pressure is applied, so peak and mean airway pressure, PEEP and inspiratory time all feed the leak (ARDS-28).

**Peak pressure <30; tidal volume 4–6 mL/kg (3–4 for one lung); lowest possible PEEP; short inspiratory time; low rate; permissive hypercapnia; pressure support or spontaneous breathing if tolerated.** Small breaths and a short inspiration shorten the time the gradient is high; low PEEP removes the gradient during expiration; a low rate reduces the number of high-pressure periods per minute. Spontaneous breathing lowers mean airway pressure most, so early weaning is part of the treatment.

**Avoid negative suction: water seal only. Check the tube’s position and patency; consider an unexpandable lung. Intrapleural pressure can be matched to PEEP.** Suction makes pleural pressure more negative, which widens the gradient and keeps the fistula open. Applying positive pressure to the drain during expiration, equal to PEEP, removes the expiratory gradient.
traps: “Chest-drain suction helps a bronchopleural fistula heal” (RSC-29e)
Suction widens the gradient and increases flow through the fistula; water seal only.
“High PEEP is used with an air leak” (RSC-29f)
The lowest PEEP that keeps oxygenation acceptable.
decode: [pattern] Ventilated patient with a large bronchopleural fistula — which change reduces the leak?
Lower PEEP, smaller tidal volume, shorter inspiratory time, water seal instead of suction.
RSC-24.punch: Whatever lowers airway pressure, or the time it is applied, lowers the leak: small breaths, short inspiration, minimal PEEP, spontaneous breathing, and a drain on water seal rather than suction.

RSC-25.sub: Respiratory → Air leak → Lung isolation and high-frequency ventilation
RSC-25.intro: When the leak is too large for ordinary settings, the healthy lung can be separated from the leaking one, or breaths made so small that little gas escapes. The questions test high-frequency jet ventilation and the bedside check of a double-lumen tube.
why: **Double-lumen tube; single-lumen tube with a bronchial blocker; endobronchial blocker (Arndt).** Isolation lets each lung be ventilated separately, or the leaking one rested. The bronchial limb goes into the healthy lung, away from the fistula and any suture line, so that lung is protected from spill and ventilated without pushing gas through the hole. A left-sided tube is the usual default, because the right upper lobe bronchus arises close to the carina and is easily blocked, but a left-sided fistula (such as a left pneumonectomy stump) needs a right-sided tube or a blocker. If a double-lumen tube is thought to have moved, position is checked by bedside fibreoptic bronchoscopy, not by transporting the patient.

**Synchronous: the same rate to both lungs, with different tidal volume, flow, PEEP and FiO₂. Asynchronous: everything differs, including the mode.** Two ventilators are used; synchronous ventilation links them so both lungs inflate together. Each lung gets settings matched to its own mechanics, so the leaking lung can take small volumes and low PEEP.

**High-frequency ventilation: tidal volume 2–5 mL/kg at 100–200/min; it raises airway impedance and so lowers fistula flow; weak evidence, selected patients. These are jet-ventilation figures; oscillation runs at 3–15 Hz.** Jet ventilation pulses small jets near the dead-space volume with passive expiration, keeping peak pressure low, so less gas passes through the fistula with each breath. It is not recommended for adult ARDS (OSCAR and OSCILLATE, ARDS-34); its niche is the large leak and airway surgery. VV-ECMO allows ultra-protective ventilation and may let the fistula close.
mimic: Jet ventilation vs oscillation

Jet: small pulses at high rates (the card gives 100–200 a minute; devices and reports vary, and neonatal jets run faster), passive expiration. Oscillation: 3–15 Hz (180–900 a minute), active expiration, high mean airway pressure.
traps: “Jet ventilation gives larger tidal volumes, or removes the need for PEEP”
It gives very small volumes at high rates; minimising lung injury is its theory, not a proven benefit in ARDS (93% right).
“Suspected double-lumen tube migration: take the patient for a chest X-ray or CT”
Confirm at the bedside with a fibreoptic bronchoscope.
decode: Severe influenza ARDS, considering high-frequency jet ventilation — primary advantage? [DocT, 93% right]
Very small tidal volumes at high rates, minimising ventilator-induced lung injury.
After thoracic surgery, suspected double-lumen tube migration — next step? [Marrow]
Bedside flexible bronchoscopy.
RSC-25.punch: A large leak is managed by isolating the lungs, ventilating each to its own needs, or making the breaths so small with jet ventilation that little gas escapes, with ECMO as the last step.

RSC-26.intro: If the leak persists and the patient cannot go to surgery, the hole can be plugged from inside the airway. The technique depends on the size and site of the defect.
why: **Small defects (<5 mm): occlusive material — fibrin glue, gel foam, tetracycline, autologous blood patch.** A small hole can be sealed directly, or made to scar shut by inflammation.

**Proximal defects: airway stents, Watanabe spigots, Amplatzer occluder.** A stent covers a hole in the trachea or a main bronchus; an occluder device plugs a larger stump fistula. Watanabe spigots are silicone plugs placed in the bronchus that leads to the leak, and are also used for peripheral leaks.

**Distal defects: one-way endobronchial valves.** The valve lets air and secretions out during expiration but stops air entering, so the segment beyond collapses and the leak seals. The leaking segment is found by blocking segmental bronchi in turn with a balloon until the bubbling stops; in one series of 40 patients (Travaline 2009) the leak resolved or decreased in about 93%.
traps: “One-way valves are for proximal stump defects”
Valves are for distal leaks; proximal defects need stents or occluders (RSC-29g).
decode: [pattern] Persistent distal air leak in a patient unfit for surgery — bronchoscopic option?
One-way endobronchial valves.
RSC-26.punch: Small holes are glued, proximal defects are stented or occluded, and distal leaks are closed with one-way valves that collapse the segment beyond.

RSC-27.sub: Respiratory → Lung donor → Why so few donor lungs
RSC-27.intro: The last step is the brain-dead patient whose lungs could save someone else. The lung is the organ most often lost during donor care, because brain death and the ICU stay injure it before retrieval.
why: **Only 15–25% of donors yield lungs.** Far fewer than kidneys or liver, because the lungs are exposed to aspiration, infection and ventilator injury as well as the effects of brain death. The usual ideal criterion is a PaO₂ above 300 mmHg on FiO₂ 1.0 and PEEP 5 cmH₂O, though no firm lower limit has been defined.

**Sympathetic storm (neurogenic pulmonary oedema, inflammation), then atelectasis, aspiration, trauma, ventilator-associated pneumonia and VILI.** As the brainstem herniates a catecholamine surge raises systemic and left atrial pressure, forcing fluid into the lung and damaging capillaries; brain death then releases inflammatory mediators that injure the lung further. The ICU adds collapse, infection and ventilator injury.

**Extended donor criteria; ex vivo lung perfusion; optimised donor management.** Ex vivo perfusion ventilates and perfuses retrieved lungs outside the body, so marginal lungs can be assessed and improved before transplant. Donor management is the part the ICU controls (RSC-28).
traps: “Donor lungs are lost mainly to the original trauma”
Most are lost to brain-death injury and to what happens in the ICU, much of which can be prevented.
decode: [pattern] What share of brain-dead donors yield transplantable lungs?
About 15–25%.
RSC-27.punch: Only 15–25% of donors yield lungs, because the sympathetic storm and then collapse, aspiration, infection and ventilator injury damage them; better donor care and ex vivo perfusion recover more.

RSC-28.sub: Respiratory → Lung donor → Ventilating the donor
RSC-28.intro: Step 6 continues with what the ICU can change. The donor’s lungs are injured lungs, so the same protective principles apply, with the apnoea test as an extra hazard.
why: **Volume control; tidal volume 6–8 mL/kg PBW; rate 8–16; PEEP 5–10; FiO₂ 100% then down to 40%.** Protective volumes limit stretch, PEEP prevents collapse, and FiO₂ is lowered to avoid absorption atelectasis and oxygen toxicity.

**PaCO₂ 35–45 mmHg; peak pressure <30.** Normocapnia avoids acidosis in a circulation that is already unstable; protective-ventilation protocols usually state the 30 cmH₂O limit as a plateau pressure.

**Protective ventilation (tidal volume ≤8 and PEEP ≥8) raised the odds of lung procurement (odds ratio 1.43).** In a French national cohort of 1,626 brain-dead donors (2020) recipients’ 1-year survival did not differ (82.7% vs 82.3%). In Mascia’s trial (JAMA 2010, 118 donors) tidal volume 6–8 mL/kg PBW, PEEP 8–10, an apnoea test on CPAP and closed suction, compared with 10–12 mL/kg and PEEP 3–5, raised the share of donors with eligible lungs from 54% to 95% and lungs harvested from 27% to 54%, with similar 6-month recipient survival (69% vs 75%).

**Closed suction, positioning, VAP bundle. Kidneys want fluid; lungs want restriction.** Disconnection for an apnoea test or open suction collapses the lung; a recruitment manoeuvre after the apnoea test reversed the fall in P/F in a small study. Fluid is given to a euvolaemic target rather than liberally, because the lung leaks.
traps: “The apnoea test is done disconnected from the ventilator”
Disconnection collapses the lung; Mascia used CPAP during the test, then re-recruited.
decode: [pattern] Brain-dead donor — which ventilation strategy increased lungs harvested?
Tidal volume 6–8 mL/kg PBW, PEEP 8–10, apnoea test on CPAP, closed suction (Mascia 2010).
RSC-28.punch: Ventilate the donor as an injured lung: 6–8 mL/kg PBW, PEEP 8–10, apnoea test on CPAP, closed suction; in Mascia’s trial this doubled the lungs harvested.

RSC-29.sub: Respiratory → Immunocompromised, air leak and donor → Revision: true or false
RSC-29.intro: A sweep through the deck. Each statement turns on one detail from an earlier card.
why: **False — neutropenia is not linked to mortality** in immunocompromised ARDS (RSC-22c).
**False — diffuse alveolar haemorrhage comes in the first 30 days** (RSC-19b).
**False — no difference in mortality** with high flow vs standard oxygen (RSC-21c).
**False — water seal only;** suction widens the gradient through the fistula (RSC-24c).
traps: “Settings that protect the ARDS lung also suit a fistula”
Protective volumes do, but the higher PEEP of ARDS feeds the leak; with a fistula PEEP is kept as low as possible.
decode: [pattern] True/false on immunocompromised failure and air leak
Neutropenia not predictive, Aspergillus after neutropenia, DAH early, HIGH no difference, no suction, low PEEP, valves distal.
RSC-29.punch: In the immunocompromised the cause and organ failures decide outcome, not neutropenia or the oxygen device; with a fistula, everything that lowers airway and pleural pressure gradients lowers the leak.

spine: Who fails, and from what

In the immunocompromised patient with respiratory failure infection causes most cases, bacteria first, and the kind of immune defect predicts which organism; a cause left undetermined carries a worse outcome.
The transplant lung by calendar

After stem-cell transplant the date tells you the likely cause: neutropenic infection, engraftment syndrome and alveolar haemorrhage in the first month, CMV, Pneumocystis and idiopathic pneumonia syndrome to day 100, and bronchiolitis obliterans after that.
Pattern to pathogen
On CT, ground glass points to Pneumocystis or a virus, nodules to moulds and Nocardia, and the non-invasive tests come before a risky bronchoscopy.
Support and outcome

NIV and high-flow oxygen have not lowered mortality in the large trials, so they are time-limited trials, and once ARDS develops it is ventilated as any ARDS, with organ failures and an undetermined cause, not neutropenia, predicting death.
The leaking lung

Flow through a bronchopleural fistula follows the transpulmonary pressure and the time it is applied, so the ventilator and the drain are set to keep that pressure low, with lung isolation, high-frequency ventilation and bronchoscopic plugs or valves for leaks that persist.
The brain-dead lung donor
Only a small share of donors yield lungs, because brain death injures them and ventilation can add to it; protective donor ventilation and an apnoea test on CPAP roughly doubled the lungs harvested.
RESP04.primer: Each arm of immunity guards against its own set of organisms: neutrophils clear bacteria and moulds, T cells control viruses, Pneumocystis and intracellular organisms, and antibodies with the spleen clear encapsulated bacteria. After a stem-cell transplant the patient is neutropenic until engraftment, the day the donor marrow starts making neutrophils, usually in the second to fourth week; T-cell and antibody immunity take months to return. The P/F ratio (PaO₂ divided by FiO₂) grades hypoxaemia, and in the Berlin definition ARDS is mild at 200–300, moderate at 100–200 and severe below 100 mmHg. Transpulmonary pressure is airway minus pleural pressure, the pressure that holds the lung open and that pushes gas through any hole in it.

SWAN-01.intro: Step 1 starts with the device. The pulmonary artery (Swan–Ganz) catheter is a long, balloon-tipped tube that the blood itself carries through the right heart; each lumen opens at a set distance from the tip, so each reads a different chamber once the tip is in the pulmonary artery.
why: **110 cm long, 4–8 Fr, passed through an introducer sheath.** The adult catheter is usually 7–7.5 Fr, marked every 10 cm so the operator knows how far it has gone. The sheath is a larger cannula left in the vein, so the catheter can be advanced, withdrawn or changed without new venepuncture.

**1.5 mL of air.** That is the maximum for the adult (7 Fr) balloon; the smaller 5 Fr balloon takes 0.75–1 mL, which is why your notes show both. Air, not liquid, is used, so the balloon deflates at once and so a rupture releases only a small bubble. Over-inflation, or inflating with the tip already in a small distal branch, is the main route to pulmonary artery rupture (SWAN-12).

**Distal (yellow): PA pressure, wedge and mixed venous blood; proximal (blue): opens in the RA, for CVP, drugs, fluids and the cold injectate; thermistor: blood temperature near the tip; balloon (red): inflation.** The proximal port lies about 30 cm from the tip, so it sits in the right atrium when the tip is in the pulmonary artery; the thermistor lies about 4 cm from the tip. When the balloon is inflated, the distal lumen looks forward past a blocked branch and reads the pressure downstream — the wedge or pulmonary artery occlusion pressure. Nothing caustic or hyperosmolar goes down the distal lumen, because it opens into a small pulmonary artery.
mimic: Distal port vs proximal port
Distal (tip) reads the pulmonary artery and, with the balloon up, the wedge; proximal (about 30 cm back) reads the right atrium and is where the injectate goes.
traps: “The balloon is inflated to measure central venous pressure”
CVP comes from the proximal port with the balloon down; the balloon is inflated to measure the occlusion (wedge) pressure, which reflects left atrial pressure. 25% of the DocT GT cohort missed this.
“Continuous cardiac output or RV ejection fraction is the balloon’s job”
Those come from special catheters with a heating filament or a fast-response thermistor; the balloon’s only jobs are flotation and occlusion.
decode: Septic shock patient with a PAC; the balloon at the tip is inflated to occlude a small PA branch — purpose of this feature? [DocT GT]
Measuring pulmonary artery occlusion (wedge) pressure, a stand-in for left atrial pressure.
[pattern] Maximum balloon volume in an adult PAC?
1.5 mL of air.
SWAN-01.punch: Four lumens, each opening at a fixed point: the tip reads the pulmonary artery and, with the 1.5 mL balloon up, the wedge; the proximal port reads the right atrium and takes the injectate; the thermistor times the cold.

SWAN-02.sub: Respiratory → Pulmonary artery catheter → Measured and derived values
SWAN-02.intro: Step 1 continues: what the catheter actually measures, and what is only calculated. Examiners test the line between the two.
why: **Directly measured: CVP or RA pressure, RV and PA pressures, wedge pressure, cardiac output, mixed venous saturation.** Pressures come from the transducer, cardiac output from thermodilution (SWAN-11), and mixed venous saturation from blood drawn from the distal port or read by a fibreoptic catheter. Systemic blood pressure and heart rate come from the arterial line and ECG, not the catheter.

**Derived: SVR and PVR, cardiac index, stroke volume index, LV and RV stroke work index, oxygen delivery and uptake.** Each is arithmetic on measured values (SWAN-09, 10), so any error in the measurement — a wedge read outside zone 3, a bad thermodilution curve — is carried into every derived number.
mimic: Wedge pressure vs LV preload
Wedge ≈ left atrial pressure ≈ LV end-diastolic pressure only when there is no mitral disease, no zone 1–2 lung and normal LV compliance; preload itself is a volume.
traps: “Stroke volume and SVR are measured by the catheter”
Both are calculated: stroke volume is CO ÷ HR, SVR is the pressure drop ÷ CO.
decode: [pattern] Which of these is derived rather than measured by a PAC?
SVR, PVR, cardiac index, stroke volume index, stroke work, DO₂ and VO₂.
SWAN-02.punch: The catheter measures pressures, cardiac output and mixed venous saturation; resistances, indices and oxygen transport are arithmetic on those, and carry their errors.

SWAN-03.sub: Respiratory → Pulmonary artery catheter → Indications today
SWAN-03.intro: Step 2 asks when the catheter is still worth floating. After the trials (SWAN-13) it moved from routine ICU monitoring to a few situations where the right-heart pressures themselves are the diagnosis or decide the treatment.
why: **Pulmonary hypertension: diagnosis and evaluation.** Right-heart catheterisation is the reference test: the 2022 ESC/ERS definition is a mean PA pressure above 20 mmHg, and a wedge ≤15 mmHg with PVR above 2 Wood units makes it pre-capillary, while a wedge above 15 mmHg makes it post-capillary. Echo can only estimate these.

**Heart, lung and liver transplant candidacy.** Fixed pulmonary hypertension or a high PVR can rule out heart transplant (the donor right ventricle fails against it) or liver transplant (portopulmonary hypertension), so it is measured directly.

**Cardiogenic shock and right ventricular failure.** Here the catheter separates LV from RV failure and guides inotropes and mechanical support. The best data are observational: in the Cardiogenic Shock Working Group registry (Garan, JACC Heart Failure 2020; 1,414 patients) no PAC assessment carried higher in-hospital mortality than complete haemodynamic profiling (adjusted OR 1.57, 95% CI 1.06–2.33), which shows association, not cause. The randomised test is the Pulmonary Artery Catheter in Cardiogenic Shock Trial (PACCS, NCT05485376; early PAC versus delayed or no PAC, primary outcome in-hospital mortality), still listed as recruiting at its last registry update.

**Mixed shock, or volume status unclear in shock.** When echo and bedside signs disagree, the catheter separates hypovolaemic, distributive and cardiogenic components, and cardiogenic from non-cardiogenic pulmonary oedema (wedge above or below about 18 mmHg).
**High-risk cardiac surgery.** It is still common in cardiac theatres, though observational studies have not shown benefit (SWAN-14).
mimic: Diagnostic use vs therapeutic use
The catheter is a diagnostic tool: it shows tamponade (equalised diastolic pressures), a left-to-right shunt (an oxygen step-up), or cardiogenic oedema; it treats nothing by itself.
traps: “PAC-guided therapy improves survival in septic shock”
No randomised trial showed benefit (SWAN-13); in a general ICU there are few if any absolute indications.
decode: [pattern] Strongest current indication for a PAC?
Diagnosis of pulmonary hypertension (and transplant work-up); in the ICU, cardiogenic shock and RV failure.
SWAN-03.punch: The catheter now earns its place where the right-heart numbers are the answer: pulmonary hypertension, transplant work-up, cardiogenic shock and RV failure.

SWAN-04.sub: Respiratory → Pulmonary artery catheter → Contraindications and high-risk states
SWAN-04.intro: Step 2 continues with the other side: when the catheter should not cross the right heart, or crosses it at real risk. Each item follows from where the catheter goes and what it touches.
why: **Absolute: infection at the site, RV assist device, RA or RV thrombus or mass, no consent.** A clot or tumour in the right heart can be dislodged into the lungs; an RV assist device has cannulae in the right heart that the catheter can tangle with or be drawn into, and the device itself carries the flow the catheter is meant to measure. Many texts (for example the UCSF Hospital Handbook) also list right-sided endocarditis and a mechanical tricuspid or pulmonary valve as absolute, because the catheter can dislodge vegetations into the lung or be trapped by, and damage, a mechanical valve (see FLAGS).

**Relative: coagulopathy, platelets <50,000, electrolyte disturbance that favours arrhythmia, severe acid–base disturbance.** The catheter touches the RV wall and outflow tract, so low potassium or magnesium and acidosis make ectopics turn into sustained VT; bleeding risk applies to the puncture and to any rupture.

**High risk: severe pulmonary hypertension or Eisenmenger, LBBB, pacemaker or ICD, tricuspid or pulmonary stenosis or prosthesis, persistent left SVC.** In pulmonary hypertension the stiff vessels rupture more easily (SWAN-12). In LBBB, the catheter brushing the right bundle can add RBBB, and both bundles blocked means complete heart block, so external pacing must be ready. Transient catheter-induced RBBB is uncommon (about 0.05–5% of insertions), and in one series of 82 patients with LBBB none developed complete block during insertion, so the risk is real but small; the precaution is cheap. Pacing leads can be dislodged or entangled; a left SVC drains into the coronary sinus, so a left-sided catheter will not follow the usual path.
mimic: LBBB vs RBBB before insertion
Pre-existing RBBB adds little risk; pre-existing LBBB is the one that can become complete heart block.
traps: “LBBB is no concern because the catheter stays on the right”
The catheter can cause RBBB as it passes the RV outflow tract; on top of LBBB that is complete heart block.
decode: [pattern] Which conduction disturbance makes PAC insertion high risk, and why?
LBBB: catheter-induced RBBB gives complete heart block.
SWAN-04.punch: Avoid floating through a heart that holds clot or a device, and in LBBB have pacing ready, because the catheter can block the right bundle as well.

SWAN-05.intro: Step 3 floats the catheter. The site decides how easily the catheter follows the natural curve into the pulmonary artery, and the 10-cm markings tell the operator which chamber to expect next, so a missing waveform at the expected depth means coiling.
why: **Right IJV > left subclavian > right subclavian > left IJV.** The right internal jugular gives the straightest route to the tricuspid valve, and the left subclavian’s curve matches the catheter’s curve into the outflow tract; the left IJ has the most bends.

**RA at 15–20 cm; about 10 cm more to each of RV, PA and wedge.** From the right IJ that gives roughly RV 25–30 cm, PA 35–40 cm and wedge 40–50 cm. If the RV trace has not appeared by about 30 cm, or the PA trace by about 50 cm, the catheter is coiling in the atrium or ventricle: deflate, withdraw to the RA and try again, because coils knot.

**Inflate in the right atrium, before crossing the tricuspid valve; always deflate before withdrawing.** Inflated, the balloon is carried by the flow like a sail and cushions the tip, so it is less likely to irritate the RV wall or perforate it; your notes’ ‘inflate once the RV trace appears’ is not standard practice. Withdrawing with the balloon up can tear the tricuspid or pulmonary valve, and leaving it up after wedging occludes the branch, causing infarction or rupture (SWAN-12).

**Depth to wedge: subclavian 35–50 cm, internal jugular 40–55 cm, femoral 60 cm.** From the femoral vein the catheter has the IVC and a sharp turn to make, so it is longer and often needs fluoroscopy.
mimic: Balloon left up vs catheter knotting
A balloon left inflated causes infarction and rupture; knotting comes from advancing too far without the expected waveform change.
traps: “Balloon left inflated after placement: the worst risk is knotting in the atrium”
Knotting comes from over-advancing a coiling catheter; the balloon left up occludes the branch, and the most serious result is pulmonary artery rupture (66% right in DocT QBank).
“Inflate the balloon once the RV trace appears”
Inflate in the RA so the tip is cushioned as it crosses the RV.
decode: Balloon accidentally left inflated after placement — most serious complication? [DocT]
Pulmonary artery rupture (not knotting, pacing wire displacement or thrombus).
[pattern] From the right IJ, at what depth should the RV trace appear?
About 25–30 cm; no RV by 30 cm suggests coiling.
SWAN-05.punch: Inflate in the right atrium, expect a new chamber every 10 cm, deflate before every withdrawal, and never leave the balloon up.

SWAN-06.sub: Respiratory → Pulmonary artery catheter → Flotation trace
SWAN-06.intro: Step 3 continues with the trace on the monitor as the catheter advances: right atrium, right ventricle, pulmonary artery, wedge. Each transition is recognised by one change in the waveform, and both real questions test whether you can name the chamber from its shape, not from the number alone.
why: **1 = right atrium; 2 = right ventricle; 3 = pulmonary artery; 4 = wedge.** The atrial trace is a low venous waveform (mean about 2–6 mmHg) with a, c and v waves; the wedge looks like it again, because it is a left atrial waveform seen through the lung.

**RA → RV: systolic pressure jumps; diastolic stays near zero.** The ventricle generates 20–30 mmHg in systole but relaxes to near the atrial pressure in diastole, so the trace becomes tall and wide-swinging. Its diastolic part slopes upward as the ventricle fills. This is when ectopics and VT appear, so the catheter is advanced through the ventricle without pausing.

**RV → PA: diastolic pressure rises (the diastolic step-up) and a dicrotic notch appears; systolic is unchanged.** Systolic is the same because the open pulmonary valve joins the RV and PA in systole. In diastole the pulmonary valve closes and holds the arterial pressure at 8–15 mmHg instead of letting it fall to near zero; the notch is that valve closing. The diastolic part now slopes downward as blood runs off into the lung, the opposite of the ventricle’s upward filling slope; this contour is a useful extra sign, but the diastolic step-up and the notch are the main ones.

**PA → wedge: the pulsatile trace is lost, replaced by an atrial-type trace at or below PA diastolic pressure.** The inflated balloon stops flow in that branch, so the tip sees the still column of blood leading to the left atrium. A wedge reading above PA diastolic pressure is wrong (over-wedging, or a zone 1–2 tip reading alveolar pressure, SWAN-08) unless there are large v waves from mitral regurgitation.
mimic: RV vs PA trace
Same systolic. PA has a raised diastolic, a dicrotic notch and a downward diastolic slope; RV has diastolic near zero sloping upward.
Wedge vs RA trace
Both are atrial waveforms; the wedge is reached only after the PA trace, and its mean normally sits a few mmHg below PA diastolic.
traps: “A low pressure of 10 mmHg must be the wedge”
A dicrotic notch means the pulmonary valve is behind the tip, so the trace is pulmonary artery; a wedge trace has no notch and no arterial pulsation. The number alone does not name the chamber.
“RV to PA is recognised by a rise in systolic pressure”
Systolic is shared; the rise is in diastolic (SWAN-15d).
decode: Septic shock patient with a Swan–Ganz; low-amplitude waveform with a clear dicrotic notch, pressure 10 mmHg — which pressure? [DocT GT · PYQ]
Pulmonary artery pressure: the dicrotic notch decides it, not the value.
PA catheter waveforms as the catheter advances [NEET 2024]
RA → RV (systolic jumps) → PA (diastolic steps up, dicrotic notch) → wedge (pulsation lost, atrial-type trace).
SWAN-06.punch: Systolic jumps when the catheter enters the ventricle; diastolic steps up and a dicrotic notch appears when it enters the pulmonary artery; pulsation vanishes when it wedges — the shape names the chamber, not the number.

SWAN-07.sub: Respiratory → Pulmonary artery catheter → Normal right-heart pressures
SWAN-07.intro: Step 3 ends with the numbers each chamber should read. The relationships matter more than the exact ranges, which vary between texts.
why: **Right atrium 0–3 mmHg; RV 20–30/0–8; PA 20–30/8–15; wedge 8–12.** References differ: a widely used set (Edwards) gives RA 2–6, RV 15–25/0–8, PA 15–25/8–15 and wedge 6–12, and others give PA diastolic as low as 4; normal mean PA pressure is about 10–20 (see FLAGS). The fixed relationships are: RV and PA systolic are equal (open valve in systole), PA diastolic is above RV diastolic (closed valve), and wedge is a few mmHg below PA diastolic. A mean PA pressure above 20 mmHg is pulmonary hypertension (SWAN-03a).
mimic: PA diastolic vs wedge
Normally wedge is 1–5 mmHg below PA diastolic; a widening gap means raised PVR (pre-capillary disease), since PA diastolic then exceeds left atrial pressure.
traps: “PA systolic is higher than RV systolic”
They are the same in the absence of pulmonary stenosis.
decode: [pattern] Normal PA pressure and wedge?
PA about 25/10 (mean under 20) mmHg; wedge 6–12 mmHg.
SWAN-07.punch: RV and PA share the systolic, the pulmonary valve lifts PA diastolic above RV diastolic, and the wedge sits just below PA diastolic.

SWAN-08.sub: Respiratory → Pulmonary artery catheter → West zones and the wedge pressure
SWAN-08.intro: Step 4 is the card asked most often in this deck. The wedge is meant to read left atrial pressure through a still column of blood, but the pulmonary capillaries run through the alveolar walls; wherever alveolar pressure is higher than the vascular pressure, it squeezes the capillaries shut and the catheter reads the alveolus instead. West’s zones describe where that happens, and the questions test the zone order, the zone for the wedge, the effect of PEEP and the V/Q gradient that comes from the same physics.
why: **Zone 1: PA > Pa > Pv. Zone 2: Pa > PA > Pv. Zone 3: Pa > Pv > PA (PA = alveolar).** Upright, gravity adds about 1 cmH₂O of vascular pressure per centimetre below the top of the lung, while alveolar pressure is the same everywhere. At the apex alveolar pressure can exceed arterial pressure, so capillaries collapse and there is no flow (zone 1, alveolar dead space); normally zone 1 hardly exists, but it appears with low pulmonary pressure or high airway pressure. In the middle, flow depends on arterial minus alveolar pressure (zone 2, the ‘waterfall’). At the base both arterial and venous pressure exceed alveolar pressure, the vessels stay open and flow depends on arterial minus venous pressure (zone 3).

**Zone 3: only there is there a continuous column of blood from the tip to the left atrium; elsewhere the wedge reads alveolar pressure.** With the balloon up, flow stops and the tip is connected to the left atrium by a still column of blood, but only if no capillary along that path is compressed. In zones 1 and 2 alveolar pressure exceeds pulmonary venous pressure, the capillaries collapse, and the transducer reads airway pressure. Because a flow-directed catheter follows the most flow, it usually goes to dependent, zone 3 lung on its own, which in a supine patient is posterior.

**Tip at or below the left atrium on a lateral film; respiratory swing in the wedge <50% of the swing in alveolar pressure (plateau – PEEP); wedge changes by <50% of a change in PEEP.** Each check asks the same thing: does the wedge follow the left atrium or the airway? If it rises and falls with each breath by as much as the airway pressure, or moves almost one-for-one with PEEP, it is reading the alveolus. Other signs of zone 3: wedge below PA diastolic, and clear a and v waves (a smooth trace suggests zones 1–2).

**End-expiration.** That is when pleural and alveolar pressures are closest to atmospheric, so the intravascular reading is nearest the true transmural pressure. On a ventilator end-expiration is the low point just before the inspiratory rise; breathing spontaneously it is the high point just before the inspiratory dip. PEEP still adds to the reading at end-expiration, so high PEEP overestimates the true filling pressure.
mimic: Zone 2 vs zone 3
In both arterial pressure exceeds alveolar; in zone 3 venous pressure also exceeds alveolar, so the whole path stays open when flow stops.
Wedge high from fluid vs high from PEEP
Fluid raises a wedge with clear a and v waves and little respiratory swing; PEEP-driven readings swing with each breath and move almost one-for-one with PEEP changes.
traps: “Excess PEEP converts zone 2 to zone 3 and improves V/Q”
The reverse: excess PEEP raises alveolar pressure above vascular pressure, converting zones 2 and 3 to zone 1, which adds alveolar dead space and makes the wedge read airway pressure.
“Excess PEEP lowers PVR as volume approaches TLC”
PVR is lowest near FRC; at high lung volumes alveolar vessels are stretched and compressed and PVR rises.
“Upright, V/Q is greater at the bases” (or “ventilation is greater at the apex”)

Both ventilation and perfusion are greater at the bases, but perfusion rises more steeply, so V/Q is highest at the apex (about 3) and lowest at the base (about 0.6). Only 35% of the DocT GT cohort chose this as the false statement; supine, the same gradient runs from posterior (low V/Q) to anterior (high V/Q).
“Hypovolaemia makes the wedge more reliable”
Low vascular pressures let alveolar pressure win, converting zone 3 to zone 2 or 1, so the wedge reads high and misleads.
decode: Pressures Pa > Pv > PA (alveolar) — which West zone? [NEET 2025]
Zone 3.
PAC in a ventilated patient — in which West zone is the wedge most accurate? [DocT GT]
Zone 3: continuous blood column to the left atrium.
Most likely consequence of excessive PEEP in ARDS, by West zones? [DocT GT]
Increase in alveolar dead space by converting zone 2 or 3 into zone 1.
All true except: ventilation greater at bases / perfusion greater at bases / V/Q greater at bases / V/Q greater anteriorly when supine [DocT GT]
V/Q greater at the bases is false: V/Q is highest at the apex.
SWAN-08.punch: The wedge reads the left atrium only through open zone 3 vessels, so the tip must sit below the left atrium and the reading taken at end-expiration; high PEEP or hypovolaemia turn zone 3 into zones 2 and 1, adding dead space and making the wedge read the airway.

parts.q: Why is V/Q highest at the apex if ventilation is lowest there?
parts.a: Gravity affects blood far more than gas: perfusion falls steeply from base to apex while ventilation falls only gently, so the ratio rises towards the apex (about 3) and falls towards the base (about 0.6).

SWAN-09.sub: Respiratory → Pulmonary artery catheter → Derived haemodynamic formulae
SWAN-09.intro: Step 5 turns measurements into derived numbers. Each resistance is the pressure drop across a bed divided by the flow through it; the only real question here (Marrow) tests a perfusion pressure built the same way.
why: **SVR = 80 × (MAP − CVP) ÷ CO.** The systemic bed runs from the aorta (MAP) to the right atrium (CVP). The 80 converts Wood units (mmHg·min/L) to dyn·s·cm⁻⁵; normal SVR is 800–1200 dyn·s·cm⁻⁵.

**PVR = 80 × (mean PAP − wedge) ÷ CO.** The pulmonary bed runs from the pulmonary artery to the left atrium, which the wedge stands in for. Normal is below about 250 dyn·s·cm⁻⁵ (about 3 Wood units); the 2022 pulmonary hypertension definition uses above 2 Wood units for pre-capillary disease.
**Cardiac index = CO ÷ body surface area.** Normal 2.5–4 L/min/m²; below 2.2 with a high wedge is the classic cardiogenic shock profile.
**Stroke volume index = cardiac index ÷ heart rate.** Normal about 33–47 mL/m² per beat. A low cardiac index with a normal SVI means the problem is rate, not pump.
mimic: SVR vs PVR
SVR uses MAP minus CVP; PVR uses mean PAP minus wedge. Mixing up the downstream pressure is the common slip.
traps: “LV coronary perfusion pressure = MAP − CVP”
The LV is perfused in diastole against its own end-diastolic pressure: LV CPP = diastolic BP − wedge (LVEDP). With DBP 72 and PAOP 10 that is 62 mmHg.
decode: LV coronary perfusion pressure from SBP 133, DBP 72, PAOP 10? [Marrow]
62 mmHg: diastolic BP − PAOP.
[pattern] Formula for PVR?
80 × (mean PAP − wedge) ÷ CO.
SWAN-09.punch: Every resistance is pressure drop ÷ flow × 80: MAP − CVP for the body, mean PAP − wedge for the lung; LV coronary perfusion is diastolic pressure minus wedge.

parts.q: Coronary perfusion pressure of each ventricle
parts.a: LV: diastolic BP − PAOP (LVEDP), because the thick LV wall squeezes its own vessels shut in systole and it fills only in diastole. RV: MAP − mean RV pressure, because the thin RV is perfused through the whole cycle; a rising RV pressure in pulmonary hypertension starves the RV of flow.

SWAN-10.sub: Respiratory → Pulmonary artery catheter → Oxygen transport
SWAN-10.intro: Step 5 continues with oxygen. Because the catheter samples truly mixed venous blood from the pulmonary artery, it measures the arterial–venous difference directly, and with the cardiac index that gives delivery and uptake.
why: **DO₂I = CI × 13.4 × Hb × SaO₂.** Flow times arterial oxygen content (dissolved oxygen ignored). The 13.4 is 1.34 mL O₂ per gram × 10, converting Hb in g/dL to per litre. Normal is about 500–600 mL/min/m².
**VO₂I = CI × 13.4 × Hb × (SaO₂ − SvO₂).** The reverse Fick: uptake is flow times the content taken out. Normal is about 120–160 mL/min/m², an extraction of about 22–30%.

**Mixed venous saturation 60–80%.** About 65–75% in most texts. A low SvO₂ means delivery is short of demand (low output, anaemia, hypoxaemia, high demand); a high SvO₂ in shock means the tissues are not extracting (sepsis, shunting, cytotoxic hypoxia), not that all is well. Central venous ScvO₂ from the SVC is normally 2–3% lower than SvO₂, but in shock the order reverses and ScvO₂ runs about 5% higher, because splanchnic blood in the IVC is extracted more.

**Fick cardiac output = VO₂ ÷ (10 × arteriovenous content difference); content difference = 1.34 × Hb × (SaO₂ − SvO₂).** The ×10 again turns mL/dL into mL/L. In practice VO₂ is often assumed (about 125 mL/min/m²), which makes the Fick output an estimate.
mimic: SvO₂ vs ScvO₂
SvO₂ (pulmonary artery) mixes SVC, IVC and coronary sinus blood; ScvO₂ (SVC) misses the lower body and heart. They move together but are not interchangeable.
traps: “A high SvO₂ in septic shock excludes tissue hypoxia”
It may mean the tissues cannot extract oxygen; lactate and the CO₂ gap help.
decode: [pattern] Normal mixed venous saturation, and what a low value means?
About 65–75% (card 60–80%); low means delivery is not meeting demand.
SWAN-10.punch: Delivery is flow times content, uptake is flow times the content removed, and SvO₂ is the balance between them.

SWAN-11.sub: Respiratory → Pulmonary artery catheter → Thermodilution cardiac output
SWAN-11.intro: Step 5 ends with how the catheter measures flow. A known amount of cold is added upstream and its dilution is timed downstream; the more blood flows past, the faster and smaller the temperature dip.
why: **Cold dextrose or saline is injected through the proximal (RA) port; the thermistor near the tip records the fall in blood temperature.** About 10 mL is usual in adults; 5 mL (your notes) also works, but the smaller temperature dip makes rewarming and technique errors weigh more. It is injected rapidly, three to five times at the same phase of respiration (usually end-expiration, since output varies by up to about 10% with breathing), and the readings averaged.

**Output is inversely proportional to the area under the curve (Stewart–Hamilton).** CO = V × (Tb − Ti) × K ÷ ∫ΔTb dt: the injectate volume and the temperature gap are known, so a large area under the temperature–time curve means the cold lingered, which means slow flow.

**High output: small, quick curve. Low output: large, prolonged curve.** Errors follow from the formula: anything that shrinks the area overestimates output, so too little or too warm injectate overestimates it, and too much underestimates it. Tricuspid regurgitation usually underestimates output, because cold blood washes back and forth and the curve is drawn out; intracardiac shunts make the reading unreliable, as the catheter measures right-sided flow, which then differs from left-sided output.
mimic: Area under the curve vs output
Inverse: a big area means low output (SWAN-15g).
traps: “Output is proportional to the area under the curve”
It is inversely proportional.
decode: [pattern] Large, prolonged thermodilution curve indicates?
Low cardiac output.
SWAN-11.punch: Fast flow washes the cold past quickly, so a small curve is high output and a large curve low output.

SWAN-12.intro: Step 6 opens with harm, the second most-asked card. Complications fall into three groups by when they happen — getting into the vein, passing through the heart, and leaving the catheter in — and all three questions test the most dangerous of them: pulmonary artery rupture after balloon inflation.
why: **Venous access: bleeding, arterial puncture, pneumothorax, air embolism, neuropathy.** These are the same as for any central line; in PAC-Man they made up most of the 10% complication rate (haematoma 4%, arterial puncture 3%, a few pneumothoraces), alongside arrhythmias needing treatment in 3%.

**Passage: atrial and ventricular ectopics, VT or VF, RBBB, knotting.** The tip touching the RV outflow tract triggers ectopics, which are common and usually stop once the catheter moves on; sustained VT is unusual and VF rare (in two large series only about 1.3–1.5% needed drugs, a thump or cardioversion). Transient RBBB occurs in about 0.05–5% and matters in LBBB (SWAN-04). Knotting (about 1% in one review) comes from advancing too far without the expected trace change (SWAN-05b).

**Residence: thromboembolism, pulmonary infarction, infection and endocarditis, valve and endocardial damage, minor tricuspid regurgitation.** Infarction follows a tip that migrates distally into a permanent wedge, or a balloon left up: the branch is occluded for hours, and a wedge-shaped opacity appears (0–1.4% in one large series, often only a new shadow on the film). Infection rises with the days the catheter stays in.

**Pulmonary artery rupture: 0.03–0.2%, mortality 41–70%.** Published figures vary: a 17-year series of 32,442 catheterised patients found 0.031% with 7 of 10 dying (70%), other large series 0.06–0.2%, and one review quotes 0.2% with 30% mortality; the card’s range sits within these. The message is the same: rare and often fatal. It happens when the balloon is inflated in a distal or stiff branch, or over-inflated: pulmonary hypertension, age over 60, female sex, anticoagulation, hypothermia (a stiffer catheter) and mitral disease raise the risk. It presents at once with haemoptysis, hypoxaemia and often collapse, usually right-sided. Management: do not pull the catheter out (some advise withdrawing it slightly and re-inflating the balloon to occlude the bleeding branch); secure the airway and isolate the lung (double-lumen tube, bronchial blocker or main-bronchus intubation of the good side); until the lung is isolated, put the bleeding side down so blood does not flood the good lung, and add PEEP; reverse anticoagulation; definitive control is angiographic embolisation or surgery. A pseudoaneurysm can form and rebleed days later.
mimic: Rupture vs air embolism
Air embolism comes from an open line or a burst balloon and causes collapse without haemoptysis; rupture brings blood up the airway.
Rupture vs knotting
Knotting causes failure to advance or withdraw and arrhythmias, not haemoptysis.
traps: “Balloon left inflated: knotting is the most serious risk”
Knotting is a passage problem from over-advancing; the inflated balloon leads to infarction and, most seriously, rupture. DocT QBank 66% right (93% on the GT repeat).
“Sudden haemoptysis just after wedging is pulmonary infarction”
Infarction develops over hours with minor haemoptysis; sudden haemoptysis with collapse right after inflation is rupture.
“The balloon may be inflated with saline to make it safer”
Always air, at most 1.5 mL, inflated slowly while watching the trace; stop as soon as it wedges.
decode: Balloon accidentally left inflated after placement — most serious potential complication? [DocT, DocT GT]
Pulmonary artery rupture.
Septic shock, PAC; shortly after balloon inflation for wedge — sudden haemoptysis, hypoxaemia, collapse [DocT GT]
Pulmonary artery rupture (not infarction, air embolism or knotting).
[pattern] Incidence and mortality of PA rupture?
About 0.03–0.2%; mortality roughly 30–70% (card 41–70%).
SWAN-12.punch: The balloon causes the worst harm: left up it infarcts the lung, inflated in a distal or stiff branch it ruptures the artery — sudden haemoptysis and collapse at inflation is rupture until proved otherwise.

Pulmonary infarction
