PE-23.sub: Respiratory → Pulmonary embolism → When thrombolysis fails or is contraindicated
PE-23.intro: Step 5 is the patient who needs the clot out but cannot be lysed, or was lysed and is still in shock. The options remove clot mechanically, either with the chest open or through a catheter, and catheters can deliver a small dose of lytic exactly where it is needed.
why: **Surgical embolectomy for high-risk and selected intermediate-high-risk patients; done on normothermic cardiopulmonary bypass, clot removed down to segmental level.** ESC 2019 recommends it for high-risk PE when lysis is contraindicated or has failed, and as an alternative to rescue lysis in the deteriorating patient. It is also favoured for a clot in transit through a patent foramen ovale. Bypass takes over the circulation so the pulmonary arteries can be opened without the heart beating against them.

**Without lysis: pigtail fragmentation, rheolytic (AngioJet), suction and rotational thrombectomy; with lysis: catheter-directed, ultrasound-assisted (EKOS) and pharmacomechanical.** Catheter lysis delivers a small fraction of the systemic dose straight into the clot, so it lowers RV strain with less bleeding; ultrasound loosens the fibrin to let the drug in. ESC 2019 suggests it for high-risk PE when lysis is barred or fails, and for the deteriorating intermediate-high patient. HI-PEITHO (NEJM 2026; 544 patients) tested EKOS plus heparin against heparin alone in intermediate-high-risk PE: the 7-day primary composite (led by PE-related death and decompensation) fell from 10.3% to 4.0%, driven by decompensation (3.7% vs 10.3%); there was no intracranial bleeding, major bleeding did not differ significantly (about 4% vs 2–3%), and mortality did not differ. The commonest complication of catheter lysis is access-site and minor bleeding; intracranial haemorrhage is rare.
mimic: Surgical vs catheter embolectomy
Surgery needs bypass and a cardiac surgeon but removes clot completely and handles clot in transit; catheter methods need only a cath lab and work through a vein.
traps: “The commonest complication of catheter-directed thrombolysis is haemorrhagic stroke” [Marrow key]

Access-site and other minor bleeding is commonest; intracranial haemorrhage is rare with the small catheter doses (none in either arm of HI-PEITHO). Choose the key only if it is the sole bleeding option offered.
decode: Massive PE on day 1 after hip replacement — therapy? [Marrow]

PE-23.punch: When lysis is barred or fails, take the clot out: surgical embolectomy on bypass or catheter treatment, with or without a small dose of local lytic, which bleeds far less than systemic lysis.

PE-24.sub: Respiratory → Pulmonary embolism → Inferior vena cava filters
PE-24.intro: Step 5 ends with a device that stops clot reaching the lung but does nothing to the clot in the leg. That is its whole trade-off, and it is why the filter is for patients who cannot have the drug that does treat the clot. The questions test the indication and what to do when PE happens with a filter in place.
why: **Absolute contraindication to anticoagulation; recurrent PE despite adequate anticoagulation; routine use is not recommended.** Active gastrointestinal bleeding with an acute PE is the classic case: place a retrievable filter, and start anticoagulation and remove the filter once the bleeding stops. PREPIC2 (399 patients with PE and DVT, retrievable filter plus anticoagulation vs anticoagulation alone) found no reduction in recurrent PE at 3 months (3% vs 1.5%), so a filter adds nothing when the patient can be anticoagulated.

**Infrarenal IVC; retrievable or permanent.** Below the renal veins, so a filter thrombus does not threaten the kidneys; a suprarenal filter is used when clot extends above the renal veins or in pregnancy. Retrievable filters should come out once anticoagulation is possible, because complications rise with time.

**Fewer recurrent PEs at the cost of more DVT.** In PREPIC at 8 years, symptomatic PE was 6.2% vs 15.1%, but DVT was 35.7% vs 27.5%, with no survival difference. The filter catches clot, and the caught clot and the device itself slow flow and make more.

**Recurrent DVT, IVC occlusion, migration, tilting, caval wall penetration, fracture and fragment embolisation, device thrombosis.** A new PE with a filter in place suggests clot on or above the filter, or through collaterals; after anticoagulation, image the filter (Doppler ultrasound or CT of the IVC), and a retrievable filter with thrombus may need thrombectomy and removal.
mimic: Filter vs anticoagulation
Anticoagulation treats the clot and prevents new ones; a filter only intercepts emboli and increases DVT, so it substitutes only when anticoagulation is impossible.
traps: “Acute PE with active GI bleeding: systemic lysis, catheter lysis, or a routine filter for proximal DVT”
Bleeding bars both kinds of lysis; the answer is a retrievable IVC filter, with anticoagulation once bleeding stops (60–74% right). ‘Routine filter’ is wrong because filters are never routine.
“IVC filters reduce DVT”
They increase DVT (PE-26h).

PE-24.punch: An IVC filter is for the patient who cannot be anticoagulated (active bleeding) or clots through full anticoagulation; placed infrarenally and retrieved when possible, it trades fewer PEs for more DVT and is never routine.

PE-25.sub: Respiratory → Pulmonary embolism → PE in pregnancy
PE-25.intro: Step 6 brings the whole pathway into pregnancy, the card asked most in this deck. Nothing about PE changes its danger, so the same rules apply — treat on suspicion, image to confirm, lyse in shock — but three things change: D-dimer rises naturally, imaging must count fetal radiation, and the drug must not cross the placenta. The seven questions test each of these and what happens after delivery.
why: **A leading cause of maternal death in developed countries; risk highest post-partum, especially after caesarean section.** Pregnancy is hypercoagulable (more fibrinogen and factors VII, VIII and X, less protein S), the gravid uterus slows venous return from the legs, and delivery adds vessel injury; risk peaks in the 6 weeks after birth.

**Start LMWH; chest X-ray, and leg ultrasound if DVT is suspected (a proximal DVT ends the work-up); normal X-ray: CTPA or perfusion scan; abnormal X-ray: CTPA.** Heparin starts while tests are done, as in any patient with high or intermediate probability (PE-13); both DocT GT questions key ‘begin IV heparin immediately’, and either heparin answers that. A proximal DVT confirms VTE without chest radiation. A normal film makes a perfusion scan readable; an abnormal one makes it non-diagnostic, so CTPA. D-dimer rises through pregnancy, so a fixed cut-off is positive in most women by the third trimester; a negative result still helps, but only within a validated pathway. In the Artemis study (van der Pol, NEJM 2019; 498 women) the pregnancy-adapted YEARS algorithm (leg ultrasound if DVT signs; no YEARS item and D-dimer <1000 ng/mL, or ≥1 item and <500, excludes PE) missed one VTE at 3 months (0.21%) and avoided CTPA in 39% — 65% in the first trimester but only 32% in the third. ESC 2019 recommends formal assessment with a validated pathway in pregnancy.

**Fetal danger threshold 50 mSv (ESC 2019: 50–100); all tests fall well below it.** ESC 2019 writes the threshold in mSv; strictly, fetal absorbed dose is measured in mGy, and for X-rays the two numbers are the same. ESC lists fetal doses of 0.05–0.5 mGy for CTPA and a similar fraction of a milligray for perfusion scanning, so both are at least a hundred times below the threshold. The real difference is the mother’s breast dose, which is far higher with CTPA (3–10 mGy). So neither test is withheld for fear of the fetus.

**LMWH is the drug of choice; UFH is also safe (neither crosses the placenta). Vitamin K antagonists cause embryopathy and fetal bleeding; NOACs are contraindicated.** LMWH is given in a fixed therapeutic dose based on early-pregnancy weight. Warfarin crosses the placenta: in weeks 6–12 it causes nasal hypoplasia and stippled epiphyses, and later fetal bleeding. NOACs cross the placenta and are untested. In shock, the pregnant woman is lysed or has embolectomy as any other patient would, because pregnancy is only a relative contraindication (PE-22). After delivery, anticoagulation continues for at least 6 weeks post-partum and at least 3 months in total; warfarin and LMWH are both safe in breastfeeding, so switching to warfarin after delivery is standard, while NOACs are avoided during breastfeeding.

traps: “A negative D-dimer (<500 ng/mL) is highly reliable in the third trimester”
D-dimer rises through pregnancy and is above 500 in most women by the third trimester; only a pregnancy-adapted pathway uses it. The keyed answer is that V/Q or CTPA can be done safely.
“Thrombolysis is strictly contraindicated in pregnancy, even in shock”
Pregnancy is a relative contraindication; an unstable pregnant woman with PE is lysed (NEET 2024 recall).
“Warfarin is the safest anticoagulant for the fetus in the third trimester”
Warfarin crosses the placenta and causes fetal bleeding; LMWH is the drug in all trimesters.
“Pregnancy PE at 9 weeks: IV UFH, subcutaneous UFH or aspirin throughout”
Subcutaneous LMWH throughout (68% right); UFH is safe but needs monitoring and causes more HIT and osteoporosis.
“After delivery, stop anticoagulation, keep IV heparin for 6 months, or switch to aspirin”
Continue anticoagulation for at least 6 weeks post-partum and 3 months in total; warfarin is the keyed choice.

PE-25.punch: In pregnancy, start heparin, image without fear (fetal doses are far below 50–100 mGy), treat with weight-based LMWH throughout, lyse if she is in shock, and after delivery continue LMWH or warfarin for at least 6 weeks; NOACs never.

PE-26.sub: Respiratory → Pulmonary embolism → True or false sweep
PE-26.intro: Step 6 closes both PE decks with the beliefs that are most often wrong. Each line points back to the card that explains it, and the real questions linked here test the ECG, the D-dimer and the filter.
why: **False: sinus tachycardia is the commonest ECG finding.** S1Q3T3 appears in only about one in five; tachycardia with non-specific ST–T changes is commonest (PE-07).

**False: in high clinical probability go straight to CTPA.** A normal D-dimer cannot exclude PE when it is likely, and a raised one means little in hospital or ICU patients, where sepsis, surgery and age all raise it (PE-10).
**True: a normal perfusion scan excludes PE.** No perfusion defect means no embolus large enough to matter (PE-11).
**False: high-risk PE is defined by haemodynamic instability, not by a saddle embolus.** A saddle clot in a normotensive patient is not high risk (PE-05, PE-15).
**False: rivaroxaban needs no heparin lead-in; it starts at 15 mg twice daily for 3 weeks.** Dabigatran and edoxaban are the two that need heparin first (PE-19).
**True: NOACs are avoided in antiphospholipid syndrome.** TRAPS showed more arterial events than with warfarin (PE-19d).
**False: primary thrombolysis is not recommended in intermediate-risk PE; rescue only.** PEITHO prevented decompensation but not death and caused intracranial bleeding (PE-21d).
**False: IVC filters increase DVT.** They reduce PE (PREPIC at 8 years) at the cost of more DVT (PE-24).

topups.q: TB patient on rifampicin starts warfarin for DVT and dies of PE on day 7 — why?
a: - Rifampicin is a potent CYP2C9/3A4 (and P-gp) inducer: warfarin is cleared fast, the INR stays sub-therapeutic and the clot propagates.
- Needs 2–3 times the warfarin dose with close INR checks, or a parenteral agent (LMWH).
- DOACs interact too (levels fall) — avoid them with rifampicin.

x.sub: Respiratory → Pulmonary embolism → Rifampicin and anticoagulants
x.intro: Step 3 says every PE patient is anticoagulated, and the drug only works at the right level. Rifampicin is the strongest common inducer of drug metabolism, and a patient on TB treatment who is started on warfarin can stay unprotected for days while looking treated. The NEET 2025 recall and a Marrow question both give the death and ask why.
why: **Rifampicin is a potent CYP2C9/3A4 (and P-gp) inducer: warfarin is cleared fast, the INR stays sub-therapeutic and the clot propagates.** Rifampicin switches on the genes for these enzymes through the nuclear pregnane X receptor, so the effect starts within days and keeps building for weeks (the warfarin requirement reaches its plateau at about 4 weeks), then fades over about 4 weeks after rifampicin is stopped. The more potent S-warfarin is cleared mainly by CYP2C9. The usual loading dose then never reaches an INR of 2–3, and if heparin is stopped on schedule after 5 days the patient is left with almost no anticoagulation.

**Needs 2–3 times the warfarin dose with close INR checks, or a parenteral agent (LMWH).** In one case series the median requirement rose about 2.6-fold, and some patients need more. The danger repeats in reverse: when rifampicin stops, enzyme levels fall over weeks and the same high dose overshoots, so the INR must be followed down as well. LMWH and fondaparinux are not metabolised by the liver and are unaffected, which makes them the simplest choice during TB treatment.

**DOACs interact too (levels fall) — avoid them with rifampicin.** Rivaroxaban and apixaban are cleared partly by CYP3A4 and P-gp, edoxaban mainly through P-gp, and dabigatran is a P-gp substrate; rifampicin lowers rivaroxaban exposure by about half, apixaban by about 54% and dabigatran by about 66%. With no routine level to monitor, the labels say to avoid combining them with strong inducers.
mimic: Inducers vs inhibitors with warfarin
Rifampicin, carbamazepine, phenytoin and St John’s wort lower the INR (clot); amiodarone, fluconazole, metronidazole and co-trimoxazole raise it (bleed).
traps: “He died because the PE was too large for anticoagulation” or “warfarin is prothrombotic at the start”
The early protein C dip is real, but it is covered by the heparin overlap; the question’s point is that rifampicin kept the INR low, so he was never anticoagulated.
“Switch to a DOAC to avoid the interaction”
DOAC levels fall with rifampicin as well; use LMWH, or warfarin at a much higher dose with close INR checks.

TB on rifampin, then warfarin, dies of PE — trigger? [Marrow]

topups.q: Fat embolism syndrome — clues, Gurd criteria, management?
a: - 24–72 h after long-bone or pelvic fracture: hypoxaemia, confusion, petechiae (axillae, conjunctivae).

- Gurd major: petechial rash, respiratory insufficiency (PaO2 <60), CNS depression; diagnosis = ≥2 major, or 1 major + ≥4 minor (tachycardia, fever, retinal fat, fat in urine, falling platelets/Hb, high ESR).
- Prevention: early fracture fixation; treatment is supportive (O2, lung-protective ventilation); steroids are not recommended.

x.sub: Respiratory → Embolism → Fat embolism syndrome
x.intro: Step 6 closes with the embolus that is not a clot. After a long-bone or pelvic fracture, marrow fat enters torn veins and lodges in the lung, and in some patients passes on to the brain and skin. It looks like PE on day 2 after a fracture, but it is diagnosed clinically and treated by support alone. The Marrow questions test the clinical picture and which features are major Gurd criteria.
why: **24–72 h after long-bone or pelvic fracture: hypoxaemia, confusion, petechiae (axillae, conjunctivae).** Respiratory failure usually comes first and the rash last. Two mechanisms combine: fat globules block small vessels (mechanical), and lipase breaks the fat into free fatty acids that injure the capillary endothelium (biochemical), which explains the delay of a day or more and the ARDS-like lung. Fat passes to the systemic circulation through a patent foramen ovale or through the lung capillaries, causing confusion and petechiae; the petechiae lie on the upper body because fat floats to the non-dependent branches of the aortic arch. They are often absent and fade within days.

**Gurd major: petechial rash, respiratory insufficiency (PaO₂ <60), CNS depression; diagnosis is ≥2 major, or 1 major + ≥4 minor (tachycardia, fever, retinal fat, fat in urine, falling platelets or haemoglobin, high ESR).** Retinal changes, jaundice and renal changes are minor criteria, not major ones, which is what the Marrow ‘all except’ questions turn on. The form most often quoted (LITFL, WikEM) is at least one major plus four minor criteria; many reviews also accept two major criteria, as the card does. No test confirms the diagnosis: fat in urine or sputum is non-specific, and MRI of the brain may show a ‘starfield’ of small diffusion lesions.

**Prevention: early fracture fixation; treatment is supportive (oxygen, lung-protective ventilation); steroids are not recommended.** Fixing the fracture early, ideally within 24 hours, stops repeated release of marrow fat. Support means oxygen, ventilation as for ARDS and avoiding hypovolaemia; most patients recover fully if hypoxic brain injury is avoided. Prophylactic steroids reduced FES in a meta-analysis of small, poor-quality trials (Bederman 2009: six trials, 389 patients, no effect on mortality), so they are not routinely recommended, and they are considered ineffective as treatment of established FES.
mimic: Fat embolism vs thrombotic PE after a fracture
Both cause hypoxia within days; FES adds confusion and petechiae, typically at 24–72 h, while CTPA is usually clear. PE comes from a DVT, is usually later, and shows a filling defect.
Fat embolism vs head injury after trauma
Both cause confusion; in FES the patient was lucid after the injury and deteriorates at 24–72 h, with hypoxia and petechiae and a CT head without a bleed.
traps: “Retinal changes are a major Gurd criterion”
They are minor; the three major ones are petechial rash, respiratory insufficiency and cerebral involvement.
“Treat fat embolism with heparin or steroids”
Treatment is supportive; heparin raises free fatty acids and bleeding risk, and steroids are not recommended.

Fat embolism syndrome.
Major (Gurd) criteria for fat embolism syndrome — all except? [Marrow]
Retinal changes (a minor criterion).
x.punch: Hypoxaemia, confusion and upper-body petechiae 24–72 h after a long-bone fracture are fat embolism syndrome: the Gurd major criteria are respiratory failure, cerebral signs and rash, and care is early fixation and support, not steroids.

spine: Grading the risk

Once PE is confirmed, shock or arrest makes it high risk, and in stable patients PESI or sPESI, RV imaging and troponin sort the rest into intermediate-high, intermediate-low and low risk, which decides where and how they are treated.
Holding up the failing RV

In high-risk PE the RV is supported with oxygen while avoiding intubation where possible, little or no fluid, noradrenaline to restore its coronary perfusion, and VA-ECMO as a bridge to clot removal when it collapses.
Anticoagulation for every patient

Every PE is anticoagulated: LMWH or fondaparinux for most, UFH when reperfusion may follow or the kidneys fail, then a NOAC in preference to warfarin for at least 3 months, longer when the risk persists.
Thrombolysis for the unstable

Systemic thrombolysis is for high-risk PE and for rescue when a patient deteriorates on anticoagulation, not for stable intermediate-risk patients, and recent stroke, surgery, trauma or bleeding bars it.
When lysis fails or is barred

Surgical embolectomy or catheter-directed treatment replaces lysis when it fails or is contraindicated, and an IVC filter is kept for the patient who cannot be anticoagulated, because it trades fewer PEs for more DVT.
Pregnancy and the sweep

In pregnancy the same pathway runs with low-dose imaging and LMWH throughout, warfarin only after delivery and NOACs never, and the true/false sweep tests the beliefs most often wrong across both PE decks.
RESP06B.primer: RESP06A ended with the diagnosis made; this deck decides how dangerous the PE is and what to do about it. Troponin is released by an ischaemic right ventricle and BNP by a stretched one, so both are markers of RV strain rather than of the clot itself. Anticoagulants do not dissolve clot: they stop it growing while the body’s own fibrinolysis clears it over weeks, whereas thrombolytics (alteplase, tenecteplase) activate plasminogen to dissolve it within hours at the price of bleeding. Heparins work through antithrombin, while NOACs (DOACs) inhibit factor Xa or thrombin directly and are cleared partly by the kidneys.

PLEU-01.sub: Respiratory → Pleura → Parietal vs visceral pleura
PLEU-01.intro: Step 1 starts with the two layers, because their differences explain where pleural pain comes from and where pleural fluid is made and cleared. The parietal layer, on the chest wall, does almost all the work; the visceral layer is wrapped on the lung.
why: **Parietal: systemic arteries (intercostal, pericardiophrenic, musculophrenic). Visceral: mainly bronchial arteries.** The parietal capillaries are systemic and lie close to the pleural surface, so they are the main source of pleural fluid. The visceral pleura in humans is thick and supplied by bronchial arteries, draining largely to the pulmonary veins.

**Parietal: intercostal nerves for the costal and peripheral diaphragmatic pleura, phrenic for the central diaphragmatic pleura. Visceral: no pain fibres.** So pleuritic pain means the parietal pleura is involved. Irritation of the central diaphragm is felt at the shoulder tip (phrenic, C3–5); the peripheral diaphragm and costal pleura refer to the chest wall and upper abdomen. The visceral pleura has only autonomic supply, which is why a pneumonia or tumour inside the lung is painless until it reaches the parietal pleura.

**Parietal pleura forms the fluid (capillaries) and removes it (lymphatic stomata); the visceral pleura absorbs little.** Fluid filters from parietal capillaries into the space and leaves through stomata in the parietal pleura, mostly over the diaphragm and lower mediastinum, into lymphatics that can raise their flow many times before fluid builds up. An effusion (RESP07B) therefore needs either more filtration than the lymphatics can clear, or blocked lymphatics.
mimic: Parietal vs visceral pleura
Parietal: systemic supply, somatic nerves, pain, makes and clears fluid. Visceral: bronchial supply, no pain fibres, little role in fluid turnover.
traps: “Chest pain in lung disease comes from the visceral pleura or the parenchyma”
Neither has pain fibres; the pain comes from the parietal pleura. Only half the cohort chose this on DocT GT (PLEU-13).
“The parietal pleura is supplied by bronchial arteries”
That is the visceral pleura; the parietal pleura is systemic (PLEU-13a).
decode: Chest pain caused by respiratory disease usually originates from involvement of? [DocT GT]
Parietal pleura (50% right).
[pattern] Shoulder-tip pain with a basal pleural process — which nerve?
Phrenic (central diaphragmatic pleura).
PLEU-01.punch: The parietal pleura is the working layer: systemic blood, the pain fibres, and both the making and the draining of pleural fluid; the visceral pleura feels nothing.

PLEU-02.intro: Step 1 continues with the fluid itself. Its normal values are the baseline against which every effusion in RESP07B is judged, and the one that surprises people is the pH.
why: **About 0.2 mL/kg.** A few millilitres in each hemithorax: enough to let the layers glide, far too little to see on a film or ultrasound. Anything visible is abnormal.

**1500–1800 cells/mm³: macrophages 75%, lymphocytes about 25%, others about 2%.** Neutrophils, eosinophils and mesothelial cells are scanty, so a neutrophil-rich fluid points to an acute process such as a parapneumonic effusion, and a lymphocyte-rich one beyond the normal share points to tuberculosis or malignancy.
**1–1.5 g/dL protein.** The fluid is a low-protein filtrate, so its ratio to serum protein is well below the 0.5 that Light’s criteria use to call an exudate.

**pH 7.62, above plasma.** The pleural fluid holds more bicarbonate than plasma, so it is alkaline. A fall to below 7.2 therefore means a large acid load (bacteria and neutrophils metabolising glucose), which is why a pH under 7.2 in a parapneumonic effusion is the classic indication to drain (RESP07B).
mimic: Normal pleural fluid vs a transudate
Both are low in protein, but a transudate is a visible volume; normal fluid is too small to image.
traps: “Normal pleural fluid pH is about 7.4”
It is about 7.6, above plasma (PLEU-13b).
decode: [pattern] Predominant cell in normal pleural fluid?
Macrophages.
[pattern] Normal pleural fluid pH compared with blood?
Higher (about 7.6).
PLEU-02.punch: Normal pleural fluid is a tiny, low-protein, macrophage-rich and alkaline film; a pH below 7.2 is a long way from normal.

PLEU-03.intro: Step 2 sorts pneumothorax by where the air came from. The class matters because it tells you how much lung reserve is left: a primary pneumothorax in a healthy young man is often tolerated, while the same size in a man with COPD can cause type 2 failure.
why: **Primary spontaneous: no known lung disease, rupture of a subpleural bleb, tall thin young men, upper lobe; smoking (cannabis more than tobacco) raises the risk. Incidence 24 per lakh a year in men, 9.8 in women.** Those two figures are the English general-practice consultation rates for all pneumothorax, primary and secondary together (Gupta, Thorax 2000); BTS 2010 gives primary spontaneous pneumothorax alone as 18–28 per lakh a year in men and 1.2–6 in women. Apical blebs sit where the distending pressure on the lung is greatest in a tall chest, which is why the apex and the tall build go together. Smoking raises the risk in a dose-related way. Recurrence after a first episode is about one in three (pooled 32%, 29% within the first year, in a 2018 meta-analysis). A woman of reproductive age with recurrent right-sided pneumothorax around her periods has catamenial pneumothorax, from thoracic endometriosis (diaphragmatic defects and implants); it recurs often and needs VATS repair of the diaphragm with pleurodesis and hormonal suppression.

**Secondary spontaneous: emphysema, asthma, cystic fibrosis, tuberculosis, Pneumocystis, fibrosis, histiocytosis X, lymphangioleiomyomatosis, Marfan and Ehlers–Danlos, lung cancer.** COPD is by far the commonest. The diseased lung has little reserve, so even a small pneumothorax can cause marked hypoxaemia and hypercapnia; the card’s watch line holds — more symptoms, higher mortality, always admit (PLEU-11). In a COPD patient who suddenly worsens, think pneumothorax before ‘another exacerbation’: hyperresonance and quiet breath sounds are already present in the emphysematous chest, so the examination does not separate them, the film does.

**Traumatic: penetrating or blunt chest injury; the second commonest finding after rib fractures.** Blunt trauma ruptures alveoli or lets a rib fragment pierce the lung; many are occult on the supine trauma film and seen only on CT (PLEU-06).

**Iatrogenic: subclavian or jugular cannulation, thoracentesis, transthoracic or transbronchial biopsy, positive-pressure ventilation.** The subclavian route carries a higher pneumothorax risk than the internal jugular because the needle passes over the lung apex. Desaturation or aspiration of air during attempts means stop, get a chest X-ray, and do not try the other side before it, since a bilateral pneumothorax is far more dangerous.
mimic: Secondary pneumothorax vs COPD exacerbation
Both bring sudden breathlessness and hypercapnia in a COPD patient; the signs overlap, so the film (or ultrasound) decides. Sudden onset and unilateral reduction in breath sounds favour pneumothorax.
Catamenial vs ordinary primary pneumothorax
Catamenial: woman, right side, recurring within about 72 hours of menses, from endometriosis.
traps: “Sudden breathlessness in COPD is an exacerbation”

A third of the cohort chose COPD exacerbation or asthma; sudden deterioration in COPD is a secondary pneumothorax until imaging says otherwise. The stem’s ‘after a fall’ and bilateral hyperresonance are loose wording, and DocT’s key is still spontaneous pneumothorax.
“Try the other subclavian after a failed, desaturating attempt”
Stop and take a film first; a pneumothorax on one side plus a second on the other is the disaster to avoid.
decode: Long-standing COPD, sudden breathlessness, PaCO₂ 72, pH 7.32 — diagnosis? [DocT]
Secondary spontaneous pneumothorax (68% right).
Recurrent right-sided chest pain and dyspnoea with menstruation, small pneumothorax — cause? [DocT GT]
Thoracic endometriosis (catamenial pneumothorax; 84%).
Desaturation after failed subclavian attempts — next step? [Marrow]
Abort, chest X-ray, drain if pneumothorax.
PLEU-03.punch: Primary pneumothorax is a burst bleb in healthy lung; secondary is the same leak in diseased lung with no reserve, so the class, not the size, sets the danger.

PLEU-04.intro: Step 3 is what happens when the leak acts as a valve. Each breath adds air that cannot leave, pleural pressure climbs above atmospheric, and the patient dies of hypoxia and of a heart that cannot fill. Seven questions test it, and they ask three things: recognise it from the bedside (often in a ventilated or trauma patient), act without imaging, and know that the needle is only a bridge to a drain.
why: **A one-way valve: air enters in inspiration and cannot leave, so pleural pressure rises with each breath; the lung collapses and the mediastinum shifts.** The flap of torn lung or chest wall opens when pleural pressure is lower than airway pressure and closes when it rises. Under positive-pressure ventilation the ventilator drives air in on every breath, so pressure builds within minutes; in a spontaneously breathing patient it builds more slowly. The signs follow the pressure: absent breath sounds and hyperresonance on that side, rising peak and plateau pressures on the ventilator (stiff chest, collapsed lung), surgical emphysema tracking into the neck, and late tracheal deviation away from the affected side.

**Venous return falls (raised pressure, caval distortion) and cardiac chamber pressures equalise → shock and arrest.** Raised intrathoracic pressure compresses and kinks the venae cavae, the right heart fills poorly, and stroke volume falls; the neck veins distend unless the patient is hypovolaemic. In the awake, spontaneously breathing patient the body defends blood pressure for a long time and hypoxia and distress dominate, so hypotension is a late, pre-arrest sign. In the ventilated or hypovolaemic patient hypotension comes early. Blood pressure goes down, never up: hypertension is not a sign of tension.

**Immediate needle decompression without waiting for imaging: 14–16 G cannula, 4th–5th intercostal space, mid- or anterior axillary line.** ATLS 10th edition places it in adults at the 4th or 5th space just anterior to the mid-axillary line, because the chest wall is thinner there than at the old site, the 2nd space in the mid-clavicular line. In a meta-analysis of chest-wall thickness (Laan, Injury 2016) a 5 cm cannula was predicted to fail in about 38% at the 2nd space mid-clavicular, 31% at the 4th–5th space mid-axillary and 13% at the 4th–5th space anterior axillary line, and failure rises with body mass; many authors therefore advise a longer (7–8 cm) catheter in adults. The 2nd space mid-clavicular site is still accepted in children, whose chest wall is thin. The needle only converts tension into an open, simple pneumothorax and kinks or blocks easily, so it is temporising: the definitive treatment is a chest drain, 5th space just anterior to the mid-axillary line, above the rib (PLEU-12). In a ventilated trauma patient a finger thoracostomy at the same site is an alternative to the needle.
mimic: Tension pneumothorax vs cardiac tamponade

Both cause hypotension and distended neck veins. Tension: absent breath sounds, hyperresonance, high airway pressure, tracheal shift. Tamponade: breath sounds normal, quiet heart sounds, effusion on echo.
Tension pneumothorax vs haemothorax
Haemothorax: dull percussion and flat neck veins from blood loss; treated with a large-bore tube.
Tension pneumothorax vs mainstem intubation
Both give one silent side and high airway pressure after intubation; ultrasound with a lung pulse and no lung point, and tube depth, decide (PLEU-08).
traps: “Respiratory distress with hypertension is a sign of tension”
It is the odd one out: tension lowers blood pressure; tracheal deviation, quiet breath sounds and distended neck veins are all signs.
“Pneumothorax suspected in trauma: chest radiograph first”
Not when the bedside signs are of tension (poor compliance, silent chest, shock): decompress first. The film is for the stable patient.
“Needle decompression is the definitive treatment”
It is a bridge; the definitive treatment is a chest drain (Marrow keys tube thoracostomy for the ventilated COPD patient and for trauma with surgical emphysema and hypotension).
“Pneumothorax during a subclavian line with stable vitals: needle decompression first”
Marrow keys this, but stable vitals mean a simple pneumothorax: image, then drain. Decompression without imaging is only for tension. For Marrow pick its key; in practice and elsewhere, image first.
decode: Which is NOT a sign of tension pneumothorax? [DocT GT]
Respiratory distress with hypertension.
Ventilated trauma patient: hypotension, rising peak pressure, one silent side, cervical crepitus [DocT GT]
Pneumothorax (tension) — decompress and drain.
Trauma, decreased breath sounds, poor compliance — condition and immediate step? [NEET 2025]
Tension pneumothorax; needle decompression.
Ventilated COPD on PEEP 10, sudden desaturation and hypotension — definitive treatment? [Marrow]
Tube thoracostomy (needle is temporising).
PLEU-04.punch: Tension is a clinical diagnosis — shock, a silent side, rising airway pressure — and is decompressed at the 4th–5th space just anterior to the mid-axillary line before any film, then drained; stable vitals mean image first.

Tension pneumothorax

**chest X-ray (or ultrasound), then drain** if needed

PLEU-05.intro: Step 3 has a second way to lose pleural pressure: a hole in the chest wall rather than in the lung. The pleural space then follows atmospheric pressure, and the mediastinum swings with each breath.
why: **Penetrating trauma: a sucking chest wound; negative pleural pressure is lost.** When the wound is wide (ATLS: about two-thirds of the tracheal diameter or more), air takes the easier path through the wound rather than the trachea, so the lung on that side is not ventilated.

**Mediastinal flutter: the mediastinum shifts away from the wound in inspiration and back towards it in expiration.** In inspiration the intact side’s pleural pressure falls while the open side stays atmospheric, so the mediastinum is pulled to the intact side; in expiration it swings back. The intact lung also loses volume with each swing.

**It distorts the venae cavae (IVC torsion), so venous return falls further.** The swinging mediastinum kinks the great veins, adding a circulatory insult to the ventilatory one. Treatment: a three-sided occlusive dressing or vented chest seal (a fully sealed dressing can create tension), then a chest drain away from the wound, and surgical closure.
mimic: Open vs tension pneumothorax
Open: pleural pressure is atmospheric through a chest-wall hole and the mediastinum swings. Tension: pleural pressure is above atmospheric and the mediastinum is pushed steadily away.
traps: “Seal the wound on all four sides”
A full seal turns an open pneumothorax into tension if the lung is also leaking; tape three sides or use a vented seal.
decode: [pattern] Sucking chest wound — first-aid dressing?
Three-sided occlusive dressing (or vented seal), then a chest drain away from the wound.
PLEU-05.punch: An open pneumothorax makes pleural pressure atmospheric, so the mediastinum swings to and fro and kinks the cavae; seal on three sides and drain elsewhere.

PLEU-06.sub: Respiratory → Pleura → Pneumothorax in the ICU
PLEU-06.intro: Step 3 in the setting that matters most to you: the ventilated patient. Positive pressure drives air through any leak, the patient cannot complain, and the supine film hides the air, so the diagnosis rests on the ventilator and the monitor. The questions test the bedside signs, and what to do with a pneumothorax seen only on CT.
why: **4–15% of ventilated patients; higher in ARDS (reduced by 48 h of paralysis); up to 50% of chest trauma victims.** Barotrauma follows high transpulmonary pressure in a lung with stiff and normal regions side by side. In ACURASYS, 48 hours of cisatracurium in early severe ARDS lowered pneumothorax (about 4% vs 12%), probably by removing asynchrony and large patient-generated swings. Pneumomediastinum and pneumopericardium from barotrauma are usually managed without a drain: keep plateau pressure under 30 cmH₂O and paralyse if the patient is fighting the ventilator.

**Sudden unexplained deterioration, rising oxygen need, haemodynamic instability, a sudden rise in peak and plateau pressures.** Add surgical emphysema, which tracks from the mediastinum into the chest wall and neck. In a ventilated patient with these signs and a suspected pneumothorax, drain without waiting for a film. A rise in both peak and plateau points to the lung or chest (stiffness); a rise in peak with an unchanged plateau points to the airway or tube.

**Occult pneumothorax: seen on CT but not on the chest X-ray; up to 15% in trauma, 64% in multitrauma; ultrasound detects 92–100%.** The air lies anteriorly in the supine patient, where the AP film does not show it (PLEU-07). Ultrasound of the anterior chest finds most of these.

**Controversial: a randomised trial in ventilated trauma patients found no difference in respiratory distress between observation and a prophylactic drain.** This is OPTICC (Am J Surg 2021; 142 ventilated trauma patients): respiratory distress occurred in 38% of observed and 25% of drained patients, a difference that was not significant in an underpowered trial, and mortality was the same. About a quarter of observed patients went on to need a drain, rising to about 40% of those ventilated for 5 days or more. So a stable occult pneumothorax may be observed on positive pressure, with a low threshold to drain if it grows, the patient deteriorates or ventilation is prolonged.
mimic: Pneumothorax vs blocked tube or bronchospasm on the ventilator
Pneumothorax raises both peak and plateau pressure with one silent side; a blocked tube or bronchospasm raises peak with plateau unchanged.
traps: “An occult pneumothorax is an indication for a chest tube”
No; a stable occult pneumothorax may be observed even on positive pressure (OPTICC).
“Any pneumothorax needing positive-pressure ventilation needs a chest tube”
Also false; observation is acceptable for the stable occult one. Together these two distractors drew most of the 35% who missed the DocT GT question.
“All traumatic haemothoraces need VATS”
Only a retained haemothorax after tube drainage (more than about 300 mL) does.
decode: Trauma, haemopneumothorax drained — which is true? [DocT GT]
Persistent air leak or recurrent pneumothorax despite a working tube → look for a tracheobronchial injury (bronchoscopy) (65%).
Ventilated polytrauma on high PEEP, surgical emphysema and rising peak pressure — next? [Marrow]
Chest tubes, without waiting for a film.
ARDS, asynchrony despite deep sedation, pneumopericardium — next? [Marrow]
Neuromuscular blocker infusion.
PLEU-06.punch: On the ventilator, a pneumothorax shows as a sudden rise in peak and plateau with shock or desaturation, and is drained on those signs; one seen only on CT can be watched if the patient is stable.

parts.q: Persistent large air leak after chest trauma despite a working drain — what is it until proven otherwise?
parts.a: A tracheobronchial injury; bronchoscopy.

PLEU-07.sub: Respiratory → Pleura → Chest X-ray and CT in pneumothorax
PLEU-07.intro: Step 4 is about finding the air, and the chest X-ray fails in the patient who needs it most. In the supine patient air rises to the front of the chest and spreads over the lung instead of collecting at the apex, so there is no apical pleural line to see. The questions test the sign that replaces it.
why: **Sensitivity: lateral decubitus 88%, erect 59%, supine 37%.** These are against CT. The supine AP film misses most pneumothoraces; in one ICU series about 30% were missed at first and half of those progressed to tension, and missed cases went on to tension far more often than recognised ones. The lateral decubitus film, affected side up, lets air rise to the lateral chest wall, where it is easy to see.

**On a supine film air collects anteromedially and subpulmonically: the deep sulcus sign, a lucent upper quadrant, an unusually sharp hemidiaphragm.** In supine patients the anteromedial recess holds about 38% of pneumothoraces and the subpulmonic recess about 26%. Air in the lateral costophrenic sulcus makes it abnormally deep and lucent (the deep sulcus sign); air under the lung outlines the diaphragm unusually sharply, sometimes as two diaphragm lines (the double diaphragm sign, also a supine pneumothorax sign); air in front of the heart sharpens the cardiac border.

**Mimic: a skin fold.** A skin fold is an edge — a band of density that ends abruptly, with lung markings continuing beyond it, and it often runs beyond the chest wall. A pneumothorax shows a thin white visceral pleural line with no lung markings beyond it.

**CT is the gold standard: sizing, separating a bulla from a pneumothorax (avoids draining a bulla and creating a fistula), checking tube position.** A drain pushed into a large bulla in emphysema makes a bronchopleural fistula; CT shows which is which. After previous thoracic surgery adhesions loculate the air, so drains go in under CT or ultrasound guidance. Ultrasound beats the supine film but does not beat CT.
mimic: Pneumothorax vs bulla
Pneumothorax: pleural line parallel to the chest wall, no markings beyond. Bulla: wall concave towards the chest wall, thin strands may cross it; CT settles it.
Deep sulcus sign vs normal supine film
A unilateral, unusually deep and lucent costophrenic angle in a supine patient is pneumothorax until proven otherwise.
traps: “Visible lung point sign” on the X-ray
The lung point is an ultrasound sign (PLEU-08); the supine X-ray sign is the deep sulcus.
“A radiolucent costophrenic angle after a jugular line is a skin fold or a normal supine variant”
It is a supine pneumothorax (the deep sulcus sign).
“Double diaphragm sign” as the wrong answer
It too can appear in supine pneumothorax, so the image decides; DocT keys deep sulcus for its picture.
“Ultrasound is superior to both chest X-ray and CT”
False (Marrow): ultrasound beats the supine film, but CT is still the reference standard.
decode: Ventilated ICU patient, suspected pneumothorax — most suggestive supine X-ray finding? [DocT GT]
Deep sulcus sign (87%).
Supine portable film after a jugular line, lucent costophrenic angle — diagnosis? [DocT GT]
Pneumothorax in a supine patient.
Ventilated trauma patient, acute hypoxia, image shown — the sign? [DocT GT]
Deep sulcus sign.
False statement on ultrasound for pneumothorax? [Marrow]
‘Ultrasound is superior to CXR and CT.’
PLEU-07.punch: Supine, the air goes to the front and the base, so look for a deep, lucent costophrenic angle rather than an apical line; the supine film misses most, and CT is the reference.

PLEU-08.sub: Respiratory → Pleura → Lung ultrasound for pneumothorax
PLEU-08.intro: Step 4 moves to the bedside test that has replaced the supine film. Every sign rests on one fact: the visceral pleura can be seen only where it touches the parietal pleura. Air between them hides it, so anything generated by the visceral pleura — sliding, B-lines, the lung pulse — proves the layers are apposed at that point, and only the lung point proves air. This card was asked ten times, and the commonest error was treating absent sliding as a diagnosis.
why: **Lung sliding present = no pneumothorax at that spot.** Sliding is the visceral pleura moving on the parietal pleura with breathing, seen at the pleural line about half a centimetre below the rib line (the ‘bat sign’ of two ribs and the line between them). Because air rises, scan the least dependent part — the anterior chest in a supine patient. Absent sliding is sensitive for pneumothorax but not specific: about 91% specificity in the critically ill, less in ARDS or after pleurodesis, because anything that stops the lung moving or glues the layers abolishes it (part e).

**B-lines present = rules out pneumothorax there (negative predictive value 100%).** B-lines are vertical, hyperechoic, laser-like artefacts that start at the pleural line, reach the edge of the screen without fading, erase A-lines and move with sliding. They arise from the visceral pleura and fluid-thickened septa beneath it, so they cannot form where air separates the layers. The lung pulse — the heartbeat transmitted to a still pleural line — rules out pneumothorax in the same way: no sliding, but the visceral pleura is there and touching. A-lines, horizontal reverberations of the pleural line, are seen both in normal lung and in pneumothorax, so they decide nothing alone.

**Lung point: where sliding meets no sliding — 100% specific for pneumothorax.** It is the edge of the pneumothorax, where the collapsed lung touches the chest wall intermittently with breathing; on M-mode, seashore and barcode patterns alternate. In Lichtenstein’s study (Intensive Care Med 2000) it was never seen without a pneumothorax, but it was found in only 66% of pneumothoraces (75% of radio-occult ones): a totally collapsed lung never reaches the chest wall, so a large pneumothorax may have no lung point. The more lateral or posterior the lung point, the larger the pneumothorax.

**Barcode (stratosphere) sign: the M-mode pattern of absent sliding. Normal is the seashore sign.** In M-mode the still chest wall gives horizontal lines above the pleural line; normally the moving lung below gives a granular ‘sand’ pattern (seashore). Without sliding, horizontal lines continue below the pleural line too, like a barcode. The barcode shows only that sliding is absent; it does not prove air. The sinusoid sign is something else — the lung line moving towards the pleural line in an effusion.

**Other causes of absent sliding: mainstem intubation (the other lung), pleural adhesions, endobronchial obstruction, diaphragm paralysis.** Add atelectasis from a mucus plug, ARDS, pleurodesis and apnoea. Right after intubation, absent sliding on the left with a lung pulse is a right mainstem tube: the left lung is touching but not ventilated. Pull the tube back, do not drain the chest.
mimic: Pneumothorax vs right mainstem intubation
Both abolish sliding on the left. Lung pulse, no lung point and a tube too deep point to the tube; a lung point means pneumothorax.
Barcode vs seashore vs sinusoid
Barcode: no sliding. Seashore: normal sliding. Sinusoid: effusion.
traps: “Absent sliding, A-lines, lung pulse after intubation: drain the left chest”
The lung pulse excludes pneumothorax; this is a mainstem intubation — adjust the tube. Only 22% got this DocT GT question right.
“B-lines or a lung pulse confirm the pneumothorax”
Both exclude it; only the lung point confirms. A third of the cohort missed this (67%).
“B-lines are horizontal hyperechoic lines”
Those are A-lines; B-lines are vertical.
“Ultrasound is superior to both chest X-ray and CT”
It beats the supine film; CT remains the reference standard.
“No lung point, so no pneumothorax”
Sensitivity is only 66%; a completely collapsed lung has no lung point.
decode: Absent sliding and barcode on M-mode — which finding confirms pneumothorax? [DocT; DocT GT]
Lung point (67%).
COPD intubated, SpO₂ falls, peak 45, no sliding on left with A-lines and lung pulse — next step? [DocT GT]
Adjust the endotracheal tube (22%).
Absent sliding; M-mode shows parallel horizontal lines above and below the pleural line — which sign is absent? [DocT GT]
Seashore sign.
Tall young man, sudden dyspnoea, M-mode image — which sign? [Marrow]
Barcode sign.
PLEU-08.punch: Sliding, B-lines or a lung pulse at a spot exclude pneumothorax there; absent sliding and a barcode only raise the question, and the lung point alone answers it (specific, not sensitive).

parts.a: Mainstem intubation of the other side; pull the tube back.

PLEU-09.intro: Step 4 widens from one diagnosis to the breathless patient. The BLUE protocol (Lichtenstein, Chest 2008) is a decision tree: check sliding, then the anterior artefact (A or B), then the leg veins, then the posterolateral bases. Each combination is a ‘profile’ that points to one diagnosis. The questions give you the findings and ask for the diagnosis, and the hard one is separating ARDS from cardiogenic oedema.
why: **Pulmonary oedema: B profile (sliding + bilateral anterior B-lines).** Three or more B-lines in an intercostal space (lung rockets) on both sides anteriorly, with sliding preserved: fluid in the septa of a lung that still moves. In the 2008 study: sensitivity 97%, specificity 95%. Cardiogenic oedema gives homogeneous B-lines from the bases up with a smooth pleural line and often effusions; ARDS gives patchy B-lines with spared areas, an irregular thickened pleural line, small subpleural consolidations and reduced sliding.

**Pneumothorax: A′ profile (no sliding, A-lines) + lung point.** The prime means sliding is abolished. In the 2008 study there were 9 pneumothoraces and A′ with a lung point found 8 of them: sensitivity 88%, specificity 100%, as on the card and in Lichtenstein’s own later review. The 2008 abstract prints 81%, which cannot be a fraction of 9 and is a misprint. A′ without a lung point is not a diagnosis: it needs another test (CT or film), because the lung point may be absent in a complete collapse (PLEU-08).

**Pulmonary embolism: A profile + venous thrombosis.** The anterior lung looks normal (sliding with A-lines) because embolism does not wet the lung; a thrombus on venous compression of the legs supplies the diagnosis. Sensitivity 81%, specificity 99%.

**COPD or asthma: A profile, veins free, no PLAPS.** A normal-looking lung, no thrombus and nothing at the bases: the cause is in the airways, which ultrasound cannot see. Sensitivity 89%, specificity 97%.

**Pneumonia: A + PLAPS; B′; A/B; C.** PLAPS is the posterolateral alveolar or pleural syndrome (consolidation or effusion at the bases); B′ is B-lines with abolished sliding (inflammatory adhesion); A/B is B-lines on one side only; C is anterior consolidation. Combined, sensitivity 89%, specificity 94%. Overall, the profiles gave the right diagnosis in 90.5% of 260 patients, a figure drawn from experienced operators after excluding patients with unclear or multiple diagnoses, so it is likely to be lower in ordinary hands.
mimic: Cardiogenic oedema vs ARDS
Both are B-line lungs. Oedema: homogeneous, smooth pleural line, sliding kept, effusions. ARDS: patchy with spared areas, irregular pleural line, subpleural consolidations, reduced sliding.
Pulmonary embolism vs COPD
Both give the A profile; the leg veins separate them.
traps: “Irregular pleural line with subpleural consolidations and B-lines = cardiogenic oedema”
That pattern is ARDS; cardiogenic oedema has a smooth pleural line and uniform B-lines. Only 44% got this right.
“Diffuse bilateral B-lines with sliding could be pneumothorax or massive effusion”
B-lines exclude pneumothorax, and an effusion is an anechoic space at the bases, not a B-line field.
“A′ profile alone diagnoses pneumothorax”
Not without a lung point.
decode: Acute dyspnoea, more than 3 B-lines per field with preserved sliding — diagnosis? [DocT]
Pulmonary oedema (86%).
Multiple bilateral B-lines in all zones in a ventilated patient — diagnosis? [DocT GT]
Alveolar (interstitial) oedema (87–93%).
Irregular pleural line, subpleural consolidation, B-lines in the same space, bilateral infiltrates — diagnosis? [DocT GT]
ARDS (44%).
Right: no sliding, no B-lines, lung point, barcode — diagnosis? [DocT GT]
Pneumothorax (94%).
PLEU-09.punch: BLUE reads sliding, then A or B anteriorly, then the leg veins, then the bases: B profile is oedema, A′ with a lung point is pneumothorax, A with a clot is embolism, A with nothing is COPD or asthma, and the rest is pneumonia.
