PLEU-10.sub: Respiratory → Pleura → BTS management of primary spontaneous pneumothorax
PLEU-10.intro: Step 5 turns to treatment. The card is BTS 2010; the 2023 BTS pleural guideline kept its spirit (treat symptoms, not size) but went further, and an exam may test either.
why: **Large = more than 2 cm from lung margin to chest wall at the level of the hilum; symptoms matter more than size.** A 2 cm rim at the hilum is roughly half the hemithorax by volume. In BTS 2023 size no longer decides whether to intervene; it mainly tells you whether a drain can safely be placed at the bedside.

**Small and not breathless: consider discharge, outpatient review in 2–4 weeks.** BTS 2023 extends this: a minimally symptomatic PSP can be managed conservatively whatever its size, after Brown (NEJM 2020; 316 patients with moderate to large PSP): re-expansion at 8 weeks 94.4% with observation vs 98.5% with intervention, non-inferior, and only 15% of the observed group needed a procedure.

**Large or breathless: needle aspiration, 16–18 G, up to 2.5 L; success = less than 2 cm and breathing better.** Aspiration works as well as a large-bore drain and shortens stay. BTS 2023 adds an ambulatory device as an option, by shared decision: in RAMPP (Hallifax, Lancet 2020; 236 patients) it cut median stay from 4 days to 0 and needed fewer further procedures, at the cost of more adverse events.
**If aspiration fails: small-bore chest drain, 8–14 Fr, and admit; suction is not routine.** Bilateral or haemodynamically unstable pneumothorax goes straight to a drain.
mimic: BTS 2010 vs BTS 2023 for PSP

2010: size and breathlessness choose observation or aspiration. 2023: symptoms and high-risk features choose; conservative care allowed regardless of size; aspiration, ambulatory device or drain by shared decision.
traps: “Primary pneumothorax is first treated with a large-bore drain”
No; aspiration (or observation if symptoms are minimal) first (PLEU-13g).
decode: [pattern] Young man, first PSP, 3 cm rim at the hilum, mildly breathless — first step (BTS 2010)?
Needle aspiration.
[pattern] Large PSP, minimal symptoms — acceptable under BTS 2023?
Conservative management.
PLEU-10.punch: For primary pneumothorax, breathlessness, not the rim, chooses the treatment: observe if comfortable, aspirate if breathless, drain small-bore if aspiration fails; BTS 2023 allows observation whatever the size.

PLEU-11.sub: Respiratory → Pleura → BTS management of secondary spontaneous pneumothorax
PLEU-11.intro: Step 5 continues with the patient who has no reserve. Because a small leak can cause respiratory failure in diseased lung (PLEU-03), the thresholds are lower and every patient is admitted.
why: **Treated as secondary: underlying lung disease, or age over 50 with a significant smoking history.** Over 50 with smoking, occult emphysema is likely even without a diagnosis, so the patient is managed as secondary. BTS 2023 keeps this as a high-risk feature.

**More than 2 cm or breathless: chest drain 8–14 Fr at once.** Aspiration fails more often in diseased lung, and the patient cannot afford a failed attempt. Ambulatory devices have weak evidence here: in a small 2021 trial (Walker, 41 patients) length of stay was no shorter, and one device, an 8 Fr pleural vent, failed early in 6 of 13 patients against 3 of 20 with a standard drain (46% vs 15%, not significant), so an ambulatory device is not a routine choice in SSP.
**1–2 cm: aspirate; if still more than 1 cm, chest drain.**

**Less than 1 cm: admit, high-flow oxygen, observe for 24 hours.** So not every secondary pneumothorax needs a tube; the small one is observed. High-flow oxygen speeds reabsorption of the air (it washes nitrogen out of the blood), but in CO₂-retaining COPD it is titrated to target saturation.

**All admitted for at least 24 h; thoracic surgical referral at 3–5 days for a persistent leak or failure to re-expand (thoracotomy with pleurectomy). No air travel until resolved; no diving unless treated surgically.** Open pleurectomy has the lowest recurrence, but VATS is now the usual approach for its lower morbidity, and BTS also lists a second ipsilateral pneumothorax, and a first contralateral one as indications. For a persistent leak in someone unfit for surgery, autologous blood patch or endobronchial valves are options.
mimic: Secondary vs primary pneumothorax management
Secondary: always admit, drain if more than 2 cm or breathless, aspirate only at 1–2 cm, observe under 1 cm. Primary: observe or aspirate, often as an outpatient.
traps: “Most should be treated with thoracotomy, stapling of blebs and pleural abrasion” as a true statement

That is old textbook wording; surgery today is for persistent leak, failure to re-expand or recurrence. DocT GT keys a different statement as false (‘all patients with secondary pneumothorax don’t need tube thoracostomy’), yet that one is true by BTS: under 1 cm is observed. Statement C is the more defensible false one; for DocT pick its key. Only 53% got it.
“Severe dyspnoea, cyanosis, large pneumothorax in a smoker of 50: oxygen only”
Large and breathless in a patient managed as secondary means a drain; DocT keys decompression then tube (98%).
decode: COPD, no air entry on the left — which is false about management? [DocT GT]
Keyed: ‘All patients with secondary pneumothorax don’t need tube thoracostomy’ (53%; key disputed).
50-year-old smoker, severe dyspnoea, cyanosis, large pneumothorax on CT — next step? [DocT]
Needle decompression then chest tube (98%).
Long-standing COPD, sudden breathlessness, hypercapnia — diagnosis? [DocT]
Spontaneous (secondary) pneumothorax (68%).
PLEU-11.punch: Secondary pneumothorax is treated harder because the lung has no reserve: admit everyone, drain if over 2 cm or breathless, aspirate at 1–2 cm, observe under 1 cm with oxygen, and refer to surgery for a leak lasting days.

PLEU-12.sub: Respiratory → Pleura → Chest drain insertion and removal
PLEU-12.intro: Step 6 is the drain itself. The safe triangle keeps the tube away from the heart, liver, spleen and the long thoracic nerve, and the rules for removal are mostly about not clamping a drain that is still doing its job.
why: **Safe triangle: the lateral edge of pectoralis major, the anterior (lateral) edge of latissimus dorsi, the line of the 5th intercostal space; apex at the base of the axilla.** Below the 5th space the diaphragm, liver and spleen rise in expiration. Go just above the rib, because the intercostal vessels and nerve run under the lower border of the rib above. For air, BTS prefers a small-bore drain inserted by Seldinger technique (guidewire, dilator, drain); large-bore drains for trauma or haemothorax go in by blunt dissection, a finger sweeping the pleura before the tube, and a trocar is never used to push a drain in.

**Large anterior pneumothorax: apico-anterior approach.** The 2nd intercostal space in the mid-clavicular line is an alternative for an apical pneumothorax, with the cosmetic and muscle-bulk drawbacks of the front of the chest.

**Removal: lung expanded and air leak stopped; suction off; clamp for up to 12 h after the leak ceases; chest X-ray at 24 h, then remove.** BTS 2010 does not advise routine clamping for pneumothorax, and a bubbling drain must never be clamped, because the leak continues and can produce tension. The usual practice is to remove the drain once bubbling has stopped and the film shows re-expansion, pulling it out during expiration or a Valsalva manoeuvre so that air is not sucked in.
mimic: Seldinger vs blunt dissection
Seldinger: small-bore, for air or free fluid. Blunt dissection: large-bore, for blood, trauma or thick fluid. Never a trocar.
traps: “Insert just below the rib”
Just above the rib; the bundle runs under the rib above.
“Clamp a bubbling drain before removal”
Never; clamping a drain that is still leaking can cause tension.
decode: [pattern] Borders of the triangle of safety?
Pectoralis major, latissimus dorsi, 5th intercostal space, apex below the axilla.
[pattern] Should a chest drain for pneumothorax be clamped before removal (BTS)?
Not routinely; never if bubbling.
PLEU-12.punch: Drains go through the safe triangle, just above a rib, small-bore by Seldinger for air, and come out when the lung is up and bubbling has stopped, without routine clamping.

PLEU-13.sub: Respiratory → Pleura → Review: true or false
PLEU-13.intro: This review runs the whole story from step 1 (the pleura) to step 5 (treatment). Each statement is a belief the questions show people hold.
why: **False: the parietal pleura is supplied by systemic arteries.** Bronchial arteries supply the visceral pleura (PLEU-01).
**False: normal pleural fluid pH is 7.62.** It holds more bicarbonate than plasma, so it is alkaline (PLEU-02).
**False: a supine chest film has a sensitivity of 37%.** Air lies anteriorly and the film looks through it (PLEU-07).
**True: the lung point is 100% specific.** But only about two-thirds sensitive (PLEU-08).
**False: B-lines exclude a pneumothorax.** They are made by the visceral pleura, which air would hide (PLEU-08).
**True: large is more than 2 cm at the hilum (BTS 2010).** In BTS 2023, symptoms rather than size decide treatment (PLEU-10).
**False: primary spontaneous pneumothorax is first treated with needle aspiration.** Or observed if symptoms are minimal (PLEU-10).
mimic: Lung point vs B-lines
Lung point confirms pneumothorax; B-lines exclude it.
traps: “Pleuritic pain comes from the visceral pleura”
Only half the cohort knew it comes from the parietal pleura.
decode: Chest pain caused by respiratory disease usually originates from? [DocT GT]
Parietal pleura (50%).
PLEU-13.punch: Parietal pleura is systemic and painful, normal fluid is alkaline, the supine film misses most pneumothoraces, B-lines exclude one and a lung point confirms it, and primary pneumothorax starts with aspiration or observation.

topups.q: Sudden hypotension and tachycardia hours after pneumonectomy — diagnosis and action?
a: - Cardiac herniation through a pericardial defect, usually within 24 h (often on coughing, turning onto the operated side, or suction on the drain); may cause SVC obstruction or arrhythmia.
- CXR/echo/CT show the heart displaced into the empty hemithorax.
- Turn the operated side UP, stop suction, and re-operate immediately to repair the pericardium; mortality is high if delayed.

x.sub: Respiratory → Pleura → Cardiac herniation after pneumonectomy
x.intro: Step 6 ends with a pleural space that has been emptied on purpose. After a pneumonectomy, especially an intrapericardial one, the pericardium may be left with a defect, and the heart can swing through it into the empty hemithorax. Anything that pulls the heart towards that side — suction on the drain, coughing, turning the patient onto the operated side, or a large pressure difference between the two hemithoraces — can trigger it.
why: **Cardiac herniation through a pericardial defect, usually within 24 h (often on coughing, turning onto the operated side, or suction on the drain); it may cause SVC obstruction or arrhythmia.** Most cases occur in theatre (about three-quarters in one review) or in the first hours, often at the moment of turning; late cases are reported. On the right the heart rotates into the empty chest and kinks the superior and inferior venae cavae: obstructive shock with a high central venous pressure, a congested face and neck, and tachycardia. On the left the ventricle is strangled by the edge of the defect: ischaemia, arrhythmia and ventricular fibrillation.

**Chest X-ray, echo or CT show the heart displaced into the empty hemithorax.** The cardiac silhouette lies in the operated side, rotated or with an abnormal contour; echo shows the displacement and the kinked cavae. Imaging must not delay action in a patient who is crashing.

**Turn the operated side up, stop suction, and re-operate at once to repair the pericardium; mortality is high if delayed.** Putting the operated side up lets gravity draw the heart back towards the midline, and removing suction ends the pull into the empty space (some reports also inject air into the operated hemithorax to push the heart back); keep tidal volumes and airway pressures modest. These buy time only: the definitive treatment is immediate re-thoracotomy, reduction of the heart and closure of the defect with a patch (direct suture can tear again). Mortality is about half when it is recognised and treated, and close to all when it is not.
mimic: Cardiac herniation vs post-operative bleeding or tamponade

All cause hypotension and tachycardia after pneumonectomy. Bleeding shows on the drain and the haemoglobin; tamponade shows a pericardial effusion; herniation shows the heart in the wrong hemithorax and often follows a position change or suction.
Cardiac herniation vs mediastinal shift from the post-pneumonectomy space
Gradual shift towards the operated side is normal as the space fills; herniation is sudden, with shock.
traps: “Turn him onto the operated side to help the remaining lung”
That swings the heart into the empty hemithorax; the operated side goes up.
“Put the pneumonectomy drain on suction to evacuate the space”
Suction on a pneumonectomy drain pulls the mediastinum and heart across; the drain is kept off suction (clamped with periodic release, or a balanced drainage system, by local practice).
decode: Sudden hypotension and tachycardia hours after pneumonectomy — diagnosis and action? [Marrow]
Cardiac herniation: operated side up, stop suction, immediate re-operation.
x.punch: Sudden shock in the first day after pneumonectomy, often on turning, coughing or suction, is cardiac herniation until shown otherwise: operated side up, suction off, back to theatre.

spine: The pleura and its fluid
The parietal pleura carries the pain fibres, makes the pleural fluid from systemic capillaries and drains it through lymphatic stomata, and normal fluid is a small, alkaline, macrophage-rich film.
Where the air comes from

Pneumothorax is classified by its cause — primary with no lung disease, secondary on diseased lung with less reserve, traumatic and iatrogenic — and the class decides how ill the patient is and how it is treated.
Air under pressure

When air enters and cannot leave, rising pleural pressure kills by hypoxia and by stopping venous return, fastest under positive-pressure ventilation, so tension is treated on clinical signs before any film.
Finding the air

Air rises anteriorly in a supine patient, so the supine film misses most pneumothoraces, CT is the reference, and ultrasound excludes one wherever sliding, B-lines or a lung pulse are seen and confirms one only with a lung point.
Treat the patient, not the rim

BTS management is driven by symptoms and by whether the lung was healthy: primary pneumothorax can be observed or aspirated, secondary needs admission and usually a drain, and the 2023 guideline allows conservative care of a minimally symptomatic primary pneumothorax whatever its size.
Draining the pleural space

A drain goes in through the safe triangle just above a rib, small-bore by Seldinger for air, and comes out once the lung is up and the leak has stopped, while a space emptied by pneumonectomy is never put on suction.
RESP07A.primer: The pleural space is a film of fluid a few millilitres thick between the visceral pleura on the lung and the parietal pleura lining the chest wall, diaphragm and mediastinum. At rest its pressure is about −5 cmH₂O, held negative because the lung recoils inward while the chest wall springs outward; once air enters, that coupling is lost and the lung shrinks towards its own resting volume. In a spontaneously breathing patient air is drawn in by the patient’s effort, but under positive-pressure ventilation the ventilator pushes air through any leak with every breath. On lung ultrasound the probe sees only the pleural line and the artefacts it makes: horizontal A-lines (reverberation), vertical B-lines (fluid-thickened septa) and sliding, the shimmer of visceral pleura moving on parietal pleura.

PLEU-14.sub: Respiratory → Pleura → Physiological effects of an effusion
PLEU-14.intro: Step 1 asks what an effusion does to the patient before asking what caused it. The surprise is that the lung loses much less volume than the fluid takes up, because the chest wall moves out to make room, so the breathlessness has to be explained by something else.
why: **Chest-wall expansion accommodates most of the fluid; lung volume falls by only one-third of the fluid volume at FRC and one-fifth at TLC.** The chest wall springs outward at FRC, so adding fluid pushes it further out rather than squeezing the lung. In the dog experiments behind these figures (Krell and Rodarte 1985; Dechman 1994) the lung gave up about one-third of the added volume and the chest wall expanded by about two-thirds, at TLC as well as at FRC. A litre of fluid therefore costs the lung only a few hundred millilitres, which is why gas exchange is often only modestly impaired by a large effusion and changes little after it is drained.

**The diaphragm is flattened, then inverted: an unfavourable length–tension relation, so dyspnoea improves after thoracentesis even if gas exchange changes little.** A flat or inverted dome shortens the muscle fibres and loses the curvature that turns tension into pressure, so each breath takes more effort. Draining the fluid restores the dome; the patient feels better at once although the PaO₂ may hardly move. In the PLEASE study (Muruganandan 2020) a flattened or everted hemidiaphragm, or absent or paradoxical movement, on ultrasound before drainage independently predicted relief of breathlessness afterwards, whether or not the lung re-expanded.

**Raised pleural pressure → lung collapse, higher pulmonary vascular resistance, RV failure; a tamponade-like picture that reverses with drainage.** A large effusion raises the pressure around the heart and compresses the collapsed lung’s vessels. The right ventricle fills less and faces a higher afterload, and the echo can show diastolic collapse of the right-sided chambers without any pericardial fluid. In a ventilated patient with unexplained hypotension and a large effusion, drainage can restore the blood pressure.

**Tension hydrothorax: a massive unilateral effusion compressing the mediastinum; mostly malignant.** It behaves like a tension pneumothorax made of fluid: the mediastinum is pushed away, venous return falls, and the patient may be shocked. Drainage relieves it; drain it in stages (PLEU-26).
mimic: Tension hydrothorax vs tension pneumothorax
Both push the mediastinum away and drop venous return. Hydrothorax: dull percussion, fluid on ultrasound, usually malignant. Pneumothorax: hyperresonance, no sliding, lung point.
traps: “An effusion makes you breathless because it collapses the lung”
The chest wall takes most of the volume; the flattened diaphragm and its poor mechanics explain most of the breathlessness, and they are what drainage fixes.
decode: [pattern] Why does dyspnoea improve after thoracentesis when the PaO₂ barely changes?
The diaphragm recovers its dome and its length–tension relation.
[pattern] Ventilated patient, large effusion, hypotension, RV diastolic collapse without pericardial fluid
Tamponade physiology from the effusion; drain it.
PLEU-14.punch: The chest wall, not the lung, makes room for most of an effusion; the breathlessness comes from a flattened diaphragm, and a big one can tamponade the heart, so drainage helps more than the gas exchange predicts.

PLEU-15.sub: Respiratory → Pleura → Detecting an effusion on examination and film
PLEU-15.intro: Step 2 starts with the chest X-ray. Free fluid falls to the lowest point, which in an upright patient is the posterior costophrenic sulcus, so the lateral film shows it before the PA film does, and the supine film, where the fluid spreads along the back, shows it last.
why: **Examination is normal below about 300 mL.** Dullness, reduced breath sounds and reduced vocal resonance need a few hundred millilitres between the lung and the chest wall.

**Posterior sulcus blunted at 75 mL (lateral view); lateral sulcus at 175 mL.** The posterior sulcus is the deepest point, so it fills first, and only the lateral film sees it. The figures most often quoted now come from Blackmore (1996): a meniscus on the lateral film at about 50 mL and on the PA film at about 200 mL; the order, lateral view before PA, is what is tested.

**About 500 mL obscures the diaphragm.** By then the meniscus rises up the lateral chest wall and the hemidiaphragm outline is lost. A subpulmonic effusion collects under the lung and mimics a raised hemidiaphragm, with its peak shifted laterally; a lateral decubitus film or ultrasound shows the fluid.

**Supine film: a blunted costophrenic angle (earliest), a homogeneous veil-like density over the lung, a lost hemidiaphragm outline, less visible lower-lobe vessels, an apparent elevation of the hemidiaphragm.** Supine, the fluid layers posteriorly behind the lung, so it shows as a haze through which vessels can still be seen, with no meniscus and no air bronchograms. The supine film misses a good deal of fluid, so in the ICU ultrasound has replaced it for detection (PLEU-16).
mimic: Supine effusion vs consolidation
Effusion: a graded veil with vessels visible through it, no air bronchograms. Consolidation: dense opacity with air bronchograms, vessels obscured.
traps: “The PA film is the most sensitive plain film”
The lateral film sees fluid in the posterior sulcus first; ultrasound beats both.
decode: [pattern] Smallest effusion seen on a lateral film vs a PA film?
About 50–75 mL lateral; about 175–200 mL PA.
[pattern] Supine ICU film with a haze over one hemithorax through which vessels are visible
Layering effusion.
PLEU-15.punch: Fluid fills the posterior sulcus first, so the lateral film sees it before the PA film, the supine film shows only a veil, and the examination misses anything below about 300 mL.

PLEU-16.sub: Respiratory → Pleura → Ultrasound and CT for pleural effusion
PLEU-16.intro: Step 2 moves to the tests that see much more than a film. Ultrasound finds a few tens of millilitres, shows whether the fluid is free or partitioned, and guides the needle; CT shows what the pleura and the lung behind it look like. The two questions linked here both test one ultrasound sign, and the trap is what it does and does not prove.
why: **Volume (mL) = 20 × interpleural distance (mm) at the lung base, at end-expiration.** This is Balik’s formula, measured in the supine patient with the trunk raised about 15°, the probe on the posterior axillary line, as the largest distance between visceral and parietal pleura. It is an estimate for deciding whether there is enough fluid to tap or drain, not a precise volume. Ultrasound reliably detects effusions above about 20 mL.

**Four patterns: anechoic; complex non-septated; complex septated; homogeneously echogenic.** Complex means echoes within the fluid (strands, debris); septated means fibrin strands crossing it to form a honeycomb; homogeneously echogenic means uniformly bright, swirling fluid, typical of pus or blood. In Yang’s series (1992) transudates were anechoic, an anechoic effusion could be either, and the three other patterns were always exudates (the card’s watch line); later series report occasional echogenic transudates, so the fluid analysis still decides.

**Ultrasound beats CT at detecting septations, and it guides thoracentesis.** Thin fibrin strands are often invisible on CT but plain on ultrasound, and septations predict that a simple drain may fail (PLEU-21). BTS 2023 says every pleural procedure for fluid should be image-guided, which has cut the pneumothorax and organ-puncture rate.

**Contrast CT separates pleural thickening from fluid and a mass from a loculated effusion; pleural enhancement suggests an exudate.** In empyema, the thickened, enhancing visceral and parietal layers are separated by fluid (the split pleura sign). Leung’s CT features of malignant pleural disease are circumferential thickening, nodular thickening, parietal thickening of more than 1 cm and mediastinal pleural involvement, each highly specific (about 88–100%) but individually insensitive. CT density helps only for blood: fluid of about 35 HU or more strongly suggests a haemothorax (PLEU-24), while transudates and exudates overlap too much to be separated by density.
mimic: Sinusoid sign vs barcode sign
Sinusoid: on M-mode the lung line swings towards the pleural line with each breath, so there is free fluid. Barcode: no sliding (RESP07A, PLEU-08).
Effusion vs consolidation on ultrasound
Effusion: an echo-free or echoic space with the sinusoid sign and a floating lung. Consolidation: tissue-like lung with air bronchograms, no sinusoid sign.
traps: “The sinusoid sign proves a transudate”

It proves free-flowing, low-viscosity fluid, nothing more. DocT keys ‘simple transudative effusion’ as the best of its options (61% right), but an anechoic free effusion can equally be an exudate; only the fluid analysis decides (PLEU-17).
“A viscous empyema or organised haemothorax gives a sinusoid sign”
Septated or thick collections damp the swing; the sign belongs to free fluid.
“Anechoic means transudate”
Anechoic can be either; it is the complex and echogenic patterns that are always exudates.
decode: POCUS in sepsis: dependent anechoic collection that moves sinusoidally with breathing — what does it mean? [DocT]
Simple (free-flowing) effusion (61%); it does not prove a transudate.
Sinusoid sign on lung ultrasound [NEET 2024]
Pleural effusion.
[pattern] Which is better than CT at showing septations?
Ultrasound.
PLEU-16.punch: Ultrasound measures the effusion (20 × the gap in mm), shows septations better than CT, and its sinusoid sign means free fluid, not a transudate; any complex or echogenic pattern is an exudate.

PLEU-17.intro: Step 3 is the first fork after a tap: is this a transudate, where the pleura is healthy and the cause lies elsewhere (heart, liver, kidney), or an exudate, where the pleura itself is diseased and must be investigated? Light’s criteria (1972) answer it with three numbers, and five real questions test them in three ways: the criteria themselves, applying them to a set of results, and the mechanism behind an exudate. The detail that separates strong answers is why the criteria overcall exudates and how to rescue a heart-failure effusion that looks exudative.
why: **Pleural/serum protein >0.5; pleural/serum LDH >0.6; pleural LDH greater than two-thirds of the upper limit of normal for serum LDH.** Protein in the fluid reflects capillary leak: a healthy pleura lets little through, so the ratio stays low. LDH reflects local inflammation and cell turnover in the pleura. The third criterion uses the laboratory’s upper limit of normal for serum LDH, not the patient’s own serum value (the card’s watch line corrects the notes): with an upper limit of 320 U/L, the cut-off is 213 U/L, and a pleural LDH of 300 U/L meets it.

**Any one criterion = exudate.** The test was built to miss no exudate, because a missed exudate is a missed cancer, tuberculosis or empyema. Requiring all three would raise specificity but let exudates through; the exam phrasing ‘all three must be met’ is false (PLEU-27a).

**Sensitivity 97%, specificity 85%.** The figures vary between series, but the pattern does not: Light’s criteria identify about 98% of exudates and label about a quarter of transudates as exudates (Porcel 2013). High sensitivity, modest specificity: a negative result (no criterion met) is a reliable transudate; a positive one may be a transudate in disguise.

**Heart failure after diuresis looks exudative; a serum minus pleural albumin gradient >1.2 g/dL shows it is a transudate.** Diuretics remove water from the pleural space faster than protein and LDH, so the fluid concentrates and crosses the 0.5 and 0.6 ratios. The albumin gradient asks a different question — how much less albumin is in the fluid than in the blood — and a gap of more than 1.2 g/dL says the capillary barrier is intact. In Bielsa’s series (2012) Light’s criteria mislabelled 29% of cardiac and 18% of hepatic transudates; the albumin gradient reclassified about 83% of the mislabelled cardiac effusions; the serum–pleural protein gradient >3.1 g/dL does the same job less well (about 55%). A raised serum NT-proBNP supports heart failure (BTS 2023). For a hepatic hydrothorax that looks exudative, a pleural/serum albumin ratio below 0.6 works better (about 77% reclassified, against 62% for the albumin gradient).
mimic: Exudate vs pseudo-exudate (diuresed heart failure)
Both meet Light’s criteria. Pseudo-exudate: known heart failure on diuretics, ratios just over the cut-offs, albumin gradient >1.2 g/dL, high NT-proBNP. True exudate: gradient ≤1.2 g/dL.
Transudate vs exudate by mechanism
Transudate: raised hydrostatic or lowered oncotic pressure across a normal pleura. Exudate: raised capillary permeability and blocked lymphatic drainage in a diseased pleura.
traps: “Heart failure” for an exudate in a patient with heart disease

The DocT stem lists heart disease among his comorbidities, but pleural protein 80 g/L against serum 60 and LDH 4000 against 500 are exudate values, and weight loss with a very high LDH points to malignancy (77% and 81% right across two sittings). Heart failure, renal failure and cirrhosis all give transudates.
“Malignant effusion is from raised hydrostatic pressure or low oncotic pressure”
Those make transudates; tumour on the pleura raises capillary permeability and blocks lymphatic drainage, and the lymphatic block is why it keeps coming back (94% right).
“Thoracic duct disruption” for a malignant exudate
That gives chyle, with triglyceride >110 mg/dL (PLEU-19).
“Pleural LDH less than two-thirds of the upper limit” or ratios below the cut-offs as exudate findings
All reversed; only ‘protein ratio >0.5’ is right in the PYQ.
“Compare pleural LDH with the patient’s serum LDH for the third criterion”
It is compared with the upper limit of normal for serum LDH.

Malignancy (77–81%).
Metastatic breast cancer, protein ratio 0.65, LDH ratio 0.75, cytology positive — pathophysiology? [DocT GT]
Raised vascular permeability and impaired lymphatic drainage (94%).
By Light’s criteria, which finding indicates an exudate? [DocT GT PYQ]
Pleural/serum protein >0.5.

Exudate if any: protein ratio >0.5, LDH ratio >0.6, LDH > two-thirds of the upper limit of normal.
PLEU-17.punch: Light’s criteria call an exudate on any one of protein ratio >0.5, LDH ratio >0.6 or pleural LDH above two-thirds of the serum upper limit, so they catch nearly every exudate but overcall diuresed heart failure, which an albumin gradient >1.2 g/dL rescues.

PLEU-18.sub: Respiratory → Pleura → Causes of pleural effusion
PLEU-18.intro: Step 3 sorts the causes by mechanism. A transudate means the pleura is innocent and the problem is pressure — the heart, the liver, the kidney, the protein level — so you treat the cause. An exudate means the pleura is diseased and you look for infection, cancer, tuberculosis or inflammation.
why: **Transudate: LV failure (commonest), cirrhosis, hypoalbuminaemia, nephrotic syndrome, peritoneal dialysis, hypothyroidism, mitral stenosis; rare — constrictive pericarditis, urinothorax, Meigs.** Heart failure is the commonest cause of any effusion, usually bilateral, larger on the right. A hepatic hydrothorax is ascites drawn through small diaphragmatic defects by the negative pleural pressure, so it is usually right-sided and can occur with little visible ascites. Peritoneal dialysis fluid crosses the same way and has a very high glucose. A urinothorax is the one transudate with a low pH and a pleural/serum creatinine ratio above 1. Meigs’ syndrome (ovarian fibroma, ascites, effusion) is often exudative by Light’s criteria in practice.

**Exudate: malignancy, parapneumonic, tuberculosis, pulmonary embolism, autoimmune pleuritis, benign asbestos effusion, pancreatitis, post-MI, post-CABG.** Parapneumonic and malignant effusions are the commonest exudates in most series; in India tuberculosis is a leading cause of a lymphocytic exudate in a young adult (PLEU-19, 20). Pulmonary embolism usually gives a small exudate, though some are transudates. Lung and breast cancer and lymphoma cause most malignant effusions. Pancreatitis gives a left-sided effusion with a high amylase; post-MI (Dressler) and post-CABG effusions are inflammatory and usually left-sided.
mimic: Heart failure vs malignancy as the cause of an effusion in an older patient
Heart failure: bilateral, transudate, cardiomegaly, high NT-proBNP. Malignancy: often unilateral and large, exudate, weight loss, very high LDH, low glucose and pH when extensive.
traps: “Heart failure, renal failure or cirrhosis” for an exudate
All three produce transudates; an exudate with weight loss points to malignancy (DocT, 77%).
decode: Weight loss, effusion with exudative protein and LDH, comorbid heart disease — diagnosis? [DocT]
Malignancy (77%).
[pattern] Right-sided transudate in cirrhosis with little ascites
Hepatic hydrothorax.
PLEU-18.punch: Transudates come from pressure problems with a normal pleura — heart failure first, then liver, kidney and low protein — and exudates from a diseased pleura: infection, cancer, tuberculosis, embolism and inflammation.

PLEU-19.sub: Respiratory → Pleura → Pleural fluid chemistry cut-offs
PLEU-19.intro: Step 4 reads the fluid once Light’s criteria have called it an exudate. Each test answers a separate question: is something burning glucose and making acid (pH, glucose, LDH)? Is there fat in the fluid (triglyceride, cholesterol)? Did something leak in from the gut (amylase)? Is it tuberculosis (ADA)? Five questions use this card, and they come as a set of fluid results with one value that decides the answer, so the skill is spotting which value matters.
why: **Protein <3 g/dL points to a transudate.** This is the old single cut-off. It misclassifies more effusions than Light’s criteria, so use it only as a rough screen; protein in an exudate is often above 3 g/dL, and very high protein (above 7–8 g/dL) suggests myeloma or Waldenström’s.

**LDH >1000 IU/L points to empyema, rheumatoid effusion or malignancy.** LDH is released by dying neutrophils and tumour cells, so a very high value means intense inflammation or a heavy tumour load. In parapneumonic effusion BTS 2023 uses LDH >900 IU/L, measured when the pH is borderline (7.2–7.4), as a reason to consider a drain (PLEU-21).

**Cholesterol >55 mg/dL (the notes also give >45) points to an exudate.** Cholesterol is a large molecule that crosses only a leaky pleura, so it is an extra exudate test, useful in the diuresed heart-failure patient. A very high cholesterol (above about 200 mg/dL) with cholesterol crystals and a low triglyceride is a pseudochylothorax: a long-standing effusion (old tuberculosis, rheumatoid) in a thickened pleura, milky but not chyle.

**Triglyceride >110 mg/dL means chylothorax; <50 mg/dL excludes it; 50–110 needs lipoprotein analysis for chylomicrons.** Chyle is lymph from the thoracic duct, carrying dietary fat as chylomicrons, so the triglyceride is high and the cells are mostly lymphocytes. Trauma and surgery (oesophagectomy, cardiac surgery) and lymphoma are the main causes; in a patient with CLL or lymphoma, a milky, lymphocytic, high-triglyceride fluid is chylothorax. A fasting patient’s chyle may be clear, so the triglyceride decides, not the colour.

**Glucose <60 mg/dL (3.3 mmol/L) or a pleural/serum ratio <0.5 points to rheumatoid effusion, empyema, malignancy, tuberculosis or oesophageal rupture.** Glucose falls when it is consumed faster than it diffuses in: by bacteria and neutrophils in empyema, by tumour cells, or across a thickened pleura in rheumatoid disease, where glucose is often below 30 mg/dL and can be near zero. An exudate with normal glucose points away from these, towards an uncomplicated parapneumonic effusion, pulmonary embolism or most other exudates.

**pH <7.2 means empyema or a complicated parapneumonic effusion.** Normal fluid is about 7.6, so 7.2 reflects a large acid load from glycolysis by neutrophils and bacteria. Measure it anaerobically in a heparinised syringe in a blood-gas analyser, not with pH paper or a laboratory meter; residual air or delay raise the pH, and lidocaine or excess heparin lower it. BTS 2023: pH ≤7.2 → drain; 7.2 to 7.4 → measure LDH and consider a drain if >900 IU/L; ≥7.4 → no drain; if pH cannot be measured, glucose <3.3 mmol/L. Low pH also occurs in rheumatoid effusion, malignancy (where it predicts short survival and failed pleurodesis), tuberculosis and oesophageal rupture.

**Raised amylase points to pancreatitis, oesophageal rupture or malignancy.** Pancreatic amylase comes from pancreatitis or a pancreaticopleural fistula; salivary amylase comes from a ruptured oesophagus, where the fluid also has a very low pH and food particles, or from an adenocarcinoma.

**ADA >35–50 U/L points to tuberculosis.** Adenosine deaminase comes from activated T lymphocytes. A meta-analysis of 40 Indian studies (3,524 patients) found a pooled sensitivity of 94% and specificity of 89%; 40 IU/L was the commonest cut-off, and the authors judged it better at excluding tuberculosis than at confirming it. BTS 2023: in high-prevalence populations ADA may be used to diagnose tuberculous pleurisy; in low-prevalence ones it is mainly an exclusion test. So in India a lymphocytic exudate with ADA above 40 is treated as tuberculosis, with culture and, if doubt remains, pleural biopsy. ADA is also raised in empyema (neutrophilic), lymphoma and rheumatoid effusion; a very high value (above about 250) suggests empyema or lymphoma rather than tuberculosis.
mimic: Chylothorax vs pseudochylothorax

Both milky. Chylothorax: triglyceride >110 mg/dL, chylomicrons, lymphocytes, acute (trauma, surgery, lymphoma). Pseudochylothorax: cholesterol >200 mg/dL with crystals, triglyceride low, years-old effusion in a thick pleura.
Chylothorax vs empyema
Both can look white. Empyema: pus with neutrophils, low pH and glucose, high LDH, fever. Chylothorax: normal pH and glucose, low LDH, lymphocytes.
Rheumatoid effusion vs empyema
Both have low glucose, low pH and high LDH. Rheumatoid: glucose often near zero, sterile, joint disease, often a pseudochylous chronic effusion. Empyema: fever, organisms, pus.
traps: “Pseudochylothorax” for a milky effusion with triglyceride 240 mg/dL
Triglyceride above 110 is chyle; cholesterol 110 is not in the pseudochylous range (above 200). 38% missed this DocT GT question.
“Empyema” or “parapneumonic” for milky fluid
pH 7.45, glucose 95 and LDH 110 rule out an infected effusion; lymphocytes and high triglyceride in a CLL patient make it chylothorax.
“Rheumatoid” with pH 7.45 (Marrow)

Marrow keys rheumatoid arthritis for LDH 500, pH 7.45 and low glucose because of the low glucose, but a rheumatoid effusion classically has a pH below 7.2 as well. For Marrow pick its key; know the full rheumatoid picture: very low glucose, high LDH, low pH.
“Pulmonary embolism” for an exudate with glucose 65 (Marrow)

The point is that normal glucose argues against empyema, rheumatoid and malignancy; but an uncomplicated parapneumonic effusion also has normal glucose, so the key leans on the rest of the stem. For Marrow pick its key.
“pH by litmus paper or a lab meter”
Only the blood-gas analyser value counts; Marrow keys ‘pH 7.2 by ABG analyser’ as the empyema finding.

Chylothorax (62%).
Effusion with LDH 500, pH 7.45, low glucose — cause? [Marrow]
Rheumatoid arthritis (key; low glucose is the clue).
Exudate (protein ratio 0.6), glucose 65 — cause? [Marrow]

PLEU-19.punch: Read the one value that decides: pH ≤7.2 and glucose <60 for infection, very low glucose for rheumatoid, triglyceride >110 for chyle, cholesterol >200 with low triglyceride for pseudochyle, amylase for pancreas or oesophagus, and ADA >40 in a lymphocytic exudate for tuberculosis.

PLEU-20.sub: Respiratory → Pleura → Pleural fluid differential count
PLEU-20.intro: Step 4 continues with the cells. The dominant cell tells you how old and what kind the process is: neutrophils for an acute insult, lymphocytes for a chronic one, eosinophils mostly for air or blood in the space.
why: **Neutrophilia: parapneumonic effusion, pancreatitis, subphrenic abscess, lupus pleuritis, and pulmonary embolism.** Any acute pleural injury brings neutrophils first, including early tuberculosis, so a neutrophilic tap does not exclude it.

**Eosinophilia, >10%: haemothorax, pulmonary infarction, benign asbestos effusion, parasites, fungal infection, drugs, and pneumothorax.** Air or blood in the space is the classic cause, including air or blood from a previous tap, so repeated taps can make the fluid eosinophilic. In modern series, though, malignancy is the commonest single cause of an eosinophilic effusion, with idiopathic and parapneumonic effusions next, so eosinophilia does not exclude cancer. It does make tuberculosis less likely, because a tuberculous effusion rarely has more than 10% eosinophils.

**Lymphocytosis, >85%: tuberculosis, lymphoma, sarcoidosis, rheumatoid pleurisy; a lymphocytic effusion is >50%.** Above 50% lymphocytes, think chronic: tuberculosis and malignancy first, plus chylothorax, post-CABG and yellow-nail syndrome. Above 85%, tuberculosis and lymphoma lead; in India a lymphocytic exudate with a high ADA is tuberculosis until proved otherwise (PLEU-19h).
mimic: Tuberculous vs malignant lymphocytic exudate
Both lymphocytic. Tuberculosis: younger, ADA >40, scanty mesothelial cells. Malignancy: older, ADA low, cytology or biopsy positive.
traps: “Eosinophilic effusion means parasites”
Parasites are a rare cause; it usually means air or blood in the space (including from a previous tap) or malignancy.
decode: [pattern] Lymphocytic exudate (90%) with ADA 70 in a young Indian adult
Tuberculous pleurisy.
[pattern] Eosinophilic effusion after a pneumothorax or repeated taps
Air or blood in the pleura; not a separate disease.
PLEU-20.punch: Neutrophils mean an acute process, eosinophils mean air, blood or often malignancy but rarely tuberculosis, and lymphocytes over 85% mean tuberculosis or lymphoma.

PLEU-21.intro: Step 5 starts with the commonest infected space. A pneumonia makes the pleura leaky; at first the fluid is sterile and clears with antibiotics, but if bacteria get in, they consume glucose, produce acid, and lay down fibrin that walls the fluid into pockets. The question is when that process needs a tube.
why: **Uncomplicated (free-flowing, sterile; antibiotics alone); complicated (bacterial invasion, septations); empyema (frank pus).** These are stages of one process: exudative (sterile, free), fibrinopurulent (bacteria, falling pH and glucose, fibrin septations), and organising (a thick peel that traps the lung). Frank pus is empyema whatever its chemistry.

**A chest tube is mandated by pus, a positive Gram stain, pH <7.20, glucose <60 mg/dL, LDH >1000, or a complex septated pattern on ultrasound.** BTS 2023 states it as: pH ≤7.2 → drain if there is a safe pocket; pH above 7.2 but below 7.4 → measure LDH, and consider a drain if it is above 900 IU/L, especially with glucose ≤4.0 mmol/L, septations, pleural enhancement on CT or a large effusion; pH ≥7.4 → no drain; if pH cannot be measured, glucose below 3.3 mmol/L (60 mg/dL) suggests a complicated effusion. So the card’s LDH >1000 is the older stand-alone threshold; LDH now counts mainly when the pH is borderline.

**No septations: small-bore catheter. Septations: large-bore.** BTS 2023 now recommends a small-bore drain (14 F or smaller) for the initial drainage of pleural infection in general, flushed regularly, because small tubes drain as well as large ones and hurt less; septations are dealt with by fibrinolytics or surgery rather than by a bigger tube (PLEU-22).

**Remove the tube when sepsis has resolved and drainage is <200 mL/day.** The aim is a dry space and a well patient; a tube that has stopped draining while a collection remains on imaging is blocked or the fluid is loculated, not ‘finished’.
mimic: Uncomplicated vs complicated parapneumonic effusion
Uncomplicated: free-flowing, pH ≥7.4, glucose normal, no organisms; antibiotics only. Complicated: pH ≤7.2 or Gram stain positive or septations; drain.
Empyema vs lung abscess on CT
Empyema: lenticular, compresses lung, split pleura sign, obtuse angle with the chest wall. Abscess: round, thick wall within lung, acute angle (see top-up on lung abscess).
traps: “After a failed drain and tPA/DNase, open thoracotomy or a second tube”
VATS debridement: less morbidity and shorter stay than open decortication (Marrow; BTS 2023 prefers VATS over thoracotomy).
“Septated, so put in a large-bore tube”
BTS 2023 uses small-bore tubes first; septations call for fibrinolytics or surgery.
decode: Failed drain plus fibrinolytics in a septated empyema — surgical approach? [Marrow]
VATS debridement.
[pattern] Pneumonia, effusion, pH 7.1 on blood-gas analyser — next step?
Chest drain.
[pattern] pH 7.3, LDH 1200, septations on ultrasound
Consider a drain (BTS 2023 intermediate pH).
PLEU-21.punch: A parapneumonic effusion needs a drain when it is pus, Gram-positive, pH ≤7.2 or septated (or pH 7.2–7.4 with LDH >900); start small-bore, and send failures to fibrinolytics, then VATS.

PLEU-22.intro: Step 5 continues with treatment once the drain is in. Three things clear a pleural infection: antibiotics that reach the organisms, drainage of the pus, and breaking down the fibrin and the thick fluid that stop it draining. The question linked here tests the third, and the trial behind it, MIST2.
why: **Antibiotics for at least 3 weeks (the notes say 4–10 weeks); cover anaerobes; hospital-acquired empyema also needs MRSA and Gram-negative cover; a macrolide only if atypicals are strongly suspected; intrapleural antibiotics not recommended (BTS 2010).** Anaerobes are common in pleural infection and often fail to grow, so cover is given regardless (for example cefuroxime with metronidazole, or co-amoxiclav). The optimal length is not established: courses of roughly 2 to 6 weeks are usual, recent trials suggest shorter courses may suffice in patients who settle without surgery, and the clinical and radiological response guides it. Atypical organisms rarely cause empyema. Aminoglycosides penetrate pus poorly and are inactivated at low pH. Risk is stratified with the RAPID score (renal: urea; age; purulence; infection source; dietary: albumin): in the PILOT validation (542 patients) 3-month mortality was 2.3%, 9.2% and 29.3% for low, medium and high scores. Non-purulent fluid scores higher than pus in RAPID.

**MIST2: tPA 10 mg plus DNase 5 mg intrapleurally, twice daily for 3 days.** Each dose is instilled through the drain, which is clamped for about an hour and then opened. tPA activates plasminogen and dissolves the fibrin septations; DNase cuts the free DNA from dead neutrophils that makes pus viscous. BTS 2023: consider the combination when drainage has stopped but a collection remains; single agents and streptokinase are not recommended.

**Better radiographic clearance, fewer surgical referrals, shorter hospital stay; either drug alone was ineffective.** In MIST2 (Rahman, NEJM 2011; 210 patients, 2×2 factorial) the pleural opacity fell by 29.5% with tPA plus DNase vs 17.2% with placebo; surgical referral at 3 months was 4% vs 16%; hospital stay was 11.8 vs 24.8 days. DNase alone had more surgical referrals than placebo (39%). The earlier MIST1 trial (Maskell, NEJM 2005; 454 patients) of streptokinase alone showed no benefit in death, surgery, radiology or hospital stay, which is why BTS 2010 advised against routine fibrinolytics (the card’s watch line).

**Main adverse effect: intrapleural bleeding, 2–12%.** MIST2 itself recorded two pleural haemorrhages among its 210 patients. In the largest series (Akulian 2022, about 1,800 patients) bleeding occurred in 4.1% overall and 9.6% of those on therapeutic anticoagulation, falling to 2.6% when anticoagulation was withheld; half-dose tPA did not lower it. So check clotting, hold anticoagulants where possible, and watch the drain for blood.
mimic: tPA vs DNase role
tPA breaks septations; DNase thins the pus. Only together do they work.
traps: “Intrapleural antibiotics” or “streptokinase” for a loculated empyema
Neither is recommended; tPA plus DNase reduces surgical referral (Marrow).
“DNase alone thins pus, so it is enough”
In MIST2 DNase alone had the most surgical referrals.
“BTS says no fibrinolytics”
That was BTS 2010, before MIST2; BTS 2023 recommends considering tPA plus DNase.
decode: Loculated empyema despite a drain — what reduces surgical referral? [Marrow]
Intrapleural tPA plus DNase.
[pattern] MIST2 regimen?
tPA 10 mg + DNase 5 mg twice daily for 3 days.
PLEU-22.punch: Pleural infection needs anaerobic cover for weeks, drainage, and, if pockets remain, tPA with DNase together, which in MIST2 cut surgical referral from 16% to 4% and halved the stay; neither drug works alone.

PLEU-23.intro: Step 5 ends with the other diseased pleura. A malignant effusion means the tumour has reached the pleura, so the aim is palliation: relieve breathlessness with the fewest procedures and days in hospital. The trials since 2010 have changed how the options are ranked.
why: **Commonest exudate after age 60; implies disseminated disease; up to 25% are asymptomatic.** Tumour on the pleura raises capillary permeability and blocks the lymphatic stomata and mediastinal nodes that drain the space, which is why the fluid is an exudate and why it recurs after drainage (DocT GT, 94%). Lung and breast cancer and lymphoma cause most cases; survival depends on the tumour and the patient’s fitness, estimated by the LENT score (BTS 2023).

**Options for a recurrent symptomatic effusion: chest drain with talc pleurodesis; thoracoscopic talc insufflation; indwelling pleural catheter (for patients unfit for anaesthesia or thoracoscopy); pleurectomy after failed pleurodesis; pleuroperitoneal shunt last.** BTS 2023 offers patients with an expandable lung a choice of talc pleurodesis or an indwelling pleural catheter (IPC) as first-line treatment, not an IPC only for the unfit. In TIME2 (106 patients) breathlessness improved equally at 6 weeks, the IPC group spent no initial days in hospital vs 4, and needed fewer further procedures (6% vs 22%), at the cost of more adverse events, mainly infection. In AMPLE (146 patients) total hospital days were 10 vs 12 and effusion-related days 1 vs 4 with the IPC. If more than about a quarter of the lung will not re-expand (non-expandable lung), talc cannot work and an IPC is preferred.

**Talc succeeds in about 90%.** That is the older figure from case series. In TAPPS (330 patients) pleurodesis failed at 90 days in 24% with talc slurry and 22% with thoracoscopic poudrage, so success is closer to three in four, and slurry and poudrage are equivalent; BTS 2023 allows either, and poudrage is done during a diagnostic thoracoscopy if one is planned anyway.

**If life expectancy is under 3 months, repeated therapeutic thoracentesis (BTS 2010: under 1 month).** The reasoning is to avoid an admission for pleurodesis in someone with little time. BTS 2023 recommends a definitive option (talc pleurodesis or an IPC) over repeated aspiration, especially when prognosis is better, because repeated aspiration commits the patient to many procedures as the fluid returns.
mimic: Talc pleurodesis vs IPC

Talc: one admission, aims to seal the space, needs an expandable lung, fewer adverse events. IPC: day case, works with non-expandable lung, drained at home, more infections, may produce spontaneous pleurodesis.
traps: “Raised hydrostatic pressure” or “low oncotic pressure” as the mechanism
Those cause transudates; malignancy raises permeability and blocks lymphatic drainage (94% right).
“An IPC is only for patients unfit for thoracoscopy”
BTS 2023 offers it as a first-line choice alongside talc.
decode: Metastatic breast cancer, large exudative effusion with malignant cells — pathophysiology? [DocT GT]
Increased vascular permeability and impaired lymphatic drainage (94%).
[pattern] Recurrent malignant effusion, lung does not re-expand after drainage — best option?
Indwelling pleural catheter.
PLEU-23.punch: A malignant effusion means pleural spread and recurs because the lymphatics are blocked; offer talc (slurry or poudrage, about three-quarters succeed) or an indwelling catheter as first-line choices, the catheter if the lung will not re-expand.

PLEU-24.intro: Step 6 turns to blood in the pleural space. The single question here gives a dense effusion on CT in an anticoagulated, hypotensive patient after a fall, and asks you to recognise blood from its density before any tap.
why: **Diagnostic criterion: pleural fluid haematocrit >50% of blood haematocrit.** Very little blood makes fluid look red, so colour alone means little; a bloodstained effusion from cancer or infarction usually has a haematocrit of a few per cent. An older haemothorax dilutes with reactive fluid, so its haematocrit may fall below half. On CT, simple fluid is close to water density, while a density of about 35 HU or more strongly suggests blood, and clot is denser still; a dense effusion with hypotension after trauma or on an anticoagulant is a haemothorax until proved otherwise.

**Massive haemothorax: >1.5 L.** ATLS means 1500 mL on immediate drainage (the card’s watch line corrects the notes’ ‘over 24 h’), and it is an indication for thoracotomy (PLEU-25). The patient is in haemorrhagic shock with a dull hemithorax and flat neck veins, unlike tension pneumothorax.

**Drain: large, 28–30 Fr, mid-axillary line.** ATLS 10th edition gives 28–32 Fr, in the 5th space just anterior to the mid-axillary line, inserted by blunt dissection; a large tube resists clotting. Smaller tubes (14 Fr pigtails) are increasingly used in stable patients. Prophylactic antibiotics are given for drains in penetrating trauma, and a malpositioned drain may be withdrawn but never pushed further in, because the outer part is no longer sterile.

**A drain is NOT inserted with clinical or radiological signs of aortic dissection or transection.** Case reports describe massive bleeding and death when the chest of a patient with a torn aorta is drained before the bleeding is controlled, because the clotted, contained haemothorax is limiting the leak. Such a patient needs CT angiography and control of the aorta (stent graft or surgery) first, then drainage.
mimic: Haemothorax vs tension pneumothorax in trauma
Both shocked with reduced breath sounds. Haemothorax: dull, flat neck veins. Tension: hyperresonant, distended neck veins.
Haemothorax vs bloodstained effusion
Haemothorax: haematocrit >50% of blood. Bloodstained effusion (cancer, infarction, trauma of the tap): haematocrit a few per cent.
traps: “Transudate” or “empyema” for a dense effusion after a fall on apixaban
35 HU is blood density; transudates are near water. 84% chose haemothorax.
“1.5 L over 24 hours defines massive haemothorax”
ATLS means on immediate drainage.
decode: Fall on apixaban, hypotension, large right effusion of 35 HU on CT — diagnosis? [DocT GT]
Haemothorax (84%).
[pattern] Bloody pleural fluid: what makes it a haemothorax?
Pleural haematocrit >50% of blood haematocrit.
PLEU-24.punch: A haemothorax is pleural fluid with more than half the blood haematocrit, dense on CT; drain it with a large tube in the 5th space, but not when the aorta may be torn.

PLEU-25.sub: Respiratory → Pleura → Urgent thoracotomy for haemothorax
PLEU-25.intro: Step 6 continues with the decision that follows the drain: is the bleeding from a vessel that needs a surgeon? Most haemothoraces stop with drainage alone, because the low-pressure lung vessels seal once the lung is up; ongoing loss means systemic arteries (intercostal, internal mammary) or the heart and great vessels.
why: **Haemodynamic instability despite resuscitation.** Physiology decides more than any volume: a patient who keeps needing blood goes to theatre.
**Initial drainage >1500 mL.** That volume at once means a major vessel. Because blood may clot in the chest, a small output from a patient who remains shocked does not reassure.
**Continued bleeding >200 mL/h for 2–4 h.** Measured once the initial volume is out; ATLS adds a persistent need for transfusion.
**Continued bleeding >1500 mL/day.** EAST guidance treats 1500 mL in 24 hours as a trigger to consider surgical exploration.

**Retained clot filling more than one-third of the pleural space.** A retained haemothorax is a nidus for empyema and later a fibrothorax that traps the lung. Clotted haemothorax with a persistent effusion is treated by VATS rather than open thoracotomy (the card’s watch line), ideally within the first 3–7 days (EAST), before the clot organises; intrapleural fibrinolysis is an alternative, especially when surgery carries high risk. A second chest tube is not recommended for retained clot.
mimic: Massive haemothorax vs retained haemothorax
Massive: active bleeding, >1500 mL at once or >200 mL/h, open thoracotomy. Retained: clot left after drainage, stable patient, VATS within days.
traps: “Insert a second tube for retained clot”
Early VATS is recommended instead.
decode: [pattern] Trauma, chest drain yields 1700 mL at once — next step?
Thoracotomy.
[pattern] Drain output 250 mL/h for 3 h after the initial evacuation
Thoracotomy.
[pattern] Stable, clotted haemothorax on day 3 despite a drain
VATS evacuation.
PLEU-25.punch: Go to theatre for instability, 1500 mL at once, 200 mL/h for 2–4 h, 1500 mL in a day, or clot filling a third of the chest, and clear a retained clot by VATS within the first week.

PLEU-26.intro: Step 6 ends with the danger of draining too much, too fast. Two questions test it: one asks you to recognise re-expansion pulmonary oedema after a tap, and one asks when to stop draining, which only 11% got right. The answer has moved from a fixed volume to the patient’s symptoms.
why: **Mechanism: a sudden fall in pleural pressure → hydrostatic shift, plus ischaemia–reperfusion capillary leak.** As the collapsed lung is pulled open, very negative pleural pressure sucks fluid into its interstitium, and the capillaries of a lung that was hypoxic for days leak when it is reperfused. The oedema is in the re-expanded lung only: unilateral B-lines and consolidation on ultrasound, usually within the first hour and up to 24 hours. Mortality in older mixed series was up to about 20%.

**Risk factors: collapse for more than 3 days, large volume, rapid drainage.** Also younger age and a large or tension pneumothorax re-expanded quickly. These are tendencies, not rules: in Mahfood’s review (1988) about a third of cases followed a short collapse or re-expansion without suction. And in a prospective study of 185 large-volume thoracenteses (Feller-Kopman 2007), clinical re-expansion oedema occurred in only 0.5% and radiographic oedema in 2.2%, and it was not related to the volume removed or the pleural pressure. Symptomatic re-expansion oedema follows fewer than 1% of drainages.

**Drain no faster than 500 mL/h, maximum 1.5 L.** The 1.5 L is per drainage session, not per day (the card’s watch line). The BTS clinical statement keeps about 1.5 L as the usual limit for one aspiration, allows more in expert hands, and makes the symptoms the stopping rule: stop for chest tightness, pain, persistent cough or worsening breathlessness, even before the planned volume. Pleural manometry has not been shown to prevent re-expansion oedema: in the Lentz trial (2019; 128 patients randomised) manometry-guided drainage did not reduce chest discomfort compared with symptom-guided drainage, though there were fewer pneumothoraces with manometry (0 vs 10%, all asymptomatic). Chest discomfort reflects the steep fall in pleural pressure as fluid comes out of a lung that cannot follow.

**Prevention and treatment: CPAP 5–10 cmH₂O, oxygen, NIV if needed.** Stop the drainage (or clamp the drain), give oxygen, take a film, and support with CPAP or high-flow oxygen, ventilating if needed; diuretics play little part because the problem is leak and suction, not fluid overload. It usually resolves in 24–72 hours.

**A chest drain is removed (general rule) when the lung is fully expanded and output is <100 mL/day.** For fluid, the threshold is a small daily output with the lung up; for air, the leak must have stopped (RESP07A, PLEU-12).
mimic: Re-expansion oedema vs non-expandable lung

Both cause chest discomfort during drainage. Re-expansion oedema: hypoxaemia, unilateral B-lines and consolidation within hours. Non-expandable lung: the lung cannot follow, pleural pressure plunges, pneumothorax ex vacuo, no oedema.
Re-expansion oedema vs post-procedure haemothorax or pneumothorax
Haemothorax: re-accumulating echogenic fluid, falling haemoglobin. Pneumothorax: absent sliding. Re-expansion oedema: B-lines and consolidation in the drained lung.
traps: “Stop at 1 L”
Only 11% chose the right answer (chest discomfort) on DocT GT; most stopped at a fixed volume. Volume alone does not predict re-expansion oedema; symptoms are the stopping rule.
“Stop when the manometer reads below −20 cmH₂O”
Manometry did not reduce discomfort (Lentz 2019) and has not been shown to prevent oedema; it is not routine.
“Stop when the patient coughs”
A brief cough is common as the lung re-expands; it is persistent cough with tightness or breathlessness that stops the tap.
decode: Large malignant effusion drained under ultrasound — when to stop to maximise drainage and minimise complications? [DocT GT]
When the patient complains of chest discomfort (11%).
Acute hypoxaemia 2 h after a large tap; ultrasound shows unilateral interstitial syndrome with consolidation [DocT GT]
Re-expansion pulmonary oedema (88%).
PLEU-26.punch: Re-expansion oedema is rare, unilateral and early; stop any large drainage when the patient feels chest tightness, pain or persistent cough, keep to about 1.5 L a session, and treat with oxygen and CPAP.
