spine: Donation in India and the law

India donates under one organ donor per million because potential donors are not identified and declared, and the law (THOA 1994, amended 2011, Rules 2014) makes the ICU doctor responsible for asking.
Preconditions before any testing
Brainstem death can be tested only when the cause is known and irreversible and every reversible look-alike — cold, drugs, paralysis, shock, metabolic upset — has been excluded.
The clinical exam and apnoea test
Every brainstem reflex must be absent and the patient must not breathe when the PaCO₂ has risen to at least 60 mmHg; spinal reflexes are allowed, posturing is not.
Ancillary tests and certification
Ancillary flow studies are used only when the exam or apnoea test cannot be completed, and in India a board of four certifies death after two sets of tests at least 6 hours apart.
What brainstem death does to the body
As the brainstem dies, a brief sympathetic storm injures the heart and lungs, then loss of sympathetic tone, diabetes insipidus and hypothermia cause the hypotension that loses organs.
Keeping and choosing the organs

Donor care switches from protecting the brain to perfusing every other organ — volume, vasopressin, hormones, lung-protective ventilation — and then each organ is judged on its own against a short list of absolute contraindications.
SPECIAL01.primer: Brain death, or death by neurological criteria, is the irreversible loss of all brain function including the brainstem; Indian and UK law use the term brainstem death, and it is legally death. The heart can keep beating for hours to days because it has its own pacemaker, as long as the ventilator supplies oxygen. The brainstem carries the cranial nerve reflexes and the respiratory centre, which is why the diagnosis rests on absent reflexes and an apnoea test. Once death is declared the patient becomes a potential donor, and the ICU’s task changes from saving the brain to keeping the other organs alive.

EOL-01.sub: End-of-life care → Definitions → The five terms
EOL-01.intro: Step 1 is naming the decisions, because every later card uses these words. The intensivist can decide not to add a treatment, to take one away, or not to attempt CPR, and the care that follows is palliative or end-of-life care. No bank question is linked to this card.
why: **Withholding: a decision not to start or escalate a life-sustaining treatment (e.g. DNR, non-escalation).** Not starting dialysis, not adding a second vasopressor, not reintubating after a planned extubation. The patient keeps what he already has.

**Withdrawal: a decision to stop or remove one.** Stopping vasopressors, dialysis or ventilation. It feels more active than withholding, but ethically the two are equivalent: if a treatment is no longer benefiting the patient, there is no reason to continue it merely because it was started, and the disease is the cause of death in both.

**DNAR: no CPR, given terminal illness and the patient’s or surrogate’s wishes.** It concerns CPR only. ICMR’s 2020 DNAR guidance is explicit that it does not mean withholding other treatment: antibiotics, fluids, vasopressors and pain relief continue unless separately limited. The form is signed, timed and dated by the patient or surrogate and the physician; when the physician is unsure, CPR is the default.
**Palliative care: from diagnosis of a life-threatening illness; quality of life alongside treatment.** It is not reserved for the dying and does not replace active treatment; it runs with it.

**End-of-life care: at the end stage — comfort, dignity, quality of dying, closure; includes the family.** It is the last part of palliative care, when the goal has changed from survival to a good death.
mimic: Withholding vs withdrawal
Not starting or not escalating vs stopping something already running; ethically and legally the same decision.
DNAR vs ‘no treatment’
DNAR removes CPR only; everything else continues unless a separate decision limits it.
traps: Believing withdrawal is morally worse than withholding
It only feels worse; ethically they are equivalent, and treating them differently makes teams reluctant to start a trial of treatment for fear they could never stop it.
Reading DNAR as an order to stop all treatment
ICMR states that DNAR does not mean withdrawal or withholding of other life-supporting treatment.
decode: A patient on noradrenaline is not started on vasopressin and not offered dialysis — what is this? [pattern]
Withholding (non-escalation).
Palliative care is appropriate from which point? [pattern]
From the diagnosis of a life-threatening illness, alongside curative treatment, not only at the end.
EOL-01.punch: Withholding is not starting, withdrawal is stopping, and the two are ethically the same; DNAR removes CPR and nothing else; palliative care begins at diagnosis and end-of-life care is its last stage.

EOL-02.sub: End-of-life care → Definitions → Ways of ending life compared
EOL-02.intro: Still step 1. The card separates five acts by two questions: what causes the death, and what the doctor intends. The first three are lawful end-of-life care; the last two are not permitted in India. No bank question is linked to this card.
why: **Withhold treatment: the underlying disease causes death; the intent is to avoid a burdensome intervention.** The patient dies of what he was dying of, without an extra burden.

**Withdraw treatment: the underlying disease causes death; the intent is to remove a burdensome intervention.** Stopping the ventilator lets the lung disease take its course; it does not introduce a new cause of death.

**Palliative sedation and analgesia: the underlying disease causes death; the intent is to relieve symptoms.** Sedatives and opioids are titrated to the minimum dose that controls a refractory symptom (ICMR: ‘at the minimal dosages necessary’). Titrated this way they have not been shown to shorten survival, and if they did, double effect covers it (EOL-04).
**Physician-assisted suicide: a drug used by the patient; the intent is to end life.** The doctor provides the means and the patient takes it. Not permitted in India.

**Euthanasia: a drug given by the doctor; the intent is to end life.** Active euthanasia, such as a lethal injection, was held illegal in Aruna Shanbaug (2011) and remains so; only Parliament could change that.
mimic: Palliative sedation vs euthanasia
Intent to relieve a symptom, dose titrated to the symptom, death from the disease vs intent to end life, dose chosen to kill, death from the drug.
Assisted suicide vs euthanasia
Who gives the final drug: the patient vs the doctor.
traps: Calling withdrawal of ventilation ‘active euthanasia’ because the doctor acts
The act is removing a treatment; death comes from the disease, and the courts call it passive euthanasia, which is lawful.
Treating ‘passive euthanasia’ as a third illegal category
In Indian law passive euthanasia is simply withdrawal or withholding, and it is lawful under the Common Cause procedure.
decode: Which of the following is permitted in India: physician-assisted suicide, active euthanasia, withdrawal of life support, lethal injection on request? [pattern]
Withdrawal of life support.
EOL-02.punch: Ask two things: what causes the death and what the doctor intends; when the disease causes it and the intent is to remove a burden or relieve a symptom, it is lawful end-of-life care.

EOL-03.sub: End-of-life care → Ethics → The four principles
EOL-03.intro: Step 2 is the ethics that justify the decisions of step 1. The four principles of Beauchamp and Childress are applied to the dying patient. Both linked DocT questions test autonomy: what respecting it does and does not allow, and which principle advance directives and surrogates serve. Only 20% chose the right answer to the first, so the common belief that autonomy means ‘do whatever the patient wants’ is the live trap.
why: **Autonomy: informed consent or refusal; needs capacity and full information. No capacity: surrogate (substituted judgment); wishes unknown: best interests.** A choice is autonomous only when the patient understands, can weigh the information and is free of pressure. Respecting it allows the doctor to persuade with honest argument and evidence; it forbids coercion (a threat) and manipulation (distorted or selective information). It gives the patient a right to refuse, not a right to demand: there is no duty to provide treatment that will not help. When capacity is lost, autonomy is carried forward by an advance directive or by a surrogate who says what the patient would have chosen (substituted judgment); only when his wishes cannot be known does the surrogate fall back on best interests. That is why advance directives and surrogates belong to autonomy, not to beneficence. A refusal protects the doctor only if it was properly informed: risks that were never explained still carry liability.

**Beneficence: act in the patient’s best interest; includes protecting the family from financial ruin. Insisting on futile care violates it.** Futile care brings burden without benefit, so it is not in the patient’s interest. The family’s finances are part of the Indian position (ISCCM) because most ICU care is paid out of pocket and ruin follows the patient’s family after his death.
**Non-maleficence: first, do no harm — pain, distress, and harm to the family.** Prolonging dying with painful procedures is a harm, even when each procedure is done well.

**Justice: fair use of resources; futile therapy violates it.** An ICU bed given to a patient who cannot benefit is denied to one who can. Policy-level budget decisions are macro-allocation; deciding who gets the last bed or ventilator is micro-allocation.
mimic: Substituted judgment vs best interests

What this patient would have chosen (his values, his directive) vs what a reasonable person would judge best for him when his wishes are unknown; Indian courts (Aruna Shanbaug 2011, Harish Rana 2026) apply a best-interests test to incapacitated patients without a directive, with his known wishes as one factor in it.
Autonomy vs justice
The family demands futile care (autonomy) while the bed is needed elsewhere (justice): resolved by repeated communication and negotiation, not by giving in or by unilateral withdrawal.
traps: ‘Physicians are obligated to do whatever the patient wants’ [DocT GT]
Autonomy is a right to refuse and to choose among appropriate options; it does not create a duty to give inappropriate treatment.
‘If a patient refuses, the physician cannot be liable’ [DocT GT]
Only an informed refusal protects; if the risks were not explained, liability remains.
‘Coercion with a credible threat is acceptable to save life’ [DocT GT]
A threat removes free choice; persuasion with legitimate argument is the limit.
Linking advance directives to beneficence because they are ‘for the patient’s good’
They express the patient’s own choice in advance, which is autonomy.
decode: Which is true regarding respect for autonomy: coercion by credible threat, persuasion by legitimate argument, doing whatever the patient wants, no liability after refusal? [DocT GT, 20% right]
Persuasion by legitimate argument.
Which principle primarily supports advance directives and surrogate decision-making in the ICU? [DocT GT]
Autonomy.
The family insists on continuing dialysis in a patient with no prospect of recovery while beds are short — which principles conflict? [pattern]
Autonomy (the surrogate’s demand) and justice (fair use of resources); also beneficence, since futile care does not serve him.
EOL-03.punch: Autonomy is the right to an informed choice and to refuse, kept alive after capacity is lost by directives and surrogates; it allows persuasion, never coercion, and never obliges a doctor to give futile treatment.

table.title: What respecting autonomy allows
head: Act
Allowed?
Why
rows: Persuading with honest argument and evidence
Leaves the choice with the patient
Manipulation by selective or false information
Corrupts the information the choice depends on
Giving any treatment the patient demands
No duty to give non-beneficial treatment
Accepting an uninformed refusal as protection
Liability remains for risks not explained

EOL-04.intro: Still step 2. Comfort drugs at the end of life can depress breathing, and teams fear that relieving suffering is the same as killing. The doctrine of double effect separates the two by intention and by dose. No bank question is linked to this card.
why: **An act with a good intention (relieving suffering) is ethical even if it has a foreseen bad effect (hastening death), provided the bad effect is not intended.** The classic conditions: the act itself is good or neutral (giving an analgesic), only the good effect is intended, the bad effect is not the means to the good one, and the good outweighs the bad. In practice, opioids and sedatives titrated to symptoms have not been shown to shorten survival, so double effect is a safeguard more often than a real trade-off.

**So: titrate opioids and sedatives to symptoms, not to death.** Intention shows in the dose: small increments in response to pain, breathlessness or agitation. A sudden large dose with no symptom to treat cannot be explained as relief.
**Document the indication and doses meticulously.** The record of the symptom, the dose and the response is what shows that the intent was relief.
mimic: Double effect vs active euthanasia
Dose titrated to a symptom, death foreseen but not intended vs a large dose given deliberately to end life.
Proportional palliative sedation vs continuous deep sedation

Consciousness lowered only as far as needed to control a refractory symptom, light or intermittent first (EAPC 2024) vs deep sedation until death, considered when lighter sedation has failed and generally in the final stage of life; EAPC 2024 sets no fixed life expectancy.
traps: Withholding morphine from a breathless dying patient for fear of respiratory depression
Titrated morphine relieves breathlessness, and any hastening of death, if it occurs, is covered by double effect; leaving the symptom untreated is the harm.
Thinking a large bolus is double effect because the motive was compassion
Given to end life, it is euthanasia; double effect needs the bad effect to be unintended and the dose proportionate.
decode: A dying patient’s dyspnoea is treated with titrated morphine; respiratory rate falls. Which principle justifies it? [pattern]
Double effect.
EOL-04.punch: Relief that may hasten death is ethical when relief is the intention, the dose is titrated to the symptom and the record shows it; a dose meant to end life is euthanasia whatever the motive.

EOL-05.sub: End-of-life care → The process → Recognising futility
EOL-05.intro: Step 3 is where the process starts. Before any family meeting or legal step, someone has to judge that further intensive treatment will not help. The card lists the situations in which that judgement is usually reached. No bank question is linked to this card.
why: **Advanced age with poor functional state.** Physiological reserve and the pre-illness function predict whether the patient can return to an acceptable life.
**Severe illness refractory to reasonable aggressive treatment.** Escalating organ failure despite appropriate treatment over a reasonable trial is the commonest ICU route to futility.
**Coma from an acute catastrophic, irreversible cause.** Massive haemorrhagic stroke or devastating brain injury.
**Severe chronic neurological disease (advanced dementia, vegetative state).**
**Prolonged poor neurological state after cardiac arrest.** Judged after an adequate interval and multimodal prognostication, not on day one.
**Any comparable situation with a predicted low chance of survival.** Futility is a reasonable prediction, not a certainty; the experience of the team and a mortality estimate support it.
mimic: Quantitative vs qualitative futility
Treatment very unlikely to work vs treatment that may keep the patient alive but cannot restore a life he would value.
traps: Waiting for certainty before discussing futility
Prognosis is never certain; the standard is a reasonable prediction, and delay prolongs suffering.
Declaring futility on age alone
Age counts with poor function and refractory illness, not by itself.
decode: Which is the first and most difficult step of end-of-life care in the ICU? [pattern]
Recognising futility.
EOL-05.punch: Everything starts with a reasonable, experienced judgement that more intensive treatment will not help; age, function, refractory illness and irreversible brain injury are the usual grounds.

EOL-06.sub: End-of-life care → The process → The ISCCM steps
EOL-06.intro: Step 4 turns the judgement of step 3 into a decision. The ISCCM–IAPC policy (2014, updated 2024) sets an order that protects the family from mixed messages: the team agrees first, then speaks once, honestly. Both linked DocT questions test this card: one on how the decision is made with an emotional surrogate (78% right), one on what palliative care involvement achieves (95% right).
why: **1. Recognise futility and the dying process.** EOL-05.

**2. Consensus among all caregivers before meeting the family.** If the cardiologist offers hope that the intensivist has given up, the family hears disagreement and trust is lost. Disagreement inside the team is resolved first, with a second opinion if needed.

**3. Honest, early disclosure of prognosis: imminent death, futility, natural death; respect hope, stay realistic.** Early disclosure gives the family time; hope is redirected to comfort and to time together, not denied.
**4. Discuss modalities: DNR, withdrawal, withholding (non-escalation).** The family is told what will be continued (comfort, nursing, presence) as well as what will stop.

**5. Shared decision-making; no consensus yet → continue and review.** The doctor gives a clear recommendation, the family contributes the patient’s values, and the decision is made together. Neither extreme is right: the physician deciding and merely informing, or the family deciding alone with the full burden. A surrogate who is struggling needs emotional support within the shared process, not to hand everything to an ethics team. If there is no agreement, current treatment continues and the discussion is repeated.
**6. Document discussions, process and decision.** Who was present, what was said, what was decided and why; this is also the legal protection.

**7. Implement: prepare staff, family, room; limitation form signed by family and team.** Plan the order of withdrawal; stop investigations and non-comfort drugs; stop tube feeds (they add aspiration and bloating, not comfort; the Supreme Court in Harish Rana, March 2026, held that clinically assisted nutrition and hydration is medical treatment that the boards may withdraw); stop neuromuscular blockers before ventilation is withdrawn so distress can be seen and treated.

**8. Compassionate palliative care (symptoms, preferred place, rituals, liberal visiting). Then after-death care (certify early, dignified exit) and bereavement support (starts before death).** Comfort measures continue: opioids, anxiolytics, glycopyrrolate, oxygen if it eases breathlessness, mouth and eye care (EOL-08).
mimic: Shared decision-making vs informed consent
The team brings a recommendation and the family brings the patient’s values, decided together vs the doctor offers options and the family carries the choice alone.
Palliative care consult for triggered cases vs for every patient

Proactive involvement for poor-prognosis ventilated patients often shortens stay and lowers cost; the Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021 suggests (conditional) against routine formal consultation for every septic patient, partly because trials gave mixed effects on families.
traps: ‘Physician decides and informs the family’ [DocT GT]
Paternalism ignores the patient’s values carried by the surrogate; the recommended model is shared decision-making with emotional support.
‘Surrogate defers all choices to the ethics team’ [DocT GT]
An ethics committee helps resolve conflict; it does not replace the surrogate.
Telling the family first and then reaching consensus in the team
Consensus comes first (EOL-12e); otherwise the family hears contradictory messages.
Accepting DAMA/LAMA for financial reasons

The patient dies at home or on the way without palliation; the right answer is limitation of treatment with comfort care in hospital. The Supreme Court (Harish Rana, 2026) also disapproved of using discharge against advice once treatment has stopped.
Believing palliative involvement increases stay or invasive procedures [DocT GT]

It reduces non-beneficial procedures, ICU readmission and cost without raising mortality. Effects on families are mixed: one trial of palliative-care-led family meetings (Carson, JAMA 2016) did not reduce relatives’ anxiety or depression and may have increased post-traumatic stress symptoms.
decode: Ventilated patient with poor prognosis; benefit most consistently associated with multidisciplinary palliative care involvement? [DocT GT, 95% right]
Reduced ICU readmission and cost savings.
Multi-organ failure despite maximal support; the daughter-surrogate struggles emotionally with withdrawal — best approach? [DocT GT, 78% right]
Shared decision-making with emotional support.
Family not yet ready to agree to withdrawal — next step? [pattern]
Continue current treatment and review with repeated meetings; do not withdraw unilaterally.
EOL-06.punch: Agree as a team, tell the family early and honestly, decide with them while supporting them, write it down, and keep treating if agreement has not come; then make comfort the whole of the care.

table.title: Withdrawing support: what stops, what continues
head: Stop
Continue
rows: Opioids and anxiolytics titrated to symptoms
Glycopyrrolate for secretions, mouth and eye care

EOL-07.intro: Still step 4. The disclosure and shared decision of EOL-06 happen at a family meeting, and how it is run decides whether the family trusts the team. No bank question is linked to this card.
why: **Intensivist coordinates; consensus among specialists first; meeting with all significant family.** One coordinator speaks for one agreed team. Having all decision-makers present avoids the relative who arrives later and reverses the plan.

**Disease process, likely prognosis, time available, comfort options.** The family should leave knowing what is happening, how it is likely to end, roughly how long, and what will be done for comfort. Listening matters more than talking: in a French trial (Lautrette, NEJM 2007), a proactive end-of-life conference in which relatives spoke for about half the time, plus a bereavement brochure, reduced their anxiety, depression and post-traumatic stress symptoms at 90 days.

**SOLER: Squarely face at eye level, Open posture, Lean toward, Eye contact (no phone), Relaxed.** These are the non-verbal signals of attention (Egan). Sitting at eye level rather than standing over a family is the single most visible one.
mimic: Coordinator-led meeting vs separate specialist conversations
One agreed message vs several partial and sometimes contradictory ones.
traps: Holding the family meeting before the specialists agree
Consensus comes first (EOL-06 step 2).
decode: Who should coordinate end-of-life discussions with the family in the ICU? [pattern]
The intensivist, after consensus among the specialists.
EOL-07.punch: One coordinator, one agreed message, the whole family present, attention shown by posture, and the family leaves knowing the prognosis, the time and the comfort plan.

EOL-08.intro: Step 5 is comfort once the goal has changed. Four symptoms dominate dying in the ICU, and each has a first-line drug. Doses are titrated to the symptom, which is also what keeps them within double effect (EOL-04). No bank question is linked to this card.
why: **Pain: mild — paracetamol, ibuprofen, ketorolac; moderate — oxycodone, morphine, fentanyl; severe — infusion or PCA; pain team.** In the ICU most dying patients cannot report pain, so behavioural scales guide dosing. Fentanyl is preferred when renal failure would let morphine’s active metabolites accumulate.

**Secretions: gentle suction; glycopyrrolate; scopolamine patch.** Antimuscarinics reduce new secretions but cannot clear what is already there, so start them early. Glycopyrrolate is a quaternary amine that does not cross the blood–brain barrier, so it does not sedate or cause delirium; hyoscine hydrobromide (scopolamine) does cross and can cause both. The noise distresses the family more than the patient; positioning and explanation help.

**Dyspnoea: oxygen as needed; morphine; lorazepam if anxious.** Low-dose opioids reduce the sensation of breathlessness. Oxygen helps only if the patient is hypoxaemic or feels better with it; a fan on the face also helps.

**Agitation: look for pain, hypoxia, poor sleep; lorazepam; haloperidol.** Treat a cause first (pain, full bladder, hypoxia). Haloperidol for delirium; benzodiazepines for anxiety or as palliative sedation, midazolam being the first-line drug (EAPC 2024). Opioids and haloperidol are not used as sedatives: raising an opioid to sedate adds toxicity without reliable sedation.
mimic: Glycopyrrolate vs hyoscine hydrobromide
Peripheral only, no sedation vs crosses into the brain, sedates and can cause delirium.
traps: Giving opioids only ‘as needed’ to a dying patient with continuous pain
Dose by the clock (WHO ladder rule); on-demand dosing leaves gaps of pain.
Combining two drugs of the same class (two opioids, two NSAIDs)
Adds side effects without adding analgesia.
decode: Noisy upper-airway secretions in a dying patient; drug that will not add sedation? [pattern]
Glycopyrrolate.
Drug of choice for refractory breathlessness at the end of life? [pattern]
Morphine (low-dose opioid).
EOL-08.punch: Morphine for pain and breathlessness, glycopyrrolate for secretions, a cause and then lorazepam or haloperidol for agitation, all given by the clock and titrated to the symptom.

EOL-09.sub: End-of-life care → Comfort → A good death and its barriers
EOL-09.intro: Still step 5. The card sets out what a good death looks like and why Indian ICUs often fail to provide it. No bank question is linked to this card.
why: **Knowing death is near; symptoms controlled; wishes respected; dignity at a place of choice; life not prolonged artificially.** Each item is something the team can deliver once it accepts that the patient is dying.

**No consensus within the medical community, unawareness of ethical issues, a culture of fighting till the end, little palliative orientation, fear of litigation, no legal backing or regulatory requirement (NABH).** Fear of prosecution was the main legal barrier; Common Cause (2018) and its 2023 simplification answered much of it, but awareness and practice lag.
**Convincing colleagues.** The hardest barrier is inside the profession, not the family: specialists who see any death as failure.
mimic: Barrier from families vs from doctors
Families usually accept honest disclosure; disagreement among doctors is the larger obstacle.
traps: Assuming the main barrier is the family’s refusal
The card names convincing colleagues as the biggest challenge.
decode: Biggest challenge to end-of-life care in Indian ICUs? [pattern]
Convincing colleagues (lack of consensus in the medical community).
EOL-09.punch: A good death means knowing it is coming, comfort, respected wishes and no artificial prolonging; in India the largest obstacle is persuading other doctors.

EOL-10.sub: End-of-life care → Law in India → The cases
EOL-10.intro: Step 6 is the law, which turns the ethics into protection for the team. The cases moved from whether there is a right to die, through allowing withdrawal under court control, to a right to die with dignity with advance directives. No bank question is linked to this card.
why: **1994, P. Rathinam vs Union of India: right to die read into Article 21 (later overruled).** A two-judge bench struck down IPC 309 (attempted suicide).
**1996, Gian Kaur vs State of Punjab: no right to die; upheld IPC 309.** A five-judge bench held that the right to life does not include a right to end it, overruling Rathinam.

**2006/2008, Law Commission reports: euthanasia; decriminalising suicide attempt.** The 196th report (2006) dealt with withholding or withdrawing treatment from the terminally ill, protecting both patients who refuse treatment and their doctors, not with active euthanasia; the 210th report (2008) called IPC 309 inhuman and recommended removing it. A later 241st report (2012) returned to passive euthanasia after Aruna Shanbaug. Attempted suicide is now effectively decriminalised: the Mental Healthcare Act 2017 (section 115) presumes severe stress, and the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, which replaced the IPC in 2024, has no general offence of attempted suicide.

**2011, Aruna Shanbaug vs Union of India: passive euthanasia allowed, via the High Court.** A two-judge bench (7 March 2011) held active euthanasia illegal but allowed withdrawal of life support from a patient in a vegetative state, on application by relatives or a ‘next friend’, with the High Court’s approval under Article 226 after a committee of three doctors examined the patient. Aruna herself was not allowed it, because the KEM hospital staff caring for her wanted to continue.

**2018, Common Cause vs Union of India: right to die with dignity (Article 21); advance directives (living wills).** A five-judge Constitution Bench (9 March 2018) held that a capable adult may refuse life-sustaining treatment, may make an advance directive for when capacity is lost, and that treatment may be withheld or withdrawn from those without capacity even without one, with palliative care continuing. It replaced the court route with medical boards (EOL-11).
mimic: Aruna Shanbaug vs Common Cause
2011, two judges, withdrawal with High Court approval, no advance directives vs 2018, five judges, right to die with dignity, advance directives, medical boards.
Gian Kaur vs Rathinam
No right to die (five judges, 1996) vs a right to die (two judges, 1994, overruled).
traps: ‘Common Cause legalised active euthanasia’
It did not; active euthanasia and assisted suicide remain illegal (EOL-12c).
Thinking Aruna Shanbaug herself had life support withdrawn
The petition was refused; she died in May 2015 of pneumonia. The first withdrawal reported as approved by the Supreme Court under the Common Cause framework was Harish Rana (March 2026).
decode: Which judgment first allowed passive euthanasia in India? [pattern]
Aruna Shanbaug (2011).
Which judgment recognised advance directives and the right to die with dignity under Article 21? [pattern]
Common Cause (2018).
EOL-10.punch: Rathinam gave a right to die, Gian Kaur took it away, Aruna Shanbaug (2011) allowed withdrawal through the High Court, and Common Cause (2018) made dying with dignity part of Article 21 with advance directives.

parts.q: Indian end-of-life guidelines in order?
parts.a: ISCCM 2005, revised 2012; joint ISCCM–IAPC policy 2014 (Myatra, IJCCM); updated joint ISCCM–IAPC statement 2024 (Mani, IJCCM); ICMR DNAR guidelines 2020; MoHFW draft guidelines on withdrawal of life support, September 2024.

parts.q: What did Harish Rana v Union of India (2026) add?
parts.a: A two-judge bench (11 March 2026) allowed withdrawal of clinically assisted nutrition and hydration from a man in a vegetative state for 13 years, reported as the first withdrawal approved under the Common Cause framework. It held that such nutrition is medical treatment, set out a holistic best-interests test, said withdrawal must not mean abandonment (palliative care continues; misuse of discharge against advice disapproved), directed that each district’s Chief Medical Officer keep a panel of doctors for secondary boards, and urged Parliament to legislate.

EOL-11.sub: End-of-life care → Law in India → The 2023 board process
EOL-11.intro: Still step 6. The 2018 procedure was so heavy (Collector, 20-year experts, a magistrate’s visit) that it was hardly workable in an ICU. On ISCCM’s application the Supreme Court simplified it on 24 January 2023, and this card is that procedure. No bank question is linked to this card.
why: **Applies to: patients who have lost capacity AND are terminally ill, where further treatment would not benefit.** A patient with capacity simply refuses; no board is needed.

**1. Primary Medical Board: treating physician + 2 subject experts with 5+ years → opinion.** The hospital forms it; the order says at least two experts and asks for the opinion preferably within 48 h.

**2. Inform next of kin (or those named in the advance directive) and obtain their concurrence.** With a valid directive, the persons named in it give consent; without one, the next of kin, next friend or guardian. Directives are now signed before two witnesses and attested by a notary or gazetted officer, no longer countersigned by a magistrate.

**3. Secondary Medical Board within 48 h: a doctor nominated by the district CMO + 2 experts (5+ years) not on the first board.** It is also formed by the hospital, not the Collector, and confirms the first board’s opinion.
**4. Boards agree → hospital records and informs the Judicial Magistrate → team implements.** Intimation only; the magistrate no longer visits or authorises.

**5. Boards disagree → family, team or hospital may approach the High Court.** The order gives this route whenever a board refuses to certify withdrawal: a writ under Article 226, heard by a Division Bench, which may appoint an independent committee of three doctors of at least 20 years’ standing and decides on the patient’s best interests.
mimic: Primary vs secondary board
Treating physician + 2 experts vs CMO nominee + 2 different experts; both 5 years, both about 48 h.
traps: Still teaching 20-year experts or the magistrate’s visit
That is the 2018 procedure, replaced in January 2023.
‘Secondary board decides within 7 days’
Preferably within 48 h (EOL-12h).
decode: Minimum experience of experts on the medical boards after the 2023 modification? [pattern]
5 years.
After both boards agree, whom does the hospital inform? [pattern]
The jurisdictional Judicial Magistrate First Class (intimation, not permission).
EOL-11.punch: Two hospital boards of 5-year experts, each in about 48 hours, the family’s or named persons’ consent, then a note to the magistrate; only disagreement goes to the High Court.

table.title: 2018 vs 2023
head: Step
rows: Two witnesses + notary or gazetted officer
Formed by the Collector, chaired by the CDMO, 20-year experts
Formed by the hospital: CMO nominee + ≥2 experts, 5 years, ~48 h

parts.q: What did the MoHFW draft guidelines (September 2024) add?
parts.a: They restate the 2023 boards for ICUs: PMB members may be from the treating team and the CMO nominee from the same hospital; terminal illness includes severe traumatic brain injury with no recovery after ≥72 h; the listed conditions are brainstem death, advanced disease unlikely to benefit from aggressive treatment, documented informed refusal by patient or surrogate, and compliance with the Supreme Court procedure (worded ‘must apply’, though the first two are really alternatives); the magistrate form is notification only, not approval; hospitals may set up clinical ethics committees. Released for comment in late September 2024; no final version had been published as far as could be found (November 2026).

EOL-12.sub: End-of-life care → Sweep → True or false
EOL-12.intro: The sweep tests the whole story, one statement per step. No bank question is linked to it; each statement is the form an examiner would use.
why: **Withholding and withdrawing are ethically equivalent: true.** Stopping a treatment that no longer helps is the same decision as not starting it (EOL-01).
**After withdrawal, the cause of death is the withdrawal: false — the underlying disease.** Removing treatment lets the disease take its course (EOL-02).
**Active euthanasia is legal in India since 2018: false — not permitted.** Common Cause allowed withdrawal, withholding and advance directives only (EOL-10).
**Titrating morphine for dyspnoea is justified by double effect: true.** Intent is relief and the dose follows the symptom (EOL-04).
**Family is told first, then caregivers reach consensus: false — among caregivers first.** (EOL-06 step 2).
**DAMA is the preferred route for financial futility: false — discouraged.** The patient dies without palliation (EOL-06).
**Aruna Shanbaug (2011) allowed passive euthanasia: true.** With High Court approval (EOL-10).
**The secondary medical board decides within 7 days: false — within 48 h.** Preferably within 48 h under the 2023 order (EOL-11).
mimic: Withdrawal (lawful) vs active euthanasia (unlawful)
Removing a treatment, death from the disease vs giving a drug, death from the drug.
traps: Reading ‘since 2018’ as making the euthanasia statement true
2018 legalised the right to die with dignity through withdrawal, not active euthanasia.
decode: Which statement about end-of-life care in India is true? [pattern]
Look for withholding = withdrawal, double effect for titrated opioids, Aruna Shanbaug 2011, and 48 h for the boards.
EOL-12.punch: Withholding equals withdrawal, the disease is the cause of death, titrated morphine is double effect, the team agrees before the family is told, and the boards work in 48 hours; active euthanasia and DAMA for money are wrong.

topups.q: ICU palliative care: the main barriers, and the triggers for a consult?
a: - Barriers: deficient communication training (prognosis talks are a skill), unrealistic family/team expectations, prognostic uncertainty, belief that palliation = giving up.
- Triggers: ICU stay >10 days, multi-organ failure, advanced dementia/frailty, metastatic cancer, post-arrest poor neurology, family conflict.
- Also whenever tracheostomy or PEG (prolonged life support) is being considered.
- SSC: discuss goals of care within 72 h; no routine consult for every patient (SEP-59).

x.sub: End-of-life care → The process → Palliative care in the ICU
x.intro: Step 4 was the team reaching a decision with the family. Bringing in palliative care is how many ICUs do that well, but it happens late or not at all. Two DocT GT questions ask why it is held back and when a consult should be triggered.
why: **Barriers: deficient communication training (prognosis talks are a skill), unrealistic family/team expectations, prognostic uncertainty, belief that palliation = giving up.** Each one delays the conversation. Uncertainty is a frequent reason given for waiting, but prognosis is never certain, and palliative care runs alongside full treatment (EOL-01), so starting it does not mean giving up.

**Triggers: ICU stay >10 days, multi-organ failure, advanced dementia/frailty, metastatic cancer, post-arrest poor neurology, family conflict.** These are the patients with a high chance of dying or of surviving with a heavy burden, and the families most likely to need help with decisions. Using fixed triggers removes the need for one doctor to ‘give up’ first.
**Also whenever tracheostomy or PEG (prolonged life support) is being considered.** That is the moment the team commits to long-term support, so goals of care should be clear before it is done.

**SSC: discuss goals of care within 72 h; no routine consult for every patient (SEP-59).** SEP-59 is the matching card in the sepsis deck. The Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021 recommends discussing goals and prognosis with patients and families and suggests doing it early (within 72 hours, weak recommendation), but suggests against a routine formal palliative consult for every septic patient (conditional), because trials showed mixed effects on families; the ICU team integrates palliative principles itself and refers by trigger or judgement.
mimic: Primary vs specialist palliative care
Symptom control and goals-of-care talks by the ICU team for every patient vs a palliative-care team consult for triggered or complex cases.
traps: Waiting for prognostic certainty before involving palliative care
Uncertainty is a barrier, not a reason; the triggers act on a high risk, not on certainty.
Thinking SSC recommends a palliative consult for every septic patient
It advises early goals-of-care discussion for all, but against a routine formal consult for all.
decode: 79-year-old with advanced dementia, frailty, multi-organ failure and prolonged ventilation develops septic shock; tracheostomy and PEG are being considered. Strongest trigger for early palliative consult: vasopressors, PEG and tracheostomy consideration, broad-spectrum antibiotics, fever? [DocT GT]
PEG and tracheostomy consideration: it marks a commitment to prolonged life support; vasopressors reflect severity but many patients recover.

Metastatic cancer, septic shock, ventilated; the intensivist thinks more treatment will not help but struggles to say so at the family meeting. Barrier illustrated: lack of diagnostic resources, poor symptom-control protocols, deficient communication training, limited reimbursement? [DocT GT]
Deficient communication training: the prognosis is understood, the skill to convey it is missing.
x.punch: Barriers are poor communication skills, unrealistic hopes, uncertainty and the idea that palliation is surrender; consult on fixed triggers or before a tracheostomy or PEG, and discuss goals of care within 72 hours, but not with a routine consult for everyone.

topups.q: Macro- vs micro-allocation of healthcare resources?
a: - Macroallocation: system/policy decisions by government or payers on splitting a budget (e.g. capping hospital reimbursement to fund outpatient care).
- Microallocation: bedside decisions on which patient gets a scarce resource (last ICU bed, ventilator, organ), guided by justice and triage criteria.

x.sub: End-of-life care → Ethics → Justice: allocating resources
x.intro: Step 2 named justice as fair use of resources (EOL-03). Allocation decisions happen at two levels, and one DocT GT question asks you to tell them apart.
why: **Macroallocation: system/policy decisions by government or payers on splitting a budget (e.g. capping hospital reimbursement to fund outpatient care).** It is made away from the bedside, for populations, before any patient is known.

**Microallocation: bedside decisions on which patient gets a scarce resource (last ICU bed, ventilator, organ), guided by justice and triage criteria.** It is about named patients competing for one resource; triage criteria such as likely benefit keep it fair rather than first-come or by influence.
mimic: Macro- vs microallocation
Policy and budgets for a population vs choosing between identified patients for one bed, ventilator or organ.
traps: Calling a hospital’s choice of who gets the last ventilator ‘macroallocation’ because a hospital made it
It concerns identified patients and one resource, so it is microallocation; macro is budget-level policy.
decode: A health minister caps hospital reimbursement to expand outpatient coverage — macroallocation, microallocation by a physician, evidence-based restriction, or equality-based prioritisation? [DocT GT]
Macroallocation for system-level cost control: a policy decision about budgets, made for a population.
x.punch: Macroallocation is a government or payer splitting a budget; microallocation is choosing which patient gets the last bed, ventilator or organ, guided by justice and triage criteria.

spine: Naming the decisions

Withholding means not starting or not escalating a treatment, withdrawal means stopping it, and in both the disease, not the doctor, causes the death; only euthanasia and assisted suicide use a drug to end life.
The ethics that justify them

Autonomy (or a surrogate’s substituted judgment) decides what is accepted, doctors are not obliged to give futile treatment, and double effect allows symptom relief that may hasten death as long as death is not the intention.
Recognising futility
The process starts when the team judges, from age, function and response to treatment, that further intensive care will not return the patient to a life worth having, and this is the hardest step.
Consensus, disclosure, shared decision
The team agrees among itself first, then tells the family honestly and early, decides with them, documents, and continues treatment while consensus is not yet reached.
Comfort and a good death

Once the goal is comfort, pain, breathlessness, secretions and agitation are treated by the clock with opioids, glycopyrrolate and sedatives titrated to symptoms, and the family is cared for before and after the death.
The law in India

Active euthanasia is illegal; withdrawal and withholding are lawful since Aruna Shanbaug (2011) and Common Cause (2018), and since January 2023 they need two hospital medical boards of 5-year experts and an intimation to the magistrate, not a court.
SPECIAL02.primer: Life-sustaining treatment is anything that keeps a patient alive without curing the illness: ventilation, vasopressors, dialysis, artificial nutrition, CPR. In the ICU most deaths now follow a decision to limit such treatment, so the questions are who decides, on what ethical grounds, by what steps, and with what legal protection. A patient with capacity decides for himself; for one without, a surrogate speaks for him, ideally guided by an advance directive. In India the courts used the term ‘passive euthanasia’ for withdrawal or withholding, and ISCCM prefers to call it limitation of life support.

NUT-01.intro: Step 1 is why ICU feeding works differently from ordinary feeding. Illness switches the body into a catabolic state in which it breaks itself down for fuel and does not listen to incoming food. Every later decision about how much and how fast follows from this.
why: **Stress hormones (cortisol, glucagon, adrenaline) and insulin resistance.** These counter-regulatory hormones, with cytokines such as IL-6 and TNF, push the liver to release glucose and the tissues to resist insulin, so glucose stays high for the brain, immune cells and wounds. Stress hyperglycaemia is the visible result.

**Catabolism: glycogenolysis, gluconeogenesis from amino acids, lactate and glycerol, proteolysis (muscle to liver), lipolysis; hyperglycaemia.** Glycogen lasts about a day, so after that glucose is made from amino acids taken out of muscle, which is why the patient wastes fast.

**The body makes 50–75% of its glucose needs itself early on; feeding cannot switch this off.** In health, eating suppresses hepatic glucose output; in critical illness it does not. Full feeding in the first days is added on top of this endogenous supply, so the patient is overfed even when the figure on the chart says 100%. That is the reason for ESPEN’s hypocaloric start (no more than 70% of expenditure early, NUT-10).

**Energy expenditure rises about 10–15% in critical illness and about 50% in trauma.** Expenditure is raised less than most people assume, and sedation, ventilation and paralysis lower it further; burns raise it most. Overestimating needs is the commoner error.

**Early protein may be essential: 0.8 g/kg/day, building to over 1.2.** Protein loss cannot be stopped by feeding, but delivery of amino acids may limit how much muscle is used. EFFORT Protein (2023) found no benefit from pushing to 2.2 g/kg/day and possible harm in patients with AKI, so the target is moderate and reached gradually.
mimic: Stress response vs simple starvation
In starvation insulin falls, ketones rise and protein is spared; feeding reverses it. In critical illness insulin resistance and proteolysis continue whatever is fed.
traps: “Feeding to 100% from day 1 stops the catabolism”
Endogenous glucose production continues, so early full feeding overfeeds without sparing muscle.
decode: Why is hypocaloric feeding advised in the first days of critical illness? [pattern]
Endogenous glucose production (50–75% of needs) is not suppressed by feeding, so full feeding overfeeds.
NUT-01.punch: Early in critical illness the body feeds itself from its own muscle and the feed cannot stop it, so the first days are fed gently and protein is built up rather than calories pushed.

NUT-02.sub: Nutrition → Metabolism → Why the gut is fed
NUT-02.intro: Still in step 1: the gut is not only a route for calories but an organ that deteriorates when unused. That is the case for preferring enteral to parenteral nutrition when both are possible.
why: **Without luminal nutrition: villous atrophy, enterocyte apoptosis and inflammatory infiltration.** Enterocytes take much of their fuel straight from the lumen (glutamine, short-chain fatty acids), so an empty gut thins its own lining.

**Dysbiosis, loss of gut immune function (GALT) and bacterial translocation.** The gut holds a large share of the body’s lymphoid tissue; an atrophic, leaky mucosa lets bacteria and endotoxin cross, which is thought to feed sepsis and organ failure.

**Early EN reduces infections.** Meta-analyses of early versus delayed EN show fewer infections, which is why ESPEN and ASPEN both recommend starting within 24–48 hours. Against parenteral nutrition the gap is smaller than once believed: CALORIES (2014) found no difference in infections when PN was not overfed (NUT-14).
mimic: Benefit of early EN vs benefit of EN over PN
Early EN versus late EN: fewer infections. EN versus PN at similar calories: mortality and infections similar in CALORIES and NUTRIREA-2.
traps: “PN causes more infections because it is PN”
Older trials overfed with PN and hyperglycaemia; at matched, moderate doses the infection difference largely disappears.
decode: Main physiological reason to prefer enteral feeding [pattern]
Preserves the mucosal barrier and gut immunity, reducing translocation and infection.
NUT-02.punch: An unused gut atrophies and leaks, so feeding it early is treatment for the barrier as much as nutrition.

NUT-03.intro: Step 2 asks who is at risk. In the ICU the usual ward tools fail because the patient is oedematous and cannot answer questions, so assessment leans on history, muscle and illness severity.
why: **Gather weight and weight history, pre-admission intake, BMI, body composition, electrolytes, illness severity, comorbidities, drugs (propofol), expected stay, days in hospital before ICU, and signs of oedema, wasting or micronutrient deficiency.** Weight loss and poor intake before admission identify the malnourished and those at refeeding risk (NUT-12). Days in hospital before ICU and severity are themselves NUTRIC items (NUT-04). Propofol is listed because its lipid is a source of calories (NUT-16).

**Skinfold thickness, bioimpedance and mid-arm muscle circumference are unreliable in ICU (oedema).** Fluid in the tissues thickens skinfolds and limbs and changes the electrical resistance bioimpedance measures, so all three misread body composition after resuscitation.

**CT or ultrasound muscle thickness; urea:creatinine ratio (rises with muscle catabolism).** A CT slice at L3 or ultrasound of the quadriceps measures muscle directly and is not distorted much by oedema. A rising urea with a stable creatinine reflects protein breakdown.

**NUTRIC (critically ill).** NUTRIC is the ICU-specific risk score. NRS-2002 is the other score in ASPEN guidance (3 or more at risk, 5 or more high risk). ESPEN adds that any patient in ICU for more than 48 hours should be considered at risk of malnutrition.
mimic: Nutritional risk vs malnutrition
Risk scores (NUTRIC, NRS-2002) predict who benefits from feeding; malnutrition is diagnosed from weight loss, low BMI and reduced muscle (GLIM criteria).
traps: “Bioimpedance gives reliable body composition in ICU”
Oedema makes it unreliable (NUT-17c).
“Albumin measures nutritional status in ICU”
Albumin falls with inflammation and dilution; it is a marker of illness, not of nutrition.
decode: Which method of assessing nutritional status is reliable in an oedematous ICU patient? [pattern]
CT or ultrasound muscle measurement, not skinfolds, bioimpedance or albumin.
NUT-03.punch: Oedema defeats skinfolds and bioimpedance, so ICU assessment rests on history, muscle imaging and a risk score built from illness severity.

NUT-04.intro: Still in step 2: NUTRIC is the score that is calculated in exam stems. It was built to find the ICU patients in whom more nutrition changes mortality, so it scores how sick and how vulnerable the patient is rather than what he weighs. All three real questions are arithmetic or application of the high-risk cut-off.
why: **Age under 50 / 50–74 / 75+ scores 0 / 1 / 2.** Older patients have less muscle reserve and lose it faster.
**APACHE II under 15 / 15–19 / 20–27 / 28+ scores 0 / 1 / 2 / 3.** Severity of acute illness carries the most points.
**SOFA under 6 / 6–9 / 10+ scores 0 / 1 / 2.** Organ failure adds to APACHE because it captures what develops after admission.
**Days from hospital admission to ICU 0 / 1+ scores 0 / 1.** Days on the ward before ICU are usually days of poor intake, so they stand in for pre-existing deficit.
**IL-6 under 400 / 400+ scores 0 / 1.** It marks inflammation, but it is rarely measured and adds little.

**High risk: 6–10 with IL-6, or 5–9 on the modified score without IL-6; these patients have worse outcomes and benefit most from aggressive feeding. Low: 0–5 or 0–4.** The original validation showed that in high scorers more delivered calories went with lower mortality, while in low scorers it made no difference. ASPEN therefore advises that high-risk patients (NUTRIC 5 or more, or NRS-2002 5 or more) or the severely malnourished be advanced to goal as quickly as tolerated over 24–48 hours, while low-risk, well-nourished patients need no specialised nutrition for the first week.
mimic: NUTRIC vs NRS-2002

NUTRIC: ICU-specific, built from severity (APACHE, SOFA), no weight or intake. NRS-2002: weight loss, intake and BMI plus disease severity and age 70 or more; used on wards and by ASPEN alongside NUTRIC.
traps: “5 or 7” for age 68, APACHE 25, SOFA 9, two comorbidities, two days in hospital (59–63% right)
Common slips: APACHE 25 scores 2 (20–27 band), not 1 or 3; SOFA 9 is still in the 6–9 band (1); two days before ICU scores 1. Total 6.
“Young multitrauma” or “elderly elective lobectomy” is the patient to feed to goal fastest (26% right)

Feed to goal in 24–48 h by NUTRIC risk: the 76-year-old with urosepsis and renal failure scores on age (2), severity, SOFA and comorbidity. A 24-year-old scores little on age; an elective lobectomy has a short, low-severity stay.
“A modified NUTRIC of 5 is low risk”
On the modified score 5 or more is high risk; on the original with IL-6 the cut-off is 6.
decode: 68-year-old, septic shock, APACHE II 25, SOFA 9, two comorbidities, ICU 2 days after admission — NUTRIC? [DocT GT ×2]
6 (high risk on the modified score). Score each band carefully.
Which patient should have EN advanced to goal within 24–48 h rather than waiting up to a week? [DocT GT]
The one with the highest NUTRIC: 76-year-old with COPD, hypertension, urosepsis and renal failure (26%).
NUT-04.punch: Add age, APACHE, SOFA, comorbidities and days before ICU: 5 or more without IL-6 is high risk, and those patients are fed to goal within 24–48 hours while low scorers can wait.

NUT-05.sub: Nutrition → Enteral feeding → When to start
NUT-05.intro: Step 3 is starting the gut. The rule is early but gentle: begin within 24–48 hours at a low rate, and hold only when the circulation cannot yet support the gut. The two real questions test the timing and the true reasons to delay.
why: **Early EN within 24–48 h of ICU admission, at low dose.** ESPEN (2019, kept in 2023) and ASPEN both recommend it in a patient who cannot eat. Bowel sounds, flatus and extubation are not prerequisites; the gut absorbs before peristalsis can be heard.

**Advance gradually and avoid early rapid advancement to full target (ESPEN).** Full early feeding overfeeds (NUT-01) and NUTRIREA-3 (2023) found that a deliberately low intake in the first week (about 6 kcal/kg) did as well on survival as 25 kcal/kg, with faster recovery and fewer GI complications.

**On vasopressors: low-dose (trophic, 10–20 mL/h) EN if shock is controlled on small or moderate doses; withhold if shock is uncontrolled.** ESPEN delays EN when shock is uncontrolled and perfusion goals are not met, and starts low-dose EN as soon as shock is controlled with fluids and vasopressors, watching for signs of bowel ischaemia. Being on a vasopressor is therefore not itself a reason to delay. ESPEN’s other reasons to delay are uncontrolled hypoxaemia, hypercapnia or acidosis, active upper GI bleeding, overt bowel ischaemia, a high-output fistula without distal access, abdominal compartment syndrome and a gastric aspirate over 500 mL in 6 hours.

**NUTRIREA-2: early full-dose EN in shock gave about 4-fold more bowel ischaemia and colonic pseudo-obstruction.** In 2,410 ventilated patients in shock, normocaloric EN versus PN gave the same 28-day mortality (37 vs 35%), but bowel ischaemia was 2% vs under 1% (19 vs 5 patients) and acute colonic pseudo-obstruction 1% vs under 1%, with more vomiting and diarrhoea. The lesson is not to avoid EN in shock but not to push it to full dose: digestion raises splanchnic oxygen demand that a hypoperfused gut cannot meet.
mimic: Trophic vs full EN

Trophic: 10–20 mL/h (EDEN about 400 kcal/day) to keep the mucosa fed. Full: the calculated target. EDEN (2012) found no difference in ventilator-free days or mortality between them for 6 days in lung injury.
traps: “On vasopressors, so delay EN” (72% right)
Vasopressors alone do not delay feeding; uncontrolled shock does. The answer was the high-output fistula that cannot be bypassed.
“Wait for bowel sounds” or “until extubated” (81% right)
Neither is required; start within 24–48 h.
“Lactate 2 mmol/L means delay”
A normal lactate supports starting; a rising lactate on escalating vasopressors is the warning.
decode: TBI, stable, soft abdomen, briefly on vasopressors now off, 24 h after admission — when to start EN? [DocT GT]
Within 24–48 h of ICU admission (81%).
In which situation is EN delayed? [DocT GT]
High-output fistula that cannot be bypassed (72%); not vasopressors as such, not a lactate of 2, not a stable patient.
NUT-05.punch: Start low-dose feed within 24–48 hours once shock is controlled, even on modest vasopressors; delay for uncontrolled shock, ischaemia, obstruction or a fistula with no distal access, and never push to full dose early in shock.

NUT-06.intro: Still in step 3: where the tube goes. The stomach is the default because it is easy and physiological; the tube moves beyond the pylorus when the stomach will not empty or when aspiration risk is high, and a permanent route is chosen when feeding will last more than a month.
why: **Nasogastric: short-term default.** It is quick to place at the bedside, and the stomach tolerates bolus or continuous feed. ESPEN and ASPEN both make gastric feeding the standard first route.

**Post-pyloric (nasojejunal): gastric intolerance despite prokinetics; acute pancreatitis; placed under endoscopic guidance (Freka tube 110–120 cm).** Gastroparesis in critical illness affects the stomach more than the small bowel, so jejunal feed is absorbed when gastric feed sits. ESPEN uses it when intolerance is not solved by prokinetics. ESPEN and ASPEN also accept high aspiration risk as an indication: prior aspiration, a ventilated patient who must lie flat or prone, poor gastric emptying. The tube length on the card could not be confirmed: Fresenius Kabi lists its endoscopically placed Freka nasojejunal tubes (Endolumina, EasyIn) at 270 cm, cut to length after placement, so treat 110–120 cm as an approximate working length rather than the tube itself. In pancreatitis gastric feeding is acceptable for most; jejunal feeding is used when the stomach does not tolerate it.
**PEG or PEJ: feeding expected over 4 weeks.** Nasal tubes beyond a month cause sinusitis, nasal ulceration and displacement.

**Surgical gastrostomy: ascites, altered anatomy, or at the time of surgery.** Ascites stops the stomach adhering to the abdominal wall and leaks around a percutaneous tube; an obstructing tumour or previous surgery may make endoscopy impossible.
mimic: Post-pyloric for intolerance vs for aspiration risk
Both are accepted indications. Intolerance: high residuals despite prokinetics (NUT-13). Aspiration risk: prior aspiration pneumonia or a ventilated patient at high risk.
traps: “Ventilated COPD with prior aspiration pneumonia — continue nasogastric feeding”
High aspiration risk is itself an indication for post-pyloric feeding (Marrow).
“PEG when feeding is expected for over a week”
Over 4 weeks (NUT-17f).
decode: Ventilated COPD patient with previous aspiration pneumonia — feeding route? [Marrow]
Post-pyloric feeding.
Long-term feeding needed, tense ascites — route? [pattern]
Surgical gastrostomy (PEG is contraindicated by ascites).
NUT-06.punch: Stomach first; past the pylorus for intolerance that prokinetics do not fix or for high aspiration risk; a gastrostomy when feeding will last more than 4 weeks, surgical if there is ascites.

NUT-07.intro: Still in step 3: when the gut cannot be used. The absolute group are situations in which feed would harm the bowel itself; the relative group mean ‘feed with care, often at a low rate’. The real question, shared with NUT-05, asks which situation delays EN.
why: **Absolute: severe (uncontrolled) shock, bowel ischaemia, abdominal compartment syndrome, perforation or obstruction.** In each, feed either cannot pass or adds oxygen demand and distension to a gut that is already failing. ESPEN’s ‘delay EN’ list adds uncontrolled hypoxaemia, hypercapnia or acidosis, active upper GI bleeding, a high-output fistula without distal access and a gastric aspirate over 500 mL in 6 hours.

**Relative: GI intolerance, upper GI bleeding, short bowel syndrome, spinal cord injury and abdominal trauma.** ESPEN treats active upper GI bleeding as a reason to delay until it stops, then feed. For spinal cord injury and abdominal trauma once gut continuity is confirmed, ESPEN actually recommends early EN rather than withholding it, as it does in TBI, ECMO, prone position, an open abdomen and diarrhoea. A high-output fistula with no access beyond it is the classic additional reason to delay: feed above it simply pours out.
mimic: Proximal vs distal fistula
Proximal high-output with no distal access: delay EN or feed beyond the fistula. Distal low-output: EN can usually continue.
traps: “Vasopressors are a contraindication to EN”
Only uncontrolled shock is; controlled shock gets low-dose EN (NUT-05).
“Spinal cord injury or open abdomen means no EN”
ESPEN recommends early EN in both.
decode: In which situation is enteral nutrition delayed? [DocT GT]
High-output fistula that cannot be bypassed (72%).
NUT-07.punch: Withhold EN when the bowel is ischaemic, obstructed, perforated, under compartment pressure or bypassed by a high-output fistula, or when shock is uncontrolled; most other ‘contraindications’ mean feed slowly.

NUT-08.intro: Still in step 3: what goes down the tube. Formulas differ in how far their nutrients have been pre-digested. The one real question is about fat absorption in pancreatic insufficiency, which is why the MCT row matters most.
why: **Elemental: free amino acids, glucose and oligosaccharides, MCT fat, no fibre; used in malabsorption.** Nothing needs digesting, so it suits a gut that cannot digest, at the cost of high osmolality (diarrhoea) and price.
**Semi-elemental: peptides (hydrolysed), oligosaccharides, MCT, no fibre; used in poor absorption.** Peptides are absorbed by their own transporter and well tolerated in a damaged mucosa.

**Polymeric: whole protein, polysaccharides, long-chain fat, fibre available; the standard formula.** ESPEN and ASPEN advise a standard polymeric formula for almost every ICU patient; peptide formulas have shown no outcome advantage.

**Why MCT in malabsorption.** Medium-chain triglycerides are hydrolysed with little need for pancreatic lipase or bile, absorbed without forming micelles or chylomicrons, and go straight into portal blood. They are the fat of choice in pancreatic insufficiency, cholestasis, cirrhosis, short bowel and chylothorax. Long-chain and omega-6 rich fats all need lipase and bile. Energy-dense formulas (1.5 kcal/mL) give more calories in less volume, but TARGET (2018) found no survival benefit and more residuals and vomiting.
mimic: MCT vs LCT
MCT: portal vein, no bile or chylomicrons, no essential fatty acids. LCT: lymph via chylomicrons, needs lipase and bile, supplies essential fatty acids.
traps: “Pure long-chain triglycerides” or “high total fat” for steatorrhoea despite enzymes
Both need lipase and bile; MCT is the answer.
“Elemental formula should be routine in ICU”
Standard polymeric is the default; elemental only for genuine malabsorption.
decode: Chronic pancreatitis and cirrhosis, steatorrhoea despite enzymes — which lipid improves fat absorption? [DocT GT]
Medium-chain triglycerides.
NUT-08.punch: Standard polymeric feed for nearly everyone; the less the gut can digest, the more pre-digested the formula, and MCT is the fat that needs no lipase, bile or lymph.

NUT-09.sub: Nutrition → How much → Measuring energy needs
NUT-09.intro: Step 4 is how much to give, and it starts with how much the patient burns. This is the most-asked card in the deck: two questions on the target in kcal/kg, two on what indirect calorimetry measures and when it fails, and one on a quick equation. The reasoning that links them is simple: measure if you can, estimate if you must, and know what the estimate is based on.
why: **Indirect calorimetry is the gold standard: it measures VO₂ and VCO₂ (Weir equation, RQ).** The analyser samples inspired and expired gas over a short steady-state period at rest (AARC accepts 5 minutes if the gas readings vary by 5% or less, longer if not) and converts oxygen consumption and carbon dioxide production into energy expenditure with the Weir equation, then extrapolates to 24 hours. ESPEN (2019, 2023) recommends it whenever available, because equations are wrong by 20% or more in a large share of ICU patients. The respiratory quotient (VCO₂/VO₂) is about 1.0 for carbohydrate, 0.7 for fat and 0.8 for protein; above 1 means lipogenesis from overfeeding. Physiological values lie between about 0.67 and 1.3, so a result outside that range means the measurement is wrong, not the patient. It becomes unreliable at FiO₂ above 0.6, because the analyser cannot resolve the small inspired–expired oxygen difference, and with air leaks (bronchopleural fistula, chest drain, cuff leak), during RRT or ECMO (which remove CO₂ outside the lungs), and when the patient is not in steady state. A pulmonary artery catheter gives VO₂ by the Fick method, but that is not indirect calorimetry and underestimates it.

**Harris-Benedict: men 66 + 13.7W + 5H − 6.8A; women 655 + 9.6W + 1.8H − 4.7A (W kg, H cm, A years).** It predicts resting expenditure in health and needs a stress factor in illness. Age is subtracted because metabolic rate falls with age. A quicker version in Harrison is men 900 + 10W and women 700 + 7W, so a 50 kg man has about 1,400 kcal/day. In the ICU, guidelines more often use a simple weight-based estimate: ASPEN 2016 25–30 kcal/kg/day; ASPEN 2022 12–25 kcal/kg/day in the first 7–10 days; ESPEN, when nothing can be measured, a simple 20–25 kcal/kg/day, given at no more than 70% of it early.

**Stress factors: pneumonia with ARDS 1.2–1.3; minor surgery 1.1–1.3; major surgery 1.2–1.4; multiple trauma 1.4–1.6; trauma with closed head injury 1.5–1.7.** The resting value is multiplied by these to estimate illness-related expenditure. They are rough, which is one more reason to measure.

**Obesity: use ideal body weight.** Fat burns little energy, so actual weight overestimates needs. ASPEN gives 11–14 kcal/kg of actual weight per day for BMI 30–50 and 22–25 kcal/kg of ideal weight for BMI over 50, with protein 2.0 g/kg of ideal weight (up to 2.5 when BMI is 40 or more). ESPEN uses an adjusted body weight (its 2023 commentary: ideal weight plus 20–25% of the excess) for energy and for protein (1.3 g/kg/day).
mimic: Indirect calorimetry vs Fick VO₂ from a PA catheter
Calorimetry measures gas exchange at the mouth or tube; Fick calculates VO₂ from cardiac output and the arteriovenous oxygen difference and misses lung oxygen consumption.
Indirect vs direct calorimetry
Direct calorimetry measures heat released in a sealed chamber; it is a research tool.
traps: “1,800 kcal/day” or “1,500” for an 80-kg ventilated trauma patient (32% right)

The key uses 25–30 kcal/kg (2,000–2,400), so 2,100 is the only option in range. Under ESPEN’s early hypocaloric approach or ASPEN 2022’s 12–25 kcal/kg, 1,800 or 1,500 would be a reasonable first-week dose, so read whether the stem asks for the goal or the early dose.
“Measures O₂ consumption and CO₂ production over 24 hours” (44% right)
It measures at rest over a short steady-state period and extrapolates.
“FiO₂ 0.40” or “measurement duration” explains an RQ of 1.55
FiO₂ 0.90 does: above 0.6 the analyser error explodes; any RQ above about 1.3 is an artefact.
decode: 39-year-old 80-kg intubated trauma patient — daily calorie goal for tube feeding? [DocT GT]
2,100 kcal/day (25–30 kcal/kg), 32%.
Indirect calorimetry determines energy expenditure by measuring? [DocT GT]
O₂ consumption and CO₂ production at rest (44%).
Ventilated, indirect calorimetry RQ 1.55 — which factor explains the unreliable result? [DocT GT]
FiO₂ 0.90.
Resting energy expenditure of a 50-kg man? [Marrow]
NUT-09.punch: Indirect calorimetry measures resting VO₂ and VCO₂ and fails at high FiO₂, leaks and extracorporeal circuits; when it is unavailable the goal is 25–30 kcal/kg, with less in the first days.
