overfeeds early in the stress phase

NUT-10.sub: Nutrition → How much → Energy and protein over time
NUT-10.intro: Still in step 4: the targets change as the patient moves from the acute catabolic phase to recovery. The card’s schedule is the hypocaloric-then-build approach that the large trials of the last decade support.
why: **Early (first days): 20 kcal/kg/day, hypocaloric; protein starts at 0.8 g/kg/day.** ESPEN gives no more than 70% of expenditure early. Trials comparing less with more in the first week (EDEN, PermiT, TARGET, NUTRIREA-3) showed no mortality difference; where GI tolerance was reported the lower arms did better (fewer GI events with trophic feeding in EDEN and with low intake in NUTRIREA-3, more vomiting and larger residuals with the energy-dense feed in TARGET).

**End of week 1: 25 kcal/kg/day; protein ramps to over 1.2–1.3 g/kg/day.** ESPEN increases to 80–100% of measured expenditure after day 3 and gives 1.3 g/kg/day protein progressively; ASPEN gives 1.2–2.0 g/kg/day. EFFORT Protein (2023) found that prescribing 2.2 g/kg/day or more did not improve outcomes, with signals of harm in patients with AKI or higher SOFA scores (exploratory subgroups).

**Recovery (anabolic): 30 kcal/kg/day with high-protein formulas (protein without excess non-protein calories).** Only now can the body build muscle, so energy and protein rise and rehabilitation begins.
mimic: Permissive underfeeding vs trophic feeding
PermiT: 40–60% of calories with full protein. EDEN: trophic about 400 kcal/day with little protein. Neither changed mortality.
traps: “More protein is always better”
EFFORT Protein found no benefit from high doses and possible harm in AKI; monitor urea and renal function when pushing protein.
decode: Energy and protein target in the first days of critical illness [pattern]
Hypocaloric (about 20 kcal/kg or ≤70% of measured expenditure), protein built progressively towards 1.3 g/kg/day.
NUT-10.punch: Low calories and modest protein early, 25 kcal/kg and about 1.3 g/kg by the end of the first week, and more of both only when the patient turns anabolic.

NUT-11.sub: Nutrition → How much → Micronutrients and immunonutrition
NUT-11.intro: Still in step 4: the small components. Basic replacement is routine; pharmacological doses meant to modify the illness have mostly failed, and one of them harmed. The single real question is about a low zinc level, which tests how plasma levels behave in inflammation.
why: **Trace elements and vitamins support metabolism, immunity, antioxidant defence and wound healing.** Requirements rise with losses (burns, drains, fistulae, CRRT), while plasma levels of zinc, selenium, iron and vitamin C fall in inflammation because they move into tissues, not because stores are empty. A low level with a high CRP is therefore hard to interpret.

**Early IV multi-trace elements and multivitamins alongside EN, plus thiamine 100–300 mg.** Daily maintenance doses are given with PN and when EN covers too little. Thiamine (100–300 mg a day for the first days) is given to those at risk of refeeding or alcohol-related deficiency (NUT-12).

**Not routinely recommended: glutamine, arginine, taurine, omega-3, γ-linolenic acid, carnitine; pharmacological vitamin C, E, β-carotene, selenium and zinc.** REDOXS (2013) found that high-dose glutamine increased mortality in multi-organ failure. ESPEN still allows enteral glutamine in burns over 20% of body surface and in trauma, and says it should not be given to other ICU patients.
mimic: Deficiency vs redistribution
Deficiency: losses or poor intake, clinical signs (rash, poor wound healing, diarrhoea for zinc). Redistribution: low plasma level with raised CRP and no signs.
traps: “Plasma zinc is low, so give pharmacological zinc”

Marrow keys ‘monitor zinc, no treatment yet’: low plasma zinc in acute illness is mostly redistribution. Replace when deficiency is clinically likely or losses are high. The Marrow explanation contradicts its key, and 0.2 µg/mL is very low, so the key is debatable.
“Routine glutamine improves outcome”
Not recommended; harmful in REDOXS (NUT-17h).
decode: Severe TBI on tube feeds, day 7 zinc 0.2 µg/mL — management? [Marrow]
Monitor zinc; no treatment yet (keyed). Supplement if signs of deficiency or high losses.
NUT-11.punch: Give maintenance trace elements, vitamins and thiamine; a low plasma level in inflammation is often redistribution, and pharmacological ‘immunonutrition’, glutamine above all, is not routine.

NUT-12.intro: Step 5 is when feeding itself harms, and refeeding is the classic case. A starved patient has adapted to burning fat; when carbohydrate arrives, insulin rises and pulls electrolytes into cells faster than the depleted body can supply them. Both real questions ask how to manage it: one a low phosphate, the other a malnourished patient about to be fed.
why: **Feeding after severe malnutrition: insulin drives phosphate, potassium and magnesium into cells.** Total body stores are low but plasma levels can be normal before feeding. Insulin moves these ions into cells and phosphate is consumed to make ATP and 2,3-DPG for glycolysis, so plasma levels fall within 2–3 days.

**Labs: low phosphate, potassium and magnesium; thiamine deficiency.** Phosphate is the defining one. In the ICU refeeding trial (Doig 2015) refeeding hypophosphataemia was defined as a fall below 0.65 mmol/L (2.0 mg/dL), by more than 0.16 mmol/L, within 72 hours of starting feed. To convert, mg/dL × 0.323 gives mmol/L, so 1.8 mg/dL is about 0.58 mmol/L.

**Effects: arrhythmia, cardiomyopathy, hypotension, respiratory and muscle weakness, kidney dysfunction, confusion, seizures, Wernicke’s.** Without phosphate, muscle (including the diaphragm and heart) cannot make ATP, so weaning fails and the heart fails; low potassium and magnesium add arrhythmias; salt and water retention with carbohydrate refeeding adds fluid overload.

**Risk: eating disorders, chronic illness with malnutrition, alcohol, prolonged starvation.** NICE CG32 gives high risk as one of: BMI under 16, unintentional weight loss over 15% in 3–6 months, little or no intake for over 10 days, or low potassium, phosphate or magnesium before feeding; or two of: BMI under 18.5, weight loss over 10%, little intake for over 5 days, alcohol misuse or drugs such as insulin, chemotherapy, antacids or diuretics.

**Prevention: thiamine first; restrict fluid and calories (500 kcal/day or 25% of target); advance in four 25% steps; replace and monitor electrolytes.** The schedules differ by source. NICE starts at no more than 10 kcal/kg/day (5 kcal/kg/day in extreme cases such as BMI under 14) and reaches full needs over 4–7 days, with thiamine 200–300 mg daily. ESPEN: when refeeding hypophosphataemia appears in ICU, restrict energy for 48 hours and then increase gradually, with electrolytes checked 2–3 times a day; in the Doig trial (339 patients) this restriction, starting at about 480 kcal/day for 2 days, did not change the primary outcome (days alive after ICU discharge) but 60-day mortality, a secondary outcome, was lower. Thiamine goes in before carbohydrate in a planned feed, because glucose metabolism uses it up. Treat low phosphate by severity: IV replacement for severe levels (under about 0.3 mmol/L, 1 mg/dL), for symptoms, or when the oral or enteral route is unreliable, which in ventilated, tube-fed ICU patients often makes IV the choice for moderate levels (0.3–0.6 mmol/L) too.
mimic: Refeeding hypophosphataemia vs ICU hypophosphataemia from other causes
Refeeding: within 72 h of starting or increasing feed in a malnourished patient. Others: diuretics, RRT, DKA treatment, respiratory alkalosis, sepsis.
traps: “Oral phosphate for 1.8 mg/dL in a tube-fed MOF patient”

Marrow keys IV potassium phosphate. Ward tables reserve IV for under 1.0 mg/dL or symptoms, but in critical illness enteral absorption is unreliable and the patient is often ventilated, so IV is the ICU answer; the qpack notes the conflict.
“Malnourished BMI 16 with ARDS — start full feeding to reverse the deficit”
BMI under 16 is high refeeding risk: low-rate EN (about 10 kcal/kg), advanced slowly, with thiamine and electrolytes (Marrow).
“Start glucose before thiamine” in a planned refeed
Thiamine first (NUT-17e). In hypoglycaemic coma glucose is never delayed (TOX-01).
decode: MOF on tube feeds, day 5 phosphate 1.8 mg/dL — best management? [Marrow]
IV potassium phosphate (keyed); oral absorption is poor in critical illness.
Severe ARDS, malnourished (BMI 16), volume overloaded — feeding strategy? [Marrow]
Low-rate EN, advance slowly.
NUT-12.punch: In a starved patient insulin from the first feed drives phosphate into cells; give thiamine first, start low (about 10 kcal/kg), build over days, check phosphate, potassium and magnesium often, and give phosphate IV in the ICU.

parts.q: NICE CG32 high refeeding risk — one criterion?
parts.a: BMI <16, weight loss >15% in 3–6 months, little or no intake >10 days, or low K/PO₄/Mg before feeding. Two criteria: BMI <18.5, loss >10%, little intake >5 days, alcohol or insulin, chemotherapy, antacids, diuretics.

NUT-13.intro: Still in step 5: feed that the gut will not take. The approach depends on where the problem sits: the stomach that will not empty, the small bowel that distends, or the colon that empties too much. Both real questions are about what to do next, one with high residuals and one with diarrhoea.
why: **Gastric (vomiting, large GRV, distension): stop or slow EN, then prokinetics, then post-pyloric feeding if there is no bowel distension. Small bowel (distension, no stool, rising IAP): stop EN or keep a low rate, measure IAP, laxatives and prokinetics. Lower GI: diarrhoea — keep EN (low rate if severe), stop laxatives, find the trigger (C. difficile); consider Ogilvie’s and ischaemia. GRV over 500 mL in 6 h is intolerance; routine GRV checks are no longer recommended.** For the stomach, ESPEN makes IV erythromycin the first-line prokinetic (metoclopramide is the alternative, or both together) for 24–48 hours, stopping prokinetics after 3 days because they lose effect, and moves to post-pyloric feeding when prokinetics do not solve it; a severe ARDS patient, ventilated and often prone, at high aspiration risk can go straight to a post-pyloric tube (NUT-06). In the small bowel, rising intra-abdominal pressure with distension is the route to abdominal compartment syndrome, which is a reason to stop EN (NUT-07). Diarrhoea in ICU is usually from drugs (laxatives, sorbitol-containing syrups, antibiotics) or infection, rarely the feed alone; stopping EN does not cure it and leaves the patient unfed, so ESPEN recommends early EN even with diarrhoea. On residuals, ESPEN delays EN when the gastric aspirate exceeds 500 mL in 6 hours and adds a prokinetic; ASPEN advises against routine GRV monitoring and, where it is still used, not to hold feed for a GRV under 500 mL, because residuals correlate poorly with aspiration and checking them mostly stops feeding.
mimic: High GRV vs bowel obstruction or ischaemia
High GRV alone with a soft abdomen: prokinetic or post-pyloric. Distension, pain, rising lactate or IAP: stop feed and look for ischaemia; never push post-pyloric into an ischaemic gut.
traps: “Septic patient with large watery stools — stop the feed”
Reduce the rate (Marrow keys 20 mL/h), stop laxatives and send C. difficile; keep feeding.
“Hold feed for any GRV over 250 mL”
The threshold is 500 mL (in 6 h for ESPEN), and routine checks are discouraged.
“Prokinetics before post-pyloric” vs the Marrow key

The card ladder uses prokinetics first; Marrow keys post-pyloric for severe ARDS with high residuals at 12 h. If prokinetics are offered and aspiration risk is not stressed, prokinetics; if the stem stresses ventilated, severe ARDS or failed prokinetics, post-pyloric.
decode: Severe ARDS on trickle feeds, high gastric residuals at 12 h — next step? [Marrow]
Post-pyloric feeding tube (keyed).
Septic patient on tube feeds, large watery stools every 2 h — next step? [Marrow]
Reduce feed rate to 20 mL/h (and test for C. difficile).
NUT-13.punch: Slow the feed, add erythromycin, then go past the pylorus for a stomach that will not empty; for diarrhoea keep feeding at a low rate and find the drug or bug; 500 mL is the only residual that matters.

table.title: Where the intolerance sits
head: Level
Signs
Action
rows: stop or low-rate EN, measure IAP, laxatives + prokinetics
**keep EN at low rate**, stop laxatives, test C. difficile; think Ogilvie’s, ischaemia

NUT-14.sub: Nutrition → Problems and PN → Enteral vs parenteral
NUT-14.intro: Step 6 is the vein. Older teaching that PN is dangerous came from trials that overfed it with glucose; at matched, moderate doses CALORIES and NUTRIREA-2 found the same mortality with either route. The differences that remain are cost, the gut barrier, the central line and metabolic complications, and the three real questions are all about the last two.
why: **Cost: enteral lower, parenteral higher.** PN needs sterile compounding, a line and more monitoring.
**Physiology: enteral is physiological and preserves the gut barrier; parenteral bypasses the gut.** NUT-02 gives the reason.

**Infection: enteral lower; parenteral has CLABSI.** The line is the main infection risk. CALORIES (2014, 2,388 patients) found no difference in infections or 30-day mortality (33.1 vs 34.2%) when PN was dosed modestly, with less hypoglycaemia and vomiting on PN. A sudden new hyperglycaemia in a patient on unchanged PN often heralds catheter-related sepsis: infection causes insulin resistance before fever appears.

**Access: enteral needs no central line; parenteral needs a central line, PICC or midline.** Standard PN is hyperosmolar, far above the roughly 850–900 mOsm/L a peripheral vein tolerates, so it needs a central vein; only dilute peripheral PN can use a peripheral vein.

**Specific risks: enteral aspiration and bowel ischaemia; parenteral hyperglycaemia, steatosis (lipid over 50%) and hypertriglyceridaemia.** Hyperglycaemia is the commonest metabolic complication of PN, so it is the answer when offered. Refeeding hypophosphataemia, hypokalaemia and hypomagnesaemia are next. Hepatic steatosis comes mainly from excess calories, especially glucose beyond about 5 mg/kg/min, which is turned into fat; high soybean lipid doses add cholestasis. Other PN complications are cholestasis and gallbladder sludge (no enteral stimulus to empty it). Stopping PN abruptly can cause rebound hypoglycaemia, because insulin secreted in response to the glucose load outlasts it; taper the infusion or run 10% dextrose and check glucose.
**PN advantage: avoids aspiration and bowel ischaemia.** In NUTRIREA-2 the PN arm had less vomiting, bowel ischaemia and colonic pseudo-obstruction than full-dose EN in shock.
mimic: Rebound hypoglycaemia vs other causes of sudden obtundation after stopping PN
Check glucose first: high circulating insulin with no incoming glucose makes it the immediate cause, treated with IV glucose.
traps: “Hyponatraemia is the lab abnormality associated with TPN”
Marrow keys it, but the key is doubtful: hyperglycaemia is the commonest metabolic complication of TPN, then refeeding hypophosphataemia and hypokalaemia. If hyperglycaemia is offered, choose it.
“Trauma patient on TPN, line pulled, obtunded 4 h later — CT head first”
Give IV glucose: rebound hypoglycaemia after an abrupt stop (Marrow).
“Stable PN, glucose suddenly rises — the PN is too concentrated”
Nothing changed in the bag; new hyperglycaemia points to infection, usually the line (Marrow).
decode: Post-laparotomy TPN through a central line — associated lab abnormality? [Marrow]
Keyed hyponatraemia; hyperglycaemia is the better answer when offered.
Trauma, on TPN, line removed for an infected site, obtunded 4 h later — next step? [Marrow]
IV glucose (rebound hypoglycaemia).
Gunshot wound, ventilated on unchanged TPN, day 6 glucose rises sharply — cause? [Marrow]
Infection (catheter sepsis).
NUT-14.punch: Dosed sensibly, PN is as safe as EN for survival; its problems are the line and glucose, so new hyperglycaemia on steady PN means sepsis and an abrupt stop means rebound hypoglycaemia.

NUT-15.sub: Nutrition → Problems and PN → When to start PN
NUT-15.intro: Still in step 6: when PN is added. The trials say that hurrying it in a well-nourished patient does harm, while waiting too long in a starved patient with a useless gut also harms. The single real question names EPaNIC, so the answer follows that trial.
why: **Supplemental PN when EN covers under 60% of target despite efforts.** The 60% figure is ASPEN 2016’s threshold (consider SPN if EN cannot meet more than 60% of energy and protein needs after 7–10 days) and the trigger in the Heidegger SPN trial (EN under 60% by day 3, SPN from day 4). ESPEN says PN should not be started until every reasonable strategy to improve EN tolerance has been tried, and weighs supplemental PN case by case, suggesting days 4–7.

**Timing: low risk after about day 7 (ASPEN); high risk or EN contraindicated, early (ESPEN, within 3–7 days).** ASPEN 2022 recommends not starting SPN before day 7 of ICU admission, except in the malnourished or those with little lean mass, where clinical judgement applies. EPaNIC (2011, 4,640 patients) found that late PN from day 8 led to fewer new infections (22.8 vs 26.2%), more patients discharged alive from ICU by day 8 and lower cost than early PN, with no mortality difference. When EN is impossible, ESPEN starts PN within 3–7 days, and ASPEN starts it as soon as possible in the severely malnourished or high-risk patient.
**Absolute contraindications: adequate oral intake, or EN meeting targets.** PN then adds only line risk.

**Relative contraindications: no central access, substrate intolerance (renal, cardiac or hepatic failure), terminal illness.** Fluid volume, glucose and lipid loads can be hard to give in these patients, and in terminal illness PN rarely changes the outcome.
**Separate infusions or all-in-one bags.** All-in-one (three-chamber) bags have fewer line manipulations and lower contamination risk; separate infusions allow flexible lipid and glucose doses.
mimic: Supplemental PN vs total PN
Supplemental: adds to inadequate EN. Total: the only source, when the gut cannot be used.
traps: “Start TPN immediately on day 3 to avoid caloric debt” (EPaNIC stem)
In a well-nourished patient (BMI 26) in shock, delay PN until day 8 and keep trying trophic EN.
“Start supplemental PN to 100% of target by day 4”
Full early feeding overfeeds in the acute phase (NUT-01); EPaNIC and ASPEN 2022 favour waiting.
“Post-pyloric tube with protein over 2 g/kg/day”
Post-pyloric is reasonable, but over 2 g/kg/day was not beneficial in EFFORT Protein; the option is wrong on dose.
decode: Faecal peritonitis, septic shock on noradrenaline 0.2 µg/kg/min, BMI 26, failed EN on day 3 — by EPaNIC, next step? [DocT GT]
Delay PN until day 8 while continuing trophic EN.
NUT-15.punch: In a well-nourished patient, PN waits until about day 8 (EPaNIC, ASPEN 2022) while trophic EN continues; the malnourished patient with no usable gut gets it early.

NUT-16.intro: Back to step 5: harm from too much. Overfeeding is easy in the ICU because calories come from sources nobody counts and because the stressed body is already making glucose. The one real question asks for a sensible dextrose–lipid prescription, which is really a test of the limits.
why: **Harms: hyperglycaemia, raised CO₂ production (harder weaning), liver steatosis.** Carbohydrate beyond what can be oxidised is turned into fat (lipogenesis), which produces extra CO₂ (RQ over 1) and loads the lungs of a patient being weaned; the fat is stored in the liver. ESPEN keeps glucose (PN) or carbohydrate (EN) at or below 5 mg/kg/min and IV lipid, counting non-nutritional sources such as propofol, at or below 1.5 g/kg/day; in practice lipid is commonly about 20–30% of calories.

**Hidden calories: propofol (1.1 kcal/mL in lipid), dextrose infusions, citrate.** Propofol 1% is in a 10% lipid emulsion: 20 mL/h gives about 530 kcal/day, so the PN lipid should be cut. 5% dextrose gives 50 g (170 kcal) per litre. Citrate used for anticoagulation of CRRT is metabolised and adds calories.

**Obesity: feed by ideal body weight, hypocaloric and high-protein.** ASPEN gives obese patients fewer calories and more protein per kg of ideal weight (NUT-09d), so that fat is used while muscle is protected.
mimic: Overfeeding vs refeeding
Overfeeding: too much for any patient, hyperglycaemia, CO₂ and steatosis. Refeeding: even modest feed in a starved patient, electrolyte crash.
traps: “The Marrow PN regimen is fine because it is keyed” (12.5% dextrose 100 mL/h + 20% lipid 50 mL/h)

Over 24 h that is 300 g dextrose (about 3 mg/kg/min in 70 kg, acceptable) but 1,200 mL of 20% lipid, about 2,400 kcal and 240 g fat (over 3 g/kg/day), far above the limits. The key only fits if the lipid runs for part of the day; the Marrow explanation’s arithmetic is wrong.
“Propofol only sedates”
It is a lipid source and must be counted.
decode: Post bowel resection, starting TPN — most appropriate dextrose and lipid composition? [Marrow]
Keyed 12.5% dextrose 100 mL/h + 20% lipid 50 mL/h; check against glucose ≤5 mg/kg/min and lipid 20–30% of calories.
Failed weaning, high PaCO₂, on full PN with propofol [pattern]
Overfeeding raises CO₂ production; count the propofol and reduce carbohydrate.
NUT-16.punch: Count every calorie, including propofol, dextrose and citrate; keep glucose under 5 mg/kg/min and lipid modest, because excess becomes fat in the liver and CO₂ in the lungs.

parts.q: PN arithmetic for 70 kg — 12.5% dextrose at 100 mL/h?

NUT-17.intro: The last card runs back through the whole story, one statement per step. Each false statement is a distractor from an earlier card.
why: **True: early EN is started within 24–48 h.** ESPEN within 48 h, ASPEN within 24–48 h (NUT-05).
**False: full-dose EN is not safe on high-dose vasopressors; low-dose only, and only if shock is controlled.** NUTRIREA-2 showed more bowel ischaemia with full-dose EN in shock.
**False: bioimpedance is unreliable in ICU (oedema).** NUT-03.
**True: a modified NUTRIC of 6 is high risk.** The modified cut-off is 5 or more (NUT-04).
**False: in refeeding, thiamine comes first.** Carbohydrate uses up thiamine and can precipitate Wernicke’s (NUT-12).
**False: PEG is for feeding expected over 4 weeks, not 1 week.** NUT-06.
**True: supplemental PN is considered when EN gives under 60% of target.** NUT-15; timing after about day 7 in the well-nourished.
**False: routine glutamine is not recommended.** REDOXS showed harm; ESPEN keeps enteral glutamine only for burns and trauma (NUT-11).
mimic: Modified vs original NUTRIC cut-off
Modified (no IL-6): 5 or more. Original (with IL-6): 6 or more.
traps: “PEG after 1 week”
4 weeks.
“Thiamine after the first feed”
Before.
decode: Which statement about ICU nutrition is true? [pattern]
Early low-dose EN within 24–48 h; mNUTRIC ≥5 high risk; SPN when EN <60% of target.
NUT-17.punch: Three statements are true: early EN in 24–48 hours, a modified NUTRIC of 6 is high risk, and supplemental PN is considered below 60% of target; the rest are distractors from earlier cards.

topups.q: Wernicke encephalopathy: picture, MRI and treatment?
a: - Triad (complete in only ~10%): confusion, ataxia, ophthalmoplegia/nystagmus; alcohol, hyperemesis, bariatric surgery, refeeding.
- MRI: symmetric T2/FLAIR signal in medial thalami, mammillary bodies, periaqueductal grey and tectum.
- Treat on suspicion: thiamine 500 mg IV 8-hourly × 3 days, then 250 mg daily.
- Never delay glucose to give thiamine first (TOX-01).

x.sub: Nutrition → When feeding harms → Wernicke encephalopathy
x.intro: Step 5 covered harm from feeding a starved patient, and Wernicke encephalopathy is its neurological form. Thiamine is a cofactor for the enzymes that move glucose through the Krebs cycle, and body stores last only a few weeks, so a malnourished patient given carbohydrate uses up what is left and the most metabolically active parts of the brain fail first. The one GT question asks for the picture, the scan and the treatment together.
why: **Triad (complete in only about 10%): confusion, ataxia, ophthalmoplegia or nystagmus; causes are alcohol, hyperemesis, bariatric surgery and refeeding.** Because the full triad is uncommon (16% in Harper’s autopsy series of 131 cases, and 19% had no recorded signs), waiting for all three misses most cases; the Caine criteria, derived in alcohol-dependent patients, need only two of dietary deficiency, eye signs, cerebellar signs and altered mental state or memory. In the ICU the patient is often sedated, so the eye signs and an unexplained confusion in a malnourished or alcohol-dependent patient are enough. Hyperemesis, bariatric surgery, prolonged vomiting, cancer and refeeding (NUT-12) are the non-alcohol causes that stems use.

**MRI: symmetric T2/FLAIR signal in the medial thalami, mammillary bodies, periaqueductal grey and tectum.** These regions surround the third ventricle and aqueduct and have the highest thiamine-dependent glucose turnover, so they swell first. MRI is specific but not sensitive (it is normal in many patients), so a normal scan does not exclude the diagnosis and never delays treatment.

**Treat on suspicion: thiamine 500 mg IV 8-hourly for 3 days, then 250 mg daily.** Oral thiamine is poorly absorbed, especially in alcohol use, so high-dose IV is given; regimens differ (EFNS: at least 200 mg three times daily IV; some UK hospital protocols use two pairs of Pabrinex three times daily for 5–7 days). Eye signs improve within hours to days, ataxia and confusion more slowly; untreated, it progresses to Korsakoff’s amnesia, coma and death. Magnesium is replaced too, because the thiamine-dependent enzymes need it.

**Never delay glucose to give thiamine first (TOX-01).** A hypoglycaemic brain is injured within minutes, while a single glucose dose does not precipitate Wernicke’s; give glucose at once and thiamine alongside. The ‘thiamine first’ rule applies to a planned refeed, not to an emergency.
mimic: Wernicke vs Korsakoff
Wernicke: acute, confusion, ataxia, eye signs, reversible with thiamine. Korsakoff: chronic, anterograde amnesia with confabulation, largely irreversible.
Wernicke vs hepatic encephalopathy in an alcoholic
Both confuse; eye signs and ataxia point to Wernicke, asterixis and high ammonia to hepatic encephalopathy. Treat Wernicke anyway when in doubt.
traps: “All three features are needed before thiamine”
The triad is complete in only about a tenth; treat on suspicion.
“A normal MRI excludes Wernicke’s”
MRI is specific, not sensitive.
“Thiamine 100 mg orally is enough”
Suspected Wernicke’s needs high-dose IV thiamine.
“Hold glucose until thiamine is given”
Glucose is never delayed in hypoglycaemia (TOX-01).
decode: Wernicke encephalopathy — clinical picture, MRI findings and treatment? [DocT GT]
Confusion, ataxia, eye signs (triad often incomplete); symmetric medial thalamic, mammillary and periaqueductal T2/FLAIR signal; high-dose IV thiamine on suspicion.
Malnourished patient started on feed, becomes confused with nystagmus on day 3 [pattern]
Refeeding-induced Wernicke’s: IV thiamine, check phosphate and magnesium.
x.punch: Treat Wernicke’s on suspicion with high-dose IV thiamine, because the triad is usually incomplete and MRI often normal; and never delay glucose for a hypoglycaemic patient while waiting for it.

spine: Catabolism you cannot switch off
Critical illness drives stress hormones, insulin resistance and muscle breakdown to make glucose, and feeding cannot suppress that early production, so full feeding in the first days overfeeds.
Who is at nutritional risk

Weight, intake and muscle tell you who is malnourished, oedema makes skinfolds and bioimpedance useless, and a high NUTRIC score (6 or more, or 5 or more without IL-6) picks those who gain most from feeding.
Start the gut early, gently
Give low-dose enteral feed within 24–48 hours through the stomach unless shock is uncontrolled or the gut is ischaemic, obstructed or inaccessible, and advance slowly.
How much energy and protein
Measure energy with indirect calorimetry where possible, give no more than about 70% of it early and 80–100% after day 3, and build protein towards 1.3 g/kg/day.
When feeding itself harms
Refeeding a starved patient crashes phosphate, intolerance shows as residuals, distension or diarrhoea, and hidden calories and excess glucose overfeed.
When to use the vein
Parenteral nutrition is as safe as enteral when dosed sensibly, but it is kept for an unusable gut or a failing enteral route, and in a well-nourished patient it can wait until about day 8.
SPECIAL03.primer: A critically ill patient’s energy expenditure is set by his illness, not by what he eats, and in the first days his liver makes much of the glucose he needs whatever he is fed. Energy is counted in kcal per kg per day and protein in g per kg per day, using actual weight in most patients and an ideal or adjusted weight in the obese. The two routes are enteral (into the gut, by tube: gastric or post-pyloric) and parenteral (into a vein, usually central). The two guideline bodies quoted throughout are ESPEN (European, 2019, partly revised 2023) and ASPEN/SCCM (American, 2016, updated 2022); where they differ, the DocT stems linked to this deck mostly use ASPEN numbers.

PK-01.sub: Special topics → Pharmacokinetics → Absorption in the critically ill
PK-01.intro: Step 1 is getting the drug into the circulation at all. In a well patient a tablet or a subcutaneous injection behaves predictably; in shock the body diverts blood away from the gut and the skin to keep the heart and brain perfused, so anything placed in those beds sits there. The three real questions test three variants of this: a subcutaneous drug in shock, a high first-pass drug switched to IV, and a drug that binds to enteral feed. Most of the cohort got all three wrong.
why: **PK determinants: Vd, clearance, Cmax, Cmin, AUC₀₋₂₄.** Vd and clearance are properties of the patient and the drug; Cmax (the peak), Cmin (the trough) and the area under the concentration–time curve over 24 hours are the exposures that result from a given dose. Each antibiotic’s effect is tied to one of these exposures (PK-09), which is why the changes in this deck matter.

**Why absorption falls: shock (gut blood flow diverted), mucosal atrophy, poor motility (opioids, electrolytes), raised gastric pH (PPI, H2 blockers), reduced pancreatic function.** Splanchnic vasoconstriction in shock and on vasopressors cuts the blood flow that carries absorbed drug away. An unused gut atrophies, opioids and low potassium or magnesium slow emptying, and acid suppression stops drugs that need acid to dissolve (itraconazole capsules, ketoconazole) from going into solution. The same vasoconstriction affects the skin, so subcutaneous drugs are absorbed poorly too: on vasopressors subcutaneous enoxaparin gives low anti-Xa levels, and an IV heparin infusion is the safer choice.

**Drug–feed interactions: warfarin, phenytoin, tetracyclines, minocycline, ciprofloxacin, fluconazole bind to enteral feed.** Phenytoin binds to feed proteins and to the tube, so starting continuous feeds can drop its level sharply; hold the feed for about 2 hours before and after each dose (UK Specialist Pharmacy Service advice), or give it IV, and recheck the level. Ciprofloxacin and the tetracyclines chelate the calcium, magnesium and iron in the feed. Warfarin binds to feed protein, and its effect falls even with low-vitamin-K feeds, so the INR drifts when feeds start or stop. Fluconazole is the weakest member of this list: it is still well absorbed through a feeding tube (see FLAGS).
mimic: Poor absorption vs high first-pass metabolism

Poor absorption means less drug reaches the portal blood. High first-pass metabolism means plenty is absorbed but the gut wall and liver destroy most of it before it reaches the systemic circulation, so the IV dose is much smaller than the oral one (oral bioavailability of metoprolol is about 50%, and its label puts oral to IV doses for the same beta-blockade at about 2.5 : 1, so 5 mg IV matches roughly 12.5 mg orally).
Enteral feed vs hypoalbuminaemia as the cause of a phenytoin problem
Feeds lower absorption, so the patient under-doses and seizes. Low albumin raises the free fraction, so the patient is at risk of toxicity at a ‘normal’ total level (PK-05).
traps: “In shock, oral mycophenolate or sublingual tacrolimus is the absorption worry” (35% right)

With bowel sounds and bowel movements the gut is working, and sublingual and IV routes bypass the problem. The drug to worry about is subcutaneous enoxaparin, because vasopressors shut down skin perfusion.
“High first-pass drug: increase the IV dose” (31% right)
The opposite: IV skips gut-wall and hepatic extraction, so far less is needed; give a smaller IV dose (metoprolol, propranolol, diltiazem, verapamil, morphine).
“Seizure on day 5 on phenytoin with albumin 1.5 g/dL — hypoalbuminaemia” (20% right)

Low albumin raises free phenytoin and risks toxicity, not seizures. Enteral feeds started on day 3 bound the phenytoin and dropped the level. Kidney dysfunction does not matter much (phenytoin is hepatically cleared), and modestly raised liver enzymes do not lower its level.
decode: Septic shock on vasopressors, transplant drugs and an anticoagulant — which route are you most concerned about? [DocT GT]
Subcutaneous enoxaparin: skin perfusion falls on vasopressors.
Oral form has significant first-pass metabolism — how should the IV dose differ? [DocT GT]
Decrease it.
On oral phenytoin, enteral feeds started on day 3, seizure on day 5, albumin low — most likely cause? [DocT GT]
Enteral tube feeds.
PK-01.punch: In shock, give critical drugs IV: the gut and the skin are the first beds the body shuts down. A high first-pass drug needs a smaller IV dose, and starting enteral feeds can quietly drop phenytoin, warfarin and ciprofloxacin levels.

parts.q: Why does a low-albumin patient on phenytoin seize after feeds start, when low albumin should raise free phenytoin?
parts.a: Low albumin changes the split between bound and free drug; the feed changes how much drug is absorbed. Absorption falls, so total and free levels both drop.

PK-02.sub: Special topics → Pharmacokinetics → Volume of distribution in sepsis
PK-02.intro: Step 2 asks where the drug goes once it is in. A hydrophilic antibiotic cannot cross cell membranes, so it stays in the extracellular water, and sepsis expands that water: leaky capillaries let fluid into the tissues, the resuscitation adds litres, and drains and circuits add more. The same dose is diluted into a bigger space. The real questions check whether you know this changes the dose and not the interval, and whether you can calculate a load.
why: **Vd = the apparent volume a drug would need to fill at its plasma concentration (dose ÷ concentration).** It is a ratio, not an anatomical space. For a one-compartment drug, the dose needed for a target peak is Cmax × Vd: with a Vd of 0.6 L/kg in a 70-kg patient, Vd is 42 L, and a Cmax of 12 mg/L needs 12 × 42 = 504 mg.

**Sepsis: capillary leak + aggressive fluids + drains and circuits → extracellular water expands → hydrophilic drugs (confined to that water) dilute.** An aminoglycoside’s Vd of about 0.25 L/kg in health often rises towards 0.4 L/kg or more in septic shock, so a standard dose gives a lower peak than expected. Lipophilic drugs are already spread through cells and fat, so a few extra litres of extracellular water hardly change their much larger Vd.

**Shown for aminoglycosides, β-lactams, vancomycin; higher APACHE II → larger Vd.** The sicker the patient, the more leak and the more fluid, so the gap between the expected and the actual level is widest in the patients who most need an effective first dose.

**So: loading doses must be bigger (Vd sets the loading dose; clearance sets the maintenance).** A larger Vd also lengthens the half-life (0.693 × Vd ÷ CL), so the drug lingers at a lower level. The answer to a larger Vd is a bigger dose, not a more frequent one. In an anuric, fluid-overloaded patient, the amikacin dose goes up because of the Vd, and the anuria lengthens the interval until the next dose; it never shrinks the first one.
mimic: Larger Vd vs lower clearance
Larger Vd: lower peak, same total removal, so give a bigger dose. Lower clearance: drug accumulates, so give the same load and extend the interval or lower the maintenance.
Hydrophilic vs lipophilic drugs in sepsis
Hydrophilic drugs (β-lactams, aminoglycosides, glycopeptides) have a small Vd that rises in sepsis. Lipophilic drugs (fluoroquinolones) have a large Vd that barely changes (PK-03).
traps: “Anuric septic shock on amikacin: decrease the dose for renal function” (14% right)
Renal failure lengthens the interval, never the load; the expanded Vd from leak and 3 L of fluid needs a bigger dose.
“Increase the dosing frequency because of the increased Vd”
Frequency is set by clearance; a larger Vd is answered with a bigger dose, and in anuria the doses must come less often, not more.
“Decrease the dose because of decreased protein binding”
Aminoglycosides are barely protein bound (under 10–20%), so binding is irrelevant here.
“Critical illness decreases the Vd of hydrophilic drugs” (NEET 2025 distractor)
It increases it. The keyed answer to that recall is altered protein binding (PK-05).
decode: Septic shock, anuric, volume-overloaded after 3 L, broadened to meropenem, amikacin, daptomycin, micafungin — amikacin dose consideration? [DocT GT]
Increase the dose because of the increased Vd.
Vd 0.6 L/kg, 70 kg, target Cmax 12 mg/L — loading dose? [DocT GT]
Which PK change in critically ill poisoned patients most complicates management? [NEET 2025]
Altered plasma protein binding; the Vd of hydrophilic drugs rises, it does not fall.
PK-02.punch: Sepsis pours water into the space hydrophilic drugs occupy, so the same dose gives a lower level. A bigger Vd needs a bigger dose, not a shorter interval, and failing kidneys never shrink the first dose.

PK-03.sub: Special topics → Pharmacokinetics → Hydrophilic vs lipophilic antibiotics
PK-03.intro: Step 2 continues with the property that predicts how sepsis will change a drug. Whether an antibiotic dissolves in water or in fat decides where it goes, which organ clears it and how much critical illness disturbs it. No real question tests this table directly, but it is the reason behind PK-02, PK-07 and PK-08.
why: **Examples: hydrophilic — β-lactams, aminoglycosides, glycopeptides, linezolid, colistin; lipophilic — fluoroquinolones, macrolides, lincosamides, tigecycline.**

**Vd: hydrophilic low, rises in sepsis; lipophilic high, little change.** Hydrophilic drugs stay in the extracellular water, which leak and fluids expand. Lipophilic drugs enter cells and fat; tigecycline’s Vd is several litres per kilogram.

**Clearance: hydrophilic renal; lipophilic hepatic.** A water-soluble drug is filtered and leaves in urine unchanged; a fat-soluble drug is reabsorbed in the tubule and must first be metabolised by the liver. Linezolid does not fit this row: only about 30% leaves unchanged in urine and about two-thirds of its clearance is non-renal, which is why it needs no renal dose change (see FLAGS).
**Cell penetration: hydrophilic poor, lipophilic good.** So intracellular organisms (Legionella, Chlamydia, Mycoplasma) need a lipophilic drug such as a macrolide or a fluoroquinolone.

**In sepsis: hydrophilic — bigger load, clearance follows the kidneys (ARC or AKI); lipophilic — dose by liver function.** Hydrophilic drugs are hit twice in critical illness: a larger Vd and a clearance that may rise (PK-07) or fall (PK-08).
mimic: Hydrophilic drug on CRRT vs lipophilic drug on ECMO
CRRT removes small, poorly bound hydrophilic drugs. The ECMO circuit absorbs lipophilic, highly bound drugs (fentanyl, midazolam, propofol, voriconazole).
traps: “Fluoroquinolones need a bigger loading dose in sepsis”
Their large Vd barely changes; the loading-dose problem belongs to hydrophilic drugs.
decode: Which antibiotic’s Vd changes most in septic shock? [pattern]
A hydrophilic one: an aminoglycoside, a β-lactam or vancomycin, not a fluoroquinolone.
Which antibiotic needs hepatic, not renal, dose adjustment? [pattern]
A lipophilic one, for example tigecycline.
PK-03.punch: Water-soluble antibiotics live in the extracellular water and leave by the kidney, so sepsis changes both their volume and their clearance. Fat-soluble ones live in tissue, leave by the liver and change little.

PK-04.sub: Special topics → Pharmacokinetics → Dosing weight in obesity
PK-04.intro: Step 2 includes the obese patient, in whom the question is how much of the extra weight the drug actually spreads into. Fat holds little water, so a hydrophilic drug does not distribute into it fully, but lean mass, blood volume and kidney size also rise with obesity. No real question tests this card; it is a likely recall item.
why: **Aminoglycosides: adjusted body weight.** Adjusted weight = ideal weight + 0.4 × (total − ideal): aminoglycosides distribute into extracellular water, and about 40% of the excess weight behaves like lean tissue for them. Dosing on total weight would give toxic peaks; on ideal weight, low ones.

**β-lactams, daptomycin: lean body weight.** In practice β-lactams are not dosed by weight: obese patients get the top of the usual dose range, often as an extended infusion. Daptomycin is the exception that does not fit the card. Its label and most guidance use total (actual) body weight (see FLAGS).

**Vancomycin: total (actual) body weight.** Vancomycin’s Vd and clearance both rise with total weight, so the load is 20–25 mg/kg of actual weight in obesity, capped at 3 g (2020 consensus), and later doses are set by AUC-guided monitoring.
mimic: Loading vs maintenance in obesity
The load follows Vd and so the weight the drug distributes into. Maintenance follows clearance, which rises less than the weight does, so it is adjusted by levels.
traps: “Vancomycin in obesity: dose on ideal weight”
That under-loads; vancomycin loads are on actual weight, capped at 3 g.
“Aminoglycosides on total weight in obesity”
This overshoots the peak and raises toxicity; use adjusted weight.
decode: Obese patient, gentamicin once daily — which weight? [pattern]
Adjusted body weight.
Obese patient with MRSA bacteraemia — vancomycin loading weight? [pattern]
Actual (total) body weight, maximum 3 g.
PK-04.punch: Aminoglycosides use adjusted weight, vancomycin uses actual weight with a 3 g cap, and β-lactams get the top of the range by infusion. Obesity also predicts β-lactam and linezolid failure, because fixed doses are spread through a larger body.

PK-05.sub: Special topics → Pharmacokinetics → Hypoalbuminaemia and protein binding
PK-05.intro: Step 2 ends with protein binding, which decides how much of the drug in the plasma is free to act and free to be cleared. Albumin falls early and steeply in critical illness, so the free fraction of highly bound acidic drugs rises. The four real questions test two consequences: a total level that looks therapeutic while the free level is toxic (phenytoin), and which drugs a binding change really matters for.
why: **Low albumin in 40–50% of septic patients.** Albumin falls through capillary leak, reduced hepatic synthesis in the acute-phase response and dilution by fluids, and the fall is often below 25 g/L.

**Highly bound drugs: more free fraction → bigger Vd and faster clearance → low troughs.** Only free drug crosses into tissues and is filtered by the glomerulus. When albumin falls, the extra free drug spreads into the expanded interstitium and is cleared faster, so total levels drop; in hypoalbuminaemic patients on ceftriaxone both Vd and clearance roughly double. For a time-dependent antibiotic the trough falls below the MIC early in the interval. The rise in Vd is the dominant effect, so give the full loading dose and, for β-lactams, dose more often or by continuous infusion.

**Matters for ceftriaxone, daptomycin, flucloxacillin, vancomycin (also ertapenem, teicoplanin).** These bind more than 70%: ceftriaxone and ertapenem 85–95%, flucloxacillin about 95%, daptomycin and teicoplanin about 90%. Vancomycin is only moderately bound (30–60%), so it belongs on this list less than the others (see FLAGS). The same reasoning applies outside antibiotics to phenytoin and valproate.

**Albumin falls but α₁-acid glycoprotein rises (binds basic drugs) in critical illness.** Albumin carries acidic drugs (phenytoin, warfarin, ceftriaxone). α₁-acid glycoprotein is an acute-phase protein that carries basic drugs (lidocaine and other local anaesthetics), so their free fraction can fall in inflammation.
mimic: Total vs free phenytoin

Total measures bound plus free; only free (normal 1–2 mg/L) acts. In low albumin or uraemia a total of 10 mg/L can carry a free level that is toxic. Measure free phenytoin, or correct the total (Winter–Tozer: total ÷ (0.2 × albumin g/dL + 0.1), using 0.1 × albumin in end-stage renal disease; this is the classic form, revised versions exist, and a measured free level is more reliable).
Low albumin vs uraemia
Both raise free phenytoin: low albumin by removing binding sites, uraemia because retained toxins displace the drug from albumin.
traps: “A total phenytoin of 10 mg/L is therapeutic, so the signs are not toxicity”
In dialysis patients the free fraction rises from about 10% to 20–30%, so the free level is high (89–100% right on DocT GT).
“The total level is low, so increase the phenytoin dose”
Chasing the total in hypoalbuminaemia causes toxicity; dose by the free level.
“High protein affinity” or “low fu, oral use” is what makes binding changes matter (55% right)
For a low-extraction or oral drug the free level re-equilibrates; it is the high-extraction drug given IV (and narrow-index drugs) where a change in binding lastingly changes the free concentration.
“More free drug means more effect”
For antibiotics, the extra free drug is cleared faster, so the net result is underdosing of time-dependent drugs.
decode: Haemodialysis, phenytoin total 10 mg/L, signs of toxicity — explanation? [DocT GT ×2]
Increased fraction unbound.
Which drug characteristic makes protein-binding changes most clinically relevant? [DocT GT]
High extraction, IV use.
Critically ill poisoned patient — which PK change most complicates management? [NEET 2025]
Alterations in plasma protein binding (hypoalbuminaemia, acidosis and uraemia raise the free fraction of phenytoin, valproate and warfarin).
PK-05.punch: Low albumin raises the free fraction. For an antibiotic, that extra free drug spreads out and is cleared, so levels fall. For phenytoin, it means a ‘therapeutic’ total can hide a toxic free level, so measure the free drug.

table.title: When does a binding change alter the free (active) level?
