Example
Effect of a fall in binding
rows: free level returns to normal as clearance of the free drug rises; **only the total falls** (reading trap)
clearance is set by liver blood flow, so the total stays put and **the free level rises** (real effect)
the transient rise in free drug can still cause toxicity

PK-06.intro: Step 3 turns to how the body removes the drug, starting with the liver. Hepatic clearance is liver blood flow multiplied by the fraction of drug the liver extracts in one pass, and that one number divides drugs into two families that respond to critical illness quite differently. The two real questions ask which change matters for fentanyl, and when a change in binding matters.
why: **Extraction ratio: flow-limited high; capacity-limited low.** A high-extraction drug (above about 0.7: fentanyl, morphine, propofol, lidocaine, propranolol) is almost completely removed in one pass. A low-extraction drug (below about 0.3: phenytoin, warfarin, diazepam) mostly passes through unchanged.

**Clearance depends on: flow-limited — liver blood flow (shock lowers it); capacity-limited — enzyme activity (CYP3A4) and protein binding.** If the liver removes almost all the drug it receives, the only way to change clearance is to change how much blood arrives: clearance ≈ hepatic blood flow. If it removes little, clearance depends on the free fraction and on how fast the enzymes work (fu × intrinsic clearance), and blood flow hardly matters.

**Sensitive to: flow-limited — haemodynamics; capacity-limited — inflammation, binding changes.** In shock, low cardiac output and vasopressors cut liver blood flow, so fentanyl, morphine and lidocaine accumulate. Inflammation (IL-6) down-regulates CYP enzymes, so capacity-limited drugs slow down in sepsis, and a fall in binding speeds their clearance.
mimic: High-extraction drug IV vs orally

Given IV, its clearance follows liver blood flow. Given orally, most is removed on first pass, so liver disease or portosystemic shunting raises bioavailability sharply and the oral dose must fall (PK-01).
traps: “Fentanyl is most affected by decreased intrinsic clearance or fewer hepatocytes” (47% right)
Fentanyl is high-extraction: the liver has spare enzyme capacity, so the limit is blood flow. Decreased hepatic blood flow is the answer.
“Decreased protein binding is the main issue for fentanyl”
For a high-extraction drug, binding changes do not change total clearance. They change the free level (PK-05), not the clearance this stem asks about.
decode: Fentanyl, a high-extraction drug, is most influenced by which critical-illness change? [DocT GT]
Decreased hepatic blood flow.
Which drug characteristic makes protein-binding changes most clinically relevant? [DocT GT]
High extraction, IV use (PK-05).
PK-06.punch: High-extraction drugs such as fentanyl, morphine and lidocaine are cleared at the rate blood reaches the liver, so shock makes them accumulate. Low-extraction drugs depend on enzymes and binding, so inflammation and low albumin change them.

parts.q: Watch line: which phase of hepatic metabolism suffers more in inflammation, and which antibiotics are reduced in hepatic dysfunction?
parts.a: Phase I (CYP oxidation) more than phase II (glucuronidation). Reduce tigecycline (keep the 100 mg load, halve the maintenance in severe impairment), rifampicin and metronidazole.

PK-07.sub: Special topics → Pharmacokinetics → Augmented renal clearance
PK-07.intro: Step 3 continues with the kidney, and with the surprise that it often clears drugs faster than normal in the critically ill. A young patient with trauma, a head injury, burns or sepsis has a high cardiac output and high renal blood flow, and his glomerular filtration can run at 150–200 mL/min with a normal creatinine. Renally cleared antibiotics then leave the body too fast. Both real questions are about recognising the resulting underdosing and fixing it.
why: **Definition: creatinine clearance over 130 mL/min.** The accepted threshold is over 130 mL/min/1.73 m²; some studies require it on more than half of measurements rather than once. It is common: 14–80% of ICU patients depending on the unit and the definition, and in one study of septic and trauma patients with a normal plasma creatinine, 58% had it (86% of the trauma patients).

**Who: young polytrauma, TBI, meningitis, post-operative, burns, VAP, pregnancy.** The common thread is a hyperdynamic circulation from systemic inflammation, often with plenty of fluid, in a young person with good renal reserve. Age under 50, trauma, male sex and a low severity score (SOFA 4 or less) are the consistent predictors. The ARC score adds age ≤50 (6 points), trauma (3) and SOFA ≤4 (1): 7–10 is high risk.

**Measurement: Cockcroft-Gault, MDRD, CKD-EPI are not valid; use measured urinary creatinine clearance.** These equations assume a stable creatinine and a normal relationship between muscle mass and creatinine, and they are built for diseased kidneys. A timed urine collection (8–24 hours; at least one 8-hour collection in patients at risk) is the bedside measure, repeated because ARC changes from day to day.

**Drugs affected: vancomycin, aminoglycosides, β-lactams — subtherapeutic levels, treatment failure.** They are hydrophilic and renally cleared, so their clearance tracks the GFR. Time-dependent β-lactams suffer most, because a fast clearance means the level falls below the MIC early in each interval.

**Response: higher or more frequent doses; extended infusions; TDM.** For example, meropenem 2 g 8-hourly as an extended infusion, piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g 6-hourly or 4-hourly (or continuously), and AUC-guided vancomycin. The loading dose does not change. Extended or continuous infusion keeps the level above the MIC despite the fast clearance; cutting the dose or giving standard short boluses does the opposite.
mimic: ARC vs AKI
Both change renal clearance of the same drugs, in opposite directions. AKI is suspected from a rising creatinine, but ARC is hidden behind a normal one, so it is missed unless clearance is measured.
traps: “Trauma patient with CrCl 145 on pip-tazo: standard intermittent dosing” (37% right)
At that clearance standard boluses leave long periods below the MIC; extended (or continuous) infusion is the fix. Reducing the dose is the opposite of what is needed.
“Switch to aminoglycoside monotherapy”
Aminoglycosides are also cleared faster in ARC, and monotherapy for septic shock is inadequate.
“Poor response despite susceptibility means resistance was induced” (51% right)

In the critically ill the commonest reason is underdosing. Standard-dose ceftolozane-tazobactam is a clear example: the VAP dose is 3 g 8-hourly, double the dose for intra-abdominal or urinary infection, and leak plus ARC lower levels further.
“A normal creatinine means normal clearance”
A young trauma patient with a normal creatinine may clear 200 mL/min.
decode: 45-year-old trauma patient, CrCl 145 mL/min/1.73 m², pip-tazo for septic shock — which intervention optimises therapy? [DocT GT]
Extended-infusion dosing.
Pseudomonas VAP on standard-dose ceftolozane-tazobactam, susceptible, poor response — best explanation? [DocT GT]
Drug underdosing in critically ill patients.
PK-07.punch: Young, injured or septic patients often clear renally excreted antibiotics far faster than their normal creatinine suggests. Measure the clearance, keep the full load, and give β-lactams more often or by extended infusion.

PK-08.sub: Special topics → Pharmacokinetics → Antibiotics on renal replacement therapy
PK-08.intro: Step 4 is clearance by a machine. When the kidneys fail, the filter takes over part of their job, but it is a sieve with fixed rules: it removes what is small, free in the plasma and not hidden in the tissues, and it removes it in proportion to how much effluent is made. The real questions test the commonest reason for dose change in the ICU and, twice, what to do when CRRT starts on a drug dosed for anuria.
why: **What decides removal: protein binding, hydrophilicity, RRT mode, filter porosity, flows.** Only free drug passes the membrane, so the sieving coefficient is roughly the unbound fraction (1 − protein binding). Most antibiotics (vancomycin about 1.5 kDa included) are far below the cut-off of a high-flux filter, so size rarely limits removal. Extracorporeal clearance ≈ sieving coefficient × effluent rate: a 25%-bound drug at 25–35 mL/kg/h is cleared at roughly 25–35 mL/min, more than the CrCl under 20 its dose was set for. A large Vd means only a small share of the body’s drug is in the plasma at any moment, which matters for short intermittent sessions (and rebound after them) more than for continuous therapy. Removal matters most for drugs normally cleared by the kidneys.

**Predictability: hard to predict; easier on CRRT than SLED; risk of over- and under-dosing.** On CRRT, clearance is steady and can be estimated from the effluent rate, but delivered dose falls with filter clotting and downtime. For β-lactams underdosing is the greater danger, because their therapeutic index is wide and failure to treat the infection kills.

**Early dosing: β-lactams — use full (non-AKI) doses for the first 48 h; higher doses, extended infusion.** In the first two days the Vd is at its largest, the kidneys may recover, and the machine adds clearance. Cutting β-lactam doses for the creatinine during this period is the common error.

**SLED removes antibiotics more efficiently than CRRT or intermittent HD, especially small, renally cleared, poorly bound drugs (β-lactams).** During a session SLED clears drug at a high rate, close to that of intermittent haemodialysis and higher than CRRT, then stops. So time doses to come after the session or give a supplement, rather than assuming steady removal (see FLAGS on the word ‘efficiently’).

**Aminoglycosides: higher dose, infrequent; TDM.** Give the full Vd-based load for the peak, then redose only when the level has fallen, because the trough drives toxicity. For vancomycin, use a weight-based load and then AUC-guided levels on CRRT.
mimic: CRRT vs ECMO circuit

CRRT removes small, poorly bound hydrophilic drugs into the effluent. The ECMO circuit absorbs lipophilic and highly protein-bound drugs (fentanyl, midazolam, propofol, voriconazole) onto the oxygenator and tubing, and its priming volume dilutes small-Vd drugs.
Continuous vs intermittent therapy
On CRRT, Vd barely limits removal over a day. In intermittent HD the short session clears mainly the plasma, so large-Vd drugs rebound from the tissues after it.
traps: “Maintain the dose because of the large Vd” for a 25%-bound, small, 60%-renally-cleared drug on CVVHD (39% right)

On continuous therapy, removal depends on the free fraction and the effluent rate, not on Vd; the machine adds about 25–35 mL/min of clearance to a dose set for CrCl under 20, so increase it. DocT’s own explanation hints that a large Vd limits removal; that applies to intermittent dialysis.
“Changes in protein binding are the commonest reason to adjust ICU drug doses” (60% right)
Reduced renal clearance (AKI or CKD) is. Most antibiotics, LMWH and many opioid metabolites are renally eliminated.
“Subtherapeutic vancomycin on CRRT: de-escalate or use rapid diagnostics”
A low level is a dosing problem; the stewardship answer is therapeutic drug monitoring (82% right).
decode: Which change in critically ill patients most often makes dose adjustment necessary? [DocT GT]
Decreased renal clearance.
New CRE drug dosed for CrCl <20, CVVHD started; 60% renal, Vd 3 L/kg, 25% bound, small — change? [DocT GT]
Increase the dose because of low protein binding and small molecular weight.
On CRRT, subtherapeutic vancomycin despite standard dosing — stewardship strategy? [DocT GT]
Therapeutic drug monitoring.
PK-08.punch: A filter clears free, small, hydrophilic drugs in proportion to the effluent rate, so a drug dosed for anuria is often too low once CRRT starts. Give full β-lactam doses for the first 48 hours and let levels guide aminoglycosides and vancomycin.

PK-09.sub: Special topics → Pharmacodynamics → Time- vs concentration-dependent killing
PK-09.intro: Step 5 moves from what the body does to the drug to what the drug must do to the bacterium. Antibiotics fall into three killing patterns, and each pattern names the exposure (from PK-01) that predicts success. Getting the pattern right decides whether you lengthen the infusion, raise the peak or raise the daily total. The one real question tests the pairs, and only 23% got it.
why: **Time-dependent: index %fT>MIC; β-lactams, carbapenems, linezolid, erythromycin, clarithromycin, lincosamides; extended or continuous infusion; PAE minimal to moderate.** Above about 4 × MIC, β-lactam killing does not get faster, so what counts is how long the free level stays above the MIC. With little post-antibiotic effect against Gram-negatives, regrowth starts as soon as the level falls below it.

**Concentration-dependent: index Cmax/MIC; aminoglycosides, fluoroquinolones, daptomycin, metronidazole; big dose, long interval; PAE prolonged.** The higher the peak, the faster and more complete the kill. The long post-antibiotic effect suppresses regrowth after levels fall, which is why aminoglycosides are given once daily. The low trough before the next dose also limits renal and ear toxicity.

**Concentration + time: index AUC₀₋₂₄/MIC; fluoroquinolones, glycopeptides, linezolid, tigecycline, azithromycin, tetracyclines, colistin; enough total daily dose; PAE moderate.** What matters is the total exposure over the day, so the daily dose is set to reach the target, however it is divided. The card puts fluoroquinolones and linezolid in two columns because both indices predict their effect; AUC/MIC is the better predictor for both, and exams still call fluoroquinolones ‘concentration-dependent’.
mimic: Vancomycin vs aminoglycoside
Vancomycin is AUC-dependent, not peak-dependent, so it is monitored by AUC (formerly trough). Aminoglycosides are peak-dependent and dosed once daily for a high Cmax.
traps: “Vancomycin is concentration-dependent” (option B)
Vancomycin is AUC/MIC-dependent; calling it concentration-dependent makes B wrong even though cefazolin is time-dependent.
“Daptomycin is time-dependent” (option C)
Daptomycin is concentration-dependent (Cmax/MIC and AUC/MIC), like amikacin.
“Levofloxacin is time-dependent” (option D)
Fluoroquinolones are concentration-dependent (AUC/MIC); meropenem is time-dependent.
decode: Which correctly pairs the pharmacodynamics with the antibacterial agents? [DocT GT]
Oxacillin (time-dependent), moxifloxacin (concentration-dependent) — 23% right.
PK-09.punch: β-lactams need time above the MIC, aminoglycosides need a high peak and vancomycin needs total daily exposure. That is why β-lactams go by extended infusion, aminoglycosides once daily and vancomycin by AUC.

PK-10.intro: Step 5 puts numbers on the killing patterns. Each target is the exposure that predicted cure (or a fixed amount of bacterial kill) in animal and clinical studies; critically ill patients and resistant organisms need the upper end. The two real questions are both about matching the dosing strategy to the target: a big once-daily aminoglycoside dose, and a prolonged meropenem infusion.
why: **β-lactams: 50–70% fT>MIC (penicillins, cephalosporins).** About 50% for penicillins and 60–70% for cephalosporins is needed for maximal killing in classic animal studies.
**Carbapenems: 40% fT>MIC.** Carbapenems kill faster and have some post-antibiotic effect, so less time is needed.

**Critically ill / MDR: 100% fT>MIC; maximal killing at 4–5 × MIC.** In the critically ill, levels need to stay above the MIC for the whole interval. French guidance (2019) aims for a free level of 4–8 × MIC throughout; the higher concentration also helps prevent resistance and reach tissues.

**Aminoglycosides: Cmax/MIC 8–10.** A peak 8–10 times the MIC gives the best kill and limits resistance. In septic shock that means a large once-daily dose (amikacin 25–30 mg/kg; DocT keys this) because the Vd is large.

**Fluoroquinolones: AUC/MIC 125 (Gram-negatives); Cmax/MIC 10.** For Gram-positives (pneumococcus) about 30–50 is enough; 125 is the Gram-negative target from ciprofloxacin studies (see the card’s watch line on 87.5).

**Vancomycin: AUC/MIC 400 (Staph aureus).** The 2020 consensus target is AUC₂₄/MIC 400–600, assuming an MIC of 1 mg/L, estimated with Bayesian software from 1–2 levels. Above 600, kidney injury becomes more likely. Trough targets of 15–20 mg/L have been dropped (see FLAGS).

**Daptomycin: Cmax/MIC; AUC/MIC 100.** It is concentration-dependent, and AUC/MIC is the index most studies use. The number quoted varies widely between studies and reviews, so know the index rather than the figure (see FLAGS).

**Colistin: AUC/MIC 53–141 (Pseudomonas).** The 2019 international polymyxin consensus states the clinical target as an AUC of about 50 mg·h/L (an average steady-state level of about 2 mg/L), which is also the point above which kidney injury rises. That is the number to quote (see FLAGS).

**Linezolid: 40–80% fT>MIC; AUC/MIC.** In a retrospective study of seriously ill patients, success was higher at an AUC/MIC of about 80–120 and when levels stayed above the MIC for the whole interval; the two indices were closely correlated.
mimic: Extended infusion vs higher bolus dose of a β-lactam
Doubling a 30-minute bolus raises the peak, which β-lactams do not need, and adds little time above the MIC. Extending the infusion buys time above the MIC with the same daily dose.
traps: “Amikacin 5 mg/kg three times daily to keep a steady trough”
Divided doses lower the peak and keep the trough up, which loses the Cmax/MIC effect and raises toxicity; give one large daily dose.
“Continuous aminoglycoside infusion at 10 µg/mL”
Concentration-dependent drugs need a high peak and a low trough, the opposite of a flat infusion.
“Meropenem: bolus for a high Cmax/MIC” or “rely on the PAE for long intervals”
Carbapenems are time-dependent; the answer is extended or continuous infusion for fT>MIC.
“Double the 30-minute meropenem dose to beat the Vd”
A bigger bolus mostly raises the peak; extended infusion is the PD answer.
decode: Amikacin in septic shock, 70 kg — preferred strategy in the acute phase? [DocT GT]
A large once-daily dose (25–30 mg/kg) to maximise Cmax/MIC.
Meropenem in septic shock after big fluids, CrCl 120 — most consistent with stewardship? [DocT GT]
Continuous or extended infusion to maximise fT>MIC.
Vancomycin target for serious MRSA infection? [pattern]
AUC₂₄/MIC 400–600 (2020 consensus).
PK-10.punch: β-lactams need the free level above the MIC for the whole interval in the critically ill, aminoglycosides a peak 8–10 times the MIC and vancomycin an AUC of 400–600. Choose the infusion method that hits that number.

PK-11.sub: Special topics → Pharmacokinetics → Antibiotic dosing in the critically ill
PK-11.intro: Step 6 puts the deck together into a prescription. The loading dose answers ‘how big is the space?’ (step 2), the maintenance answers ‘how fast is it cleared?’ (steps 3–4), the method of infusion answers ‘what does the bug need?’ (step 5), and the level answers ‘did it work?’. The four real questions test each piece, and one of them is keyed wrongly.
why: **Loading dose for aminoglycosides, β-lactams, glycopeptides, tigecycline, colistin: sized by Vd, independent of renal function.** The first dose fills the volume, and the kidneys have not yet had any time to act, so their function cannot affect it. Examples: vancomycin 20–35 mg/kg of actual weight (maximum 3 g) in the seriously ill; colistin 300 mg colistin base activity (about 9 million IU); tigecycline 100 mg.

**Maintenance: by the eliminating organ (kidneys, liver).** Renally cleared drugs follow measured clearance, high in ARC (PK-07), low in AKI, added to by RRT (PK-08). Hepatically cleared drugs follow liver function (PK-06).

**Time-dependent: bolus then continuous or extended (4 h) infusion; best studied with pip-tazo and meropenem (also vancomycin, ceftriaxone, cefepime); large RCTs show no distinct advantage, meta-analyses conflict (BLING III: no significant 90-day mortality difference).** The bolus reaches the target at once; the infusion keeps the level above the MIC. BLING III (JAMA 2024, 7,202 patients on pip-tazo or meropenem) found 90-day mortality of 24.9% with continuous infusion vs 26.8% with intermittent (p = 0.08), but clinical cure was higher (55.7% vs 50.0%). The companion meta-analysis of 18 trials (9,108 patients) found lower 90-day mortality with prolonged infusion (RR 0.86). The 2026 Surviving Sepsis Campaign guideline now makes a strong recommendation for prolonged infusion for maintenance after a loading bolus. So ‘no distinct advantage’ is outdated (see FLAGS).

**Aminoglycosides: large once-daily dose on adjusted weight.** The goal is a high peak (Cmax/MIC 8–10) with a drug-free period before the next dose: amikacin 25–30 mg/kg in septic shock, repeated by level, not by the clock, if the kidneys fail.

**TDM: established for aminoglycosides and vancomycin; useful for β-lactams in ARC.** For vancomycin, AUC-guided dosing (Bayesian) has replaced troughs. β-lactam TDM aims for 100% fT>MIC (free level 4–8 × MIC in French guidance). International position papers now recommend it in the critically ill wherever it is available, not only in ARC: on RRT, in obesity, on ECMO and for resistant organisms.
mimic: Load vs maintenance in AKI
AKI never changes the load; it lengthens the interval or lowers the maintenance. ARC is the reverse: same load, more frequent or prolonged maintenance.
traps: “The loading dose of vancomycin needs to be decreased in CKD” — the DocT GT key (9% right)

The key is wrong: the load depends on Vd, not renal function. Of the other options, reducing tobramycin in CKD and cisatracurium not being prolonged (Hofmann elimination is organ-independent) are both true, and propofol induction does not need a big cut. The bank’s pasted explanation is about morphine. Pick the true statement; know that the bank keys A.
“Standard-dose ceftolozane-tazobactam failed because of resistance induction” (51% right)
Underdosing in the critically ill is the answer; the VAP dose is double the standard one.
“Cut the first dose because of AKI”
Renal function changes the interval, never the load.
“Extended infusion makes no difference — BLING III was negative”
Its primary outcome narrowly missed significance, clinical cure was better, the meta-analysis shows a mortality benefit, and SSC 2026 recommends it strongly.
decode: Drug dosed for CrCl <20, CVVHD started; small, 25% bound — dose change? [DocT GT]
Increase it (PK-08).
Which statement on drug dosing in CKD is correct? [DocT GT]
Keyed ‘vancomycin load decreased’ — wrong; the load is Vd-based. True: tobramycin reduction, cisatracurium unaffected.
Amikacin in septic shock — preferred strategy? [DocT GT]
Large once-daily dose (25–30 mg/kg).
Pseudomonas VAP, standard-dose ceftolozane-tazobactam, poor response — why? [DocT GT]
Underdosing in the critically ill.
PK-11.punch: Load by volume whatever the kidneys show, maintain by the clearing organ, infuse β-lactams over hours, give aminoglycosides once a day, and check with levels.

topups.q: Pharmacokinetics of monoclonal antibodies?
a: - ~150 kDa → cannot cross membranes → small Vd (plasma + interstitium, ~3–8 L).
- Not renally cleared; proteolysis and target-mediated disposal (non-linear at low doses).
- FcRn recycling protects IgG → long half-life (~3 weeks).
- Anti-drug antibodies increase immune clearance → falling troughs, loss of response.

x.sub: Special topics → Pharmacokinetics → Monoclonal antibodies
x.intro: Step 2 explained that where a drug goes depends on whether it can cross membranes. Monoclonal antibodies take that to an extreme: they are proteins several hundred times the size of a typical antibiotic, so they stay almost entirely in the plasma and interstitial fluid, and they are removed by being broken down, not by the kidney or the liver. The two bank questions ask why their Vd is small and why their levels fall over months of treatment.
why: **~150 kDa → cannot cross membranes → small Vd (plasma + interstitium, ~3–8 L).** A small-molecule drug diffuses across cell membranes; an IgG antibody is far too big and too polar to do so. It leaves the blood only slowly, by convection through gaps in the capillary wall, and reaches the interstitium but not the inside of cells. So its central Vd is close to plasma volume (about 3 L) and its total Vd only a few litres more.

**Not renally cleared; proteolysis and target-mediated disposal (non-linear at low doses).** At about 150 kDa an IgG is far above the glomerular filtration cut-off, and the liver’s CYP enzymes do not act on it, so renal and hepatic failure barely change its dose. It is taken up into cells by pinocytosis and digested in lysosomes. It is also removed when it binds its target and the complex is internalised. That route saturates once the target is occupied, so clearance is faster at low doses and the kinetics are non-linear.

**FcRn recycling protects IgG → long half-life (~3 weeks).** Inside the endosome the neonatal Fc receptor binds the antibody’s Fc portion at acid pH and carries it back to the cell surface, where it is released into the blood instead of being digested. This salvage gives IgG1 a half-life of about 21 days and allows dosing every 2–8 weeks.

**Anti-drug antibodies increase immune clearance → falling troughs, loss of response.** The patient’s immune system may make antibodies against the therapeutic antibody, especially against chimeric or humanised regions. The immune complexes are cleared quickly, so trough levels fall and the disease returns despite unchanged dosing. Measuring the trough level and anti-drug antibodies separates this from true failure of the drug’s target; co-prescribed methotrexate or azathioprine reduces it.
mimic: Monoclonal antibody vs small-molecule drug
Antibody: small Vd, no renal or CYP clearance, half-life of weeks, cleared by proteolysis and its target. Small molecule: crosses membranes, filtered or metabolised, half-life of hours.
Anti-drug antibodies vs target-mediated clearance

Anti-drug antibodies appear over weeks to months of treatment and cause a new fall in levels. Target-mediated clearance is there from the first dose and is greatest when the target burden is high or the dose is low.
traps: “Their small Vd is due to high protein binding or rapid renal clearance”
Antibodies are themselves proteins and are not filtered; the cause is that they cannot diffuse across membranes (50% right on DocT GT).
“Falling levels on a mAb mean the drug is cleared faster by the kidney or liver”
Neither organ clears intact IgG; the usual cause is anti-drug antibodies increasing immune clearance (64% right on DocT GT).
“Reduce the dose in renal failure”
Renal function does not change IgG clearance.
decode: Why do monoclonal antibodies have small central volumes of distribution? [DocT GT]
Limited membrane diffusion.
Autoimmune disease on a mAb, drug levels falling, response lost — mechanism? [DocT GT]
Increased immune clearance (anti-drug antibodies).
x.punch: An antibody is too big to cross membranes or be filtered, so it stays in plasma and interstitium and is removed by proteolysis and by its target. FcRn salvage gives it a half-life of weeks, and anti-drug antibodies are what make its levels fall.

spine: Getting the drug in
In shock the gut and the skin lose their blood supply, so oral, enteral and subcutaneous drugs are absorbed unpredictably and critical drugs go intravenously.
Where the drug goes
Capillary leak, fluids and low albumin expand the space hydrophilic drugs must fill, so the same dose gives a lower level and the loading dose has to be bigger.
How the body clears it

The liver clears high-extraction drugs in proportion to its blood flow and low-extraction drugs by its enzymes, while the young septic or injured kidney may clear far more than the creatinine suggests.
Clearance by the machine
Renal replacement therapy removes small, poorly bound, hydrophilic drugs in proportion to the effluent rate, so doses set for anuria are often too low on CRRT.
What the bug needs
Beta-lactams kill by time above the MIC, aminoglycosides by peak height and vancomycin and fluoroquinolones by total exposure, and each has a target number.
Putting the dose together
The volume sets the loading dose whatever the kidneys are doing, the eliminating organ sets the maintenance, the drug’s killing pattern sets how it is infused, and levels check the result.
SPECIAL04A.primer: Volume of distribution (Vd) is the volume a drug would need to fill to give the concentration measured in plasma; it is a ratio (amount in the body ÷ plasma concentration), not a real space, so a drug that hides in fat or tissue has a Vd far larger than the patient. Clearance (CL) is the volume of plasma cleared of drug per unit time, and the two together set the half-life (0.693 × Vd ÷ CL). The first dose is sized by Vd (dose = target concentration × Vd) and the doses that follow are sized by clearance. Only the free, unbound drug acts on bacteria and receptors, is filtered and is metabolised, and the minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) is the lowest free concentration that stops a given organism growing.

PK-12.sub: Pharmacology → Special circuits → Drug handling on ECMO
PK-12.intro: Step 2 takes the rule of step 1 to its extreme. The ECMO circuit adds litres of priming fluid, and its tubing and oxygenator bind some drugs, while the patient is septic, hypoalbuminaemic and often in organ failure. The card lists four forces and what each does to the dose; no real question is linked, so this is the short version.
why: **Priming and haemodilution: ↑ Vd of hydrophilic drugs (β-lactams, aminoglycosides) → bigger load.** The circuit is primed with crystalloid, colloid or blood and adds this to the patient’s plasma volume at once, so a drug that stays in body water is diluted and its first peak is low. The fix is a larger first dose; clearance is unchanged by the prime itself.

**Circuit sequestration: lipophilic drugs (fluoroquinolones, fentanyl, midazolam, propofol) are bound and lost → bigger load, more often.** Lipophilic and highly protein-bound drugs stick to the PVC tubing and the oxygenator membrane until binding sites saturate, which acts as a large extra volume and keeps removing drug from the blood. Voriconazole behaves the same way. How much is lost varies with the circuit materials and falls as binding sites saturate, so sedative needs often rise early and the dose has to be retitrated later.

**Low albumin: ↑ free fraction of highly bound drugs (teicoplanin, ceftriaxone) → load, give more often.** With less albumin more drug is unbound; unbound drug is both active and the part the kidney can filter, so it is cleared faster and the total level falls between doses. The free fraction, not the total, sits above or below the MIC.

**Sepsis and organ failure: ↑ Vd and ↓ clearance of hydrophilic, renal or hepatic drugs → load, then stretch the interval.** Capillary leak enlarges Vd, so the load is still full or larger; AKI or liver failure slows elimination, so it is the interval or the maintenance dose that is reduced, guided by levels where they exist (vancomycin, aminoglycosides).
mimic: Sequestration vs haemodilution
Haemodilution affects hydrophilic drugs and is a one-off fall at the start of the circuit. Sequestration affects lipophilic or highly bound drugs and keeps removing drug until the circuit saturates.
ECMO vs CRRT drug loss
CRRT removes small, unbound, hydrophilic drugs by filtration; ECMO adsorbs lipophilic drugs. A patient on both can lose both kinds.
traps: “Hydrophilic drugs bind to the ECMO circuit”
Sequestration is a property of lipophilic and highly protein-bound drugs (PK-22 i); hydrophilic drugs are affected by dilution, not binding.
“Reduce the load because the patient is in renal failure on ECMO”
The load follows Vd, which is larger; only the maintenance follows clearance.
decode: [pattern] Which drug is most sequestered by the ECMO circuit — fentanyl, gentamicin, meropenem, vancomycin?
Fentanyl: lipophilic and highly bound.
[pattern] Patient on VA-ECMO needs ever-higher midazolam and fentanyl in the first days — why?
Circuit sequestration of lipophilic drugs, on top of raised Vd.
PK-12.punch: On ECMO, hydrophilic drugs are diluted and lipophilic ones are soaked up by the circuit, so both need a bigger first dose; organ failure changes only how often the next doses come.

PK-13.sub: Pharmacology → Special circuits → Antibiotics in burns
PK-13.intro: Still step 2: a major burn changes kinetics twice. In the first two days the patient is in burn shock with a leak and a low GFR; after that he becomes hyperdynamic and clears drugs faster than almost any other ICU patient. No real question is linked; the point to carry is that standard doses usually run low after the first two days.
why: **Early (first 48 h): hypovolaemia, low albumin, low GFR. Late (after 48–72 h): hyperdynamic, raised cardiac output, high renal and non-renal clearance, low albumin, liver dysfunction.** In the ebb phase capillary leak and large volumes of resuscitation fluid raise the Vd of hydrophilic drugs while poor perfusion lowers renal clearance. In the flow (hypermetabolic) phase cardiac output and renal and hepatic blood flow rise and ARC is common, so drugs are cleared fast; reviews date its onset from 48–72 h to about day 5, and it can persist for months, in large burns for a year or more. The low albumin persists throughout.

**Highly bound drugs (ertapenem, daptomycin, ceftriaxone, oxacillin): high free levels, fast clearance → subtherapeutic.** Without albumin, more of the dose is free, so more is filtered and cleared quickly; the free level is briefly high and then falls below the MIC well before the next dose. Once-daily highly bound drugs such as ertapenem and ceftriaxone are the ones most at risk of running out before the next dose.

**Aminoglycosides penetrate eschar well; usual β-lactam doses inadequate.** Aminoglycosides are small, water-soluble molecules that diffuse through the oedematous interstitium; biopsies of burn eschar in patients on gentamicin or tobramycin found measurable tissue levels in every patient, with an effect on the eschar flora. They are still dosed by weight with peak and trough levels, often at gentamicin 7 mg/kg or tobramycin 10 mg/kg daily and sometimes more often, because clearance is high. For β-lactams the fix is the top of the dose range given as extended infusions (piperacillin–tazobactam 4.5 g 6-hourly over 4 h, cefepime 2 g 8-hourly, meropenem 1–2 g 8-hourly).

**Vancomycin: ↑ Vd and clearance; standard doses rarely hit targets → TDM. Higher linezolid and colistin doses.** Burn patients often need 40–70 mg/kg/day of vancomycin to reach an AUC of 400–600, so it is given after a load with early levels; linezolid is commonly given 8-hourly instead of 12-hourly.
mimic: Early vs late burn phase
Early: leak, low GFR, raised Vd, normal or slow clearance. Late: hyperdynamic, ARC, fast clearance. Both have low albumin.
traps: “Burn patients need lower doses because of renal hypoperfusion”
Only in the first 48 h; afterwards clearance is high and standard doses fail.
“A high free fraction means toxicity, so reduce highly bound antibiotics”
For renally cleared antibiotics the extra free drug is cleared quickly and levels end up low; the toxicity concern applies to narrow-window drugs such as phenytoin.
decode: [pattern] Day 7 after a 50% burn, vancomycin troughs low on standard dosing — why?
Hyperdynamic phase with augmented renal clearance and raised Vd; increase the dose and dose to levels.
PK-13.punch: After the first two days a burn patient clears antibiotics fast, so give the top doses as extended infusions and dose vancomycin and aminoglycosides by levels.

PK-14.intro: Step 3 is the time-dependent drugs. β-lactams kill only while the free level stays above the MIC, and peaks above about 4–5 times the MIC add nothing, so the question is always how to keep the level up between doses in a patient whose Vd and clearance are both raised. No real question is linked to this card.
why: **Hydrophilic, low Vd (0.1–0.6 L/kg in your notes), doubled in the critically ill; mainly renal clearance (ceftriaxone is biliary).** In healthy people most β-lactams have a Vd of about 0.2–0.3 L/kg, the extracellular water; leak and fluid can double it, so the first dose must be full. Most are filtered and secreted by the kidney, so they need maintenance changes in AKI and run low with ARC. Piperacillin–tazobactam is mostly renal with some biliary excretion and still needs renal adjustment; ceftriaxone is cleared by both bile and kidney and needs no renal adjustment.

**Moderate protein binding (20–50%) for most.** The exceptions are the highly bound ones: ceftriaxone and ertapenem (85–95%), oxacillin and flucloxacillin (about 90–95%) and cefazolin (about 80%). For these, low albumin raises clearance and shortens the time above the MIC (PK-13 b).

**Carbapenems: half-life about 1 h, low protein binding (2–20%). Ertapenem: 95% bound, half-life 4 h (once daily).** Meropenem is about 2% bound and imipenem about 20%, so their short half-lives require 8-hourly (meropenem) or 6-hourly (imipenem) dosing. Ertapenem’s binding gives it a long half-life and once-daily dosing, but it also makes it the carbapenem most likely to fail in hypoalbuminaemia, and it does not cover Pseudomonas or Acinetobacter.

**Reconstituted meropenem and imipenem are stable only 1–4** hours at room temperature, so a single bag cannot run for 24 hours. The US meropenem label allows 1 hour at room temperature once diluted in saline for infusion and 3 hours in water for a bolus; imipenem in saline lasts about 4 hours.

**h at room temperature: infuse within 1–3 h.** This is why carbapenems are given as 3-hour extended infusions (prepared freshly for each dose) rather than continuous infusions; piperacillin–tazobactam and cefepime are more stable and can run continuously. The watch line gives the target: about 40% of the dosing interval with the free level above the MIC for carbapenems (50% for penicillins, 60–70% for cephalosporins), and in the critically ill or with MDR organisms 100% fT>MIC, with maximal killing at 4–5 × MIC.
mimic: Meropenem vs ertapenem
Meropenem: 2% bound, half-life 1 h, 8-hourly, covers Pseudomonas. Ertapenem: about 95% bound, half-life 4 h, once daily, no Pseudomonas or Acinetobacter cover.
Extended vs continuous infusion
Extended (3–4 h) suits unstable drugs such as meropenem; continuous suits stable ones such as piperacillin–tazobactam. Both always start with a loading dose.
traps: “Ceftriaxone needs renal dose reduction”
It is cleared by bile as well as kidney; no renal adjustment.
“Run meropenem as a 24-hour continuous infusion from one bag”
It degrades within hours at room temperature; use 3-hour infusions or bags changed every few hours.
decode: [pattern] Which carbapenem is once daily and why? Which one fails in severe hypoalbuminaemia?
Ertapenem, because it is about 95% protein bound (half-life 4 h); the same binding makes its free level fall fast when albumin is low.
[pattern] PK/PD target of meropenem?
Time above the MIC: 40% fT>MIC, 100% in the critically ill.
PK-14.punch: β-lactams are hydrophilic, renally cleared and time-dependent: load fully, then keep the free level above the MIC with extended infusions, remembering that meropenem lasts only an hour or two in the bag.

PK-15.intro: Step 4 is the concentration-dependent drugs, and this card sets the two classes side by side: one lipophilic and orally available, one hydrophilic and needing levels. No real question is linked; PK-22 b and h and PK-19 a carry the asked points about aminoglycosides.
why: **Nature: fluoroquinolones lipophilic, large Vd, oral 70–90% bioavailable; aminoglycosides hydrophilic.** Fluoroquinolones enter cells and tissues, so lung and prostate levels exceed plasma, and the oral dose gives levels close to IV (levofloxacin and moxifloxacin almost 100%). The card’s ‘aminoglycosides penetrate tissues well’ is only partly right: they reach the interstitial fluid of well-perfused tissues and even burn eschar, but they stay in extracellular water (Vd about 0.25 L/kg), barely enter cells, reach lung epithelial lining fluid, CSF and bone poorly, and are inactivated in acidic, anaerobic pus, which is why they are nebulised for pneumonia or given intraventricularly for ventriculitis.

**Clearance: ciprofloxacin and levofloxacin renal unchanged; moxifloxacin hepatic, no renal adjustment. Aminoglycosides renal; half-life 1.5–3.5 h.** Levofloxacin is about 85% excreted unchanged, so its dose falls in AKI; ciprofloxacin is partly renal. Moxifloxacin needs no renal change but is avoided in severe liver failure. Aminoglycosides are filtered unchanged, so their half-life lengthens in step with falling GFR.

**Killing: both concentration-dependent; fluoroquinolones by AUC/MIC; aminoglycosides with a post-antibiotic effect and synergy with cell-wall drugs.** The post-antibiotic effect means bacterial growth stays suppressed for hours after the level falls below the MIC, which is what makes once-daily dosing work. β-lactams and glycopeptides damage the wall and let the aminoglycoside in, hence the synergy used in enterococcal endocarditis.

**Key ratio: fluoroquinolone AUC/MIC over 87.5–125; aminoglycosides AUC/MIC for Enterobacterales, peak/MIC for Pseudomonas.** For Gram-negatives the classic fluoroquinolone target is an AUC24/MIC of 125 or more (ciprofloxacin in seriously ill patients, Forrest 1993), and about 87 or more predicted eradication with levofloxacin in nosocomial pneumonia (Drusano 2004), which is where the lower figure comes from; for pneumococcus about 30–40 is enough. For aminoglycosides the standard target is a peak (Cmax) of 8–10 times the MIC, with AUC/MIC used by some dosing programmes; the split by organism is the notes’ framing.

**TDM: yes for aminoglycosides, especially in renal dysfunction.** A peak (after the first dose) checks efficacy and a trough or a timed level guides the interval; a high trough means drug is building up in the renal cortex and inner ear. Fluoroquinolones are not routinely monitored.
mimic: Levofloxacin vs moxifloxacin
Levofloxacin: renal, reduce in AKI, covers Pseudomonas. Moxifloxacin: hepatic, no renal change, poor urine levels and no Pseudomonas cover.
traps: “Aminoglycosides penetrate tissues well”
They are hydrophilic and penetrate lung, CSF and abscesses poorly; this is a card statement to unlearn (FLAGS).
“Moxifloxacin for a urinary infection in AKI”
No renal adjustment, but also little reaches the urine.
decode: [pattern] Which fluoroquinolone needs no renal dose adjustment?
Moxifloxacin.
[pattern] Why can aminoglycosides be given once daily?
Concentration-dependent killing plus a post-antibiotic effect, with less cortical uptake when the trough is low.
PK-15.punch: Fluoroquinolones are lipophilic and oral, aminoglycosides hydrophilic and monitored; both kill by concentration, and the aminoglycoside’s post-antibiotic effect is what allows one big daily dose.

PK-16.intro: Still step 4: colistin is the concentration-dependent drug with the most awkward kinetics. It is given as an inactive prodrug that converts slowly, so without a load the active drug sits below target for two to three days, the very days a carbapenem-resistant infection kills. No real question is linked, but PK-22 a tests the load.
why: **Given as colistimethate (CMS), an inactive prodrug; peak colistin about 7 h after a dose; half-life 14 h → steady state takes 2–3 days without a load; about 60% protein bound.** CMS is cleared mainly by the kidney, and only the part that is not excreted hydrolyses to active colistin. The 2019 consensus quotes colistin protein binding as about 50%, a little below the card’s 60%. Five half-lives of 14 hours is about 3 days, which is why the load matters. Doses are written in million units (MU) of CMS or mg of colistin base activity (CBA): 1 MU is about 30–33 mg CBA, so 9 MU is roughly 300 mg CBA.

**Poor penetration into lung, CSF, bone, pleura → nebulise (intrathecal for CNS).** Colistin is a large polycationic molecule, so systemic levels in alveolar fluid and CSF are low. Nebulised CMS is added for XDR ventilator pneumonia (a weak consensus recommendation; ESCMID advises against routine nebulised antibiotics), and for ventriculitis CMS is given intraventricularly (consensus about 125,000 IU, roughly 4 mg CBA, daily) alongside IV dosing.
**PD index: fAUC/MIC.** The consensus target is an average steady-state plasma colistin of about 2 mg/L. Above that, nephrotoxicity becomes more likely, so the therapeutic window is narrow.

**Loading 9 MU (9–12 MU by ideal weight; 12 MU for 70 kg), independent of renal function.** The 2019 international consensus gives a fixed load of 300 mg CBA, about 9 MU, infused over 30–60 minutes. The older weight-based formula (with ideal or actual weight, whichever is lower) gives about 280 mg CBA, roughly 9 MU, for 70 kg, so the card’s 12 MU for 70 kg is higher than either source. What is asked is the rule: the load fills Vd, so it is never reduced in AKI (PK-22 a).

**4.5 MU every 12 h, starting 24 h after the load (consensus 12–24 h); cut by eGFR (30–60: 3 MU; 10–30: 2 MU; under 10: 1 MU, every 12 h).** 4.5 MU 12-hourly is the European label dose of 9 MU a day; the consensus gives 300–360 mg CBA (9–10.9 MU) a day in two doses, with the first maintenance dose 12–24 hours after the load (12 h with normal kidneys). In renal failure the consensus reductions are smaller than the card’s: about 195 mg CBA (roughly 6 MU) a day at CrCl 30–40, 160 mg (about 5 MU) at 10–20, and about 130–145 mg (about 4 MU) under 10, so the card’s 2 MU a day under 10 would under-dose. The European label’s bands are similar: 5.5–7.5 MU a day at CrCl 30–50, 4.5–5.5 MU at 10–30 and 3.5 MU under 10, so both sources give more than the card at the bottom. CRRT removes CMS and colistin, so patients on CRRT need more than the anuric dose: the consensus gives 440 mg CBA (about 13 MU) a day, 220 mg 12-hourly.
mimic: CMS dose units
MU (million units of CMS) and mg CBA are different scales: 9 MU ≈ 300 mg CBA ≈ 720 mg CMS. Confusing them gives a two- to three-fold error.
traps: “Halve the colistin load in AKI”
The load depends on Vd, not on the kidneys (PK-22 a).
“Start maintenance straight after the load”
The first maintenance dose comes 12–24 h later, at the usual interval.
decode: [pattern] Colistin loading dose for a 70 kg patient with CRAB pneumonia and creatinine 3?
9 MU (300 mg CBA), whatever the renal function; maintenance reduced for CrCl, nebulised CMS added.
[pattern] Why give a loading dose of colistin?
CMS is a slowly converting prodrug and colistin’s half-life is about 14 h, so without a load the level is subtherapeutic for 2–3 days.
PK-16.punch: Colistin is a slow prodrug, so load 9 MU (300 mg CBA) whatever the kidneys do, start maintenance 12–24 hours later, and cut only the maintenance for renal failure.

PK-17.sub: Pharmacology → Antibacterials → Colistin vs polymyxin B
PK-17.intro: Step 4 again: the two polymyxins are almost the same molecule (they differ by one amino acid) but reach the body in opposite ways. Colistin arrives as a prodrug cleared by the kidney; polymyxin B arrives active and is barely excreted in urine. That single difference decides which one to use where. No real question is linked.
why: **Form: colistin as a prodrug (CMS → colistin); polymyxin B as the active drug.** Polymyxin B reaches target levels quickly after a load and its plasma levels are predictable; CMS converts slowly and variably.

**Renal handling: CMS cleared by the kidneys → high urine levels; polymyxin B undergoes tubular reabsorption → low urine levels, no renal adjustment.** Because most CMS is filtered into the urine and converts there, the bladder sees high colistin levels. Polymyxin B is cleared mainly by non-renal routes, so the 2019 consensus doses it on total body weight (load 2–2.5 mg/kg, then 1.25–1.5 mg/kg 12-hourly) with no change for renal failure or RRT.
**Plasma levels: colistin slow and variable; polymyxin B predictable.** This is why polymyxin B is preferred when the blood level is what matters.

**Toxicity: colistin more nephrotoxic; polymyxin B less nephrotoxic, with neurotoxicity and skin pigmentation.** Both damage the proximal tubule and can cause paraesthesia and neuromuscular blockade; observational data favour polymyxin B for renal toxicity. Skin hyperpigmentation is a polymyxin B effect.
**Best for: colistin for urinary infection; polymyxin B for systemic infection (bloodstream, pneumonia).** This is the consensus recommendation, and it follows directly from row b.
mimic: Colistin vs polymyxin B in a CRE urinary infection
Colistin: high urine levels. Polymyxin B: little reaches the urine.
traps: “Polymyxin B needs renal dose reduction like colistin”
It is not renally cleared; consensus gives no adjustment, even on dialysis.
“Polymyxin B for a lower urinary tract infection”
Its urine levels are low; colistin is the polymyxin for the bladder.
decode: [pattern] Which polymyxin for CRE pyelonephritis, and which for CRAB bacteraemia?
Colistin (CMS) for the urine; polymyxin B for the blood.
PK-17.punch: Colistin is a kidney-cleared prodrug, so it suits the urine and needs renal adjustment; polymyxin B is active, non-renally cleared and predictable, so it suits blood and lung and is never renally reduced.

PK-18.sub: Pharmacology → Antibacterials → Glycopeptides, tigecycline, linezolid, azithromycin
PK-18.intro: Step 5 is the Gram-positive drugs. Each has one kinetic fact that the exam turns into a question: vancomycin is renally cleared and dosed to levels, teicoplanin has a very long half-life, tigecycline lives in tissue rather than blood, and linezolid needs no renal change. Both real questions are about the renally impaired patient, and one of them shows how that last fact misleads.
why: **Vancomycin: Vd 0.4–0.9 L/kg; 80–90% renal unchanged; half-life 4–6 h; AUC/MIC 400; obese: actual weight; load 25–30 mg/kg; CVVHD every 36–48 h.** Vancomycin is filtered unchanged, so its clearance tracks creatinine clearance; with ARC levels run low, in AKI they accumulate. The 2020 consensus targets an AUC/MIC of 400–600 (MIC 1) and no longer uses a trough of 15–20 alone. The load is 20–35 mg/kg of actual body weight (max 3 g) in the critically ill, 20–25 mg/kg in obesity, then 15–20 mg/kg 8–12-hourly. On CRRT (effluent 20–25 mL/kg/h) the consensus gives a load of 20–25 mg/kg and 7.5–10 mg/kg 12-hourly, with levels within 24 h; the card’s 36–48-hourly interval belongs to older, low-intensity CRRT. On intermittent haemodialysis it is given after each session, aiming for a pre-dialysis level of 15–20 mg/L.

**Teicoplanin: Vd 0.9–1.4; half-life about 150 h (14 days to steady state); load 12 mg/kg 12-hourly × 3–5, then 12 mg/kg daily (CRRT 6); glomerular filtration; not removed by HD or CAPD.** Teicoplanin is about 90% albumin bound, which gives it its very long half-life (100–170 h). Without a load it would take two weeks to reach steady state, so it is loaded 12-hourly (6 mg/kg × 3 for ordinary infections, 12 mg/kg × 3–5 for bone, joint and endocarditis). Renal adjustment starts only from day 4, and haemodialysis does not remove it.

**Tigecycline: lipophilic, Vd 7–10 L/kg; biliary; about 80% bound; AUC/MIC; low serum levels → higher doses.** It moves into tissue so completely that blood levels are low, which is why it is a poor choice for bacteraemia and why a 200 mg load and 100 mg 12-hourly are used for MDR infections. Biliary elimination means no renal adjustment.

**Linezolid: oral about 100%; 30% bound; 30% renal, 70% metabolised; no renal adjustment; AUC/MIC.** Oral and IV doses are interchangeable. Its metabolites accumulate in renal failure (more thrombocytopenia), but the dose is not changed. It is bacteriostatic against staphylococci, which matters for bacteraemia.

**Azithromycin: long half-life (about 64–68 h); once daily; macrolides Cmax/MIC (notes).** The long half-life comes from huge uptake into cells, which allows once-daily dosing and short courses. Its PK/PD index is usually given as AUC/MIC rather than Cmax/MIC; older teaching classes erythromycin and clarithromycin as time-dependent.
mimic: Vancomycin vs teicoplanin
Vancomycin: half-life 4–6 h, dosed to AUC, removed by high-flux dialysis and CRRT. Teicoplanin: half-life 4–7 days, 12-hourly loading, not removed by haemodialysis.
Tigecycline vs linezolid
Both need no renal change. Tigecycline: tissue drug with low blood levels, biliary. Linezolid: full oral bioavailability, good blood and lung levels.
traps: “Linezolid” keyed for MRSA CLABSI with septic shock on haemodialysis (49% right)

The key is disputed. Its only advantage is no renal adjustment; it is bacteriostatic and IDSA guidance makes vancomycin or daptomycin first line for MRSA bacteraemia, with renal failure handled by dosing vancomycin to levels or daptomycin 48-hourly. The AVERT trial in the stem is irrelevant. Pick linezolid only if neither vancomycin nor daptomycin is offered.
“De-escalate” or “rapid diagnostics” for low vancomycin levels on CRRT
A low level is a dosing problem: therapeutic drug monitoring with AUC-guided dosing (82% right).
“Dose vancomycin on ideal body weight in obesity”
Actual weight, with the load capped at 3 g (PK-22 d).
decode: ICU patient on CRRT, subtherapeutic vancomycin despite standard dosing — which stewardship strategy? [DocT GT]
Therapeutic drug monitoring (82%): AUC-guided dosing to 400–600 after a load, adjusted for effluent rate.
AKI on haemodialysis, MRSA CLABSI, septic shock — initial therapy? [DocT QBank]
Keyed linezolid (49%); by guideline, vancomycin (load, then to levels) or daptomycin (48-hourly).
[pattern] Which glycopeptide is not removed by haemodialysis and needs 12-hourly loading?
Teicoplanin.
PK-18.punch: Vancomycin is renally cleared, so load on actual weight and dose to an AUC of 400–600 with levels, especially on CRRT; ‘no renal adjustment’ makes linezolid convenient but not the first choice for MRSA bacteraemia.

PK-19.sub: Pharmacology → Antibacterials → Empirical ICU and CRRT doses
PK-19.intro: Step 5 ends with the dose table, where steps 1, 3 and 4 become numbers. Two rules run through it: the first dose is the same or bigger in the critically ill whatever the kidneys, and on CRRT only the maintenance falls. The one real question asks how amikacin is given in septic shock.
why: **Amikacin: 25–30 mg/kg once, then TDM; CRRT 12–15 mg/kg, interval by TDM.** A single large dose gives a peak of 8–10 times the MIC (about 60–80 mg/L), uses the post-antibiotic effect, and lets the trough fall low, which reduces uptake into the renal cortex and inner ear. Sepsis raises Vd, so the critically ill need the top of the range on actual weight (adjusted weight if obese). Your notes print 30 mg/kg.

**Gentamicin: 7–10 mg/kg; CRRT 3–4 mg/kg, then TDM.** Extended-interval gentamicin is usually 5–7 mg/kg, with 7 mg/kg the common ICU and burn dose; French guidance allows up to 8 mg/kg in severe sepsis, aiming at a peak of 30–40 mg/L (8–10 times the MIC). The card’s 10 mg/kg is above these recommendations, so a peak level after the first dose is essential.

**Meropenem: 1 g load, then 1 g 8-hourly as extended or continuous infusion (ARC: 6–8-hourly); CRRT 0.5–1 g 8–12-hourly.** 2 g 8-hourly is used for Pseudomonas with high MICs and for meningitis. Stability limits continuous infusion (PK-14 d).
**Piperacillin–tazobactam: 4.5 g load, then 4.5 g 6-hourly (ARC: 4–6-hourly); CRRT 4.5 g 8-hourly.** Given as extended (over 3–4 h) or continuous infusion after the load.

**Cefepime: 2 g load, then 2 g 8-hourly (ARC 6–8); CRRT 1–2 g 12-hourly.** Cefepime accumulates in renal failure and causes encephalopathy and non-convulsive status, so the renal adjustment matters more than for other β-lactams.
**Ciprofloxacin 400 mg 8-hourly, levofloxacin 750 mg daily, moxifloxacin 400 mg daily; CRRT ciprofloxacin 400 mg 12-hourly.** Moxifloxacin is unchanged on CRRT (hepatic, PK-15 b).

**Vancomycin: load 25–30 mg/kg, then 15–20 mg/kg 8–12-hourly; CRRT 20 mg/kg load, then 10–15 mg/kg 24–48-hourly.** The 2020 consensus gives 20–35 mg/kg (max 3 g) as the load and, on CRRT at effluent 20–25 mL/kg/h, 7.5–10 mg/kg 12-hourly to levels; the card’s 24–48-hourly interval under-doses modern CRRT (PK-18 a).

**Daptomycin: 10–12 mg/kg; CRRT 8 mg/kg 24–48-hourly.** Licensed doses are 4–6 mg/kg; 8–12 mg/kg is used for bacteraemia, endocarditis and in the critically ill. It is inactivated by surfactant, so never for pneumonia; check creatine kinase weekly.
**Linezolid: 600 mg 8–12-hourly; usual on CRRT.** 600 mg 12-hourly is standard; 8-hourly is used with ARC, burns or obesity.
mimic: What changes on CRRT
Unchanged: β-lactam and vancomycin loads, linezolid, moxifloxacin. Reduced: β-lactam maintenance, aminoglycoside doses and intervals, vancomycin maintenance, ciprofloxacin.
traps: “Divide amikacin into 5 mg/kg three times a day” or “continuous infusion at 10 µg/mL”
Both throw away the peak that drives killing and raise the trough that drives toxicity; amikacin is given once daily at 25–30 mg/kg.
“Avoid aminoglycosides in sepsis because ATN is certain”
A short once-daily course with level monitoring has a modest risk; the absolute wording is the giveaway.
decode: Septic shock, 70 kg, amikacin in combination — preferred dosing in the acute phase? [DocT GT]
One large daily dose of 25–30 mg/kg to maximise Cmax/MIC.
[pattern] Which antibiotic dose is NOT changed on CRRT?
The loading dose of any of them; for maintenance, linezolid and moxifloxacin.
PK-19.punch: In the septic patient the first dose is always full: amikacin 25–30 mg/kg once, vancomycin 20–35 mg/kg, β-lactams at full dose; CRRT trims only the doses that follow.

PK-20.intro: Step 6 is the antifungals, and the first question is always where the drug goes. Choosing an antifungal for Candida in the urine, eye or brain is a penetration question before it is a spectrum question. Both real questions are Candida in the bladder, and the second key is disputed.
why: **Fluconazole: nearly everywhere — CSF, eye, urine.** It is small, water-soluble and poorly protein bound, and about 80% is excreted unchanged in the urine, so bladder levels are many times the MIC; CSF and vitreous levels are about 70–80% of serum. It is the drug of choice for susceptible Candida cystitis and pyelonephritis, and the step-down for Candida endophthalmitis and meningitis.
**Voriconazole: not into urine.** It is metabolised in the liver and less than 2% appears unchanged in urine, so it does not treat Candida UTI, although it does reach the eye and CNS well.

**Echinocandins: poor in urine, CSF and vitreous.** They are large, highly protein-bound molecules cleared by slow non-renal degradation, so very little reaches the urine, CSF or eye. They are first line for candidaemia but should not be relied on for cystitis, endophthalmitis or meningitis.

**Liposomal amphotericin: high serum and CNS levels.** The liposome gives high blood levels and good brain tissue levels (it is used for cryptococcal meningitis and CNS candidiasis), though CSF levels themselves are low. Liposomal amphotericin reaches the urine poorly; for Candida cystitis by a fluconazole-resistant species the IDSA choice is amphotericin B deoxycholate (0.3–0.6 mg/kg, with or without bladder irrigation) or flucytosine.
mimic: Liposomal vs deoxycholate amphotericin
Liposomal: less nephrotoxic, better tissue and CNS levels, poor urine levels. Deoxycholate: reaches the urine, so it is the amphotericin for resistant Candida cystitis.
traps: “Caspofungin” for symptomatic Candida UTI
Echinocandins barely reach the urine; fluconazole is the answer.
“Anidulafungin” keyed for lower UTI by C. auris (82% chose it)

The key is disputed: an echinocandin reaches the bladder poorly, and IDSA 2016 advises amphotericin B deoxycholate (± bladder irrigation) or flucytosine for fluconazole-resistant Candida cystitis; it was written for C. glabrata and C. krusei and is applied to C. auris by extension. CDC’s echinocandin-first advice is for invasive C. auris, gives nothing specific for the bladder, and advises against treating C. auris in urine without symptoms. If amphotericin is offered for a symptomatic bladder infection, pick it, after checking susceptibility, since some C. auris isolates resist amphotericin.
“Voriconazole” for Candida UTI
It is not excreted unchanged in urine.
decode: ICU patient, symptomatic Candida UTI, no fungus ball or abscess — agent with high urinary concentrations? [DocT GT]
Fluconazole.
Drug of choice for lower UTI by Candida auris? [DocT GT]
Keyed anidulafungin (82%); by IDSA logic, amphotericin B deoxycholate.
PK-20.punch: Fluconazole goes everywhere, including the bladder; echinocandins treat the blood but not the urine, eye or CSF; for a resistant Candida in the bladder, amphotericin deoxycholate is the drug that gets there.

PK-21.sub: Pharmacology → Antifungals → PK/PD indices and drug levels
PK-21.intro: Step 6 continues with how hard and how often to give each antifungal, and which ones need levels. The polyenes and echinocandins kill by peak; the azoles by exposure over time, with voriconazole and posaconazole dosed to troughs. The one real question is about voriconazole, and its key is wrong.
why: **Amphotericin B: Cmax/MIC 2–4 (lipid 5; liposomal over 40); concentration-dependent.** Its killing rises with the peak and it has a long post-antifungal effect, so it is given once daily at a high dose (liposomal 3–5 mg/kg).

**Echinocandins: Cmax/MIC (5–7 parapsilosis/glabrata; 10–20 albicans); AUC/MIC; large, infrequent doses.** They are concentration-dependent and fungicidal against Candida, so a loading dose and once-daily dosing are standard; there is no renal adjustment.

**Voriconazole: trough 1–2 mg/L (effective); over 4.5–6 toxic; hepatic; IV cyclodextrin accumulates in renal failure.** The usual target range is a trough of 1–5.5 mg/L, with more than 1–2 needed for efficacy and visual hallucinations, encephalopathy and hepatotoxicity above about 5.5. Its metabolism by CYP2C19 is genetically variable and non-linear, hence TDM. The IV form is carried in sulfobutylether-β-cyclodextrin (SBECD), which is renally cleared and accumulates when CrCl is under 50, so oral voriconazole is preferred in renal failure; the clinical harm of SBECD is debated and has been shown only in animals. Voriconazole is fungistatic against Candida and has no activity against Mucorales.

**Posaconazole: trough over 0.5–1 mg/L; over 98% bound; Vd 5–25 L/kg; IV cyclodextrin, renal accumulation, neurotoxicity.** Current targets are a trough of 0.7 mg/L or more for prophylaxis and 1 mg/L or more for treatment. The 3.5–4 mg/L your notes mention elsewhere is not a protective level: some licensing authorities suggest about 3.75 mg/L as an upper limit (pseudo-hyperaldosteronism, hypertension and hypokalaemia at high levels). Its IV form contains the same SBECD as voriconazole.

**Isavuconazole: load 200 mg 8-hourly × 6, then 200 mg daily; renal safe; over 90% bound; no cyclodextrin.** The IV form is a water-soluble prodrug (isavuconazonium), so it needs no cyclodextrin and no renal adjustment, and TDM is not routine. It covers Aspergillus and Mucorales and shortens rather than prolongs the QT.

**Fluconazole: AUC/MIC 25–44 (preclinical); 55–100 (clinical).** In practice this is the dose/MIC ratio: a daily dose in mg at least 100 times the MIC, so higher doses (800 mg load, then 400–800 mg daily, or 12 mg/kg) are used in the critically ill and for less-susceptible species.
mimic: Voriconazole vs isavuconazole in renal failure
Voriconazole IV: SBECD accumulates, so switch to oral. Isavuconazole IV: no cyclodextrin, no change.
Voriconazole vs posaconazole vs isavuconazole for mucormycosis
Voriconazole: no activity. Posaconazole and isavuconazole: active, used for step-down or salvage after liposomal amphotericin.
traps: “Oral voriconazole is preferred in renal dysfunction” keyed as the INCORRECT statement

The key is wrong: that statement is true, because the IV SBECD accumulates. The false statements are ‘IV voriconazole is preferred in renal dysfunction’, ‘first line for mucormycosis’ (amphotericin B is; voriconazole has no mucor activity) and ‘fungicidal against Candida’ (it is fungistatic). If the mucor option is offered, it is the clearest incorrect statement.
“Posaconazole target trough 3.5–4 mg/L”
That is near the suggested upper limit; the targets are 0.7 (prophylaxis) and 1 mg/L (treatment).
decode: Which of the following is incorrect about voriconazole? (oral preferred in renal dysfunction / IV preferred in renal dysfunction / first line for mucor / fungicidal against Candida) [DocT GT]
Keyed A, which is actually true; choose the mucormycosis statement.
[pattern] Which mould-active azole needs no renal adjustment of its IV form?
Isavuconazole (no cyclodextrin).
PK-21.punch: Amphotericin and echinocandins kill by peak, so give big daily doses; voriconazole is dosed to a trough of 1–5.5 mg/L and switched to oral in renal failure because of its cyclodextrin, and it never treats mucor.

PK-22.intro: This sweep comes back to step 1, the rule under the whole deck: the first dose depends on how much water the drug spreads into, and only the later doses depend on the kidneys. The one real question was answered correctly by only 14%: an anuric, fluid-overloaded patient in septic shock, and the majority reached for ‘decrease the amikacin dose’.
why: **False: the colistin load is independent of renal function.** The load fills the volume of distribution; renal function decides only the maintenance (PK-16 d, e).

**True: sepsis raises the Vd of aminoglycosides.** Aminoglycosides distribute in extracellular water, normally about 0.25 L/kg. Capillary leak, fluid resuscitation and oedema can raise this to 0.35–0.5 L/kg, so a standard dose gives a lower peak and may miss the Cmax/MIC of 8–10. The answer is a larger single dose by weight (amikacin 25–30 mg/kg). Anuria lowers clearance, which changes when the next dose is given (by levels, often days later), not the size of the first.

**False: ARC is a creatinine clearance over 130 mL/min/1.73 m².** It is common in young patients with trauma, burns, sepsis or brain injury and causes subtherapeutic β-lactam and vancomycin levels; serum creatinine looks normal or low, so it is found only by measuring an 8- or 24-hour urinary creatinine clearance.

**False: vancomycin is dosed on total body weight.** It distributes into lean and some adipose tissue, so actual weight predicts its Vd. The load is capped (20–25 mg/kg, max 3 g, in obesity) and the maintenance is then set by AUC. Aminoglycosides, by contrast, use adjusted body weight in obesity, and older colistin formulas used the lower of ideal and actual weight.
**True: meropenem is time-dependent.** Its index is fT>MIC (PK-14), so extended infusions and shorter intervals help; a higher single peak does not.
**False: echinocandins barely reach the urine and do not suit Candida UTI.** Fluconazole, or amphotericin B deoxycholate for resistant species (PK-20).
**False: linezolid needs no renal adjustment.** Its metabolites accumulate in renal failure but the dose stays at 600 mg (PK-18 d).
**True: aminoglycosides have a post-antibiotic effect.** Bacterial regrowth is suppressed for hours after the level falls below the MIC, which allows once-daily dosing (PK-15 c).
**False: lipophilic drugs, not hydrophilic ones, are sequestered by the ECMO circuit.** Hydrophilic drugs are affected by haemodilution and raised Vd (PK-12).
mimic: Load vs maintenance in AKI
Load: depends on Vd, unchanged or bigger. Maintenance: depends on clearance, reduced or spaced.
traps: “Decrease the amikacin dose because of diminished renal clearance” (the commonest wrong answer; 14% right)
That is the maintenance rule applied to the first dose. In shock with fluid overload Vd is up, so the dose is increased (option C) and the interval is lengthened by levels.
“Increase the dosing frequency because of the increased Vd”
Vd changes the dose size, clearance changes the frequency; an anuric patient needs less frequent, not more frequent, doses.
“Decrease the dose because of decreased protein binding”
Aminoglycosides are barely protein bound, so albumin is irrelevant.
“ARC is CrCl over 90”
90 is normal; ARC starts at 130.
decode: Septic shock on noradrenaline and vasopressin, 3 L of Ringer’s, anuric, volume overloaded; started on meropenem, amikacin, daptomycin, micafungin — amikacin dose consideration? [DocT GT]
Increase the dose because of the increased Vd (14%); the anuria lengthens the interval.
[pattern] Obese patient, vancomycin load — which weight?
Actual (total) body weight, capped at 3 g.
PK-22.punch: Size the first dose by the volume, time the next one by the clearance: a septic, fluid-overloaded, anuric patient gets more amikacin up front and waits longer for the second dose.
