x.sub: Trauma → Complications → Fat embolism syndrome
x.intro: Step 4 linked mechanism to injury; a long-bone or pelvic fracture predicts this delayed complication. Fat from the marrow enters the circulation, blocks capillaries and then triggers an inflammatory reaction, which explains both the delay of a day or more and the three organs affected. Five bank questions test two things: which features are major Gurd criteria, and that treatment is supportive with early fixation.
why: **24–72 h after long-bone or pelvic fracture (also IM nailing, liposuction, sickle crisis).** The delay reflects the time it takes fat globules to be broken down to free fatty acids that injure the endothelium. Intramedullary reaming forces more marrow into the veins.

**Gurd MAJOR: respiratory insufficiency, cerebral signs, petechial rash (non-dependent; only about 1/3).** The lung is the first capillary bed reached; fat passing through it (or through a patent foramen ovale) reaches the brain and skin. The rash appears on the upper chest, axillae, neck and conjunctivae, and is present in only about a third of patients.

**MINOR: tachycardia over 120, fever, retinal changes, jaundice, renal change, fall in Hb or platelets, high ESR, fat macroglobulinaemia; need 1 major + 4 minor.** Tachycardia and retinal changes are the two minor criteria that bank questions offer as ‘major’. Gurd and Wilson’s criteria set the tachycardia threshold at over 110 a minute and fever at over 38.5 °C.

**Clinical diagnosis: CT chest non-specific (ground glass), MRI brain ‘starfield’ DWI; fat in urine or BAL supportive only.** No test confirms FES; imaging and laboratory tests are done to exclude other causes (missed head injury, pneumothorax, pulmonary embolism). The MRI pattern of many small diffusion-restricting dots supports it.

**Supportive care (O₂/ventilation, haemodynamics); early fracture fixation (24 h or less) limits further embolisation; no proven role for steroids, heparin or IVC filters.** Lung-protective ventilation for the ARDS-like picture. A filter cannot catch fat, heparin does not dissolve it, and steroids have no outcome evidence as treatment.
mimic: FES vs pulmonary embolism
FES: 24–72 h after fracture, with confusion and petechiae. PE: later, usually without rash or encephalopathy, and a filling defect on CT angiography.
traps: “Tachycardia is a major Gurd criterion”
It is minor (47% right on DocT GT).
“Retinal changes are a major criterion”
Minor (Marrow, asked twice).
“Diagnosis is made with CT of the chest”
That was the false statement: FES is a clinical diagnosis of exclusion (69% right).
“Give steroids or heparin, or place an IVC filter”
None is proven; treatment is supportive with early fixation.
decode: ORIF of femur, sudden tachycardia, hypotension, hypoxia — all are major Gurd criteria EXCEPT [DocT GT]
Tachycardia.
Day 1 after femoral fixation: confusion, dyspnoea, petechiae on neck and trunk — all true EXCEPT [DocT GT]
‘Diagnosis is made with CT of the chest’.
Bilateral femur fractures, day 2, confusion, petechiae, P/F 150 — management? [DocT GT]
Supportive care with early operative fixation.
x.punch: Fat embolism is hypoxia, confusion and a non-dependent petechial rash 24–72 hours after a long-bone fracture; it is diagnosed clinically and treated by support and early fixation, and tachycardia and retinal changes are minor criteria.

topups.q: Blunt chest trauma: aortic injury, cardiac injury and posterior sternoclavicular dislocation — how to diagnose and act?
a: - Aorta: deceleration tear at the isthmus. CXR clues: mediastinum >8 cm, lost aortic knob, apical cap, left haemothorax, trachea/NG deviated RIGHT, LEFT main bronchus depressed, 1st/2nd rib fracture; a normal CXR does not exclude → CT angiography (not TTE/TEE).
- Aortic treatment: anti-impulse (HR <100, SBP <100) + TEVAR; minimal intimal injury observed.

- Blunt cardiac injury: screen all with ECG + troponin I; both normal → ruled out, no telemetry (EAST); abnormal → monitor 24–48 h, echo if hypotension/arrhythmia; sternal fracture alone does not predict BCI.
- Posterior SC dislocation threatens great vessels, trachea, oesophagus → CXR + CT angiography, reduction with CT-surgery backup.
topups.src: DocT GT:70; Marrow:QB61-Q07; Marrow:QB61-Q13; DocT GT:CGT2-Q46; DocT GT:GT5-Q140

x.sub: Trauma → Chest → Blunt aortic injury, blunt cardiac injury and posterior sternoclavicular dislocation
x.intro: Step 4 predicted injuries from the mechanism; rapid deceleration (a fall, a frontal crash) predicts injury to the structures in the mediastinum. The five bank questions test the imaging choice and the CXR signs of aortic injury, and who can be cleared of cardiac injury. The cohort did badly on both: 36% on the imaging question and 27% on cardiac clearance.
why: **Aorta: deceleration tear at the isthmus. CXR clues: mediastinum over 8 cm, lost aortic knob, apical cap, left haemothorax, trachea/NG deviated RIGHT, LEFT main bronchus depressed, 1st/2nd rib fracture; a normal CXR does not exclude → CT angiography (not TTE/TEE).** The isthmus, just beyond the left subclavian, is where the mobile arch meets the descending aorta fixed by the ligamentum arteriosum, so shear concentrates there. The haematoma lies to the left of the trachea and above the left main bronchus, so it pushes the trachea and NG tube to the right and the left bronchus down. No CXR finding is sensitive enough on its own, so a normal film does not exclude injury after a major deceleration. CT angiography is the test; TOE needs sedation and a cleared spine and misses parts of the arch.

**Aortic treatment: anti-impulse (HR under 100, SBP under 100) + TEVAR; minimal intimal injury observed.** A beta-blocker first (esmolol), then a vasodilator if needed, lowers the shear on the torn wall until it is repaired; many sources set tighter targets than the card, a heart rate of about 60–80 and a systolic pressure of 100 mmHg or less. Endovascular repair has replaced open repair because it has lower mortality and less paraplegia.

**Blunt cardiac injury: screen all with ECG + troponin I; both normal → ruled out, no telemetry (EAST); abnormal → monitor 24–48 h, echo if hypotension or arrhythmia; sternal fracture alone does not predict BCI.** The danger of a cardiac contusion is arrhythmia, which usually announces itself with an abnormal admission ECG; EAST recommends an ECG for every patient in whom blunt cardiac injury is suspected, and troponin I routinely. EAST (2012) states that a normal ECG with a normal troponin I rules out blunt cardiac injury, so no serial testing or telemetry is needed; a normal ECG with a raised troponin still needs a monitored bed, and echocardiography is for haemodynamic instability or a persistent new arrhythmia.

**Posterior SC dislocation threatens great vessels, trachea, oesophagus → CXR + CT angiography, reduction with CT-surgery backup.** The medial clavicle displaced backwards lies against the brachiocephalic vessels and trachea; a missing medial clavicle prominence after a steering-wheel or shoulder impact is the clue.
mimic: Aortic injury vs other causes of a wide mediastinum
A supine AP film widens any mediastinum; the specific signs are a lost aortic knob, rightward tracheal or NG deviation, and a depressed LEFT bronchus.
traps: “Definitive evaluation of BTAI is with TTE or TEE”
That was the false statement; CT angiography is the test (36% right).
“Depression of the right main bronchus suggests aortic injury”
The left main bronchus is depressed; ‘right’ was the false statement.
“Normal ECG and troponin I at 8 h: start serial troponins or 72-h telemetry”
Both normal rules out blunt cardiac injury: discharge (27% right).
“A sternal fracture means cardiac contusion”
A sternal fracture alone does not predict BCI.
decode: Fall from 20 ft, widened mediastinum — all true about BTAI EXCEPT [DocT GT]
‘TTE or TEE for definitive evaluation’.
Blunt chest trauma, normal ECG, troponin I under 1.5 ng/mL at 8 h — next? [DocT GT]
Discharge with follow-up.
Stable BCI with abnormal ECG and raised troponin — plan? [Marrow]
Serial ECG and troponin with echocardiography.
Unrestrained driver, medial clavicle deformity, SC joint not felt — management? [Marrow]
Chest X-ray then CT angiography.
x.punch: Deceleration tears the aorta at the isthmus: the haematoma pushes the trachea right and the left bronchus down, CT angiography confirms, and TEVAR follows anti-impulse control. A normal ECG and troponin together rule out blunt cardiac injury.

topups.q: Incomplete cord syndromes: lesion and deficit?
a: - Brown-Séquard (hemisection, stab): ipsilateral motor + proprioception loss, contralateral pain/temperature loss; best prognosis.
- Central cord (elderly, hyperextension on spondylosis): arms > legs (arm fibres medial), sacral sparing.
- Anterior cord (flexion injury; anterior spinal artery infarct after thoracic aortic repair): motor + pain/temperature lost, proprioception spared; worst prognosis.
- Posterior cord: proprioception/vibration lost only.
topups.src: DocT GT:33; DocT GT:58; Marrow:QB47-Q06; DocT GT:AIM2-Q55

x.sub: Trauma → Spine → Incomplete spinal cord syndromes
x.intro: Step 5 examined the spinal level under D. The incomplete cord syndromes follow from where the three main tracts run: the corticospinal tract (motor) and dorsal columns (proprioception, vibration) stay on the same side until the brainstem, while the spinothalamic tract (pain, temperature) crosses within a segment or two of entry. Which modality is lost on which side therefore locates the lesion.
why: **Brown-Séquard (hemisection, stab): ipsilateral motor and proprioception loss, contralateral pain/temperature loss; best prognosis.** Cutting one half of the cord takes the uncrossed motor and dorsal-column fibres of that side and the already-crossed spinothalamic fibres from the other side.

**Central cord (elderly, hyperextension on spondylosis): arms more than legs (arm fibres medial), sacral sparing.** The commonest incomplete syndrome. In the cervical cord the fibres for the arms lie nearest the centre, so central damage weakens the arms most; sacral fibres lie outermost and are spared.

**Anterior cord (flexion injury; anterior spinal artery infarct after thoracic aortic repair): motor and pain/temperature lost, proprioception spared; worst prognosis.** The single anterior spinal artery supplies the front two-thirds; the dorsal columns have their own paired posterior arteries and are spared. After aortic surgery this gives flaccid paraplegia below the level of the infarct, with loss of pain and temperature below it and preserved joint position and vibration sense.
**Posterior cord: proprioception and vibration lost only.** Rare after trauma; motor power and pain sensation are preserved.
mimic: Brown-Séquard vs anterior cord
Brown-Séquard: losses split between the two sides. Anterior cord: bilateral motor and pain loss with proprioception preserved on both sides.
traps: “Post-aortic repair cord infarct: bilateral loss of proprioception”

That is the posterior pattern; anterior spinal artery infarct spares proprioception. The keyed answer was flaccid paralysis at T8 (54%); its wording ‘complete loss of sensory function’ overstates the deficit, since dorsal columns are spared.
“Central cord affects the legs more than the arms”
Arms more than legs, because the arm fibres lie centrally.
decode: Stab in the back: ipsilateral weakness and proprioception loss, contralateral pain/temperature loss below T8 [DocT GT]
Brown-Séquard (78%).
Elderly fall backwards, arms weaker than legs, sacral sensation preserved [DocT GT]
Central cord syndrome (83%).
Most likely finding after thoracic aneurysm repair cord infarction [DocT GT]
Flaccid paraplegia at the level with motor and pain/temperature loss (anterior cord).
x.punch: Where the deficit falls locates the lesion: split sides are a hemisection, arms worse than legs is central cord, and motor plus pain loss with preserved proprioception is anterior cord, the worst prognosis.

topups.topic: Spinal column injury: stability and mechanism
topups.q: Spinal column injury: which patterns are unstable, and how are they imaged?
a: - Three columns: anterior (ALL + front half of body), middle (back half + PLL), posterior (arch, ligaments). Wedge compression = anterior only, stable.
- Burst = anterior + middle (retropulsion can hit the cord); Chance (flexion–distraction, lap belt) = all three, UNSTABLE, with hollow-viscus/mesenteric injury.
- Facets: unilateral jump (flexion + rotation, <50% translation, cord often spared) vs bilateral (flexion + distraction, >50%, cord injury usual, unstable).
- Subluxation = ligamentous instability: in-line immobilisation, CT for bone, MRI for cord/disc/ligament/epidural haematoma; early decompression and fixation (<24 h, STASCIS).
topups.src: DocT GT:GT6-Q10; DocT GT:GT7-Q8; DocT GT:GT7-Q86

x.sub: Trauma → Spine → Column injury: stability and mechanism
x.intro: Step 4 tied mechanism to injury; in the spine the mechanism also predicts stability. Stability means whether the column can hold its shape under normal load without endangering the cord, and the three-column model judges it by how many columns are broken. The three bank questions were each answered by only 34–53%.
why: **Three columns: anterior (ALL + front half of body), middle (back half + PLL), posterior (arch, ligaments). Wedge compression = anterior only, stable.** A compression fracture crushes the front of the body under flexion and axial load; the middle column is intact, so the canal is not narrowed and the patient is usually neurologically intact.

**Burst = anterior + middle (retropulsion can hit the cord); Chance (flexion–distraction, lap belt) = all three, UNSTABLE, with hollow-viscus or mesenteric injury.** In a burst the posterior wall of the body breaks and fragments can be pushed back into the canal. In a Chance fracture the body is folded over a lap belt and the posterior elements are pulled apart, so all three columns fail; the same belt crushes bowel and mesentery (see the blunt abdominal trauma top-up).

**Facets: unilateral jump (flexion + rotation, under 50% translation, cord often spared) vs bilateral (flexion + distraction, over 50%, cord injury usual, unstable).** One jumped facet narrows the canal a little; both jumped facets displace the body by half its depth or more and compress the cord.

**Subluxation = ligamentous instability: in-line immobilisation, CT for bone, MRI for cord, disc, ligament and epidural haematoma; early decompression and fixation (under 24 h, STASCIS).** Displacement of one vertebra on another means the ligaments have failed. CT shows bone; only MRI shows the cord, disc and ligaments. In cervical cord injury, STASCIS (Fehlings 2012) found a 2-grade or greater AIS improvement in 19.8% of patients decompressed within 24 hours against 8.8% decompressed later.
mimic: Burst vs wedge compression
Wedge: front of the body only, posterior wall intact, stable. Burst: posterior wall broken, risk of retropulsion.
traps: “Chance fractures are often stable”
False: all three columns fail (38% right).
“Subluxation with anterior displacement: collar and CT are enough”
Unstable; MRI and early surgery are needed (53% right).
“Backward fall onto the head with quadriparesis: hyperextension and rotation”
DocT keys bilateral jumped facets from hyperflexion–distraction based on the MRI (34% right); the image decides, and without it a backward fall in the elderly suggests central cord.
decode: Which is false: compression fracture neurologically intact; Chance with visceral injury; burst affects anterior and middle; Chance often stable [DocT GT]
‘Chance fractures are often stable’.
C-spine fracture with subluxation and anterior displacement — management and imaging? [DocT GT]
Surgery, with MRI for the soft tissues.
x.punch: Stability depends on the columns: wedge is anterior only and stable, burst adds the middle column, and Chance breaks all three, comes with bowel injury and is unstable. Subluxation means ligament failure, so get an MRI and early fixation.

topups.q: Alert blunt trauma patient: when no C-spine imaging, and Hangman's vs Jefferson fracture?
a: - NEXUS: no imaging if no midline tenderness, normal alertness, not intoxicated, no focal deficit, no distracting injury (Canadian rule adds age ≥65, dangerous mechanism, rotation 45°).
- If imaging: CT (not plain films); MRI for deficit or ligament concern.
- Hangman's: bilateral C2 pedicle/pars fractures from hyperextension–distraction; canal widens, cord often spared.
- Jefferson: C1 ring burst from axial load (diving); lateral masses overhang C2 on open-mouth view.
- Both unstable: collar, CT/MRI, spinal surgery.

x.sub: Trauma → Spine → C-spine clearance and C1/C2 fractures
x.intro: Step 5 protected the spine during A; this card is about when that protection can stop without imaging, and about the two upper cervical fractures that are named in stems. Both clearance rules were derived to stop imaging the many alert patients who have no injury without missing the few who do.
why: **NEXUS: no imaging if no midline tenderness, normal alertness, not intoxicated, no focal deficit, no distracting injury (Canadian rule adds age 65 or more, dangerous mechanism, rotation 45°).** NEXUS requires all five low-risk criteria. The Canadian C-spine rule works in three steps: any high-risk factor (age 65 or more, dangerous mechanism, limb paraesthesia) → image; no low-risk factor (simple rear-end collision, sitting in the ED, walking since the injury, delayed neck pain, no midline tenderness) → image; otherwise the patient must actively rotate 45° each way. In a head-to-head study (Stiell 2003) the Canadian rule was more sensitive (99.4% vs 90.7%) and more specific (45.1% vs 36.8%).
**If imaging: CT (not plain films); MRI for deficit or ligament concern.** CT misses far fewer fractures than plain films; MRI shows cord, disc and ligaments.

**Hangman’s: bilateral C2 pedicle/pars fractures from hyperextension–distraction; canal widens, cord often spared.** The fracture separates the body of C2 from its arch, which enlarges the canal, so many patients are neurologically intact. Hyperextension–distraction is the judicial-hanging mechanism; road traffic collisions, now the commonest cause, usually add axial loading to the hyperextension.
**Jefferson: C1 ring burst from axial load (diving); lateral masses overhang C2 on the open-mouth view.** The skull drives the lateral masses of the atlas outwards; the ring breaks in several places.

**Both unstable: collar, CT/MRI, spinal surgery.** Treat both as unstable until a spinal surgeon has assessed them; stability depends on the displacement in a hangman’s fracture and on whether the transverse ligament has ruptured in a Jefferson fracture.
mimic: Hangman’s vs Jefferson
Hangman’s: C2, hyperextension, cord often spared. Jefferson: C1 ring, axial load.
NEXUS vs Canadian C-spine rule
NEXUS: five clinical criteria, any age. Canadian: adds age, mechanism and an active rotation test, and is more sensitive.
traps: “Alert, no neck pain, no deficit, sober, no distracting injury: CT or a collar anyway”
He meets all NEXUS criteria: no imaging (65% right).
“Bilateral C2 fracture is a Jefferson fracture”
Jefferson is C1; bilateral C2 pedicle fractures are hangman’s (63%).
decode: Alert crash victim, no neck pain, no deficit, not intoxicated, no distracting injury — next? [DocT GT]
No imaging required.
Head-on collision, bilateral fracture of C2 — name? [DocT GT]
Hangman’s fracture.
x.punch: An alert, sober patient with no midline tenderness, deficit or distracting injury needs no imaging under NEXUS; otherwise CT. A hangman’s fracture is bilateral C2 pars from hyperextension, and a Jefferson fracture is a C1 ring burst from axial load.

topups.q: Pulmonary contusion ± flail segment: course, and when to intubate?
a: - Contusion (not the flail) drives hypoxaemia: may be absent on first CXR, blossoms 24–72 h, resolves 5–7 days unless pneumonia/ARDS.
- Judicious fluids (colloid NOT better), multimodal/regional analgesia, physiotherapy, HFNC/NIV if alert.
- Distress with SpO2 ~85%, rising work or shock → intubate, PEEP to recruit, lung-protective volumes.
- No prophylactic antibiotics or steroids; rib fixation for selected flail, not first step.

x.sub: Trauma → Chest → Pulmonary contusion and flail chest
x.intro: Step 5 dealt with breathing in the primary survey; this card covers the chest injury that worsens over the following days. Contused lung is bruised parenchyma: blood and plasma fill the alveoli, compliance falls and shunt rises. The flail segment is the visible part, but the contusion beneath it causes most of the hypoxia.
why: **Contusion (not the flail) drives hypoxaemia: may be absent on the first CXR, blossoms at 24–72 h, resolves in 5–7 days unless pneumonia or ARDS.** Most contusions are visible on the chest film within about 6 hours, but CT shows them earlier and better, and small ones can be missed on the first film; the bleeding and oedema accumulate over the first day or two, and the shadowing then clears over about a week. A lesion that worsens after that is infection or ARDS.

**Judicious fluids (colloid NOT better), multimodal/regional analgesia, physiotherapy, HFNC/NIV if alert.** Excess fluid of any kind worsens oxygenation in leaky lung, and no study shows colloid is better than crystalloid. Pain makes the patient splint and retain secretions, so regional analgesia (epidural or paravertebral) and physiotherapy prevent the slide into pneumonia.

**Distress with SpO₂ about 85%, rising work or shock → intubate, PEEP to recruit, lung-protective volumes.** Non-invasive ventilation suits an alert patient with mild failure; a patient in distress with established contusion needs a tube, and PEEP reopens the flooded alveoli.

**No prophylactic antibiotics or steroids; rib fixation for selected flail, not first step.** Neither prevents pneumonia or ARDS. Surgical fixation helps selected flail segments but does nothing for the contusion.
mimic: Contusion vs ARDS
Contusion: within hours, at the impact site, resolves in a week. ARDS: bilateral, develops later, lasts longer.
traps: “Colloid is preferred over crystalloid in pulmonary contusion”
That was the false statement; avoid over-resuscitation with any fluid (81% right).
“Flail chest, SpO₂ 85%, distress: NIV and morphine” or “an epidural”
In distress with contusion, intubate and set PEEP; the epidural treats pain, not the contusion (30% right).
decode: Rib fractures with contusions in the SICU — all true EXCEPT [DocT GT]
‘Colloid is preferred over crystalloid’.
77-year-old, paradoxical right chest, SpO₂ 85%, HR 122 — next? [DocT GT]
Intubation with PEEP adjustment.
x.punch: The contusion under the flail drives the hypoxia, worsens over 24–72 hours and is not helped by colloid; the alert patient gets analgesia and support, and the distressed one is intubated with PEEP.

topups.q: Blunt trauma with haematuria: how do you image kidney, bladder and urethra?
a: - 1. Blood at meatus, perineal haematoma, high-riding prostate → retrograde urethrogram BEFORE a Foley.
- 2. Stable with flank pain/haematuria → contrast CT with delayed phase (gold standard for renal injury; not KUB/IVP).
- 3. Pelvic fracture + gross haematuria → retrograde CT cystogram (≥300–350 mL by gravity); clamped-catheter passive filling misses ruptures.
- 4. Extraperitoneal rupture → catheter 10–14 days; intraperitoneal → surgical repair.

x.sub: Trauma → Genitourinary → Imaging kidney, bladder and urethra
x.intro: Step 5 listed the urinary catheter among the adjuncts; this card is about when it must wait, and which test answers which question. The order follows the anatomy from the outside in: urethra first (before a catheter is passed), then bladder, then kidney. One GT question was answered correctly by only 15%.
why: **Blood at the meatus, perineal haematoma, high-riding prostate → retrograde urethrogram BEFORE a Foley.** A catheter pushed blindly through a torn urethra can turn a partial tear into a complete one.

**Stable with flank pain or haematuria → contrast CT with delayed phase (gold standard for renal injury; not KUB/IVP).** CT grades the parenchymal injury, and the delayed (excretory) phase shows urine leaking from the collecting system.

**Pelvic fracture + gross haematuria → retrograde CT cystogram (300–350 mL or more by gravity); clamped-catheter passive filling misses ruptures.** A rupture only leaks contrast when the bladder is fully distended. Clamping the catheter and waiting for diluted IV contrast to fill it does not distend it enough, so small tears are missed.

**Extraperitoneal rupture → catheter 10–14 days; intraperitoneal → surgical repair.** Extraperitoneal leaks (the usual type with pelvic fractures) heal with drainage, unless the bladder neck is involved, bone fragments lie in the bladder, or the rectum or vagina is also injured; those are repaired. Intraperitoneal rupture, from a blow to a full bladder that bursts at the dome, leaks urine into the peritoneum and needs repair.
mimic: Intraperitoneal vs extraperitoneal rupture
Intraperitoneal: blow to a full bladder, dome, contrast outlines bowel, repair. Extraperitoneal: pelvic fracture, contrast in the perivesical tissues, catheter drainage.
traps: “IV contrast CT with delayed bladder images after clamping the catheter”
Passive filling under-distends the bladder; a retrograde CT cystogram is needed (only 15% right).
“Retrograde urethrogram” when the catheter passed easily and there was no blood at the meatus
The urethra is already shown to be intact; the question is the bladder.
decode: Side impact, pubic rami fractures, catheter passes easily and drains gross blood, FAST positive splenorenal, stable [DocT GT]
Contrast CT abdomen and pelvis plus retrograde CT cystogram.
Flank pain, ecchymosis, haematuria after a bike collision — imaging? [Marrow]
Contrast-enhanced CT.
x.punch: Image from the outside in: urethrogram before a catheter if there is blood at the meatus, a retrograde cystogram filled to at least 300 mL for pelvic fracture with haematuria, and contrast CT with a delayed phase for the kidney.

topups.q: Hypotensive elderly smoker with flank/back pain, suspected ruptured AAA: next step?
a: - Bedside focused aortic ultrasound, then straight to theatre/EVAR.
- No CT or departmental ultrasound in an unstable patient; permissive hypotension until control.

x.sub: Trauma → Shock → Suspected ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm
x.intro: Step 6 dealt with shock from bleeding; this is the non-traumatic version that appears in the same bank. An elderly smoker with hypotension and back or flank pain is a ruptured aneurysm until shown otherwise, and the only question is how to confirm it without delaying control.
why: **Bedside focused aortic ultrasound, then straight to theatre/EVAR.** Ultrasound in the resuscitation room shows whether an aneurysm is present in minutes; in the right patient that is enough to call the vascular team. A stable patient goes for CT angiography to plan endovascular repair.

**No CT or departmental ultrasound in an unstable patient; permissive hypotension until control.** Leaving the resuscitation room delays control. Raising the pressure to normal with fluid can blow out the retroperitoneal clot that is containing the leak, so a lower pressure is accepted as long as the patient is conscious.
mimic: Ruptured AAA vs renal colic
Both: flank pain in an older man. Hypotension or a pulsatile mass makes it the aneurysm; never call it colic before the aorta has been scanned.
traps: “CT angiography first” in a hypotensive patient
Only when stable; unstable patients go to theatre after bedside ultrasound.
decode: Hypotensive elderly smoker, flank pain, suspected ruptured AAA — next step? [Marrow]
Focused bedside abdominal ultrasound.
x.punch: Hypotension with back or flank pain in an older smoker is a ruptured aneurysm: confirm it with bedside ultrasound, keep the pressure low, and go to theatre without stopping for CT.

topups.q: Haemorrhagic shock, two failed peripheral IV attempts: next access?
a: - Intraosseous needle (proximal humerus or tibia): in place in <1 min, takes blood products and all drugs; humeral flow approaches a 16G line under pressure.
- Then large-bore central access when time allows.
- Avoid a fractured bone or a limb distal to a vascular injury.

x.sub: Trauma → Shock → Intraosseous access in haemorrhagic shock
x.intro: Step 6 needs blood going in fast, and vasoconstricted, collapsed veins are the usual obstacle. The marrow cavity drains into the systemic veins and does not collapse, so a needle in it works like a non-collapsible vein. The one bank question was answered correctly by everyone.
why: **Intraosseous needle (proximal humerus or tibia): in place in under 1 min, takes blood products and all drugs; humeral flow approaches a 16G line under pressure.** Insertion is quick and needs little skill. Flow is driven by a pressure bag. In patients, humeral and tibial lines under pressure both ran at roughly 150–165 mL/min (Ong 2009), and the evidence that the humerus is faster is inconsistent; this is useful but less than a large-bore peripheral cannula, so the card’s comparison with a 16G line is generous.

**Then large-bore central access when time allows.** Rapid infusion catheters or central lines give the highest flows for a massive transfusion. The internal jugular is awkward under a collar, so the femoral or subclavian route is usual in trauma.
**Avoid a fractured bone or a limb distal to a vascular injury.** Fluid would leak out of the fracture or out of the injured vessel instead of reaching the heart.
mimic: IO vs central line in shock
IO: seconds, minimal skill, moderate flow. Central line or rapid infusion catheter: minutes, more skill, highest flow.
traps: “After two failed peripheral attempts, attempt a subclavian or IJ line”
Takes longer and needs more skill; the IJ is hindered by the collar. IO first (100% right).
decode: Polytrauma in haemorrhagic shock, two failed peripheral attempts — next? [DocT GT]
Insert an intraosseous needle.
x.punch: When peripheral access fails in shock, put in an intraosseous needle (humerus or tibia) within a minute, avoiding a fractured or vascularly injured limb, and add large-bore central access when time allows.

spine: Who dies from trauma, and when
Bleeding and brain injury kill most trauma patients, and most of those deaths happen in the first hours, which is why the first hour of care is organised so rigidly.
Defining and triaging the injured
Polytrauma means serious injury in two regions plus a physiological failure, and field triage sends the patient with deranged vital signs or a high-risk injury pattern to the highest-level centre.
Scoring the damage
Anatomical scores (AIS, ISS, NISS) count the injuries, physiological scores (RTS) measure the derangement, and TRISS combines them to compare outcomes between centres, not to triage.
Mechanism predicts the injuries
The way the energy was delivered tells you which injuries to look for before the examination finds them.
The primary survey
xABCDE treats each threat to life as it is found, in the order in which it would kill: catastrophic bleeding, airway, breathing, circulation, disability, exposure.
Grading and resuscitating shock
Haemorrhagic shock is graded by how much blood has gone, and the shocked patient gets blood, not crystalloid, and has the circulation filled before the airway is taken.
SPECIAL05A.primer: Trauma care rests on one principle: treat the injury that will kill first before the diagnosis is complete. The primary survey (xABCDE) finds and treats immediate threats; the secondary survey is the full head-to-toe examination and history; the tertiary survey, within 24 hours, catches what both missed. Shock in trauma is bleeding until proven otherwise, and the systolic pressure is a late sign because vasoconstriction holds it until about a third of the blood volume has gone. Severity is described two ways: anatomically (how bad the injuries are) and physiologically (how deranged the patient is).

POLY-11.sub: Polytrauma → Lethal triad → Hypothermia, acidosis, coagulopathy
POLY-11.intro: Step 1 is the spiral that kills the bleeding patient. Each part of the triad makes the other two worse: cold and acid slow clotting, poor clotting means more bleeding, and more bleeding means worse perfusion, more acid and less heat production. The one real question tests how cold impairs clotting even when the laboratory numbers look normal.
why: **Hypothermia (under 34 °C), acidosis (pH under 7.2), coagulopathy: each worsens the others, and all three together carry a very high mortality.** The thresholds are where the effect on clotting becomes clinically important. Many now add hypocalcaemia as a fourth corner (the ‘lethal diamond’): over half of patients are hypocalcaemic on arrival before any blood is given, and citrate in transfused products lowers it further (POLY-22).

**pH under 7.1 (odds ratio 12.3), temperature under 34 °C (8.7), ISS over 25 (7.7), SBP under 70; all four together ≈ 98% mortality.** These figures come from Cosgriff (1997), a study of 58 massively transfused trauma patients, and what they predicted was life-threatening coagulopathy (PT and PTT more than twice normal), not death: with all four risk factors, 98% developed it. Coagulopathy of that degree carries a very high mortality, which is why the card reads them as predictors of death. Acidosis carries the highest odds because clotting enzymes fail in acid, which is why the pH or base deficit is the number most often used to choose damage control (POLY-14).

**Lost thermoregulation and shivering, low metabolism, cold fluids and exposure; a core temperature under 32 °C in trauma ≈ 100% mortality.** Heat comes from metabolism, and a hypoperfused patient makes little; cold fluids and an exposed body on a trolley remove the rest. Cold hits platelets first: adhesion and activation fall at about 33 °C, while enzyme slowing becomes important mainly below that. PT and aPTT are run at 37 °C in the laboratory, so they can be normal in a patient who is oozing, and the fix is rewarming, not more products. Trauma hypothermia is far more lethal than accidental hypothermia at the same temperature, because it marks shock.

**Poor perfusion and saline resuscitation cause it; it makes factor VIIa, the Xa/Va complex and platelets fail, and depresses the myocardium.** Lactic acid from anaerobic metabolism and the hyperchloraemia of large volumes of 0.9% saline both lower the pH. Clotting enzymes are proteases that work poorly in acid: as the pH falls towards 7.0, factor VIIa and the Xa/Va complex lose most of their activity. Correcting pH with bicarbonate alone does not restore clotting; restoring perfusion does.
mimic: Trauma hypothermia vs accidental hypothermia
In trauma, 32 °C is close to unsurvivable because the cold reflects shock; in accidental hypothermia a patient may survive far lower temperatures with rewarming.
traps: “Normal PT, aPTT and platelet count mean the bleeding is surgical”
The tests are warmed to 37 °C; at 33 °C platelet adhesion is reduced in the patient while the numbers stay normal.
“Hypothermia’s main effect on clotting is enhanced fibrinolysis or excess tissue factor”
Its main effect is reduced platelet adhesion and activation.
decode: Core 33 °C, normal platelet count and factor levels, diffuse microvascular bleeding — which defect? [DocT GT]
Reduced platelet adhesion.
Which factor most strongly predicted life-threatening coagulopathy in massively transfused trauma patients? [pattern]
Acidosis, pH under 7.1 (odds ratio about 12; Cosgriff).
POLY-11.punch: Cold, acid and poor clotting feed each other. Cold impairs platelets before the laboratory can see it, acid cripples the clotting enzymes, and the treatment of both is restoring perfusion and warmth, not correcting a number.

POLY-12.intro: Step 2 explains why the bleeding patient is coagulopathic on arrival, before any fluid has been given. Five real questions test the mechanism, and the one that only 11% got right asked exactly that: coagulopathy despite minimal crystalloid is caused by shock-driven activation of protein C, not dilution.
why: **Early (endogenous, acute traumatic coagulopathy): tissue injury exposes endothelium; shock activates protein C (anticoagulation) and hyperfibrinolysis; fibrinogen falls first.** Hypoperfused endothelium releases thrombomodulin, which binds thrombin; the thrombin–thrombomodulin complex activates protein C. Activated protein C cleaves factors Va and VIIIa (factor V is the factor most consistently depleted in shock) and inhibits PAI-1, which releases fibrinolysis. Tissue plasminogen activator from damaged endothelium adds to the clot breakdown. Fibrinogen is both consumed and broken down, so it reaches a critical level first. This is present in about a quarter of severely injured patients on arrival and needs both tissue injury and shock; neither alone produces it.

**Late (iatrogenic): consumption, dilution with clot-free fluids, hypothermia, acidosis.** Crystalloid and red cells contain no clotting factors, so each litre dilutes what is left. Cold and acid then slow the enzymes that remain (POLY-11). This layer is avoidable, which is why damage control resuscitation restricts crystalloid and gives plasma early.

**Six drivers: tissue damage, shock, inflammation, hypothermia, acidosis, haemodilution.** The first three are endogenous and start at the scene; the last three are added in hospital. The endothelium is also part of the injury: shock and catecholamines shed its glycocalyx, which raises permeability, releases heparin-like material and promotes fibrinolysis.
mimic: Acute traumatic coagulopathy vs dilutional coagulopathy
The first is present on arrival, needs shock and is driven by activated protein C and fibrinolysis; the second follows large volumes of factor-free fluid.
Trauma-induced coagulopathy vs DIC
Early trauma coagulopathy is anticoagulant and fibrinolytic, with fibrinogen loss; classical DIC with widespread microthrombi is a later, inflammatory picture.
traps: “Coagulopathy on arrival in a patient given little fluid is dilutional or consumptive”
It is systemic protein C activation by shock. Only 11% chose this on DocT GT; most picked dilution or local consumption.
“PT/INR or the platelet count is the earliest marker”
Fibrinogen is the first factor to fall to a critical level.
“An LY30 of 5% is normal fibrinolysis”
Over 3% defines hyperfibrinolysis in trauma, with about a tenfold rise in mortality; give tranexamic acid.
“Factor IX, XI or XIII deficiency is typical of shock”
Factor V is the one most consistently depleted, because activated protein C cleaves Va.
decode: Polytrauma, minimal crystalloid, coagulopathic on admission — mechanism? [DocT GT]
Systemic protein C activation in shock (11% right).
Profound shock, oozing from venepuncture sites despite transfusion — primary mechanism of the acute coagulopathy? [DocT GT]
Thrombin–thrombomodulin–protein C activation.
Which clotting factor deficiency is most consistent in haemorrhagic shock? [DocT GT]
Factor V.
TEG LY30 5% in trauma — interpretation? / early marker of coagulopathy? [DocT GT, PYQ]
Hyperfibrinolysis with about a tenfold mortality rise; fibrinogen is the early marker.
POLY-12.punch: The bleeding patient arrives anticoagulated by his own shock: thrombomodulin turns thrombin into a protein C activator, factor V and fibrinogen fall, and fibrinolysis runs. Dilution, cold and acid come later and are the part we cause.

parts.q: What is the endotheliopathy of trauma, and why does it favour plasma over crystalloid?
parts.a: Shock and the catecholamine surge shed the endothelial glycocalyx (syndecan-1 rises and predicts death), causing capillary leak, autoheparinisation and fibrinolysis, and later ARDS and multi-organ failure. Plasma helps restore the glycocalyx; crystalloid worsens the shedding.

POLY-13.sub: Polytrauma → Lethal triad → Lactate and base deficit
POLY-13.intro: Step 1 also needs a measure of how deep the shock is. Pressure and pulse lag behind blood loss, so lactate and base deficit are used to grade hypoperfusion and to judge whether resuscitation is working. Both NEET 2025 recall questions are here: one on what a lactate of 3 means for the next step, one on the base deficit of each ATLS shock class.
why: **Initial lactate and its clearance over 6 hours independently predict death; over 3 mmol/L had a sensitivity of 0.81 and specificity of 0.73 for 24-hour mortality.** The exact figures vary between cohorts (one large trauma cohort, Dezman 2015, reported 0.86 and 0.73 for 3 mmol/L or more); the point is that a lactate of 3 or more picks up most early deaths. Lactate rises when tissue oxygen delivery is inadequate, so it detects ‘occult’ shock in a patient whose pressure is still normal. The trend matters more than a single value: falling lactate means resuscitation is reaching the tissues, so the response to a raised value is to resuscitate and repeat it.

**Alcohol raises it.** Ethanol metabolism increases the NADH/NAD⁺ ratio, which pushes pyruvate to lactate. The rise is usually modest, so a high lactate in an intoxicated trauma patient should still be treated as shock until proven otherwise.

**Base excess is the better biochemical predictor: mild −2 to −5, moderate −6 to −9, severe −10 or worse.** Base deficit measures the total metabolic acid load, not only lactate, and is less affected by alcohol. These mild/moderate/severe bands are an older grading. Questions on the ATLS shock classes use the ATLS 10th edition bands instead: class I 0 to −2, class II −2 to −6, class III −6 to −10, class IV −10 or worse (mEq/L).
mimic: Card’s base excess severity bands vs ATLS class bands
Card: −2 to −5, −6 to −9, −10 or worse. ATLS: I 0 to −2, II −2 to −6, III −6 to −10, IV −10 or worse. Answer a ‘shock class’ question with the ATLS bands.
traps: “SBP 90 and lactate 3 after a crash: go for damage control surgery”
That is early shock, not extremis; continue resuscitation and repeat the lactate. Damage control is for the patient with the triad (POLY-14).
“Base deficit in class III shock is −10 or more”
Class III is −6 to −10; −10 or worse is class IV.
decode: Road crash, BP 90/60, lactate 3 mmol/L — next step? [NEET 2025]
Further resuscitation and repeat the lactate.
Base deficit in class III shock? [NEET 2025]
−6 to −10 mEq/L (ATLS 10th edition).
POLY-13.punch: Lactate and base deficit see shock before the blood pressure does, and their clearance shows that resuscitation is working. For a class question use the ATLS bands: class III is −6 to −10.

POLY-14.intro: Step 3 begins with choosing who gets damage control rather than complete repair. The choice is driven by physiology: a patient who is cold, acidotic and coagulopathic will die on the table during a long operation, whatever the anatomy. The one linked question (NEET 2025) tests the other side: a patient in early shock who does not yet need it.
why: **Anatomical: ISS over 36; penetrating abdomen or chest; open pelvic fracture; long-bone fracture with head injury or lung contusion; truncal haemorrhage, amputation.** These are injuries that predict massive bleeding or a long operation, or in which a second hit (long-bone fixation in a patient with head or lung injury) would be dangerous.

**Physiological: weak or absent radial pulse; core under 35 °C; SBP under 100, HR over 100; P/F under 250; urine under 50 mL/h.** These show that compensation is failing. The temperature threshold here is higher than the triad’s 34 °C, because the aim is to stop before the patient reaches it.

**Laboratory: lactate over 2.5 mmol/L; platelets under 90,000; fibrinogen under 1 g/L; PT over 16 s, INR over 1.5; Hb under 11; pH under 7.2.** These measure the depth of shock and the coagulopathy already present. Low fibrinogen is the trigger (your notes print it the other way). The European guideline recommends damage control surgery for any severely injured patient in haemorrhagic shock, and also for hypothermia, acidosis, inaccessible major injury or a long procedure.
mimic: Damage control vs early total care
Damage control for the physiologically exhausted (triad, ongoing bleeding); early total care for the stable patient whose lactate has normalised (under about 2.5).
traps: “Any hypotension after trauma means damage control surgery”
BP 90/60 with lactate 3 is early shock: resuscitate and reassess first.
“Fibrinogen over 1 g/dL triggers damage control”
It is LOW fibrinogen, under 1 g/L, that does.
decode: Road crash, BP 90/60, lactate 3: early total care, damage control surgery, more tests, or resuscitate and repeat lactate? [NEET 2025]
Resuscitate and repeat the lactate.
POLY-14.punch: Damage control is chosen by physiology: the cold, acidotic, coagulopathic or persistently shocked patient gets a short operation; the patient in early shock is resuscitated first and reassessed.

POLY-15.intro: Step 3 continues with how the patient is resuscitated until the bleeding is controlled. Three ideas run together: accept a lower pressure so clots are not blown off, avoid fluids that dilute clotting factors, and give blood products early in a ratio close to whole blood. Five real questions test these, including a NEET 2025 stem on the cornerstone of the massive transfusion protocol.
why: **Permissive hypotension: SBP 70–90 (or MAP 50), normal mentation, palpable pulses, until bleeding is controlled; follow lactate and ScvO₂.** A higher pressure raises flow through the injured vessel and can dislodge a fresh clot, and the fluid needed to reach it dilutes factors. The pressure is only ‘low enough’ if the brain and tissues are still perfused, hence mentation, a radial pulse and lactate clearance. The European guideline (6th edition, 2023) sets SBP 80–90 mmHg, which it equates to MAP 50–60 (POLY-23); noradrenaline can be added if fluids alone fail to reach it.

**Not in TBI or spinal cord injury: keep MAP 80 or more if GCS 8 or less.** An injured brain or cord has lost autoregulation, so cerebral and cord perfusion follow the arterial pressure; a single episode of hypotension worsens outcome after head injury.

**Restrict crystalloid: big volumes worsen bleeding (dilution, clot disruption), oedema and hepatocellular injury.** Crystalloid carries no oxygen and no clotting factors and leaks out of the circulation. Its only early role is small amounts to keep a pressure while blood is fetched. A patient still hypotensive after the first litre or so needs blood, not more crystalloid.

**Haemostatic resuscitation: blood products first, RBC:FFP:platelets about 1:1:1.** Giving plasma and platelets with the red cells from the start replaces what is being lost, in the proportions of whole blood. Cryoprecipitate is not part of the ratio; it is given for fibrinogen under 1.5 g/L (POLY-21).

**Penetrating torso: a restrictive policy (SBP 60–70) lowers bleeding and 28-day mortality.** The classic trial is Bickell (1994): penetrating torso injury with SBP 90 or less, fluids delayed until the operating room, survival to discharge 70% vs 62%, with fewer complications. A later trial targeting MAP 50 vs 65 mmHg during surgery reported fewer early post-operative deaths at its interim analysis (Morrison 2011), but the final report (Carrick 2016, 168 patients) found no difference in 24-hour or 30-day mortality, only less blood and fluid use. The figures on the card are not those of either trial; the principle of tolerating a low pressure until surgical control is the same.
mimic: Permissive hypotension vs no resuscitation
The aim is the lowest pressure that still perfuses the brain and tissues, not ignoring shock; mentation, a pulse and lactate are the checks.
Blood products in ratio vs whole blood
Components in 1:1:1 approximate whole blood. Prehospital low-titre O whole blood was not better than components in TOWAR (NEJM 2026); either is acceptable.
traps: “Restore normotension with crystalloid before haemorrhage control”
That disrupts clots and dilutes factors; permissive hypotension is the answer.
“Permissive hypotension is fine with a head injury”
Contraindicated: keep MAP 80 or more.
“Give red cells only until Hb is over 10, then plasma”
Products are given together in a balanced ratio from the start.
“Add 6 units of cryo with 6 units of red cells”
The ratio is plasma and platelets; cryo is for low fibrinogen.
decode: Penetrating abdomen, SBP 82, active bleeding, before haemorrhage control — strategy? [DocT GT]
Permissive hypotension.
Polytrauma, still hypotensive after 2 L, Hb 6.8, INR 2.0 — cornerstone of the MTP? [NEET 2025]
Products in a balanced ratio approximating whole blood.
6 units of red cells given — what else improves success? [DocT GT]
FFP and platelets, both (94% right).
Which parameters guide adequacy of resuscitation? [DocT GT]
All: lactate clearance, urine output, SBP 90 or more.
POLY-15.punch: Until bleeding stops: accept SBP 80–90 (MAP 80 or more if the brain is injured), keep crystalloid to a minimum, and give red cells, plasma and platelets together in about 1:1:1.

parts.q: Why is blood the only colloid used in trauma?
parts.a: Starches increase kidney injury and mortality (CHEST, 6S) and impair clotting; gelatins cause anaphylaxis; albumin raised mortality in TBI (SAFE-TBI). Hypertonic saline is used only for raised ICP.

POLY-16.sub: Polytrauma → Damage control → Surgery, rewarming, haemorrhage control, REBOA
POLY-16.intro: Step 4 is stopping the bleeding itself, because no amount of resuscitation replaces it. Eight real questions are linked here, most of them about the pelvis (binder, packing, embolisation), the stages of damage control surgery and REBOA. The common thread is that the first operation is short and aims only at bleeding and contamination.
why: **Temporary sacrifice of anatomy to save physiology: (1) abbreviated laparotomy to control bleeding and contamination, (2) ICU resuscitation, (3) planned re-operation for definitive repair.** The first operation packs the liver, ligates or shunts vessels, staples bowel and closes the abdomen temporarily, in about an hour. The ICU then rewarms and corrects coagulopathy and acidosis; the patient returns at about 24–48 hours for repair. Five-stage versions add stage 0 (‘ground zero’: recognising the need in the emergency department) and a final stage of definitive abdominal-wall closure.

**Rewarming: passive external (blankets, warm room); active external (forced air); active internal (warm IV fluids, warm peritoneal lavage).** Prevention is easier than rewarming: all fluids and products go through a warmer and the patient is covered after exposure. In the profoundly cold, active internal methods or extracorporeal rewarming are used.

**Pelvic binder, compressive dressings, tourniquets; surgery is the gold standard; interventional radiology; pelvic packing or embolisation if unstable despite a binder.** A binder centred on the greater trochanters closes an open-book pelvis, reduces its volume and holds clot; it stays on until a fracture is excluded on imaging or the pelvis is fixed or embolised. A pelvic bleed with a negative FAST is retroperitoneal: laparotomy does not reach it, so after the binder the next steps are angiography with embolisation (arterial bleeding) or preperitoneal packing (venous plexus bleeding, the commoner source), not fixation or saline to a target MAP.

**REBOA: balloon in the aorta via the femoral artery; zone 3 (infrarenal to the bifurcation; notes: IMA to bifurcation) for pelvic bleeding; zone 1 (descending thoracic) for abdominal bleeding.** Zone 1 runs from the left subclavian to the coeliac trunk, zone 2 from the coeliac to the lowest renal artery (not used), zone 3 from the lowest renal artery to the bifurcation. The balloon stops flow below it and supports cerebral and coronary perfusion, buying minutes for surgery or embolisation; it is useless for bleeding above it (thoracic aorta, subclavian, intracranial). Its benefit is doubtful: UK-REBOA (JAMA 2023, mostly blunt trauma) was stopped for harm, 90-day mortality 54% vs 42%. The European guideline only suggests ‘considering’ it for non-compressible life-threatening bleeding.
mimic: REBOA vs resuscitative thoracotomy
Both occlude the aorta. REBOA is endovascular from the groin for bleeding below the diaphragm; thoracotomy opens the chest and is needed for tamponade or chest bleeding.
Angioembolisation vs preperitoneal packing
Embolisation treats arterial bleeding (a blush on CT); packing treats venous and bony bleeding and is faster where angiography is not available.
traps: “Remove the binder once the patient is stable, FAST is negative or the pelvis does not spring”
Only after a fracture is excluded on imaging (or after fixation/embolisation); springing dislodges clot and FAST misses retroperitoneal blood. 75% right on DocT GT.
“Binder on and still hypotensive: fix the pelvis internally or get a CT angiogram first”
Packing or angioembolisation is the damage control step; CT is for the stable patient.
“REBOA helps a thoracic aortic or subclavian bleed”
It controls bleeding only below the balloon: pelvic (internal iliac) and abdominal.
“REBOA has proven benefit”
UK-REBOA showed probable harm; it is a bridge used in selected centres.
decode: Hypotensive, FAST negative, open-book pelvis on X-ray — next step? [DocT GT]
Pelvic binder and interventional radiology for angiography (78% right).
Open-book pelvis, binder on, MAP 55 after 2 units, FAST negative — damage control step? [DocT GT]
Preperitoneal packing or angioembolisation.
Femoral access and an aortic balloon / temporising control of non-compressible torso bleeding — which? REBOA most useful for which site? [DocT GT]
REBOA; internal iliac (pelvic) bleeding.
When can the pelvic binder be removed? / match the stages of damage control surgery [DocT GT]
After radiological exclusion of fracture; ground zero → abbreviated surgery → ICU → planned re-look → closure.
POLY-16.punch: Damage control surgery stops bleeding and contamination quickly and leaves the repair for later. For the pelvis: binder first, and if still unstable with a negative FAST, packing or embolisation; REBOA is a temporary bridge with doubtful benefit.

POLY-17.intro: Step 3 also rests on the trials that removed colloids from trauma resuscitation. No real question is linked to this card; the trials are asked as the reason behind ‘no albumin in TBI’ and ‘no starch’.
why: **SAFE 2004 (ICU): saline vs 4% albumin, 28-day mortality similar.** Albumin was safe in general ICU patients but not better, so there was no reason to pay for it.

**SAFE-TBI 2007: albumin had higher mortality at 24 months.** In the TBI subgroup, deaths were about a third vs a fifth, mainly in severe TBI. Hypotonic 4% albumin is thought to raise intracranial pressure.

**FIRST 2011 (trauma): saline vs HES 130/0.4, HES needed less volume and gave lower lactate in penetrating injury; mortality similar.** It was small, and its kidney finding (less injury with starch in penetrating trauma) was not repeated in larger trials.
**CHEST 2012: saline vs 6% HES, mortality similar, more renal replacement therapy with HES.** With 6S (more deaths with starch in sepsis), this ended routine starch use.
**CRYSTAL 2013 (shock): crystalloid vs colloid, 28-day mortality similar.** The 90-day mortality was lower with colloid, but that was a secondary outcome and is not taken as proof.
mimic: SAFE vs SAFE-TBI
Same trial: neutral overall, harmful in the head-injured subgroup.
traps: “HES protects the kidneys in trauma (FIRST)”
The larger trials (CHEST, 6S) showed more kidney injury with starch.
decode: Preferred fluid in TBI; which fluid raised mortality in TBI? [pattern]
Isotonic crystalloid; albumin (SAFE-TBI).
Which trial showed more RRT with starch? [pattern]
CHEST (6% HES 130/0.4).
POLY-17.punch: Albumin is neutral in general ICU patients but harmful in TBI, and starch damages the kidney; in trauma the only colloid is blood.

POLY-18.sub: Polytrauma → Massive transfusion → Definitions, emergency blood, ratios, prediction
POLY-18.intro: Step 5 is where blood replaces fluid. This is the most-asked card in the deck (11 questions): when to activate the protocol, which group to give before the patient’s group is known, which ratio, and which score predicts the need. The lowest scores (13% and 18%) were on plasma compatibility and on a GT stem printed with two identical options.
why: **10 or more red cell units in 24 h; or more than 4 units in 1 h with ongoing need; or more than 50% of blood volume in 3 h.** The 24-hour definition is retrospective and biased by survival (those who die early never reach 10 units), so the rate-based definitions are more useful clinically. In practice, the protocol is activated on clinical grounds or a score (part d), not after 10 units.

**Group O red cells and group AB plasma until the group is known.** Red cell compatibility is about antigens on the donor cells: group O cells carry neither A nor B. Plasma compatibility is the reverse, about antibodies in the donor plasma: AB plasma has neither anti-A nor anti-B, so it is universal, and its RhD group does not matter because plasma contains no red cells. O RhD-positive cells are given to men and older women; O RhD-negative is kept for girls and women of child-bearing age to avoid anti-D sensitisation. Platelets carry a few red cells, so an RhD-negative woman of child-bearing age should get RhD-negative platelets, or anti-D. After several units of group O, keep giving group O even when the group comes back A, B or AB, because transfused anti-A and anti-B could haemolyse type-specific cells; switch only when the laboratory says it is safe.

**PROPPR: 1:1:1 vs 1:1:2, no difference in 24-hour or 30-day mortality, but fewer exsanguination deaths and more haemostasis. PROMMTT: higher plasma and platelet ratios linked to lower early mortality.** PROPPR (JAMA 2015, 680 patients): 24-hour mortality 12.7% vs 17.0% and 30-day 22.4% vs 26.1%, neither significant; deaths from exsanguination at 24 hours 9.2% vs 14.6%, and haemostasis 86% vs 78%, with no more complications. PROMMTT (observational) found that high ratios mattered in the first 6 hours, when haemorrhagic deaths happen, and not after 24 hours. Prehospital plasma helped in PAMPer (air transport, 30-day mortality 23% vs 33%).

**TASH (7 variables: SBP, HR, free abdominal fluid, pelvic or long-bone fracture, sex, Hb, base excess; 0–28). ABC score: SBP under 90, HR over 120, penetrating mechanism, positive FAST; 2 or more → activate.** The ABC score needs no laboratory test, so it is the fastest bedside tool; at 2 or more it has a sensitivity of about 75% and specificity of about 86%. TASH needs Hb and base excess; a score of 16 or more corresponds to roughly a 50% probability of massive transfusion and is the usual activation threshold. TEG and ROTEM guide which products, not whether to start.
mimic: Red cell vs plasma compatibility
Cells: O is universal (no antigens). Plasma: AB is universal (no antibodies).
ABC score vs TASH vs shock index
ABC: four bedside items, no labs, fastest. TASH: needs Hb and base excess. Shock index (HR ÷ SBP over 1) flags shock but is not a massive transfusion score.
traps: “O RhD-negative FFP for an O RhD-negative woman”
Group O plasma has anti-A and anti-B; AB plasma is universal and the RhD of FFP does not matter. Only 13% chose AB RhD-positive FFP on DocT GT.
“Red cells, plasma and cryo in equal numbers”
The ratio is red cells : plasma : platelets. The DocT GT stem printed options B and C identically (18% right); choose the platelets option.
“Switch to the patient’s own group AB as soon as it is known after 6 units of O”
Continue group O until the laboratory confirms no significant anti-A/B; 63% right.
“Wait for cross-matched blood, or give a fourth litre of crystalloid first”
Give uncrossmatched group O (Rh-positive in a man) now.
“4:1:1 or 1:1:2 is the ideal ratio”
decode: Stab wound, SBP 85, HR 125, FAST positive — next step? [DocT GT]
Activate the massive transfusion protocol (64% right).
Which bedside score predicts massive transfusion fastest, without laboratory tests? [DocT GT]
ABC score (66% right).
Woman O RhD-negative bleeding at caesarean — most suitable product? / 6 units O-negative given, group returns AB+ [DocT GT]
FFP group AB RhD-positive; continue group O.
Hypotensive after 3 L of crystalloid — which statement is right? [NEET 2025]
Transfuse type O Rh-positive blood (not wait for cross-match, not more crystalloid).
POLY-18.punch: Activate on the bedside picture or an ABC score of 2, start with group O cells and AB plasma, and run red cells, plasma and platelets at 1:1:1: in PROPPR this did not change 30-day mortality but cut deaths from exsanguination.

POLY-19.sub: Polytrauma → Massive transfusion → Ending the protocol
POLY-19.intro: Step 5 ends with stopping the fixed ratio. Once surgical control is achieved, products are given to laboratory or viscoelastic targets instead of by formula. The two linked questions are about viscoelastic tests, and the one most people got wrong (38%) asked which viscoelastic finding predicts death.
why: **Red cells: stop at Hb about 10 g/dL (notes).** The European guideline target during bleeding is Hb 7–9 g/dL (POLY-23); the higher figure in your notes is a stop point for the protocol, not a transfusion trigger.
**FFP: stop when PT is under 18 s and PTT under 35 s.** Plasma replaces all the soluble factors; once PT and PTT approach normal, more plasma adds volume without benefit.
**Platelets: stop when the count is above target (notes print 150,000).** The guideline targets are over 50 × 10⁹/L with ongoing bleeding and over 100 in TBI; 150,000 is a generous stop point.

**Cryoprecipitate: stop at fibrinogen over 100 mg/dL (1 g/L).** Current European practice uses a higher trigger, Clauss fibrinogen 1.5 g/L or less, or a low FIBTEM A5 on ROTEM, because fibrinogen falls first and furthest (POLY-21).
mimic: Viscoelastic tests vs PT/INR

TEG/ROTEM are whole-blood, run at body temperature, give results in 10–15 minutes and show clot strength and fibrinolysis; PT/INR is plasma-based, slow and misses both. In the ITACTIC trial (trauma, 2021), guiding treatment by viscoelastic tests did not improve survival free of massive transfusion at 24 hours or mortality over conventional tests. Cochrane reviews, mostly of cardiac surgery, suggest lower mortality, but on very low-certainty evidence.
traps: “Increased fibrinolysis is the viscoelastic finding most associated with death”
Low clot strength (TEG MA, ROTEM MCF or A5) is; most patients have fibrinolytic shutdown, not hyperfibrinolysis. Only 38% got this on DocT GT.
“INR over 1.2 is a viscoelastic variable”
INR is a conventional plasma test.
decode: Which VHA finding is most strongly associated with mortality in trauma coagulopathy? [DocT GT]
Decreased clot strength (38% right).
Which test rapidly assesses clot dynamics in trauma? [DocT GT]
TEG (100% right).
POLY-19.punch: After surgical control, stop the formula and treat to targets; on viscoelastic testing the number that predicts death is low clot strength, not fibrinolysis.

POLY-20.intro: Step 6 opens with the drug that every bleeding trauma patient should get. Tranexamic acid blocks the binding of plasminogen to fibrin and so stops clots being broken down, the hyperfibrinolysis of step 2. Three questions are linked; the one only 36% answered correctly hid it among options for a diffusely bleeding liver, and the NEET 2025 stem tested the time window.
why: **CRASH-2: 1 g over 10 minutes, then 1 g over 8 hours; fewer bleeding deaths (about 15%).** CRASH-2 (20,207 bleeding adults, SBP under 90 or HR over 110, within 8 hours of injury) reduced death from bleeding from 5.7% to 4.9% and all-cause death a little, with no rise in vascular occlusive events. It works in blunt and penetrating trauma alike.

**Within 3 hours of injury; after 3 hours it increased bleeding deaths.** The benefit was greatest when given within 1 hour (bleeding deaths RR 0.68), still present at 1–3 hours (RR 0.79), and reversed after 3 hours (RR 1.44), probably because fibrinolysis gives way to shutdown and a prothrombotic state. The 8 hours on the card is the length of the second infusion, not the window.

**CRASH-3: benefit in mild-to-moderate TBI (given early), none in severe TBI.** CRASH-3 (12,737 patients with TBI, within 3 hours) did not reduce head-injury deaths overall (18.5% vs 19.8%, not significant), but did in GCS 9–15 and when given early; in GCS 3 or with bilateral unreactive pupils there was no effect. There was no excess of thrombotic events.

**Give as early as possible to anyone bleeding or at risk; prehospital first dose.** The European guideline (Grade 1A) gives TXA as soon as possible, en route if feasible, within 3 hours, and not waiting for viscoelastic results. PATCH-Trauma (NEJM 2023, prehospital TXA) did not improve functional outcome at 6 months; deaths at 24 hours and 28 days were lower with TXA as secondary outcomes, and 6-month mortality did not differ significantly.
mimic: CRASH-2 vs CRASH-3 vs WOMAN
CRASH-2: bleeding trauma, within 3 h. CRASH-3: TBI, helps mild-moderate. WOMAN: postpartum haemorrhage, same dose, same 3-hour window.
traps: “TXA works if given within 8 (or 12) hours”
Within 3 hours; after 3 hours it increased bleeding deaths. The NEET 2025 stem asked which statement is incorrect: ‘within 12 hours, only in blunt or penetrating trauma’.
“Diffuse liver bleeding at laparotomy: cryo in equal numbers, PCC or vitamin K”
Tranexamic acid is the useful adjunct; only 36% chose it.
“TEG shows hyperfibrinolysis and weak clot: give FFP or platelets”
Hyperfibrinolysis is treated with TXA (73% right).
decode: Multiple liver lacerations with diffuse bleeding — useful adjunct along with volume? [DocT GT]
Tranexamic acid (36% right).
TEG hyperfibrinolysis, weak clot, normal platelets — targeted intervention? [DocT GT]
Tranexamic acid.
Which is incorrect about TXA in trauma? [NEET 2025]
‘Within 12 hours and only in blunt or penetrating trauma’; 1 g over 10 min, 1 g over 8 h, for all with suspected significant bleeding are correct.
POLY-20.punch: Tranexamic acid: 1 g over 10 minutes then 1 g over 8 hours, as early as possible and never after 3 hours, because late doses increased bleeding deaths in CRASH-2.

POLY-21.sub: Polytrauma → Drugs → Fibrinogen concentrate vs cryoprecipitate
POLY-21.intro: Step 5 also covers the first factor to replace. Fibrinogen falls first and furthest in bleeding trauma (step 2), and it can be replaced from two sources. The two linked questions ask the concentrate dose when the level is unknown and which product to give for a fibrinogen of 70 mg/dL.
why: **Source: concentrate is a lyophilised, pathogen-reduced powder; cryoprecipitate comes from controlled thawing of FFP.** Thawing FFP at 1–6 °C leaves a cold-insoluble precipitate rich in fibrinogen, which is collected and refrozen.

**Contents: concentrate is fibrinogen only; cryoprecipitate contains fibrinogen, factor VIII, von Willebrand factor and factor XIII.** That is why cryo was historically used for haemophilia A and von Willebrand disease, and why it is the cheaper alternative where concentrate is not available.

**Dose: concentrate (target − measured, mg/dL) ÷ 1.7 mg/kg, often about 70 mg/kg (notes); cryoprecipitate 1 unit per 5–10 kg.** The divisor 1.7 is the expected rise in mg/dL for each mg/kg; when the level is unknown, 70 mg/kg is the labelled starting dose. In trauma the European guideline suggests an initial 3–4 g of fibrinogen, equal to 15–20 single-donor units of cryo, when Clauss fibrinogen is 1.5 g/L or less or ROTEM shows a functional deficit.

**Pros and cons: concentrate is fast and needs no matching; cryo has limited availability, is allogeneic, needs thawing and is group-matched.** Concentrate has a known, standard fibrinogen content and a lower infection risk. Neither has shown a survival benefit when given early and empirically in a randomised trial: CRYOSTAT-2 (JAMA 2023, 1,604 patients) found no difference in 28-day mortality with early high-dose cryo (25.3% vs 26.1%). The ‘lower 6-hour mortality’ with concentrate comes from a registry matched-pairs study (Wafaisade 2013), in which mortality at discharge did not differ.
mimic: Cryo vs FFP for low fibrinogen
FFP contains fibrinogen at plasma concentration (about 2 g/L), so it cannot raise a low level without large volumes; cryo or concentrate is needed.
traps: “Fibrinogen 70 mg/dL with oozing: FFP, PCC or rFVIIa”
Cryoprecipitate (or concentrate); PCC contains no fibrinogen.
“Early empirical cryo improves survival”
CRYOSTAT-2 was neutral.
decode: Congenital afibrinogenaemia, level unknown — initial RiaSTAP dose? [DocT GT]
70 mg/kg IV.
Septic patient bleeding, fibrinogen 70 mg/dL, platelets 92,000, INR 1.4 — product? [DocT GT]
Cryoprecipitate 10 units.
POLY-21.punch: When fibrinogen is low (1.5 g/L or less in trauma), give cryoprecipitate or concentrate, about 3–4 g in an adult; FFP and PCC cannot replace it, and early empirical cryo did not save lives in CRYOSTAT-2.

POLY-22.sub: Polytrauma → Drugs → Calcium, factor VIIa, steroids in cord injury, antioxidants
POLY-22.intro: Step 6 continues with the other drugs. Calcium is the fourth corner of the triad, rFVIIa is a last resort, and steroids for cord injury are the classic question. The two linked questions ask about rFVIIa as a rescue agent and, with only 43% right, what improves neurological outcome after spinal cord injury.
why: **Calcium is a cofactor for clotting, cardiac contractility and vascular tone; monitor every 10 units transfused; keep ionised Ca over 0.9 mmol/L (notes).** Citrate in each unit binds calcium, and a shocked liver clears citrate slowly, so ionised calcium falls with every unit. The European guideline keeps it in the normal range (1.1–1.3 mmol/L) and recommends calcium chloride; below 0.9 mmol/L is transfusion hypocalcaemia and below 0.8 risks arrhythmias.

**rFVIIa: off-label, no outcome benefit, causes thrombosis, last resort only.** It needs fibrinogen, platelets, a normal pH, temperature and calcium to work, so it fails in exactly the patients who are given it too early. The European guideline does not recommend it first-line and suggests it only when bleeding and coagulopathy persist despite everything else.

**NASCIS II: high-dose methylprednisolone within 8 h improved motor recovery; NASCIS III: 48 h better than 24 h if started at 3–8 h. Now not recommended (CNS, CAEP): harms, no long-term benefit.** The NASCIS benefits were found in post-hoc subgroups, while steroids increased infections, GI bleeding and hyperglycaemia. What does help the cord is perfusion: the traditional target is MAP 85–90 mmHg for 7 days (AO Spine 2024 suggests a floor of 75–80 and ceiling of 90–95 for 3–7 days).
**Vitamins A, C and E reduce inflammation; vitamin C may protect the kidneys.** This is weak, experimental evidence and is not part of any trauma guideline.
mimic: Steroids vs MAP augmentation in acute cord injury
Steroids: not recommended. Keeping MAP 85–90: suggested by guidelines and the answer to ‘what improves neurological outcome’.
traps: “Methylprednisolone improves neurological outcome after cord injury”
Not recommended; MAP augmentation is the answer (43% right on DocT GT).
“SBP over 120 or CVP over 20 protects the cord”
The target is MAP, about 85 mmHg or more.
“rFVIIa is first-line, or should be given early before surgery”
It is an off-label rescue agent after surgery and full correction; 91% right.
decode: Massive PPH despite uterotonics, sutures and MTP — which statement about rFVIIa is correct? [DocT]
Off-label rescue agent for life-threatening haemorrhage.
88-year-old with cervical cord injury — what improves neurological outcome? [DocT GT]
Maintain MAP over 85 mmHg.
POLY-22.punch: Give calcium chloride to keep ionised calcium normal during transfusion, keep rFVIIa as an off-label last resort, and protect an injured cord with a MAP of about 85, not with steroids.

POLY-23.intro: Step 6 gathers the numbers into the European guideline (6th edition, 2023), the reference most of these targets come from. The one linked question tests its pelvic recommendation, which is in the card’s watch line: packing or embolisation for the patient who stays unstable despite a binder.
why: **Restricted volume replacement to a target SBP of 80–90 mmHg until bleeding is controlled (no TBI).** Grade 1B. This is a little higher than the 70–90 often taught (POLY-15).
**Severe TBI (GCS 8 or less): MAP 80 mmHg or more.** Grade 1C. Cerebral perfusion follows arterial pressure once autoregulation is lost.

**Vasopressors with fluids for life-threatening hypotension.** The guideline names noradrenaline, added when fluids alone do not reach the target, and dobutamine if the myocardium is failing. A vasopressor reduces the fluid needed to hold the pressure.

**Isotonic crystalloid; avoid excess 0.9% saline.** The 6th edition recommends starting with 0.9% saline or a balanced crystalloid (Grade 1B); its rationale adds that if saline is used it should be limited to about 1–1.5 L, because large volumes cause hyperchloraemic acidosis. Hypotonic solutions such as Ringer’s lactate are avoided in severe head injury.
**Haemoglobin 7–9 g/dL.** Grade 1C. Higher targets add risk without benefit.

**Start coagulation support with plasma:RBC at least 1:2, or fibrinogen concentrate plus RBC.** Either a plasma-based or a factor-concentrate strategy is accepted (Grade 1C), with a high platelet:RBC ratio; then goal-directed treatment guided by viscoelastic or laboratory tests.

**TXA 1 g over 10 minutes then 1 g over 8 hours, within 3 hours.** Grade 1A, the strongest recommendation in the guideline: as soon as possible, en route if feasible, and not waiting for viscoelastic results.
**Platelets over 50; over 100 with ongoing bleeding or TBI.** In the 6th edition the higher threshold of 100 × 10⁹/L applies to TBI; over 50 is the target with ongoing bleeding.
mimic: European SBP 80–90 vs SBP 70–90 / MAP 50
Both are permissive hypotension; the guideline number is 80–90 without TBI.
traps: “Pelvic binder on and still hypotensive: internal fixation, CT angiogram, or saline to MAP 80”
Preperitoneal packing or angioembolisation (the watch line).
“Hb target 10 g/dL during bleeding”
decode: Open-book pelvis, binder on, MAP 55 after 2 units, FAST negative — damage control step? [DocT GT]
Preperitoneal packing or angioembolisation.
European guideline BP target without TBI / with severe TBI? [pattern]
SBP 80–90; MAP 80 or more.
POLY-23.punch: The European numbers: SBP 80–90 (MAP 80 or more in severe TBI), Hb 7–9, plasma:RBC at least 1:2 or fibrinogen, fibrinogen if 1.5 g/L or less, platelets over 50 (100 in TBI), TXA within 3 hours, calcium normal.

parts.q: What does the European guideline say about fibrinogen, calcium and REBOA?
parts.a: Give fibrinogen concentrate or cryo if Clauss fibrinogen is 1.5 g/L or less or viscoelastic tests show a deficit (initial 3–4 g); keep ionised calcium in the normal range with calcium chloride; consider REBOA only for non-compressible life-threatening bleeding (weak, 2C).

POLY-24.intro: Step 6 closes with a sweep across both polytrauma decks. Three linked questions all test the shock index, which is statement b: they give a heart rate and systolic pressure and ask you to divide.
why: **False: BP first falls in Class III (30–40% loss).** In class II the pulse rises and pulse pressure narrows but systolic pressure is maintained by vasoconstriction (POLY-09).

**True: a shock index over 1 predicts mortality.** Shock index = heart rate ÷ systolic pressure; normal is 0.5–0.7. It rises before the systolic pressure falls, so 118/105 (1.1) or 130/92 (1.4) already signals hypovolaemia despite a ‘normal’ pressure. Over 1 is abnormal and associated with transfusion need and death.
**False: permissive hypotension is contraindicated in TBI.** The injured brain needs a MAP of 80 or more (POLY-15).
**False: TXA must be given within 3 hours.** After 3 hours it increased bleeding deaths in CRASH-2 (POLY-20).
**True: fibrinogen is the first factor to fall critically.** It is consumed, broken down by fibrinolysis and diluted (POLY-12).
**False: albumin raised mortality in TBI (SAFE-TBI).** Isotonic crystalloid is preferred (POLY-17).

**True: the Berlin definition needs AIS 3 or more in 2 or more regions plus at least one physiological factor.** The factors are SBP 90 or less, GCS 8 or less, base excess −6 or worse, INR 1.4 or more or PTT 40 s or more, and age 70 or more (POLY-02).

**False: ISS takes one injury per region (taking the three worst regardless of region is NISS).** ISS squares the highest AIS in each of the three most severely injured body regions and adds them; NISS squares the three highest AIS scores regardless of region, so it counts two severe injuries in the same region (POLY-04).
mimic: ISS vs NISS
ISS: the worst injury in each of the three worst regions. NISS: the three worst injuries anywhere.
traps: “SBP 105 and lactate 1.8 rule out early hypovolaemia”
A shock index of 1.1 already signals it.
“Shock index 120/90 is 0.75, normal”
It is 1.33, severe shock.
decode: SBP 92, HR 130, CRT 3.5 s, lactate 2.2 — which index best suggests inadequate perfusion? [DocT GT]
Shock index 1.4 (79% right).
Trauma, cool, HR 118, SBP 105 — which index most suggests early hypovolaemia? [DocT GT]
Shock index 1.1.
HR 120, SBP 90 — shock index and interpretation? [NEET 2025]
1.33, severe shock.
POLY-24.punch: Divide pulse by systolic pressure: over 1 is shock even when the pressure looks normal. And the rest: BP falls in class III, no permissive hypotension or albumin in TBI, TXA within 3 hours, fibrinogen falls first.

topups.q: Fracture or reperfused limb with pain: compartment syndrome — the path?
a: - 1. Commonest after closed tibial fracture or crush. Early signs: pain out of proportion and on passive stretch, tense compartment, paraesthesia; pulses and pallor are LATE.
- 2. Remove all circumferential dressings/splints at once.
- 3. Unreliable exam (sedated, obtunded) → measure: delta-P = DIASTOLIC BP − compartment pressure (an absolute pressure >30 alone ignores perfusion); measurement is an adjunct, not infallible.
- 4. Not relieved, or delta-P <30 mmHg → emergency fasciotomy (ideally within 6 h).
- 5. Never more opioids or delay for imaging.
